side_a_arguments: North Carolina law bars cities from imposing mandatory adequate-public-facilities school impact moratoriums or full-cost fees
State underfunding, charter/voucher enrollment dynamics, and County/DPS bond timing—not housing growth alone—drive classroom shortages
Requested better joint seat-generation forecasting without pitting housing supply against public schools
conflicts.side_b_position: Staff/DPS capacity framing emphasizing rapid residential rezoning student-yield pressures (+5,000 projected seats)
side_b_arguments: High-volume new residential entitlements accelerate enrollment spikes beyond current school facility capital budgets (~$100,000 per seat)
conflicts.resolution: Informational briefing concluded with Council directing better intergovernmental data sharing ahead of future growth coordination.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Aug 19 2024
conflicts.issue: Duke Central Campus Addition University College (UC) Rezoning Without Specific Development Plan
conflicts.summary: Council members disagreed on whether to evaluate Duke's Central Campus UC rezoning without specific development plans and broader institutional commitments before deciding to continue the case to October 7, 2024.
conflicts.side_a_position: Delay/require clearer master plan, development intentions, sustainability, housing, and transportation timing commitments before voting.
side_a_arguments: Duke has no concrete development plans for parcels acquired over decades, leaving Council without control once broad UC zoning is granted.
The ordinance states a master plan shall be submitted, yet lacks clarity on what a master plan must contain compared to NCCU's publicly available plan.
Duke's transportation commitment for a 10-foot side path lacked a binding timing component, and community/council distrust of the county's largest private landowner warrants deeper due diligence.
conflicts.side_b_position: Evaluate the UC rezoning on standard land-use grounds without litigating broader disputes with Duke.
side_b_arguments: Council has previously approved rezonings without detailed development plans by relying on lists of prohibited uses, and UC zoning is designed to provide flexibility for universities.
Broader institutional conversations and grievances with Duke should be addressed in separate forums rather than prosecuted through this land-use case.
conflicts.resolution: Council polled unanimous consent at 03:26:22 to hold the public hearing open and continue the case to October 7, 2024.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session May 23, 2024
conflicts.issue: Addressing Downtown Business Disruptions: UDO Rewrite vs. Administrative Action and Citywide Equity (Item 34)
conflicts.summary: Following DDI's urgent letter from 260 downtown businesses, Council members and DDI diverged over whether construction/streetscape reforms belong in the UDO rewrite or immediate administrative operations, and whether grants and support should extend citywide beyond downtown.
conflicts.side_a_position: Address construction communication, ADA compliance, and public goods through UDO standards, and ensure small-business support extends beyond downtown.
side_a_arguments: Large out-of-town corporate developers should have communication, sidewalk, and utility/trash allocation standards baked into the UDO rewrite and targeted amendments.
Small businesses in neighborhoods outside downtown—such as Ninth Street and Driver Street—also suffer from utility shutoffs and lack a DDI-style organization to advocate for them.
conflicts.side_b_position: Focus on immediate City operational fixes (employee parking, alert systems, fines for bad actors) without tying them to the UDO.
side_b_arguments: DDI's letter seeks pre-development meetings, enforcement of existing closure plans, employee parking relief by September, and administrative coordination rather than waiting on the UDO.
Council should stay focused on actionable operational fixes and activating the existing small business fund rather than letting out-of-town developer critiques hijack the discussion.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote; Council asked Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson to consult City Manager Wanda Page and return with a timeline of immediate vs. FY26 budgetary actions.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session May 9, 2024
conflicts.issue: Surplus City Land Disposition and Permanent Affordability Terms
conflicts.summary: Members differed on how aggressively the City should mandate permanent affordability covenants and community land trust transfers versus flexible RFP/upset-bid disposition on 10 surplus city-owned sites.
conflicts.side_a_position: Prioritize permanent affordability and community land trust stewardship over time-limited deed restrictions or open market upset bids.
side_a_arguments: Publicly owned land represents an irreplaceable asset that should stay permanently affordable beyond 30-year windows.
Conveyances to nonprofits or land trusts avoid speculative turnover on small infill lots.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain flexible disposition pathways including upset-bid and negotiated RFP authority under NC law so parcels actually get developed quickly.
side_b_arguments: State disposition statutes constrain direct transfers unless specific statutory affordable housing or nonprofit channels apply.
Overly rigid requirements can stall small, scattered-site projects identified in the HR&A inventory.
conflicts.resolution: Staff advanced Item 19 to the May 20 Consent Agenda as an initial intent-to-declare-surplus step while committing to return with disposition structure details for each parcel.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session April 18, 2024
conflicts.issue: 2024 General Obligation Bond Package Scope and Sustainability Inclusion
conflicts.summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman questioned excluding dedicated green/climate sustainability components from the $200M Parks and Streets GO Bond package favored by the majority.
conflicts.side_a_position: Include explicit green infrastructure or sustainability investments within the 2024 GO Bond referendum rather than deferring them.
side_a_arguments: Earlier bond planning discussions contemplated green and climate resilience priorities that disappeared from the final $200M split.
Addressing climate infrastructure alongside aquatics and paving aligns with City sustainability commitments.
conflicts.side_b_position: Keep the $200M bond tightly focused on $85M in aquatic/park facilities and $115M in streets and sidewalks within manageable tax impacts.
side_b_arguments: Residents prioritized sidewalk construction, road paving, unpaved street upgrades, Wheels Aquatic Center, and East End/Long Meadow pools.
Expanding bond categories further would raise the projected 2.51-cent average / 3.45-cent peak tax rate impact.
conflicts.resolution: A Council majority gave thumbs-up to advance the $200M Parks ($85M) and Streets/Sidewalks ($115M) bond package toward the May 20 Council meeting.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting April 1, 2024
conflicts.issue: Lee Valley Rezoning Transit-Oriented Area Compliance and Collector Street Design (Item 21)
conflicts.summary: A majority of Council members questioned Lee Valley's omission of commercial/civic space, private streets, and an isolated Wendell Road collector segment, contrasting with Mark-Anthony Middleton's support for advancing East Durham housing.
conflicts.side_a_position: Require Transit-Oriented Area (TOA) projects to deliver real mixed commercial/civic uses, public street grids, and coherent Wendell Road collector alignment.
side_a_arguments: The Comprehensive Plan's TOA place type expects neighborhood-serving commercial/civic elements rather than pure residential sprawl.
Private streets and a disconnected collector-road island along Wendell Road fall short of multimodal connectivity standards.
conflicts.side_b_position: Recognize the 8-5 Planning Commission approval, affordability proffers, and DPS contribution as sufficient grounds to support needed East Durham housing.
side_b_arguments: The project provides 310-340 multiplex and apartment homes, 30-year 80% AMI affordability, and $53,500 for Durham Public Schools.
Strict insistence on every TOA ideal can stall viable housing near planned transit corridors.
conflicts.resolution: Sensing insufficient support for immediate approval, applicant representatives requested and received a continuance to September 3, 2024.

conflicts.meeting_title: City Council Budget Retreat - March 1, 2024 - 9:00 a.m.
conflicts.issue: FY 2024-25 Budget Guidelines: Uniform 5% Step/Pay-for-Performance Increases vs. Graduated/Tiered Compensation Design
conflicts.summary: Council members disagreed over draft budget guidelines proposing 5% average pay-for-performance and step-plan increases across general, police, and fire employees alongside market adjustments, and whether to cap potential property tax increases now.
conflicts.side_a_position: Explore graduated or flat-dollar raise structures favoring lower-paid workers and review exact fiscal numbers before locking 5% guideline language.
side_a_arguments: Awarding a uniform percentage gives larger dollar raises to top earners than front-line workers; a flat-dollar or tiered model (like Charlotte's 2.5% cap at top tiers) would be more equitable.
Council had not yet seen the full fiscal cost numbers for bumping the general step plan from 4.8%/4% to 5% on top of market adjustments.
conflicts.side_b_position: Keep the existing pay-plan design with 5% step/performance guidelines for FY25 to deliver raises on time by June 30, and defer any structural pay-plan redesign to a future budget cycle.
side_b_arguments: Altering the pay-plan structure is a multi-month classification/redesign project that was not part of the market study's charge and would jeopardize adopting a balanced budget by June 30.
Every employee group—from public works to fire drivers—expects step values and market adjustments to be honored immediately without delaying raises.
Staff still needs Council feedback on maximum acceptable tax-rate increases (noting 1¢ generates ~$4.1M-$4.2M) when balancing market pay adjustments.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken at the retreat; staff will refine numbers and return the draft Budget Guidelines to a March work session ahead of an April formal vote.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council August 4, 2025
conflicts.issue: Cliff Street Unimproved Right-of-Way Closure vs. Future Rockwood Trail Connectivity
conflicts.summary: Council Members split over whether to vacate 42 linear feet of unimproved Cliff Street right-of-way requested by an adjoining homeowner or preserve public access for a future Rockwood Trail connection.
conflicts.side_a_position: Protect public right-of-way and greenway connectivity aligned with Transportation Policy 57 and Bike/Ped Advisory Commission concerns.
side_a_arguments: Once vacated, public right-of-way for pedestrian and trail access is permanently lost.
Staff and BPAC identified the corridor as important to future Rockwood Trail connectivity under the Comprehensive Plan.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid letting speculative long-range trail plans indefinitely restrict an adjacent resident's reasonable property and driveway use.
side_b_arguments: Speculative trail concepts without active funding or timeline should not override existing resident access requests.
Residents deserve certainty when maintaining driveway and yard boundaries.
conflicts.resolution: With the applicant's consent, Council referred the matter back to staff to explore an easement compromise and continued the public hearing to October 20, 2025.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session May 22, 2025 (livestream)
conflicts.issue: Gunfire Detection Technology (ShotSpotter) vs. Preventative Housing and Youth Investments After Q1 Crime Report
conflicts.summary: Following Chief Patrice Andrews' Q1 2025 crime briefing showing nine Q1 homicides despite overall violent crime declines, Council clashed over whether to restore ShotSpotter/law enforcement technology or prioritize root-cause housing and poverty investments.
conflicts.side_a_position: Argue Council reacts urgently to tree protection or traffic deaths while failing to equip police with gun-violence technology like ShotSpotter.
side_a_arguments: Fifteen people had been killed year-to-date despite DPD's strong clearance rates, yet residents lack an urgent, visible gun-violence response.
Council invests aggressively in Vision Zero and environmental rules while refusing tools like ShotSpotter that Chief Andrews and officers support.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject ShotSpotter as an unproven, reactionary tool and argue that housing stability, mental health resources, and poverty reduction are true gun-violence prevention.
side_b_arguments: ShotSpotter only alerts police after shots are already fired and did not justify its cost during Durham's pilot evaluation.
Homicides stem from systemic poverty, housing instability, and inadequate mental health infrastructure, which require sustained preventative investments rather than surveillance tools.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote occurred on the Q1 report; Chief Andrews emphasized DPD's focus on community engagement, youth outreach, and stolen-gun prevention.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session for May 8, 2025
conflicts.issue: Scope of Durham Racial Equity Commission Recommendations: Institutional Change vs. Individual Action & Backlash Risk
conflicts.summary: Following DREC's 2024 Annual Report, Council members differed in emphasis between pushing bold structural policies regardless of state backlash, investigating Duke's tax/resource equity, and adding individual resident-level action steps.
conflicts.side_a_position: Focus squarely on bold institutional, wealth-disparity, rent-stabilization, and livable-wage reforms rather than legislating out of fear of state pushback or shifting responsibility onto individuals.
side_a_arguments: Racial equity work is fundamentally systemic because residents do not control government purse strings or macroeconomic structures.

Durham should lead boldly on policies like rent stabilization, wealth data tracking, and equitable contributions from major institutions like Duke rather than self-censoring over potential state backlash.
conflicts.side_b_position: Include parallel recommendations for individual residents alongside institutional reforms so residents also see steps to position themselves to access opportunities.
side_b_arguments: While government bears primary responsibility, having a complete picture requires empowering individuals with actionable steps to connect to programs and services.
conflicts.resolution: DREC presenters agreed to consider resident-facing guidance while reiterating that DREC's core charge is evaluating government institutions and policies.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session February 20, 2025 (live stream)
conflicts.issue: Eviction Diversion Competitive RFP Scope: Preserving Court Legal Representation Versus Pre-Court Root-Cause Interventions
conflicts.summary: Council members debated how Community Development should structure its upcoming competitive Eviction Diversion RFP and whether the City must commit additional funds above its $650,000 base toward $1 million to ensure legal defense for tenants in court.
conflicts.side_a_position: Ensure Legal Services / Legal Aid tenant representation remains a funded core component of Eviction Diversion and increase City funding toward $1M (+$350k above $650k base).
side_a_arguments: Tenants facing eviction have significantly better housing outcomes with an attorney, and losing federal funds leaves a $350,000 gap above the $650,000 City base.
DeDreana Freeman objected to using funds solely as landlord rental payouts without tenant legal advocacy and asked whether separate legal-services budget requests were needed.

Javiera Caballero noted County DSS rental assistance rules often force residents into court first, making Legal Aid mediation and representation vital while allowing nonprofit collaborations in the RFP.
conflicts.side_b_position: Keep the competitive RFP flexible to test upstream pre-court eviction-prevention models and track 3-to-6-month housing retention outcomes without locking out non-legal nonprofits.
side_b_arguments: Restricting the RFP strictly to law firms would exclude non-profit organizations that provide upstream 'on-ramp' eviction mediation before cases reach court.
Council should evaluate post-assistance outcomes 3 to 12 months later and remains free to reject RFP bids or fund legal services separately.
conflicts.resolution: Deputy City Manager Chadwell confirmed the RFP draft would allow collaborative bids and remain competitive, while City Manager Ferguson advised Council to add any funding increase above flat base into retreat prioritization.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting February 17, 2025 with closed captioning
conflicts.issue: Item 12 (UMCNC MWBE/Section 3 Consulting Contract Amendment #1) Readiness vs. Referral Back to Staff
conflicts.summary: Mayor Pro Tem Middleton moved to approve Amendment No. 1 to Contract #18421 immediately, whereas Council Member Rist sought firm-level subcontractor and dollar breakdowns first; Middleton's motion died for lack of a second and Mayor Williams referred the item back to staff.
conflicts.side_a_position: Hold the contract amendment and refer back to Community Development staff until firm-level MWBE, Workforce, Section 3, and Davis-Bacon contract data are provided in writing.
side_a_arguments: Following concerns raised at the February 6 work session, Council still lacked firm-specific names and dollar figures showing exact subcontractor participation and compliance deliverables.
Community Development Director Reginald Johnson indicated staff could compile and provide the firm-level amounts if referred back.
conflicts.side_b_position: Approve Amendment No. 1 immediately without further delay.
side_b_arguments: There was no substantive flaw demonstrated with UMCNC's compliance monitoring work or the contract amendment itself.
Delaying approval unnecessarily slows down active compliance oversight on federally and locally funded housing projects.
conflicts.resolution: Middleton's motion to approve received no second, and Mayor Williams referred Item 12 back to staff to bring back additional firm-level data.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat - Feb 14, 2025 (livestream)
conflicts.issue: Interpreting Resident Priorities on Policing vs. Non-Police Crime Deterrence
conflicts.summary: Council members clashed over whether ETC survey and Community Conversations data indicate support primarily for policing or for non-police prevention/deterrence investments.
conflicts.side_a_position: Community engagement shows residents prioritize crime prevention, economic opportunity, youth spaces, and alternative responders like HEART rather than expanding traditional policing.
side_a_arguments: Survey framing conflates broad feelings about safety with police protection and omits dedicated evaluation of Community Safety / HEART services.
Qualitative Community Conversations explicitly called for expanding HEART to youth and funding root-cause economic and community-engagement deterrents.
conflicts.side_b_position: Both traditional policing response to lethal gun violence and non-police tools remain critical priorities backed by residents.
side_b_arguments: ETC data demonstrate Black residents do not support defunding the police, and youth/neighborhood fatalities require immediate law-enforcement and violence-intervention capacity.
With 317,000+ residents, samples of 359 to 600 participants must be weighed alongside objective crime statistics and broader constituent outreach.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote; staff noted separate ETC police-survey results would be presented at the next work session.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session January 23, 2025 (livestream)
conflicts.issue: Gun Violence Priority Parity with Vision Zero & Surveillance Cameras in Participatory Budgeting
conflicts.summary: Council members debated dedicating salaried 'Gun Violence Zero' capacity equal to traffic Vision Zero and clashed over whether resident-chosen PB security cameras represent meaningful safety or passive surveillance.
conflicts.side_a_position: Prioritize gun-violence prevention with dedicated salaried coordination and acknowledge that residents repeatedly vote for security cameras via PB.
side_a_arguments: The city pays a full-time Vision Zero coordinator for traffic deaths while lacking an equivalent dedicated coordinator to receive proposals like Dennis Garrett's or Advance Peace for gun violence.
Middleton noted residents in high-violence areas chose security cameras via democratic PB ballots when given the choice.
conflicts.side_b_position: Address systemic street-design and state-road causes of traffic deaths and prioritize active intervention (such as Advance Peace) over passive surveillance cameras.
side_b_arguments: Baker argued surveillance cameras neither call police nor dispatch ambulances, merely producing high-resolution footage after someone is already shot.
Cook emphasized winning state DOT/legislative support on multi-lane state highways (where most high-injury traffic crashes occur) and reviewing Advance Peace holistically.
conflicts.resolution: Informational discussion concluded with Mayor Williams signaling an upcoming proposal for a 'Vision Zero for gun violence' initiative.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session December 19, 2024
conflicts.issue: Proposed Citywide Reductions to Deer Bow Hunting Acreage and Setback Buffers (Item 5)
conflicts.summary: Multiple council members pushed back on lowering the minimum parcel size from 5 to 2 acres and shrinking the dwelling setback from 250 to 60 feet citywide in response to Treyburn HOA requests.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve relaxed citywide acreage and buffer limits so neighborhoods like Treyburn can manage severe deer overpopulation and tick-borne disease risk.
side_a_arguments: Treyburn has roughly 70 deer per square mile and cannot physically satisfy the 250-foot buffer requirement even on combined 5-acre parcels.
Certified bow hunters shooting downward from elevated 10-foot stands pose minimal risk and already operate safely in neighboring jurisdictions.
conflicts.side_b_position: Require stronger citywide safety data, daytime/signage restrictions, non-lethal alternatives, and consideration of neighborhood equity before weakening weapon discharge buffers.
side_b_arguments: A citywide ordinance change opens bow hunting in denser neighborhoods outside Treyburn with fewer notice protections for residents and pets.

Council lacked empirical deer-count data, exploration of sterilization options, and justification for prioritizing suburban deer culling relative to gun violence in communities like McDougald Terrace.
conflicts.resolution: Item 5 was placed on the January General Business Agenda rather than Consent for further deliberation and public hearing.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Dec 5, 2024
conflicts.issue: Retroactive Effective Date for FY24-25 Public Safety Pay Plan Correction (Item 13)
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether pay-compression adjustments for roughly 196 bypassed Fire and Police employees should take effect January 11, 2025 as proposed by staff or retroactively to the start of the fiscal year on July 1, 2024.
conflicts.side_a_position: Make the public safety pay correction retroactive to July 1, 2024
side_a_arguments: Affected Fire and Police employees missed parity increases implemented in the FY25 budget at the start of the fiscal year
Delaying implementation until January 11, 2025 shortchanges employees who were bypassed by administrative structure
conflicts.side_b_position: Staff cautioned against mid-year retroactivity due to budget tightness and payroll calculation complexity
side_b_arguments: City Manager Wanda Page cited sluggish sales tax revenue growth (~13 months into tighter post-ARPA budgeting)
Retroactively recalculating 6 months of variable public safety overtime shifts poses heavy payroll and financial uncertainty
conflicts.resolution: Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton polled at least four supporting members and referred Item 13 back to staff to recalculate costs effective July 1, 2024; Item 13 was omitted from the December 16 agenda.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 24, 2024
conflicts.issue: City Manager Recruitment Timeline, Interview Format, and Interim Governance (Item 14)
conflicts.summary: Members agreed on HR leading the search but differed on moving straight into the proposed timeline versus pausing for closed-session deliberation over interim leadership and alternative paths.
conflicts.side_a_position: Proceed briskly with the HR-led national posting, adding virtual screening, in-person finalist visits with community/stakeholder roundtables, and assessment center exercises.
side_a_arguments: Time is tight and an aggressive 30-day holiday posting window captures qualified candidates cleanly.
Bringing at least two finalists in person and using EQI/assessment centers ensures rigorous vetting.
conflicts.side_b_position: Flag that the proposed timeline extends past December 31 without a manager, necessitating closed-session discussion of an interim manager and alternative options.
side_b_arguments: Full endorsement of the posted timeline should wait until Council holds a personnel closed session to weigh interim appointment and alternative recruitment options.
conflicts.resolution: Council agreed by consensus to hold a closed session on November 4 at 6:00 PM prior to the regular meeting while HR drafts the recruitment brochure for November 7 review.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 10, 2024
conflicts.issue: Citywide Scope and Safety Protections in Proposed Deer Bow Hunting Ordinance Revisions (Item 9)
conflicts.summary: Council members questioned whether loosening bow hunting acreage and setback rules citywide for Treyburn HOA introduces safety and equity risks without sufficient data or time limits.
conflicts.side_a_position: Note existing 2013 ordinance safeguards (10-ft elevated stand requirement) and address Treyburn residents' documented deer overpopulation concerns promptly.
side_a_arguments: Treyburn cannot meet existing buffer limits even after consulting NC Wildlife and NC State.
Shooting downward from an elevated 10-foot stand is viewed by NC Wildlife officials as the primary safety protection, and no injuries have occurred under the 2013 ordinance.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defer the ordinance amendment by at least one cycle to investigate tighter calendar/daylight time limits, public notice, population thresholds, and citywide implications.
side_b_arguments: Ordinances apply the force of law citywide rather than solely to Treyburn, creating unforeseen risks for pets and pedestrians in denser areas.
Council must avoid rushing code changes for suburban deer complaints compared with gun-violence challenges elsewhere in Durham.
conflicts.resolution: Deferred one work-session cycle so DCM Bo Ferguson and the City Attorney's Office could consult NC Wildlife officials and research potential limits.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 10, 2024
conflicts.issue: 2025 Property Reappraisal Equity, Appeal Disparities, and LOHRP Grant Scaling (Item 26)
conflicts.summary: Council members pressed Durham County tax officials over whether rapid gentrification increases and unequal appeal access worsen racial tax burdens and whether local relief grants scale with post-reappraisal tax bills.
conflicts.side_a_position: Examine demographic appeal disparities, communicate relief programs more simply, and explore scaling LOHRP assistance when gentrifying home values jump above the countywide average.
side_a_arguments: Fixed-income homeowners in rapidly gentrifying neighborhoods face above-average assessment spikes, yet LOHRP grants remain tied to income rather than bill jumps.
National research documents racial disparities in effective sales ratios due to unequal access to appeals, and residents struggle to find clear guidance on County webpages.
conflicts.side_b_position: Emphasize that tax assessors follow market sales under strict state statute without demographic data and highlight Durham's 2021 UNC School of Government equity study and online evaluator.
side_b_arguments: Tax offices do not create property values and Durham's 2021 UNC SOG study found no consistent demographic bias in appeal outcomes, prompting expanded community outreach.
LOHRP is nearly unique in the South (funded $750K County / $500K City), while statutory fixes such as lifting the $36,700 state homestead cap require General Assembly action.
conflicts.resolution: Informational briefing; County staff agreed to share the UNC SOG audit and work with City Communications on clearer water-bill and web tax-relief messaging.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session August 8, 2024
conflicts.issue: Canceling or Rescheduling the July 2025 Work Session in the Annual Meeting Calendar (Item 5)
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether to eliminate the late-July 2025 work session upfront or adjust closer to summer to avoid exhausting combined meeting days.
conflicts.side_a_position: Eliminate the July 24, 2025 work session now (or move it to July 31) to protect a full July Council recess.
side_a_arguments: The original policy goal was keeping all of July meeting-free, and Mayor Williams noted planned international travel in July 2025.
conflicts.side_b_position: Wait until June 2025 to assess conflicts and avoid scheduling two full meetings on a single 14-to-15-hour Monday.
side_b_arguments: Working council members struggle with back-to-back 15-hour combined meeting days, Local Progress conference dates are not yet set, and City Attorney Kim Rehberg noted July 31 conflicts with the Municipal Attorneys Conference.
conflicts.resolution: Item 5 was moved to the General Business Agenda for final resolution.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session June 6, 2024
conflicts.issue: Durham Rail Trail Delivery Acceleration vs. Community Engagement and Anti-Displacement Policies (Item 28)
conflicts.summary: Council members differed on whether to push staff to accelerate the Durham Rail Trail timeline (currently targeting fall 2027 opening) and how urgently the City must pair the project with anti-displacement and value-capture measures.
conflicts.side_a_position: Push to accelerate infrastructure delivery timelines while pursuing value-capture overlay/tax tools.
side_a_arguments: Voters supporting a tax increase and $200M bond want to know what staffing or funding would deliver funded projects like the Rail Trail a year earlier.
Rising property values along the corridor should be paired with value capture or overlay mechanisms and stay-in-place policies.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain realistic schedules that honor equitable engagement and recognize market realities around major amenities.
side_b_arguments: Rushing project delivery risks excluding East Durham residents from equitable engagement and causing construction flaws.

High-value amenities inevitably raise surrounding market prices, and anti-displacement programming carries ongoing tax costs; Durham already replaced neighborhood-specific pilots with the County's low-income homeowner relief program.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote; Council requested an update from Durham County on the Low-Income Homeowner Relief Program at a future Joint City-County Committee meeting.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session May 23, 2024
conflicts.issue: Youth Gun Violence Response, ShotSpotter Termination, and Police Staffing Realism (Item 26)
conflicts.summary: During the Q1 Crime Report discussion, Mayor Williams sharply criticized Council's handling of gun violence after ending ShotSpotter without an alternative response, while Council members also questioned whether DPD's 535 sworn staffing target is realistic.
conflicts.side_a_position: Treat youth gun violence as Durham's top crisis and provide concrete alternatives after ending ShotSpotter.
side_a_arguments: Neighborhoods are enduring heavy gunfire (~1,500 shell casings collected YTD) and Council ended ShotSpotter without putting a response in place.
Council shut down City Hall for a Gaza ceasefire resolution while staying quiet on gun violence in Durham; public safety must be prioritized alongside bike lanes and sidewalks.
conflicts.side_b_position: Question whether filling 535 sworn positions is realistic and pair pay raises with holistic investments.
side_b_arguments: With sworn staffing at 74% (397 of 535) and modest academy class sizes, reaching 100% of authorized slots may be unrealistic without reassessing workload and vacancy metrics.
Higher pay in the FY24-25 budget (moving everyone to July raises) alongside investments in youth, Survivor Care, and community trust—including protecting immigrant reporting—are key responses.
conflicts.resolution: Item 26 remained on the June 3 Consent Agenda; staff committed to providing shooting demographics and tracking Latino youth crime trends.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session May 23, 2024
conflicts.issue: UDO Street Widths, Autocentrism, and Vision Zero Target Timelines (Item 36)
conflicts.summary: Council members debated whether Durham's street width standards and greenfield rezonings undermine Vision Zero, how quickly fatalities can be eliminated, and how to balance narrower streets with emergency and service vehicle needs.
conflicts.side_a_position: Reform UDO street standards to prevent auto-centric sprawl and accelerate Vision Zero delivery timelines.
side_a_arguments: Approving auto-centric single-family sprawl on annexed land contradicts Comprehensive Plan walkability and Vision Zero goals, and current UDO street widths may be excessive.
Setting 10-year (50% by 2035) and 20-year (0% by 2045) targets feels slow given recent traffic deaths; accelerating project delivery is vital to win federal SS4A grants.
conflicts.side_b_position: Adopt realistic timelines and coordinate street narrowing delicately with Fire, Solid Waste, and transit buses.
side_b_arguments: Setting hard target dates creates anxiety given current project-delivery capacity and NCDOT constraints, and narrow streets require testing with fire trucks, school buses, and solid waste vehicles.
conflicts.resolution: Council expressed consensus support for advancing the revised Vision Zero resolution (Item 27) onto the June 3 Consent Agenda.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting May 6, 2024
conflicts.issue: Item 25: Allocate FY24 Funds ($41,000) for Heart of a Champion Summer Camp and FY25 July/August Funding
conflicts.summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman moved to immediately allocate $41,000 from FY24 funds for Education 360 / Heart of a Champion at Cornwallis along with bridging support into July and August of FY25, citing urgent gun violence prevention needs for public housing youth. Multiple competing nonprofit youth operators spoke during the hearing requesting substantial summer allocations ranging from $200,000 to $500,000, underscoring demand across the city. Opponents of the motion—Williams, Middleton, Caballero, and Rist—argued that awarding an unbid mid-year earmark to one organization while other groups awaited process was inequitable and bypassed budget discipline, committing instead to create a larger competitive Youth Fund in FY25. Supporters Baker, Cook, and Freeman contended the modest sum was needed immediately for summer 2024 rather than waiting another year, but the motion failed 3-4.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 3-4)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (3-4)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 21, 2024
conflicts.issue: Developer Accountability in Southeast Durham Watershed Improvement Plan (Item 17)
conflicts.summary: Council members differed over whether public funds should finance $2.93M in Southeast Durham watershed remediation or if private developers should bear greater responsibility.
conflicts.side_a_position: Require stronger developer accountability rather than relying on public tax/utility dollars to fix sediment pollution.
side_a_arguments: Rapid greenfield construction in Southeast Durham generated severe erosion into Lick Creek and adjacent basins.
Spending $2.022M in City funds and $910k in County funds subsidizes damage caused by inadequate site enforcement.
conflicts.side_b_position: Proceed with the joint City-County watershed plan immediately to address legacy and ongoing stream degradation.
side_b_arguments: Downstream residents and ecosystems need remediation regardless of whether blame spans historical and current projects.
Enforcing new UDO rules proceeds separately from executing existing basin-wide stabilization.
conflicts.resolution: Item 17 advanced to the April 1 Consent Agenda as drafted.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 21, 2024
conflicts.issue: City Hall Front Door Locking, Fire-Code Capacity, and Public Comment Cutoffs
conflicts.summary: At the close of open session, Council members clashed sharply over locking City Hall doors after hours and restricting in-person public entry.
conflicts.side_a_position: Keep City Hall accessible to residents attending public meetings rather than locking front doors prematurely or capping access at 7:00 PM.
side_a_arguments: Residents attempting to attend evening meetings encountered locked entrances, chilling democratic participation.
Public institutions must prioritize open entry and transparent accommodation for late-arriving workers.
conflicts.side_b_position: Enforce fire-marshal occupancy limits, building security protocols, and established public-comment deadlines.
side_b_arguments: Chamber overcrowding triggers binding fire-code capacity violations and safety risks for attendees and staff.
Security staff must manage perimeter access consistently once chambers reach overflow limits or normal operating cutoff times.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Mayor Williams directed staff to enforce fire-code and security protocols while managing overflow accommodations.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council March 4, 2024
conflicts.issue: Authorize Three-Year Contract with SoundThinking, Inc. for ShotSpotter Gunshot Detection Services (Item 17)
conflicts.summary: Following the Duke Wilson Center evaluation, more than 15 residents and advocates (including Damon Williams, Samuel Scarboro, Leslie St. Dre, Brittany Price, Kesha Mallette, and Elle Gent) urged Council to reject the three-year ShotSpotter renewal, while East Durham resident and city employee Wilma Oliver spoke in favor. Council Members Chelsea Cook, Nate Baker, Carl Rist, and Javiera Caballero argued against renewal, emphasizing that 91% of ShotSpotter-only alerts were unconfirmed, 50 of 52 gunshot-wound incidents already had 911 calls, regression analysis showed no gains in arrests, evidence collection, or witness interviews, focus group residents lacked trust in the tool, and resources were better invested in 911 staffing, prevention, and HEART. Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton and Mayor Leonardo Williams argued in favor, contending ShotSpotter reduced median response time by 1.2 minutes, potentially saved a life, had backing from Police Chief Patrice Andrews, the Sheriff, and NCCU, and helped an understaffed police force (~120 vacancies). The motion failed 2-4, ending the city's ShotSpotter contract.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 2-4)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (2-4)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Feb 22, 2024
conflicts.issue: Interpretation of the Duke Wilson Center ShotSpotter Pilot Evaluation (Items 17 & 24)
conflicts.summary: Following Dr. Philip Cook's presentation of the Wilson Center evaluation, Council members diverged in how they weighed ShotSpotter's response-time gains against its opportunity costs and null impact on 911 investigative productivity.
conflicts.side_a_position: Question the cost-effectiveness and opportunity costs of ShotSpotter given null investigative productivity findings and limited community support.
side_a_arguments: Faster 911 response times under ShotSpotter produced no detectable improvement in arrests, evidence collection, or witness interviews.
In addition to the $225,000+ contract cost, ShotSpotter generated 2.3 extra two-car Priority 2 dispatches per day (2% of citywide Priority 2 deployments), creating officer opportunity costs.
The impact on overall gun violence could not be determined, and focus-group residents voiced skepticism about spending priorities.
conflicts.side_b_position: View the evaluation as validating ShotSpotter as an effective response tool that should not be unfairly judged on gun-violence prevention.
side_b_arguments: Proponents and SoundThinking never claimed ShotSpotter would reduce gun violence; it was intended as a response tool and succeeded in cutting median response time by 1.2 minutes (5:11 in Q4).

ShotSpotter-only alerts produced 7 arrests (+32%), nearly doubled evidence collection cases, and plausibly saved one victim's life—making it worth the ~$200K/year cost just as Council funds HEART without proof of lives saved.
Durham's strict guardrails prevented Chicago-style over-policing, and residents in high-gunfire areas asked for police protection.
conflicts.resolution: Council placed Item 17 (three-year SoundThinking renewal contract) on the March 4, 2024 General Business Agenda for formal deliberation and vote.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Jan 4, 2024
conflicts.issue: Procedural Pathway for Small Area Planning (Council Work Session Resolution vs. JCCPC Referral)
conflicts.summary: Council members differed over whether to initiate a small area planning discussion—including Walltown and Northgate Mall—directly on a City Council work session agenda or route it first through the Joint City-County Planning Committee (JCCPC).
conflicts.side_a_position: Bring the small area planning discussion or resolution to a City Council work session so all council members can provide input early.
side_a_arguments: Nate Baker noted rules of procedure were unclear and wanted a work session discussion on small area planning beyond just Northgate Mall within a feasible staff timeline.
Carl Rist noted he was no longer on JCCPC and wanted an opportunity for his voice to be heard at a full Council work session.
conflicts.side_b_position: Originate land-use work program items at the JCCPC because planning jurisdiction is shared with the County.
side_b_arguments: Javiera Caballero noted land-use issues fall under both City Council and County Commissioners and recommended placing the item on the February JCCPC agenda first.
Mark-Anthony Middleton added that resolutions are aspirational rather than binding staff directives and noted any JCCPC work product still returns to full Council for debate.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; members aired preferences ahead of staff work-program scheduling.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Jan 2, 2024
conflicts.issue: Item 23 (Motion 1): East Club Gateway Voluntary Annexation and Utility Extension Agreement (Gander Development LLC, BDG220031)
conflicts.summary: Council voted on Motion 1 to adopt an annexation ordinance effective March 31, 2024 for the 13.96-acre East Club Gateway site and authorize a utility extension agreement with Gander Development LLC. The motion failed 2-4 with Baker, Caballero, Freeman, and Rist voting no, rendering subsequent zoning and consistency motions unnecessary.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 2-4)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (2-4)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Dec. 18, 2023
conflicts.issue: Item 11: Authorize 3-Month Contract Amendment with SoundThinking Inc. for ShotSpotter Services ($52,356; Total $249,856)
conflicts.summary: Following extensive public comment overwhelmingly opposing ShotSpotter and council debate over waiting for the Wilson Center's independent evaluation of the 12-month pilot, the motion to extend the contract through March 14, 2024 failed 2-4, causing the ShotSpotter alert service to go dark.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 2-4)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (2-4)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session August 4, 2025
conflicts.issue: Strict Target Metrics vs. Flexible Underwriting for Small Business Opportunity Fund Phase 2 (Item 17)
conflicts.summary: Council Members differed on whether Phase 2 of the Durham Small Business Opportunity Fund ($25k-$75k loan guarantees administered by Carolina Small Business Development Fund) should enforce strict quantitative loan-delivery targets.
conflicts.side_a_position: Require explicit numerical performance targets for guaranteed loans and early-stage businesses served.
side_a_arguments: Clear quantitative metrics help Council evaluate return on public economic development dollars.
Targets establish accountability for reaching 50 early-stage businesses and 18-40 loan guarantees.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain underwriting flexibility rather than rigid numeric quotas for pandemic-era small business relief.
side_b_arguments: Early-stage small businesses recovering from pandemic disruption face uneven credit profiles that rigid targets could distort.
Partnering with experienced CDFIs like Carolina Small Business Development Fund requires trust in adaptive technical assistance.
conflicts.resolution: Item remained on the Consent Agenda for evening approval without imposing rigid new contract quotas.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 20, 2025 (livestream)
conflicts.issue: Applying Data-Driven Policing and Gunshot Detection Tools Versus Root-Cause Investments in Gun Violence Response
conflicts.summary: Following the Vision Zero traffic-safety presentation, Council members disagreed over whether Durham should pair Vision Zero-style data dashboards with gunshot detection/law-enforcement technology or avoid expanding policing surveillance technologies.
conflicts.side_a_position: Apply Vision Zero-level urgency, dashboards, and gunshot-detection/law-enforcement technology alongside community efforts to curb gun violence.
side_a_arguments: Gun violence kills young people in Durham at devastating rates, warranting the same measurable goal-setting and public dashboard transparency as traffic fatalities.
Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton advocated a 'both/and' approach incorporating technology (referencing ShotSpotter and law enforcement tools) alongside community interventions.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject diverting public tax dollars toward acoustic gunshot surveillance or punitive policing expansions rather than survivor and root-cause investments.
side_b_arguments: Technology like ShotSpotter did not demonstrate effective outcomes in Durham and risks diverting taxpayer funds from community-centered prevention.
Durham should prioritize investments in underlying socioeconomic causes and support for survivors and affected neighborhoods.
conflicts.resolution: Exchange ended without formal action during the Vision Zero Q&A.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat - Feb 28, 2025 (livestream)
conflicts.issue: Downtown Parking Philosophy: Subsidized First-Two-Hours Free and Asset Redevelopment Versus Higher Parking Fees to Deter Driving
conflicts.summary: Council divided over how to fix the Parking Fund's $2.5 million deficit—with some advocating discounted/free initial hours to aid downtown patrons and businesses, and others favoring higher fees and extended hours to cover costs and push mode shift to buses.
conflicts.side_a_position: Raise parking fees, extend paid enforcement hours past 7 PM, expand paid zones to other hubs, and oppose free initial hours to force cost recovery and bus usage.
side_a_arguments: Free first two hours reduces parking turnover and contradicts the City's 15-minute city and fare-free transit messaging.
Extending paid hours to 8–10 PM and charging in hubs like University Hill or Ninth Street helps the Parking Fund recover its own costs.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid across-the-board rate hikes, explore targeted first-two-hours-free validation/discounts (e.g., for Carolina Theater moviegoers), and repurpose underutilized lots or aging garages.
side_b_arguments: Durham's parking rates are already at or near the top of the NC market, and raising them further risks hurting downtown small businesses and cultural venues.
The deficit stems largely from Debt Service on overbuilt garages like Morgan-Rigsbee, so redeveloping surface lots or aging garages is a better structural fix than higher user fees.
conflicts.resolution: Council requested utilization/stay-duration/enforcement data (including Javiera Caballero and Chelsea Cook's data requests) and staff options on surface-lot redevelopment ahead of May budget proposals.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat - Feb 14, 2025 (livestream)
conflicts.issue: Fiscal Terminology ('Deficit' vs. 'Budget Gap') and Equity Program Nomenclature
conflicts.summary: Mayor Pro Tem Middleton urged staff to stop describing the early-stage budget baseline projection as a 'deficit' and suggested reframing 'Equitable Green Infrastructure' nomenclature to protect equity investments from external political scrutiny.
conflicts.side_a_position: Retire alarmist or politically vulnerable labels ('deficit', 'Equitable Green Infrastructure') while preserving balanced-budget discipline and underlying equity criteria.
side_a_arguments: Because North Carolina cities must legally adopt balanced budgets, calling an early revenue-expenditure delta a 'deficit' misleads the public into thinking the city is running in the red.
Renaming EGI to 'empowerment zones' or 'areas of focus' protects essential infrastructure investments in underserved neighborhoods amid heightened statewide and federal scrutiny.
conflicts.side_b_position: Staff agreed to adjust 'deficit' to 'budget gap' and confirmed internal discussions are underway on making EGI's name more relatable, while Freeman and Baker emphasized maintaining transparency and accessibility.
side_b_arguments: Technical terms should communicate accurately to residents without obscuring how equity criteria target underserved census block groups.
conflicts.resolution: City Manager Ferguson adopted 'budget gap' and staff confirmed EGI rebranding options are under review.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session February 6, 2025
conflicts.issue: Item 12 (UMCNC Compliance Contract Amendment #1) Use of Dedicated Housing Funds & Backup Transparency
conflicts.summary: Council Member Cook questioned using Forever Home Durham / Dedicated Housing Fund dollars and lacking original contract backup for UMCNC compliance monitoring, while Mayor Pro Tem Middleton defended external compliance oversight.
conflicts.side_a_position: Scrutinize dedicating housing program funds to external compliance consulting and require full original contract documentation and MWBE attainment metrics before final approval.
side_a_arguments: Dedicated Housing Fund / Forever Home Durham dollars are scarce affordable housing capital, and Council needs to see the original contract scope and results before expanding it.
Staff had not attached the original contract or firm-level outcome breakdown to the agenda packet.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain independent third-party monitoring of MWBE, Workforce, Section 3, and Davis-Bacon obligations so the city does not grade its own compliance.
side_b_arguments: External oversight ensures independent verification of labor and minority/women business participation rather than relying solely on internal departmental self-reporting.
Reginald Johnson reported the project exceeded citywide MWBE targets (13% minority and 12% women participation versus 11%/7% goals).
conflicts.resolution: Staff agreed to attach the original contract and supporting compliance figures ahead of the February 17 Council meeting.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session February 6, 2025
conflicts.issue: HOPWA Program Oversight, Eviction Risks & Community Engagement Following Subrecipient Collapse
conflicts.summary: Council members pressed Community Development leadership over underutilization, landlord late fees, eviction filings, and lack of lived-experience input after Central Piedmont Community Action abruptly folded.
conflicts.side_a_position: CDD must embed client/lived-experience engagement into RFP design, improve grant utilization, and institute early-warning financial checks before subrecipients collapse.
side_a_arguments: Abrupt agency failure left clients facing unpaid rent, late fees covered out of CDD's general operating budget, and eviction filings.
Community partners and clients were not adequately engaged in shaping the upcoming July 1 RFP.
conflicts.side_b_position: CDD took emergency in-house stewardship of TBRA payments to prevent client displacement while preparing a competitive July 1 RFP.
side_b_arguments: Central Piedmont Community Action ceased operations abruptly with little advance notice, forcing rapid emergency transition in-house.
CDD staff committed to incorporating oversight lessons and communicating transitions more proactively.
conflicts.resolution: Informational briefing concluded with Council direction to tighten early-warning monitoring and stakeholder outreach for the July 1 RFP.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session January 23, 2025 (livestream)
conflicts.issue: Participatory Budgeting (PB) 60% Geographic Equity Target Methodology
conflicts.summary: Mayor Pro Tem Middleton praised PB's outcomes while questioning how its 60% underserved-area project goal is operationalized in a one-person, one-vote election so staff can defend it against rising external scrutiny.
conflicts.side_a_position: Clarify and rigorously document how delegate equity scoring and targeted paper-ballot outreach drive the 60% outcome without creating legal vulnerabilities akin to quotas.
side_a_arguments: Concentrating physical polling/boots-on-the-ground paper outreach in selected areas alongside delegate scoring weights produces different demographic pools than online voting.
Amid shifting state and national legal scrutiny of municipal equity programs, Durham must be able to defend its methodology with complete precision.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defend PB's geographic equity scoring as a vital tool to include low-income, transit-dependent, and unhoused/incarcerated residents lacking digital access.
side_b_arguments: Every resident can submit ideas and vote once, while paper ballots at bus stations, convenience stores, and the jail ensure populations without cell phones or emails participate.
conflicts.resolution: Informational briefing; Middleton thanked staff for transparent demographic and survey-methodology breakdowns.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Nov 21, 2024
conflicts.issue: Public and Stakeholder Transparency in Executive Personnel Discussions (Closed Session NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6))
conflicts.summary: Although all seven members voted to enter closed session, members disagreed sharply on whether executive transition deliberations were overly shielded from community input.
conflicts.side_a_position: Executive transition and key leadership-role discussions require structured public and stakeholder engagement rather than being handled primarily behind closed doors.
side_a_arguments: Major community-facing leadership roles affect residents directly and merit public input on priorities and expectations.
Supporting the statutory closed-session vote should not be mistaken for endorsing a closed-off transition process.
conflicts.side_b_position: Personnel evaluations, candidate discussions, and contractual deliberations must remain confidential in closed session to comply with North Carolina law and protect candor.
side_b_arguments: NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6) specifically authorizes confidential personnel deliberation when evaluating individuals or terms.
conflicts.resolution: Council unanimously voted 7-0 to enter closed session at 02:19:19 after Cook and Freeman placed their process objections on the public record.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session June 6, 2024
conflicts.issue: Outsourced Consulting Contracts, In-House Capacity, and Contractor Living-Wage Compliance (Items 18 & 19)
conflicts.summary: Council members clashed over whether the City should continue outsourcing communications and technical work (such as Moss + Ross LLC at $6,000/month for Forever Home Durham) instead of hiring in-house staff, and how the City enforces livable wages and MWBE equity among contractors.
conflicts.side_a_position: Scrutinize outsourcing vs. in-house FTEs and track contractor wages and MWBE pay equity.
side_a_arguments: Paying $6,000/month over multi-year bond cycles raises questions about why communications are not brought in-house.
Council should ensure the City is not cutting costs via contracting at lower wages and should track MWBE and contractor pay against the City's minimum livable wage.
conflicts.side_b_position: Trust City Manager operational make-or-buy decisions and avoid micromanaging staffing amid tax pressures.
side_b_arguments: With a proposed 3.85-cent City tax increase and 4.5-cent County increase, Council sets policy and should trust the manager to make cost-effective operational choices.
North Carolina state law preempts municipalities from mandating contractor wages, so City contracts rely on voluntary livable-wage expectation clauses and lowest-bidder rules where applicable.
conflicts.resolution: Items 18 and 19 remained on the June 17 Consent Agenda; staff committed to checking whether Moss + Ross counted toward MWBE tracking and providing the City's contract living-wage clause.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session May 9, 2024
conflicts.issue: Discover Durham Board Nomination Bypassing Organization Recommendation
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether to respect Discover Durham's internal nominating recommendation (Sydney Cove) or advance alternative Council nominations for two board seats.
conflicts.side_a_position: Honor Discover Durham's submitted slate recommendation alongside Sean Umstead rather than bypassing its vetted nominee.
side_a_arguments: Partner tourism organizations vet candidates for operational fit and conflict-free representation.
Passing over Discover Durham's recommended nominee Sydney Cove breaks typical deference without clear rationale.
conflicts.side_b_position: Exercise Council's independent appointment authority by nominating Crystal E. Taylor and Sean Umstead to the ballot.
side_b_arguments: Council members retain discretion to nominate qualified community and hospitality leaders directly.
Nomination to the ballot still allows all Council members to vote at the regular meeting.
conflicts.resolution: Both Sean Umstead and Crystal E. Taylor were placed on the nomination slate for formal voting at the May 20 meeting, with Caballero's objection noted on the record.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session April 4, 2024
conflicts.issue: 30-Year vs. Permanent Affordability on 312 E. Umstead SRO Loan (Item 7)
conflicts.summary: Council members questioned whether a $3.2M ARPA loan to Reinvestment Partners for 17 SRO units at 312 E. Umstead should lock in permanent affordability rather than a 30-year period.
conflicts.side_a_position: Push for permanent affordability covenants on heavily subsidized nonprofit/ARPA housing investments.
side_a_arguments: Covering $3.2M for 17 SRO units equates to major public subsidy per door that warrants perpetual affordability.
Expiring 30-year terms create future displacement cliff risks.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain the 30-year standard agreement used in the current ARPA underwriting to close the transaction before federal deadlines.
side_b_arguments: Community Development staff noted Reinvestment Partners is a mission-driven nonprofit unlikely to flip the property and warned renegotiating closing terms could delay ARPA obligation deadlines.
Adding unilateral covenant changes late in deal structuring risks project delays.
conflicts.resolution: Item 7 remained on the April 15 Consent Agenda as structured, with staff noting affordability duration policy as an ongoing Council priority.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Dec. 7, 2023
conflicts.issue: Extending ShotSpotter Pilot Contract for Three Months Pending Wilson Center Evaluation
conflicts.summary: Council members debated whether to keep ShotSpotter running for three months ($52,356) while the Wilson Center analyzes data from the already-concluding one-year pilot.
conflicts.side_a_position: Question extending the contract when no additional evaluation data will be collected and move the decision to the General Business Agenda for full public debate.
side_a_arguments: The Wilson Center evaluation is limited strictly to the 12-month pilot period ending December 14, so a 3-month extension yields no extra study data.
Extending an expired pilot without completed evaluation findings creates a slippery slope.
Public and council views warrant placing Item 11 on the General Business Agenda rather than Consent.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain continuity of ShotSpotter operations for three months rather than shutting sensors off mid-review.
side_b_arguments: ShotSpotter alerts have faster response times than 911 calls, led to arrests and gun recoveries, and alerted police when residents did not call 911.
No reports of aggressive policing from the pilot have materialized.
Deactivating sensors on December 14 while awaiting the report disrupts emergency response.
conflicts.resolution: Item 11 was pulled from Consent and placed on the December 18 General Business Agenda for a formal vote.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council October 6, 2025
conflicts.issue: Item 18A: Hartland Park Annexation Ordinance and Utility Extension Agreement (1021, 1105, 1213 Doc Nichols Road)
conflicts.summary: Council held a contested public hearing on Ardent Building LLC's annexation and Utility Extension Agreement for 12.999 acres along Doc Nichols Road to construct up to 117 townhomes. Nearby residents and environmental advocates warned that steep slopes and Triassic clay soils would worsen sediment runoff into Lick Creek and Falls Lake and exacerbate traffic along Doc Nichols Road, while the developer noted the parcel sits inside the Urban Growth Boundary and raised its affordable proffer during the hearing from 5% to 7% (8 units at 80% AMI for 30 years) alongside 7-day seeding commitments. Opponents Nate Baker, DeDreana Freeman, and Chelsea Cook criticized suburban sprawl, water-quality risks, and insufficient transit connectivity, while supporters Leonardo Williams, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, and Carl Rist cited below-median-priced townhomes and infill proximity to existing utilities in passing the annexation 4-3.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council October 6, 2025
conflicts.issue: Item 18B: Hartland Park Zoning Map Change Ordinance (Rural Residential / Falls Jordan B to PDR 9.001)
conflicts.summary: Following passage of the Hartland Park annexation, Council voted on the companion rezoning ordinance converting the Doc Nichols Road parcels from county Rural Residential to City Planned Development Residential 9.001 within the Falls/Jordan B watershed overlay. Dissenting members Baker, Freeman, and Cook maintained that the density and clearing on erodible soils conflicted with environmental protection goals despite the applicant's 7% affordability proffer. The majority coalition of Williams, Middleton, Caballero, and Rist voted in favor, adopting the rezoning 4-3.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council June 2, 2025
conflicts.issue: History of Non-Police Post-Shooting Canvassing Under ShotSpotter (Item 24)
conflicts.summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton clashed factually during the Q1 Crime Report over whether Durham ever deployed unarmed/HEART-style personnel to canvass neighborhoods after ShotSpotter alerts.
conflicts.side_a_position: Durham previously saw social workers, EMS, and non-violent coalition volunteers canvass neighborhoods the day after shootings.
side_a_arguments: Community organizations and social worker/EMS volunteers repeatedly knocked doors in public housing neighborhoods after shootings in past years.
Day-after canvassing in high-gun-violence neighborhoods is not unprecedented and could be funded in future cycles.
conflicts.side_b_position: The City of Durham never deployed HEART or unarmed municipal responders specifically triggered by ShotSpotter gunshot detections.
side_b_arguments: Unlike peer cities using ShotSpotter alerts to dispatch HEART-type canvassers the next day, Durham only sent law enforcement assets and did not yet have HEART during earlier ShotSpotter periods.
Claiming Durham deployed ShotSpotter-triggered civilian responders is historically inaccurate.
conflicts.resolution: After trading statements on the record, Council moved on and unanimously adopted the Q1 Crime Report 7-0.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session May 22, 2025 (livestream)
conflicts.issue: Proposed Revisions to City Council Rules and Procedures (Item 19)
conflicts.summary: Council Member Baker raised concerns over proposed changes to Council's rules of procedure regarding how individual council members introduce agenda items and whether five votes can still add day-of items.
conflicts.side_a_position: Preserve existing avenues for council members to introduce agenda items directly and keep the five-vote mechanism to add urgent items at meetings.
side_a_arguments: Requiring council-initiated items to go through the Mayor first concentrates gatekeeping power and could delay urgent member priorities.
Removing the five-vote supermajority option eliminates flexibility when unexpected public issues arise.
conflicts.side_b_position: Streamline agenda-setting through structured committee/mayoral routing and clearer procedural rules (committee led by Javiera Caballero, who was absent).
side_b_arguments: Formal routing improves coordination and avoids ad-hoc last-minute docket additions without staff review.
conflicts.resolution: Item 19 was placed on the General Business Agenda for the June 2 meeting so absent Council Member Javiera Caballero could lead the full discussion.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council May 5, 2025 (full meeting with closed captioning)
conflicts.issue: Item 15: Annexation Ordinance and Utility Extension Agreement – Howard Property
conflicts.summary: After nearly three hours of testimony from roughly 15 opponents warning of Lick Creek/Falls Lake sedimentation, wildlife corridor fragmentation, NC 98 traffic, EMS delays, and an initial staff-report error stating no streams were on site—countered by landowners Larry Howard, Kelly Jones, and Robert Height Jr.—applicant Dan Jewell added five commitments including raising affordable units from 5% to 6% and capping impervious cover at 50%. Council Members Baker, Cook, and Freeman opposed annexation citing environmental vulnerability, greenfield infrastructure strain, and transparency flaws. Mayor Williams, Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton, Caballero, and Rist supported annexation citing Urban Growth Boundary alignment, housing need, and landowner rights, passing the ordinance 4-3.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council May 5, 2025 (full meeting with closed captioning)
conflicts.issue: Item 15: UDO Zoning Map Change Ordinance (RR & RS-20 County to PDR 5.783 City) – Howard Property
conflicts.summary: Following the 4-3 annexation vote, Council voted on the companion UDO Zoning Map Change converting the 86.41-acre Howard Property from RR and RS-20 County to PDR 5.783 City with Falls/Jordan District B Watershed Overlay for up to 499 units and 12,000 square feet of commercial space. Council Member Freeman's voting console briefly failed to register electronically, so Mayor Williams and the Clerk verbally confirmed her Nay vote for the official record. The rezoning passed on the same 4-3 split, with Williams, Middleton, Caballero, and Rist voting Aye and Baker, Cook, and Freeman voting Nay.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council March 17, 2025 with closed captioning
conflicts.issue: Item 31: Zoning Map Change — Pickett Apartments (Z2400024)
conflicts.summary: Item 31 drew nearly two and a half hours of contentious testimony and Council deliberation over rezoning 6.12 acres at 3117–3127 Pickett Road from RS-20 to PDR 36.176 for up to 140 apartments abutting Sandy Creek Park. Neighboring residents, Friends of Sandy Creek Park supporters, and environmentalists opposed the project due to narrow Pickett Road's lack of sidewalks and transit service, stormwater runoff, floodplain/riparian impacts along Sandy Creek, and tree loss, while housing advocates and the applicant cited acute housing scarcity and added modified proffers for bird-safe glass (ABC threat factor <=30) and $300,000 directed to the Durham Parks Foundation earmarked for Pickett Road/Sandy Creek connectivity. Council Members Nate Baker, Chelsea Cook, and DeDreana Freeman opposed the rezoning, arguing the site lacked safe pedestrian/transit access and stronger environmental protections (such as dark-sky lighting and pervious surfaces). Mayor Leonardo Williams, Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, and Carl Rist voted in favor, emphasizing the value of 140 infill apartments inside the Urban Growth Boundary near a park compared with 12 by-right single-family homes, passing the rezoning 4-3.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)
