conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Nov 4, 2024
conflicts.issue: Item 11: Lindley Townhouses UDO Zoning Map Amendment (RR to PDR 8.326, 1343 Ellis Rd & 1326 Clinton Rd)
conflicts.summary: Applicant representatives sought to rezone 12.25 acres from Rural Residential to Planned Development Residential 8.326 for 102 townhomes, adding a 10-foot pedestrian path proffer during the hearing alongside 5% units at 80% AMI for 30 years and 100-year stormwater detention. Nearby residents strongly opposed the project citing narrow Ellis Road access, flooding, and a 10-3 Planning Commission denial recommendation. Opponents Nate Baker, Chelsea Cook, and DeDreana Freeman argued the suburban site lacked transit, pedestrian infrastructure, and deep affordability while overriding community and Planning Commission opposition; supporters Williams, Middleton, Caballero, and Rist argued Durham urgently needs homeownership townhome supply near major job corridors and praised the stormwater and path upgrades. The rezoning narrowly passed 4-3 at 03:14:54.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Nov 4, 2024
conflicts.issue: Item 12: Sharon Grove Consolidated Annexation and Utility Extension Agreement (803, 901, 903 Sharon Rd)
conflicts.summary: Drees Homes sought annexation and rezoning of 24.2 acres along Sharon Road for 120 total single-family detached homes (57 additional lots on parcel 803), carrying a 12-1 Planning Commission denial recommendation and zero on-site affordable units. After a council break, the developer raised its proffers to $120,000 for the Affordable Housing Fund, $21,000 for Durham Public Schools, and 100-year stormwater detention. Baker, Cook, and Freeman objected to single-family-only greenfield expansion without walkable urban form or on-site affordability, while Williams, Middleton, Caballero, and Rist argued the site sits inside the Urban Growth Boundary, replaces worse county-jurisdiction outcomes, and delivers housing supply plus cash proffers. The annexation passed 4-3 at 04:09:24 after the clerk corrected an initial 5-2 readout to reflect Baker's No vote.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Nov 4, 2024
conflicts.issue: Item 12: Sharon Grove UDO Zoning Map Amendment (RR/RS-20/RS-10(D) to RS-8(D))
conflicts.summary: Following the 4-3 annexation vote, Council voted on the companion UDO zoning map amendment rezoning 803, 901, and 903 Sharon Road from RR, RS-20, and RS-10(D) to RS-8(D). Council members maintained the exact positions debated during the annexation hearing regarding greenfield infrastructure costs, car-dependent single-family sprawl, and housing supply versus cash affordable-housing contributions. The zoning map amendment passed along the same 4-3 divide at 04:10:19.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Aug 5 2024
conflicts.issue: Item 26 (Motion 1): Adopt Annexation Ordinance for Alcott Tract and Authorize Utility Extension Agreement with M/I Homes of Raleigh, LLC
conflicts.summary: Council voted by show of hands to annex the Alcott Tract into the City of Durham and authorize a utility extension agreement with M/I Homes of Raleigh, LLC; the Clerk reported the motion passed 4-3 with Chelsea Cook, Nate Baker, and DeDreana Freeman voting no.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting May 6, 2024
conflicts.issue: Item 23a (Fox Crossing 2): Approve Utility Extension Agreement with Burnham Fee Acquisition LLC
conflicts.summary: Fox Crossing 2 generated nearly two hours of testimony and debate regarding up to 320 multifamily apartments and 2,000-7,000 sq ft of commercial space near South Miami Boulevard, Lynn Road, and Spring Street. Seven neighborhood residents opposed the project, citing hazardous two-lane traffic on Spring Street, Lick Creek headwater flooding, low tree preservation (7%), and dissatisfaction with Planning Commission's 7-4 denial vote. Proponents on Council pointed out the infill parcel sits inside the Urban Growth Boundary near jobs and transit, while the applicant increased its 5% at 80% AMI affordability commitment from 20 to 30 years and added 100-year stormwater ponds, native landscaping, Energy Star buildings, and crosswalk commitments. Conducted by raised hands due to a voting clicker issue, the Utility Extension Agreement passed 4-3 with Baker, Cook, and Freeman dissenting.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting May 6, 2024
conflicts.issue: Item 23b (Fox Crossing 2 — Final Re-Vote): Adopt UDO Zoning Map Change RU-5 to PDR 12.75 with Added Commitments
conflicts.summary: Following the successful recall motion, Mayor Williams re-read the Item 23b rezoning motion to amend the zoning map from RU-5 to PDR 12.75 with the textual development plan and the five commitments added during the public hearing. Supporters Williams, Middleton, Caballero, and Rist emphasized the need for housing inside the Urban Growth Boundary, improved affordability duration, stormwater upgrades, and commercial space along South Miami Boulevard. Dissenters Baker, Cook, and Freeman maintained that Spring Street lacked safe pedestrian infrastructure, a private-parking connectivity clause undermined street design, and Lick Creek headwaters and residents deserved stronger protection. The re-vote passed 4-3 by raised hands.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 21, 2024
conflicts.issue: EBOP Ordinance 'Aspirational Goals' Language (Item 11)
conflicts.summary: Carl Rist objected to retaining 'aspirational' before 'goals' in the revised Equal Business Opportunity Program ordinance, opposed by Mark-Anthony Middleton and staff.
conflicts.side_a_position: Strike 'aspirational' so municipal contracting equity benchmarks carry stronger normative force.
side_a_arguments: Labeling goals 'aspirational' undermines accountability to local minority- and women-owned businesses.
Legal counsel should verify whether simple 'goals' terminology suffices without softening language.
conflicts.side_b_position: Retain staff's vetted disparity-study phrasing to protect the ordinance legally.
side_b_arguments: Staff and disparity attorneys drafted the phrase carefully to distinguish goals from prohibited quotas.
Changing legal terms without full review risks jeopardizing program durability.
conflicts.resolution: Item 11 stayed on the April 1 Consent docket from the work session, but Rist successfully pulled and amended it 6-1 at the April 1 Council meeting.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting March 18, 2024
conflicts.issue: Ruling Public-Hearing Remarks Out of Order and Chamber Fire-Code Access
conflicts.summary: Mayor Williams ruled DeDreana Freeman out of order during the Pickett Road hearing for thanking budget speakers, and later addressed resident frustration over locked doors tied to chamber capacity limits.
conflicts.side_a_position: Allow Council members broader latitude to acknowledge residents waiting through long hearings and keep chamber access open.
side_a_arguments: Residents who stayed for hours to participate in civic hearings deserve Council acknowledgment and unobstructed building entry.
Strict gavel enforcement on non-substantive thank-yous feels unduly punitive toward colleagues.
conflicts.side_b_position: Enforce germaneness rules during statutory zoning public hearings and uphold fire-marshal occupancy lockouts.
side_b_arguments: Council rules require remarks during an advertised zoning hearing to stay strictly germane to the specific land-use case on the floor.
Fire-code capacity caps legally require limiting entry once chambers reach maximum occupancy.
conflicts.resolution: Procedural ruling stood during the Pickett Road item, and Mayor Williams reiterated fire-code capacity protocols after the Sharon Road vote.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting March 18, 2024
conflicts.issue: Item 22a (Sharon Road Apartments): Approve Annexation Ordinance and Utility Extension Agreement
conflicts.summary: Sharon Road Apartments drew nearly two hours of debate over annexing and extending municipal utilities to a 24.87-acre tract at 4862 Wake Forest Highway for 260 apartments, following a 9-4 Planning Commission endorsement. Eleven East Durham residents opposed the project, pointing to Lick Creek watershed turbidity, rock blasting impacts, and pedestrian hazards along NC 98. Supporters Williams, Middleton, Caballero, and Rist argued the parcel satisfied 23 of 25 Comprehensive Plan policies, sat adjacent to Walgreens with a committed 10-foot shared-use path, provided 6% income-restricted units (5% at 80% AMI plus 1% at 100% AMI added at the meeting) for 30 years, and warned against imposing an unlawful de facto moratorium on East Durham housing. Dissenters Baker, Cook, and Freeman objected to private-driveway connectivity loopholes, Lick Creek erosion, and the absence of an $80,000-$100,000 ADA crosswalk across NC 98 (which staff noted was constrained by Nollan/Dolan nexus rules), resulting in a 4-3 annexation approval.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat 2/16/2024
conflicts.issue: Structure and Cost of Employee Pay Plan Policy Changes (4%-to-5% Step Increase vs. Targeted Equity Tiers)
conflicts.summary: During the budget retreat's closing compensation-study discussion, Council members disagreed over whether to advance ~$4.6 million in pay-plan design changes—particularly increasing general step raises from 4% to 5%—without first reviewing municipal comparables and targeting larger increases toward lower-paid workers.
conflicts.side_a_position: Hold off on or restructure the ~$4.6M policy changes (including the 4%-to-5% step increase) until staff provide municipal comparables, racial equity data, $25/hour minimum modeling, and options favoring lower-wage employees.
side_a_arguments: A flat 5% raise gives far more dollars to someone earning $150/hour than someone earning $19/hour and lacks flexibility to target workers facing the steepest cost-of-living barriers.
The $4.6M in policy design changes (~$3M–$3.3M for the 4%-to-5% shift) lacked comparable data from peer municipalities and could be deferred while focusing first on market adjustments.
conflicts.side_b_position: Give staff immediate direction to include the $28M market and policy-change package in budget models so pay raises stay on schedule while returning with requested data on March 1.
side_b_arguments: Delaying budget-modeling direction risks stalling employee pay relief during the current budget cycle.
The consultant's market study and established budget process already allow Council to adjust specific ranges once final study figures arrive.
conflicts.resolution: Six members gave informal nods of consensus at 07:48:16 to advance staff modeling of the presented $28M package while requesting follow-up wage and equity data for the March 1 retreat.

side_a_arguments: Supported by Council Member Cook and one additional member during pre-session Clerk polling.
conflicts.side_b_position: Support alternative candidates individually, preventing a majority consensus.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Dec. 19 2023
conflicts.issue: City Response to Calls for a Permanent Gaza Ceasefire Resolution
conflicts.summary: Following extensive public comments urging Durham to adopt UE150's permanent ceasefire resolution and redirect funds toward local wages and HEART, Mayor Leonardo Williams declined to adopt an externally authored resolution and noted Council lacked consensus on a single approach, proposing a dedicated four-hour council working session instead.
conflicts.side_a_position: Decline externally authored resolutions and convene a four-hour council session to draft an inclusive, council-authored statement or resolution.
side_a_arguments: Durham's municipal budget has no line item funding foreign wars.
Signing onto an externally authored resolution without council deliberation risks community division and broader repercussions.
Individual council members hold differing views, requiring structured space to reach a holistic response.
conflicts.side_b_position: Public speakers and community advocates demanded immediate introduction and passage of the UE150 ceasefire resolution.
side_b_arguments: Over 19,000 Palestinians have been killed and municipal resolutions apply political pressure on federal officials.
Durham has precedent taking international human rights stances such as opposing South African apartheid.
Taxpayer funds should be prioritized for $25/hour city worker wages and 24/7 HEART funding.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Council members voiced no objection to Mayor Williams's request to schedule a dedicated four-hour working session to craft a council response.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council June 3, 2024
conflicts.issue: FY2024-25 Budget Priorities: Police vs. HEART Funding and City/Solid Waste Worker Compensation (Item 37)
conflicts.summary: During the FY2024-25 budget public hearing, residents, labor advocates, and public employees presented sharply competing visions over tax increases, police vs. Community Safety (HEART) spending, and whether the City's pay plan adequately serves its lowest-paid and Solid Waste workers.
conflicts.side_a_position: Cut or halt police budget growth in favor of HEART/guaranteed income, raise the minimum wage to $25-$27/hr, and reclassify CDL Solid Waste workers.
side_a_arguments: Triangle DSA criticized increasing DPD's budget by $4M (to $82M) while increasing Community Safety/HEART by only $1M (to $7.5M).

Solid Waste workers and labor advocates argued the proposed $19.58/hr minimum falls far short of Durham's cost of living (urging $25-$27/hr) and demanded CDL-holding Solid Waste drivers be reclassified as Maintenance Specialist Seniors or Heavy Equipment Operators.
StepUp Durham and Durham for All urged adding $200,000 so the $1M guaranteed income allocation goes 100% to direct payments.
conflicts.side_b_position: Prioritize sworn Police and Fire compensation/staffing, protect taxpayers from high property tax hikes, or support the City Manager's balanced package.
side_b_arguments: Public safety advocates and city staff (John Wacka, Wilma Oliver) stressed DPD staffing shortages, rising property tax burdens, and the vital daily work of police, firefighters, and code enforcement officers.

Local 668 firefighters thanked Council for substantial raises cutting sub-livable-wage firefighters from over 100 to 31, while safe-streets and eviction-diversion advocates urged passing the proposed CIP, Vision Zero, fare-free transit, and Legal Aid items.
conflicts.resolution: Public hearing only; Council received testimony ahead of final budget deliberations and adoption later in June.

conflicts.issue: Annex Olive Branch Reserve North and Authorize Utility Extension Agreement with MCRT SFR Investments LLC (Item 25, Motion 1)
conflicts.summary: Mill Creek Residential sought annexation, utility extension, and rezoning of 87.7 acres along Olive Branch Road for up to 280 townhouse and duplex rentals, committing to preserve ~45% of the site (including a 300-ft wildlife corridor and 100-ft stream buffers), 24% tree canopy, 100-year storm detention, $23,000 for DPS, and 17 income-restricted units for 30 years. Over a dozen neighbors, Preserve Rural Durham advocates, and Neuse Riverkeeper Samantha Krop testified against the project due to severe sediment pollution in Martin Branch Creek (40x state turbidity standards), blasting impacts on nearby wells, traffic congestion on Olive Branch Road, EMS response delays, and the 10-0 Planning Commission denial. Nate Baker and Chelsea Cook voted No, arguing the car-centric development violated the Comprehensive Plan, added heavy traffic and environmental risk, and offered 100% AMI units outside the plan's 30-80% AMI affordability definition. Middleton, Caballero, Rist, and Williams voted Aye, noting the project was consistent with 22 of 25 comp plan policies, triggered stricter new UDO erosion controls, funded road improvements, and avoided 129 high-priced by-right single-family homes on wells and septic.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-2)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-2)

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session November 20, 2025 (full meeting)
meetings.executive_summary: In the complete recording of the November 20, 2025 City Council Work Session, presiding chair Javiera Caballero convened a four-member quorum (Caballero, Nate Baker, Chelsea Cook, and Carl Rist, with Leonardo Williams, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and DeDreana Freeman excused) and opened with emotional remarks condemning recent federal Border Patrol operations in North Carolina and directing residents to a centralized Durham Public Schools Foundation food and necessity fund. Council appointed members to the Environmental Affairs Board and Citizens Advisory Committee (deferring a tie-adjacent second CAC appointment), reviewed pulled items on the Durham History Museum, Open Table Ministry's White Flag threshold, and DHA's $1.5 million Calvert Place rehabilitation match, and heard the Downtown Durham Blueprint presentation before voting 4-0 to settle the December 1 agenda.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Excused Absences, and Council Remarks on Immigration Enforcement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Presiding chair Javiera Caballero called the meeting to order with a four-member quorum (Baker, Caballero, Cook, Rist) while Leonardo Williams, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and DeDreana Freeman were absent on prior excused absences. Caballero and colleagues delivered opening statements condemning recent federal Border Patrol raids across North Carolina and Durham, thanking neighborhood volunteers, and encouraging donations to the centralized Durham Public Schools Foundation relief fund.

agenda_items.title: Boards, Committees, and Commissions Appointment Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk reported board ballot outcomes appointing Lena G. Tonkan to the Environmental Affairs Board (Youth seat) and Michael A. Jones to the Citizens Advisory Committee. A second Citizens Advisory Committee seat fell short of a four-vote majority—receiving three votes for Bonita D. Green and two for David McCull—and was deferred to a future meeting.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Reading and Public Comment (Citizens Matters)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council pulled Items 4, 5, and 7 from the consent agenda for discussion and deferred public comments on December 1 public hearing Item 12 (East Geer Towns) until the formal hearing. Under Citizens Matters, speakers Jeremy Burger and Chris Perilstein commended Council Member DeDreana Freeman's tenure, Michael Harris urged pedestrian safety improvements on West Lakewood Avenue, Dr. Haley Cunningham pressed on HOPWA administration, and Thomas Hennessy commented on local transit and governance.

agenda_items.title: Durham History Museum at 500 W. Main Street
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Members raised questions regarding city property plans and lease arrangements for the Durham History Museum at 500 W. Main Street. Given outstanding details and the absence of three colleagues, Council reached consensus to refer Item 4 back to staff for further work.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Referred back to staff via Settle Agenda vote

agenda_items.title: Open Table Ministry Contract Amendment (White Flag Inclement Weather Threshold)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council examined the Open Table Ministry contract amendment funding winter emergency shelter capacity and discussed Durham's 32°F White Flag trigger versus warmer thresholds used in peer jurisdictions. Members kept the amendment on the December 1 consent agenda while requesting continued operational review of shelter thresholds.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Advanced to Dec 1 Consent via Settle Agenda vote

agenda_items.title: DHA Subrecipient Agreement ($1.5M Match) for Calvert Place and Main Street Townhomes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Housing staff presented the $1.5 million subrecipient agreement providing local match funds for Durham Housing Authority's Choice Neighborhoods Initiative (CNI) rehabilitation of Calvert Place and Main Street Townhomes. Council members confirmed rehabilitation scope and affordability commitments and left Item 7 on consent.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Advanced to Dec 1 Consent via Settle Agenda vote

agenda_items.title: Downtown Durham Blueprint Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Nicole Thompson of Downtown Durham Inc. and Interface Studio planners walked Council through the Downtown Durham Blueprint vision for residential growth, activated ground-floor retail, transit connections, and accessible public spaces. Council members discussed implementation coordination and noted the Blueprint would return for adoption on December 15–16 (Monday Council meeting / Tuesday Work Session).

agenda_items.title: Settle the Agenda for December 1, 2025 City Council Meeting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted 4-0 by voice vote to settle the December 1, 2025 agenda—placing Items 1, 3, and 5–10 on Consent, Item 2 on General Business Agenda, Item 12 on GBA Public Hearings, and referring Item 4 back to staff—and confirmed the December 15–16 meeting dates before adjourning at 3:09 p.m.

meetings.title: Durham City Council November 17, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams opened the November 17, 2025 City Council meeting by reading a joint statement with the county and school board chairs condemning federal Border Patrol operations in North Carolina and introducing special assistant Emmanuel Ago, before receiving an excused absence at 00:09:17 to travel to Washington, D.C. Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton presided over the remainder of the session, during which Council unanimously (6-0) approved the consent agenda, a $17,049,195 affordable housing loan for Villages at Hayti Phase 1, and the Durham Parks and Recreation FY2025 Annual Report. Following an emotional public hearing and a sharp council split over neighborhood notice and public right-of-way preservation, General Business Agenda Item 16 (Street Closing SC25003 for Hayti Lane) failed to pass and was discharged without taking the companion place-type map vote.

agenda_items.title: Joint Statement on Immigration Enforcement, Staff Introduction, and Mayor's Excused Absence
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams read a joint statement issued with the Durham County Board of Commissioners Chair and Durham Public Schools Board Chair denouncing Border Patrol enforcement actions and affirming Durham as a welcoming community. He then introduced his new special assistant Emmanuel Ago before requesting an excused absence at 00:09:13 to fly to Washington, D.C. for Morning Joe and New Deal Leaders appearances, handing the gavel to Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton.

agenda_items.title: Excused Absences for DeDreana Freeman and Mark-Anthony Middleton (Nov 20 Work Session)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted 6-0 (Leonardo Williams absent) on a motion by Chelsea Cook to grant excused absences to DeDreana Freeman and Mark-Anthony Middleton for the upcoming November 20, 2025 City Council Work Session.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Adoption (Items 1, 2, 4–7, 11–13)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council pulled Items 8 and 10 for separate discussion and unanimously adopted the remaining consent agenda items (Items 1, 2, 4–7, and 11–13) by a 6-0 vote.

agenda_items.title: Villages at Hayti Phase 1 Loan Agreement ($17,049,195)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council considered a pulled loan agreement of up to $17,049,195 with Durham Housing Authority / DVI affiliates to finance the 252-unit all-affordable Villages at Hayti Phase 1 redevelopment. Following clarification of project financing and unit affordability tiers, Council approved the loan agreement unanimously (6-0).

agenda_items.title: Durham Parks and Recreation (DPR) FY2025 Annual Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Victoria Peterson pulled Item 10 to raise concerns regarding ADA-accessible playground conditions at W.D. Hill and Campus Hills parks. DPR Director Wade Walcott responded on park accessibility upgrades and maintenance schedules, after which Council unanimously (6-0) accepted the FY2025 Annual Report.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Street Closing SC25003 (Hayti Lane, 229 Linear Feet East of Old Fayetteville Street)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Applicant Rob Emerson and property manager Todd Parker sought permanent closure of 229 linear feet of Hayti Lane, drawing strong opposition from nearby residents and community advocates—including Anita Scott Neville, Angel Dozier, Chris Perilstein, tenant Chris Mulvy Jr., Christian Edwards, and CJ Brick—who cited inadequate tenant notice, loss of historic street right-of-way, and absence of community benefits. Chelsea Cook, Nate Baker, and DeDreana Freeman opposed closing the public lane while Javiera Caballero and Mark-Anthony Middleton leaned supportive (and Carl Rist disclosed a conflict); after the applicant declined a continuance to February 2, the street-closing motion failed and Item 16 was discharged at 02:29:36.

agenda_items.title: Excused Absence for Leonardo Williams (Nov 20 Work Session)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Before adjourning at 9:30 p.m., Council approved an excused absence 6-0 for Mayor Leonardo Williams for the November 20, 2025 Work Session, noting that Javiera Caballero would preside with a four-member quorum.

votes.item_title: Excused Absence for Mayor Leonardo Williams (Remainder of November 17, 2025 Meeting)

Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton entertained a motion for an excused absence and directed the clerk to open the electronic vote at 00:09:21. votes.item_title: Item 16: Street Closing SC25003 — Permanently Close 229 Linear Feet of Hayti Lane East of Old Fayetteville Street
votes.notes: ASR omits the clerk's roll-call tally announcement between 02:29:23 and 02:29:36, immediately cutting to Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton stating 'All right. Well, then item number 16 is discharged' without taking the required companion Comprehensive Plan place-type map amendment vote; Carl Rist had disclosed a conflict during debate and Leonardo Williams was absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Item 16 involved a public hearing lasting nearly 90 minutes (01:00:30–02:28:58) on applicant Rob Emerson and property manager Todd Parker's petition to permanently close 229 linear feet of Hayti Lane east of Old Fayetteville Street. Neighborhood residents and housing advocates—including Anita Scott Neville, Angel Dozier, Chris Perilstein, tenant Chris Mulvy Jr., Christian Edwards, and CJ Brick—opposed the closure, citing lack of tenant notice, loss of historic public right-of-way and connectivity, and absence of community benefits. Council divided along sharp lines: Chelsea Cook, Nate Baker, and DeDreana Freeman opposed surrendering the historic public street without resident engagement or community return, whereas Javiera Caballero and Mark-Anthony Middleton expressed openness and floated a continuance to February 2, 2026 (while Carl Rist disclosed a conflict). After applicant Rob Emerson declined a continuance at 02:28:52 ('They want the vote'), the street-closing motion was opened at 02:29:23; although the automated transcript dropped the clerk's vote readout, presiding chair Middleton announced at 02:29:36 that Item 16 was discharged without advancing the companion map amendment, confirming the motion failed.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council November 17, 2025
disagreements.issue: Permanent Street Closure of Hayti Lane (SC25003) and Neighborhood Notice / Public Right-of-Way Preservation
disagreements.summary: Council divided over applicant Rob Emerson's request to permanently close 229 linear feet of Hayti Lane near Fayetteville Street amid fierce resident and tenant opposition.
disagreements.side_a_position: Reject permanent closure of Hayti Lane due to inadequate tenant outreach, loss of historic Hayti public right-of-way, and zero public benefit.
side_a_arguments: Tenants and neighboring Hayti residents reported little to no direct outreach despite repeated requests and legal notice concerns.

Permanently vacating a public right-of-way—a historic alley/street in Hayti—transfers public land to a private developer without enforceable public benefits, pedestrian access, or affordability guarantees.
disagreements.side_b_position: Either approve the street closure as an alley reconfiguration or grant a continuance to February 2, 2026 to allow additional resident engagement.
side_b_arguments: The 229-foot segment operates as an unimproved stub adjacent to applicant-controlled parcels and could facilitate redevelopment.
Continuing the item to February 2 would allow the applicant to conduct neighborhood meetings rather than forcing an immediate denial.
disagreements.resolution: Applicant declined the continuance option ('They want the vote') at 02:28:52; the closure motion failed on the floor and Item 16 was discharged at 02:29:36 (with Carl Rist recused/conflicted and Leonardo Williams absent).

development_cases.project_name: Villages at Hayti – Phase I Redevelopment Loan Agreement (formerly Fayette Place)

development_cases.development_type: Multifamily Apartments (Publicly Financed Affordable Housing Redevelopment)
development_cases.scale: Phase 1: 252 affordable apartment units (part of multi-phase redevelopment adding ~70 senior Phase 2 units, 100+ Phase 3 units, and ~40 homeownership townhomes)

proffers.affordable_housing: City loan up to $17,049,195 supporting 252 income-restricted Phase 1 rental apartments via DHA/DVI redevelopment of Fayette Place

member_justifications.stance_summary: Pulled Item 8 from consent to clarify unit counts across Phases 1–3 with DHA Interim CEO Anthony Snell (252 Phase 1 units, ~70 senior Phase 2 units, 100+ Phase 3 units, and ~40 townhomes) and check on Forest Hill Heights' 6–8 month NCDEQ radon-mitigation approval delay before voting AYE.
member_justifications.key_quote: I just wanted to touch base and kind of circle around some of the things that were floating around Phase One, Phase Two, and Phase Three, and then also touching base on how Forest Hills is connected or not connected to this project.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Asked DHA Interim CEO Anthony Snell where residents can track online updates on Phases 2 and 3 before voting AYE on the Phase 1 redevelopment loan.
member_justifications.key_quote: Is there a place where folks can access the information about phases two and three?

development_cases.location: 229 linear feet of Hayti Lane east of Old Fayetteville Street (serving 20 Hayti Lane / 19 townhomes in Hayti)
development_cases.scale: 229 linear feet (~1/3 acre right-of-way) proposed for recombination with 20 Hayti Lane (REID 119218) totaling ~1.249 acres in Transit Opportunity Area
development_cases.zoning_change: Request to permanently close entirety of Hayti Lane ROW and designate established place type as Transit Opportunity Area (motion to close defeated; Place Type motion mooted)

member_justifications.stance_summary: Questioned statutory mailed-notice choices when the applicant owned all adjacent parcels; at [01:38:42] sharply criticized the applicant's team for calling the Hayti area non-historic, failing to engage community institutions like the Hayti Heritage Center, and dismissing public residents' testimony as 'not substantive.'
member_justifications.key_quote: Folks are within their right to get up here and talk about however they relate to this land and it doesn't have to be technical and it doesn't have to be couched in statute.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Contrasted Hayti Lane sharply with Cliff Street—where council negotiated two greenway easements in a win-win trade—arguing privatizing public right-of-way with no project plan or public benefit was 'imbalanced' and set an unhealthy precedent. Reiterated at [02:16:42] that vacating public land without any redevelopment plan was 'putting the cart before the horse' and risked easing displacement of existing tenants.
member_justifications.key_quote: I don't see a persuasive argument being made that this is both beneficial to the public, to the neighborhood, to the city, to the public good and to the applicant. It seems imbalanced.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Initially leaned yes because the landlord had renovated roofs, siding, and HVAC since 2022 rather than letting the townhomes go derelict and noted no adjacent greenway existed on the cul-de-sac. Later at [02:19:23] suggested continuing the hearing so the property owner could meet directly with neighbors and the Hayti Heritage Center, before council held the vote when the applicant declined to offer a plan.
member_justifications.key_quote: Right now I'm leaning yes, but I'm open to hearing from others; most of these street closures are pretty straightforward from just a land use perspective, but I understand why there's a lot of sensitivity.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Opposed giving away public land in historic Hayti without a defined public benefit, criticized 'cultural appropriation' in the LLC name 'Hayti Properties,' and faulted the absent owner for sending a property manager. Later at [02:05:54] highlighted DOST/park review disparities in Hayti and at [02:26:27] opposed a continuance because the applicant admitted having no project to negotiate.
member_justifications.key_quote: We've got to make sure that we're clear that we're not auctioning off pieces without community benefit for the public good. ... I'm definitely not persuaded to close the street.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Pressed the applicant and City Manager Boozer-Strother on the UDO 'public interest' standard, eliciting confirmation that the city's ongoing street-maintenance cost for the short cul-de-sac was 'negligible' and saying he remained conflicted between current use and Transit Opportunity Area goals. Later at [02:10:26] suggested having BPAC review future street closure requests.
member_justifications.key_quote: This is public land... what is the public interest in closing this right of way? ... So yeah, I'm still wrestling with this one.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Contended that routine cul-de-sac closures normally pass as straightforward checkmarks and became contentious solely because of Hayti's sensitive urban-renewal history, urging council to apply uniform standards across neighborhoods. Declined to telegraph votes on a continuance and held the binding vote at [02:29:03], discharging the failed item without voting on the second Place Type motion.
member_justifications.key_quote: I don't want to pretend that this is some type of exotic case in terms of the particularities of it. We've done a bunch of these over the years and they're pretty straightforward; it is not straightforward because it's in Hayti.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session November 6, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: Following a nearly hour-long power outage at the start of the session, the broadcast of the November 6, 2025 City Council Work Session resumed mid-Citizens Matters with a sharp exchange involving DHA CEO Anthony Snell and residents over Fayette Place / Villages at Hayti financing, minority contracting, and Hayti Lane. Council spent nearly two hours reviewing the Durham Athletic Park (DAP) Feasibility Study with Perkins+Will and seven public speakers, ultimately converging on Option 1 to preserve historic baseball/softball use alongside flexible community activation. Members also reviewed the DPR FY2025 Annual Report, heard a Source Water Resiliency & Response Plan update, received a draft C-PACE resolution from Mayor Leonardo Williams, and voted unanimously by voice vote to settle the November 17 Council agenda (with Javiera Caballero having departed early at 02:19:05).

agenda_items.title: Fayette Place / Villages at Hayti Financing Q&A and Hayti Lane Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resuming mid-session after an opening power outage, residents and advocates—including Terrence and Shekika Priester, Anita Scott Neville, and Chris Perilstein—questioned Fayette Place / Villages at Hayti ownership, minority contractor participation, and the pending Hayti Lane closure. DHA CEO Anthony Snell detailed the capital stack, Harmony Housing Global/managing-member ownership structure, and the 252-unit AMI breakdown across 30% to 80% AMI.

agenda_items.title: Boards, Committees, and Commissions Appointments Report

agenda_items.title: Durham Athletic Park (DAP) Feasibility Study Presentation (Perkins+Will)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Consultants from Perkins+Will (Zena Howard), General Services staff (Stacy Poston), and the Durham Sports Commission (Marcus Manning) presented three redevelopment concepts for the historic Durham Athletic Park, drawing seven public speakers. Council debated Options 1, 2, and 3—weighing preservation of the historic baseball field, neighborhood open access versus Sports Commission tournament programming, Corporation Street activation, and financing—before giving consensus direction around Option 1.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Consensus direction for Option 1 / No formal vote

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Consultant Sid Miller and Water Management leadership updated Council on Durham's long-term source-water resiliency and utility interconnections. disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session November 6, 2025
disagreements.issue: Durham Athletic Park (DAP) Redevelopment Vision: Option 1 Preservation vs. Expanded Multi-Use Activation and Sports Commission Role
disagreements.summary: Council members and seven public speakers debated how to balance preserving DAP's historic baseball/softball diamond against multi-sport tournament partnerships, year-round community access, and adjacent street closures.
disagreements.side_a_position: Prioritize Option 1 preserving the historic baseball/softball field, free neighborhood open access, and community event flexibility over commercialization.
side_a_arguments: Historic Bull Durham / DAP baseball heritage and broad, no-barrier public neighborhood access must remain central.
Heavy emphasis on Sports Commission tournament bookings risks pricing out or locking out surrounding residents.
disagreements.side_b_position: Push stronger year-round activation, flexible event space, adjacent Corporation Street pedestrianization, and creative public-private financing alongside sports preservation.
side_b_arguments: Without high-frequency event activation and surrounding street connections, DAP risks remaining underutilized outside baseball dates.
Creative partnerships and revenue models can help finance capital upgrades without straining general funds.
disagreements.resolution: Council gave staff and Perkins+Will consensus direction to advance Option 1 (preserving the diamond while incorporating flexible community events and activation study).

meetings.title: Durham City Council November 3, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: The November 3, 2025 City Council meeting opened with proclamations honoring Durham's HEART Crisis Response Team and David Richmond Gergen Day, and an excused absence granted 6-0-1 for Chelsea Cook for the November 6 Work Session. Council adopted the Consent Agenda 7-0 before engaging in two lengthy debates on pulled items: Item 12 (the $3.42 million ST337 Unpaved Roads Phase 1 bond contract with Sunrock Industries) and Item 15 (a $44 million conduit multifamily revenue note for Fayette Place Phase 1 / Villages at Hayti). On Item 12, Nate Baker introduced and then withdrew a resident opt-out amendment for Wallace Street as Council split 6-1 (DeDreana Freeman dissenting) to award the paving contract while securing a Vision Zero review pledge, and unanimously approved the companion contingency, contract modification authority, and Item 15 revenue note.

agenda_items.title: HEART Recognition Day and David Richmond Gergen Day
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams, joined by Council Members Mark-Anthony Middleton and Javiera Caballero and Community Safety Director Ryan Smith, proclaimed HEART Recognition Day honoring Durham's unarmed crisis response program launched in 2021. Carl Rist then read a proclamation honoring journalist and Durham native David Richmond Gergen.

agenda_items.title: Excused Absence for Chelsea Cook (November 6, 2025 Work Session)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After DeDreana Freeman arrived at the dais, she moved to grant Chelsea Cook an excused absence for the November 6, 2025 City Council Work Session. Council approved the motion 6-0-1 with Cook abstaining.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Adoption (Items 1–11, 13–14, 16–22)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council pulled Items 12 and 15 for separate discussion and public comment, then adopted all remaining Consent Agenda items (Items 1–11, 13–14, and 16–22) on a unanimous 7-0 roll call vote.

agenda_items.title: ST337 Unpaved Roads Phase 1 Contract ($3,421,687.10 with Sunrock Industries LLC), Contingency, and Modification Authority
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Wallace Street resident Orlando Watson urged allowing neighbors to opt out of street paving, prompting a prolonged policy debate over neighborhood consent, traffic calming, and honoring the 70% 2024 GO Bond mandate. Nate Baker moved and Chelsea Cook seconded a 1-week unanimous-opt-out amendment for Wallace Street before withdrawing it on City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg's advice regarding scope; Council then approved the $3,421,687.10 contract 6-1 (DeDreana Freeman voting No) with a Vision Zero safety review commitment from City Manager Bo Ferguson, and approved the $171,084.36 contingency and modification authority 7-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Contract approved 6-1 (Freeman No); Contingency & Modification approved 7-0

agenda_items.title: Up to $44,000,000 Multifamily Housing Revenue Note Resolution for Fayette Place Phase 1 (Villages at Hayti)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Anita Scott Neville pulled Item 15 to question why UBE/workforce diversity goals appeared marked 'not applicable' and why the updated 'Villages at Hayti' name was not yet reflected on the public hearing notice. Housing staff Matthew Walker and DHA CEO Anthony Snell clarified the legal notice linkage to the TEFRA hearing and distinguished the tax-exempt conduit bond from direct city loans (noting an African-American general contractor is part of the project lead), after which Council approved the $44 million resolution 7-0.

votes.item_title: Excused Absence for Council Member Chelsea Cook (November 6, 2025 Work Session)
votes.notes: Chelsea Cook abstained on her own excused-absence request.
votes.discussion_detail: Upon DeDreana Freeman's arrival at the council dais around 00:29:12, she offered a motion to grant Chelsea Cook an excused absence for the upcoming Thursday, November 6, 2025 City Council Work Session. A colleague seconded the motion and Mayor Leonardo Williams directed the clerk to open the electronic vote. At 00:29:54, the clerk announced that the motion passed 6-0 with one abstention by Chelsea Cook.

votes.item_title: Consent Agenda Adoption (Items 1–11, 13–14, 16–22)
votes.notes: Items 12 and 15 pulled for discussion and separate votes.
votes.discussion_detail: After the reading of the Consent Agenda items, residents and council members pulled Item 12 (ST337 Unpaved Roads Phase 1 contract) and Item 15 ($44 million Fayette Place Phase 1 multifamily housing revenue note) for public discussion. Mayor Leonardo Williams entertained a motion to approve all remaining Consent Agenda items (Items 1–11, 13–14, and 16–22), which was moved and seconded at 00:58:44. All seven council members voted in favor, passing the Consent Agenda unanimously 7-0 at 00:58:55.

votes.item_title: Item 12 (Motion 1): Authorize Contract ST337 Unpaved Roads Phase 1 ($3,421,687.10) with Sunrock Industries LLC
votes.notes: City Manager Bo Ferguson committed to an explicit Vision Zero traffic-calming review for Wallace Street prior to construction.
votes.discussion_detail: Wallace Street resident Orlando Watson pulled Item 12 to request removing his street from the ST337 Unpaved Roads Phase 1 paving contract, citing pedestrian safety, speeding fears, and neighborhood reluctance. Council split sharply: Nate Baker moved (with Chelsea Cook seconding at 01:38:06) an amendment giving Wallace Street owners one week to file a unanimous opt-out, supported by DeDreana Freeman's concern for resident consent, while Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, Carl Rist, and Mayor Leonardo Williams argued against ad-hoc opt-outs given citywide infrastructure equity, emergency-vehicle access, and the 70% voter approval of the 2024 Streets and Sidewalks GO Bond. After City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg noted the amendment lay outside the contract motion's text, Baker withdrew his amendment at 01:43:27 in exchange for City Manager Bo Ferguson's pledge to conduct a Vision Zero safety review. The main contract motion ($3,421,687.10 to Sunrock Industries LLC) passed 6-1 at 01:46:01, with DeDreana Freeman casting the lone dissenting vote.

votes.item_title: Item 12 (Motion 2): Establish Contingency Fund ($171,084.36) for ST337 Unpaved Roads Phase 1
votes.notes: Standard 5% contingency fund accompanying the ST337 Unpaved Roads Phase 1 contract.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately after approving the base $3,421,687.10 construction contract with Sunrock Industries LLC, Mayor Leonardo Williams introduced the second companion motion for Item 12 to establish a $171,084.36 contingency fund for the ST337 Unpaved Roads Phase 1 project. With policy arguments already resolved on the main contract motion and City Manager Bo Ferguson's Vision Zero commitment on record, DeDreana Freeman joined the rest of the council on the procedural budget authorization. The motion was moved, seconded, and passed unanimously 7-0 at 01:46:24.

votes.item_title: Item 12 (Motion 3): Authorize City Manager to Execute Limited ST337 Contract Modifications
votes.notes: ASR rendered the combined contract-plus-contingency cap figure at 01:46:48 as '$3,592,0007' ($3,592,771.46 mathematical sum of base + contingency, though not altering printed transcript text).
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Leonardo Williams then read the third required motion for Item 12 authorizing the City Manager to negotiate and execute contract modifications within the combined contract and contingency budget (transcribed in ASR at 01:46:48 as '3,592,0007', corresponding to the base contract plus $171,084.36 contingency). Council members offered no additional remarks following the preceding policy exchange and Vision Zero commitment. The motion was moved, seconded, and passed unanimously 7-0 at 01:47:00.

votes.item_title: Item 15: Adopt Resolution Approving Up to $44,000,000 Multifamily Housing Revenue Note for Fayette Place Phase 1 (Villages at Hayti)
votes.notes: Tax-exempt conduit revenue bond resolution (no city funds/debt obligation); staff confirmed name update to Villages at Hayti Phase 1 on subsequent loan documentation.
votes.discussion_detail: Resident Anita Scott Neville pulled Item 15 to question why UBE and minority contracting metrics were listed as 'not applicable' on the resolution cover sheet and why the project still appeared under the name 'Fayette Place' instead of 'Villages at Hayti.' Housing staff Matthew Walker and DHA CEO Anthony Snell clarified that the resolution was a federally required TEFRA tax-exempt conduit bond approval rather than direct city expenditure—preserving continuity with the Housing Authority's public hearing notice while updating the name on the November 6 work-session city loan item—and Mayor Williams noted an African-American general contractor was serving among the project leads. Following those clarifications, a motion to adopt the up-to-$44,000,000 multifamily housing revenue note resolution was moved, seconded, and approved unanimously 7-0 at 02:03:30.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council November 3, 2025
disagreements.issue: Resident Opt-Out Policy on 2024 GO Bond Unpaved Road Paving (ST337 / Wallace Street)
disagreements.summary: Council debated whether residents on unpaved streets—specifically Wallace Street—should be permitted to opt out of Phase 1 GO Bond paving due to traffic-speeding and neighborhood-character concerns.
disagreements.side_a_position: Allow street-level resident opt-out (e.g., 1-week unanimous property-owner petition) or delay paving pending resident consent and Vision Zero traffic calming.
side_a_arguments: Forcing paving against neighborhood wishes undermines community self-determination and can increase speeding on narrow residential streets.
An opt-out would allow city bond funds to be redirected to other unpaved streets whose residents actively want paving.
disagreements.side_b_position: Execute the bond-funded paving program uniformly without street-by-street opt-outs while addressing speeding through Vision Zero engineering.
side_b_arguments: 70% of Durham voters approved the 2024 Streets and Sidewalks GO Bond to eliminate legacy dirt roads across the city.
Allowing individual street opt-outs creates patchwork maintenance burdens, emergency-vehicle access issues, and future displacement of paving costs onto later residents.
disagreements.resolution: Nate Baker withdrew his opt-out amendment at 01:43:27 on legal advice regarding motion scope after City Manager Bo Ferguson committed to a Vision Zero review for Wallace Street; the ST337 contract then passed 6-1 with DeDreana Freeman voting No.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session October 23, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton opened the October 23, 2025 City Council Work Session (with Carl Rist excused for his son's wedding) before Mayor Leonardo Williams arrived at 00:13:08 and presided over pulled items, presentations, and the afternoon strategic-planning session. The morning session centered on sharp council and public pushback over Priority Item 25—a proposed Paragrin Technologies operations management platform for Durham Police's Real Time Crime Center—which City Manager Bo Ferguson agreed to refer back to staff after council members demanded public town halls and written privacy/AI/immigration-data assurances. Council also received a progress update on the 2024 GO Bond streets and parks projects, accepted board appointments to the Planning Commission and Human Relations Commission, voted 6-0 to settle the November 3 Council agenda, and spent nearly two hours debating FY27–29 Strategic Plan goal framing and policy priorities.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Priority Adjustments, Consent Reading, and Citizens Matters
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton opened the session with Carl Rist excused and Mayor Leonardo Williams arriving at 00:13:08. City Manager Bo Ferguson added Priority Item 25 (Paragrin Technologies) and reordered presentations so Item 24 (2024 GO Bond Update) preceded Item 23 (Strategic Plan), while Council pulled Items 5, 12, 13, 15–18, 20, and 25 and heard Citizens Matters speaker Dr. Haley Cunningham on HOPWA deadlines.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / Pulled items routed to discussion

agenda_items.title: Pulled Public Works, Stormwater, Fayette Place Naming, Rail Trail, Clarity Permitting, Signal Timing, and Lift Station Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council heard public speaker Brad Johnson on Item 12 (Brutin Road unpaved-road safety), reviewed Dragonfly stormwater maintenance (Item 13), clarified the Fayette Place to Villages at Hayti naming transition (Item 15), heard Chris Perilstein on the Durham-to-Roxboro Trail (Item 16), reviewed Clarity replacing the LDO permitting software (Item 17), examined Kimley-Horn signal-timing optimization (Item 18), and discussed the Glen Road sewer lift station (Item 20).
agenda_items.vote_summary: Advanced to Nov 3 Consent via Settle Agenda vote

agenda_items.title: Paragrin Technologies Operations Management Platform / Real Time Crime Center Software
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Speakers Raina Reno and Owen Webster strongly opposed Item 25 over fears of mass surveillance, Palantir ties, and ICE data exposure. Police Chief Patrice Andrews, City Manager Bo Ferguson, and Paragrin representative Philip Casanova stated the software only indexes existing internal DPD CAD/RMS records without Palantir or ICE data-sharing, but Javiera Caballero, Chelsea Cook, DeDreana Freeman, Nate Baker, and Leonardo Williams pressed for community town halls, written answers, and AI/immigration policy review, leading the Manager to refer Item 25 back to staff.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Referred back to staff (removed from Nov 3 agenda)

agenda_items.title: 2024 General Obligation (GO) Bond Referendum Progress Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff—including Tasha Johnson on $115 million in streets, sidewalks, and unpaved-road investments, DPR Director Wade Walcott on $85 million in park upgrades (Merrick-Moore, Long Meadow, East End, and lead-in-soil park remediation), and Christina Rearden on stoplight reporting—briefed Council on bond milestones, schedules, and equity targeting.

agenda_items.title: Boards/Committees Report and Settle the Agenda for November 3, 2025
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk announced the appointment of America E. Juarez Maldonado to the Planning Commission and Kristen Barrett to the Human Relations Commission after Mark-Anthony Middleton switched his vote to form a majority. Council then voted 6-0 by voice vote to settle the November 3 regular meeting agenda (Items 1–22 on Consent; Item 25 referred back to staff).

agenda_items.title: FY27–29 Strategic Plan Refresh Afternoon Work Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Facilitated by Sherri Metcalf, Warren Miller, and Fountain Works consultant Danielle Bodaki, Council debated four equity/engagement lenses, restructuring draft goal buckets (including whether Affordable Housing stands alone or integrates with infrastructure/transportation), and specific priorities such as gun-violence reduction versus youth engagement, food/childcare deserts, worker cooperatives, rent stabilization, and 30% AMI targeting. Council wrapped up at 5:09 p.m. after flagging future work-session items on the Housing Task Force and Durham Museum of History.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 23, 2025
disagreements.issue: Paragrin Technologies Software Contract (Item 25) for DPD Operations / Real Time Crime Center
disagreements.summary: Public speakers and council members pushed back against fast-tracking a priority contract with Paragrin Technologies, demanding public education and written privacy, AI, and ICE data-sharing guardrails before any vote.
disagreements.side_a_position: Hold the contract for community town halls, written answers on data access/AI/immigration risk, and full transparency before council action.
side_a_arguments: Surveillance and data-integration tools require transparent public dialogue rather than a single priority work-session cycle.
Residents need ironclad, written guarantees prohibiting third-party data harvesting, Palantir/ICE leakage, and unchecked AI analytics.
disagreements.side_b_position: Advance the software tool as an internal search upgrade over existing DPD CAD/RMS data without new surveillance hardware.
side_b_arguments: Police Chief Patrice Andrews, City Manager Bo Ferguson, and Paragrin explained the platform only queries data DPD already possesses, with zero Palantir affiliation or ICE sharing.
Improving internal search speeds officer investigations without expanding external camera or sensor networks.
disagreements.resolution: City Manager Bo Ferguson agreed to refer Item 25 back to staff rather than place it on the November 3 agenda so DPD could host public outreach and provide written responses.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 23, 2025
disagreements.issue: FY27–29 Strategic Plan Goal Structure and Municipal Policy Scope (Housing, Rent Stabilization, Food & Childcare Deserts)
disagreements.summary: During the afternoon Strategic Plan Refresh workshop, council members differed over how to group goal buckets and how far municipal strategy should stretch into county-led social domains and market interventions.
disagreements.side_a_position: Pair housing tightly with built infrastructure/transit or test ambitious anti-displacement tools while addressing food, childcare, and co-op gaps.
side_a_arguments: Linking housing directly with transportation and infrastructure reflects how land use and mobility shape affordability (Williams, Baker), while DeDreana Freeman and Chelsea Cook stressed keeping Affordable Housing front-and-center.
Food deserts, childcare access, worker-owned cooperatives, and tenant/displacement protections directly affect equitable economic mobility.
disagreements.side_b_position: Keep municipal strategic goals focused within core city jurisdiction and practical statutory authority.
side_b_arguments: Childcare and food policy fall primarily outside core municipal utility/land-use lanes compared to county health and school systems (Javiera Caballero).
Broad rent stabilization pledges or unrealistic statutory promises risk overcommitting beyond North Carolina Dillon's Rule authority (Mark-Anthony Middleton).
disagreements.resolution: Facilitators from Fountain Works and Budget & Management Services recorded council feedback across all goal buckets to refine the draft FY27–29 Strategic Plan.

meetings.title: Durham City Council October 20, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: In a marathon nearly six-hour session running past midnight until 12:43 a.m. with all seven members present throughout, the Durham City Council took 14 formal roll-call votes across major housing, tenant-protection, and land-use items. Council unanimously approved the Consent Agenda (7-0), the $1.75 million Quorum Houses LLC Affordable ADU Loan Pilot (7-0), and the closely watched Tenant Protection Ordinance adding City Code §10-241(f) (7-0) after Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton withdrew a proposed preemption caveat in response to opposition from Chelsea Cook, DeDreana Freeman, and Nate Baker. Council also unanimously approved the Cliff Street partial street closing (Item 22), Ravenstone Commercial rezoning (Item 23), and 1607 East Cornwallis Road rezoning (Item 25), before passing the controversial 12.16-acre Wake Olive annexation and PDR rezoning (Item 24) on a 5-2 split vote with Nate Baker and DeDreana Freeman dissenting.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations: Breast Cancer Awareness Month and NCCU Men's Tennis HBCU National Champions Month
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Javiera Caballero read a proclamation recognizing October as Breast Cancer Awareness Month alongside American Cancer Society representative Richard Avaret. Carl Rist then read a proclamation celebrating North Carolina Central University's Men's Tennis team on winning its second HBCU national championship.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Adoption (Items 1–5, 7, 9–13, 15, 17–19)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mark-Anthony Middleton read the Consent Agenda and Item 16 (ADU Loan Pilot) was pulled for discussion. Council adopted the remaining consent items unanimously 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Quorum Houses LLC Contract ($1,750,000) for Affordable ADU Loan Pilot
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated the $1.75 million ADU Loan Pilot targeting 20 backyard units at 80% AMI via 30-year 2% loans. Nate Baker questioned the 80% AMI threshold and single-bidder RFP and opposed future loan forgiveness, while Chelsea Cook questioned compliance monitoring, 60-day lease-up, Airbnb bans, and SCAD origins; Carl Rist, Javiera Caballero, and Leonardo Williams backed the pilot to close a financing gap banks refuse to serve, approving it 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Tenant Protection Ordinance Amendment Adding City Code §10-241(f) (Prohibiting Rent Collection Under Imminently Dangerous Conditions)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: More than two hours of public comment pitted Riverside High School Affordable Housing Club students, NC Tenants Union, Legal Aid/Justice Center attorneys, Durham CAN, and tenants—urging adoption—against landlord and realtor representatives and DHA CEO Anthony Snell warning of legal/operational impacts. Senior Deputy City Attorney Fred Lamar reiterated state preemption concerns; after Chelsea Cook, DeDreana Freeman, and Nate Baker rejected Mark-Anthony Middleton and Carl Rist's proposed preemption caveat and code-list changes, Middleton withdrew the caveat and Council unanimously adopted the unamended ordinance 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Cliff Street Partial Street Closing SC25001 (402 Linear Feet) and Place-Type Amendment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Presiding over Item 22, Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton heard applicant representatives Hamilton and Jackson present the 402-linear-foot Cliff Street closure accompanied by two newly proffered Rockwood Trail greenway easements, drawing support from bike/pedestrian advocate Chris Perilstein. Council voted 7-0 to permanently close the segment and 7-0 to amend the Comprehensive Plan place-type map.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Street closing and map amendment approved 7-0

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Ravenstone Commercial Rezoning (5204 Wake Forest Hwy, 2.42 Acres)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Applicant Jeremy Anderson sought a zoning map change from CC with GDP to CG with TDP for 2.42 acres at 5204 Wake Forest Highway. Council approved the rezoning and consistency statement 7-0, then added and unanimously approved (7-0) an inadvertently omitted Utility Extension Agreement with Anderson Marlo flagged by Carl Rist.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Rezoning, consistency statement, and UEA approved 7-0

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: 1607 East Cornwallis Road Rezoning (1.91 Acres, 9 Parcels)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Taken ahead of Item 24 at Chelsea Cook's request, applicant Neil Ghosh presented a CN-to-CN rezoning with a prohibited-use TDP covering nine parcels totaling 1.91 acres at 1607 East Cornwallis Road. Council approved the Utility Extension Agreement, rezoning ordinance, and consistency statement unanimously 7-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: UEA, rezoning, and consistency statement approved 7-0

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Wake Olive Consolidated Annexation and PDR 17.270 Rezoning (5247/5255 Wake Forest Hwy, 12.16 Acres)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Applicant Toby Coleman (Redeeming Development Group) requested annexation and PDR 17.270 rezoning for up to 210 residential units (6% affordable) plus commercial space along NC-98/Wake Forest Highway, facing sustained opposition from Sound Rivers and Preserve Durham speakers over turbidity/erosion, 67.5% imperviousness, NC-98 crashes, blasting, and missing sidewalks to Neal Middle School. Despite mid-hearing proffers adding 100-year pond storage, outflow turbidity sampling, a 30-foot pedestrian easement, and a 2,500 sq ft commercial minimum, Council passed the annexation/UEA and rezoning 5-2 (Nate Baker and DeDreana Freeman voting No) and adopted the consistency statement 7-0 at 12:43 a.m.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Annexation/UEA & Rezoning passed 5-2 (Baker, Freeman No); Consistency passed 7-0

votes.item_title: Consent Agenda Adoption (Items 1–5, 7, 9–13, 15, 17–19)
votes.notes: Item 16 (Quorum Houses ADU Loan Pilot) was pulled for separate debate and vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton read the Consent Agenda items aloud at 00:28:34, after which Item 16 (Quorum Houses LLC ADU Loan Pilot contract) was pulled for council discussion. Mayor Leonardo Williams then presided over the consent motion covering Items 1–5, 7, 9–13, 15, and 17–19. The motion was moved, seconded, and approved unanimously 7-0 on roll call at 00:32:18 with all seven council members present and voting Aye.

votes.item_title: Item 8: Adopt Tenant Protection Ordinance Revision Adding City Code §10-241(f) (Effective Immediately)
votes.notes: Clarified at 03:26:51 to take effect immediately on October 20, 2025 without the City Attorney's preemption caveat.
votes.discussion_detail: Item 8 drew over two hours of impassioned testimony (00:52:28–03:25:20), with Riverside High School Affordable Housing Club students, Legal Aid/Justice Center advocates, NC Tenants Union, Durham CAN, and dozens of tenants urging adoption of §10-241(f) barring landlords from collecting rent on properties cited for imminently dangerous conditions, while realtor associations, the Triangle Apartment Association, and DHA CEO Anthony Snell raised operational and statutory objections. Senior Deputy City Attorney Fred Lamar reiterated that state landlord-tenant law likely preempts municipal rent-collection bans, prompting Mark-Anthony Middleton and Carl Rist to float adding a preemption disclaimer and local code cross-references. Chelsea Cook, DeDreana Freeman, and Nate Baker strongly opposed inserting a preemption caveat or weakening the already 72-hour cure structure, arguing it would chill enforcement and invite legal dismissal. Middleton withdrew his amendment at 03:22:40 to preserve council unity, and Council unanimously adopted the unamended ordinance 7-0 at 03:26:03 (effective immediately).

votes.item_title: Item 22 (Motion 1): Permanently Close 402 Linear Feet of Cliff Street (SC25001)
votes.notes: Applicant Hamilton/Jackson proffered two Rockwood Trail greenway easements during review; supported by speaker Chris Perilstein.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton presided over the public hearing on Item 22 (SC25001), a petition by applicants Hamilton and Jackson to permanently close 402 linear feet of an unimproved portion of Cliff Street. Unlike an earlier paper-street conflict, the applicants added two greenway easements connecting the Rockwood Trail network, winning public support from bicycle and pedestrian advocate Chris Perilstein during the hearing. With no speakers opposing the revised easement-backed closure, a motion to permanently close the 402-foot Cliff Street segment passed unanimously 7-0 at 03:53:20.

votes.item_title: Item 22 (Motion 2): Adopt Comprehensive Plan Place-Type Map Amendment (Established Residential) for Cliff Street Closure
votes.notes: Required companion Comprehensive Plan map amendment following permanent street right-of-way closure.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately following approval of the SC25001 Cliff Street partial street closing, Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton called up the mandatory companion Comprehensive Plan place-type map amendment designating the closed right-of-way as Established Residential. Having just endorsed the applicants' Rockwood Trail greenway easement commitments, council members raised no additional questions. The motion was moved, seconded, and passed unanimously 7-0 at 03:53:48.

votes.item_title: Item 23 (Motion 1): Adopt Ravenstone Commercial Rezoning Ordinance (5204 Wake Forest Hwy, CC w/ GDP to CG w/ TDP)
votes.notes: 2.42 acres at 5204 Wake Forest Highway; applicant Jeremy Anderson.
votes.discussion_detail: Applicant Jeremy Anderson presented Item 23, requesting to rezone 2.42 acres at 5204 Wake Forest Highway from Commercial Center with a General Development Plan (CC w/ GDP) to Commercial General with a Text-Only Development Plan (CG w/ TDP) for the Ravenstone Commercial project. With Mark-Anthony Middleton presiding and no public speakers opposing the commercial text-only adjustment, council members briefly reviewed transportation and use parameters before closing the hearing. A motion to adopt the rezoning ordinance carried unanimously 7-0 at 04:00:48.

votes.item_title: Item 23 (Motion 2): Adopt Consistency Statement (N.C.G.S. §160D-605) for Ravenstone Commercial Rezoning
votes.notes: Statutory consistency finding under N.C.G.S. §160D-605.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately after adopting the Ravenstone Commercial rezoning ordinance, Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton entertained the statutorily required consistency statement under North Carolina General Statute §160D-605 affirming alignment with Durham's Comprehensive Plan. Council members raised no further comments following the unanimous rezoning approval. The motion was moved, seconded, and passed 7-0 at 04:01:16.

votes.item_title: Item 23 (Motion 3): Authorize Utility Extension Agreement with Anderson Marlo for Ravenstone Commercial
votes.notes: Motion was inadvertently omitted from the clerk's action sheet and caught by Carl Rist at 04:01:52 after the consistency vote.
votes.discussion_detail: As Mayor Leonardo Williams resumed the gavel after Item 23's consistency vote, Carl Rist noticed at 04:01:52 that Item 23 also required approval of a Utility Extension Agreement (UEA) that had been omitted from the presiding script. Planning and legal staff confirmed the UEA with Anderson Marlo was included in the packet and necessary to serve the Ravenstone Commercial site. Council promptly entertained a motion to authorize the Utility Extension Agreement, which passed unanimously 7-0 at 04:03:13.

votes.item_title: Item 25 (Motion 1): Authorize Utility Extension Agreement with 1607 East Cornwallis LLC
votes.notes: Taken out of order ahead of Item 24 per Chelsea Cook's request at 04:01:24; covers 9 parcels totaling 1.91 acres.
votes.discussion_detail: At Chelsea Cook's request at 04:01:24, Council took up Item 25—1607 East Cornwallis Road—ahead of the lengthier Wake Olive hearing. Applicant Neil Ghosh presented the rezoning across nine parcels totaling 1.91 acres from Commercial Neighborhood (CN) to CN with a Text-Only Development Plan restricting prohibited uses, noting neighborhood-serving commercial intent and utility connection needs. After closing the brief public hearing, Council voted unanimously 7-0 at 04:21:31 to authorize the Utility Extension Agreement with 1607 East Cornwallis LLC.

votes.item_title: Item 25 (Motion 2): Adopt Zoning Map Change Ordinance for 1607 East Cornwallis Road (CN to CN w/ TDP)
votes.notes: Prohibited-use Text-Only Development Plan across 1.91 acres.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately after approving the Utility Extension Agreement for 1607 East Cornwallis Road, Mayor Leonardo Williams entertained the zoning map change ordinance rezoning the 1.91-acre assemblage to CN with a prohibited-use TDP. Council members noted that the committed TDP protections narrowed objectionable commercial uses while supporting neighborhood retail viability. The motion was moved, seconded, and passed unanimously 7-0 at 04:22:03.

votes.item_title: Item 25 (Motion 3): Adopt Consistency Statement (N.C.G.S. §160D-605) for 1607 East Cornwallis Road
votes.notes: Statutory consistency finding under N.C.G.S. §160D-605.
votes.discussion_detail: Following unanimous approval of the 1607 East Cornwallis Road rezoning ordinance, Mayor Leonardo Williams called for a motion to adopt the statutory consistency statement under N.C.G.S. §160D-605. With no additional debate needed, the motion was moved, seconded, and passed unanimously 7-0 at 04:22:23.

votes.item_title: Item 24 (Motion 1): Approve Consolidated Annexation and Utility Extension Agreement for Wake Olive (5247/5255 Wake Forest Hwy)
votes.notes: 12.16 acres; 5-2 split vote with Nate Baker and DeDreana Freeman voting No.
votes.discussion_detail: Item 24 centered on Toby Coleman and Redeeming Development Group's consolidated annexation and PDR 17.270 rezoning for 12.16 acres at 5247/5255 Wake Forest Highway proposing up to 210 units (6% affordable) plus commercial space. Sound Rivers' Samantha Crop and Preserve Durham residents Pam Andrews, Wanda Allen, Tina Motley-Pearson, Donna Stainback, and Tammy Sue warned against 67.5% imperviousness, turbidity runoff, NC-98 crash hazards, blasting, fire/EMS response strain, and lack of sidewalks to Neal Middle School. During the hearing, the applicant added proffers for 100-year storm pond capacity, outflow turbidity sampling, a 30-foot pedestrian easement, and a 2,500 sq ft commercial floor, which satisfied Chelsea Cook, Carl Rist, Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Mayor Leonardo Williams as responsive housing growth along a designated corridor. Nate Baker and DeDreana Freeman remained opposed over stormwater/watershed risk, corridor infrastructure gaps, and low (6%) affordable set-asides, resulting in a 5-2 vote approving the annexation and UEA at 05:42:05.

votes.item_title: Item 24 (Motion 2): Adopt Wake Olive Zoning Map Change Ordinance (RS-20/RR to PDR 17.270, Falls/Jordan B)
votes.notes: Includes mid-hearing committed proffers on stormwater ponding, turbidity monitoring, pedestrian easement, and 2,500 sq ft minimum commercial.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately following the 5-2 vote to annex the Wake Olive parcels and authorize the Utility Extension Agreement, Mayor Leonardo Williams entertained the companion zoning map change ordinance establishing PDR 17.270 in the Falls/Jordan B watershed protection overlay. Council members maintained the exact policy alignment established during the nearly 80-minute hearing, with five members citing the housing units, 6% affordable commitment, commercial minimum, and late-proffered stormwater and pedestrian conditions. Moved and seconded at 05:42:39, the rezoning ordinance passed 5-2 at 05:42:56, with Nate Baker and DeDreana Freeman again voting No.

votes.item_title: Item 24 (Motion 3): Adopt Consistency Statement (N.C.G.S. §160D-605) for Wake Olive Rezoning
votes.notes: Adopted at 12:43 a.m. prior to adjournment; dissenters joined the statutory procedural consistency finding after the substantive 5-2 votes.
votes.discussion_detail: In the final formal action of the night at 12:43 a.m., Mayor Leonardo Williams called for a motion to adopt the statutory consistency statement under N.C.G.S. §160D-605 for the Wake Olive rezoning. Following standard practice after substantive split votes on the annexation and zoning map change, all seven council members joined the procedural consistency finding confirming the record. Moved and seconded at 05:43:14, the consistency statement passed unanimously 7-0 at 05:43:31 immediately before adjournment.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council October 20, 2025
disagreements.issue: Tenant Protection Ordinance (§10-241(f)): Unamended Passage vs. Preemption Caveat and Code Cross-Reference Amendment
disagreements.summary: Council members split over whether to add the City Attorney's proposed state-preemption disclaimer and local code enumerations to §10-241(f) before passing the rent-collection prohibition.
disagreements.side_a_position: Adopt §10-241(f) immediately without adding a preemption caveat or altering the cure-period structure.
side_a_arguments: Inserting 'unless otherwise preempted by state or federal law' undermines enforceability and gives landlords a ready-made pretext to ignore the ordinance.
Existing housing code already incorporates a 72-hour cure framework for imminently dangerous conditions, so tenants need clear protection effective immediately.
disagreements.side_b_position: Attach legal preemption caveats and specific Durham code enumerations to mitigate litigation risk raised by the City Attorney's office.
side_b_arguments: Senior Deputy City Attorney Fred Lamar warned that state landlord-tenant statutes likely preempt municipal restrictions on rent collection.
Tailoring language and cure references could lower legal exposure while preserving neighborhood inspection triggers.
disagreements.resolution: Mark-Anthony Middleton withdrew the preemption amendment at 03:22:40 and backed the unamended ordinance, which passed 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council October 20, 2025
disagreements.issue: Structure, Affordability Targeting, and Oversight of the $1.75M Affordable ADU Loan Pilot (Item 16)
disagreements.summary: Council members scrutinized the Quorum Houses LLC ADU pilot's 80% AMI threshold, single-bidder procurement, loan forgiveness, and compliance risks while ultimately voting yes.
disagreements.side_a_position: Question 80% AMI targeting, single-bidder risk, Airbnb/lease-up enforcement, and oppose loan forgiveness.
side_a_arguments: 80% AMI rents and an ~$80,000 average city loan per unit yield modest affordability depth relative to multifamily subsidies.
Allowing loans to become forgivable turns scarce revolving housing funds into grants, while homeowners acting as landlords require strict Airbnb bans and lease-up monitoring.
disagreements.side_b_position: Launch the 20-unit pilot with Quorum Houses LLC to fill a private lending void and evaluate scalability.
side_b_arguments: Commercial banks and mission lenders have struggled to underwrite small ADU construction loans, so direct city lending fills a real market gap.
Forever Home Durham promised an ADU pilot, and Quorum Houses was the sole qualified respondent with hands-on ADU construction capacity.
disagreements.resolution: Council unanimously passed the $1.75 million pilot 7-0 with expectations of compliance enforcement and program evaluation.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council October 20, 2025
disagreements.issue: Wake Olive Consolidated Annexation and PDR 17.270 Rezoning (Item 24)
disagreements.summary: Council split 5-2 on annexing and rezoning 12.16 acres at 5247/5255 Wake Forest Highway for up to 210 homes and commercial space amid neighborhood and environmental objections.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the annexation and PDR 17.270 rezoning with the applicant's late-proffered stormwater, turbidity, pedestrian, and commercial commitments.
side_a_arguments: The project adds up to 210 housing units including 6% income-restricted units along an urbanizing Wake Forest Highway corridor.

Mid-hearing proffers—100-year pond design, outflow turbidity self-monitoring, a 30-foot pedestrian easement toward Neal Middle School, and a 2,500 sq ft commercial floor—addressed key public concerns.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose annexation and high-imperviousness rezoning due to watershed turbidity, NC-98 traffic safety, school connectivity gaps, and low affordability.
side_b_arguments: 67.5% impervious coverage in the Falls/Jordan B watershed poses erosion and sediment hazards even with self-monitored sampling.
NC-98 crash rates, lack of continuous sidewalks to Neal Middle School, and only 6% affordable units fall short of transit-oriented community standards.
