meetings.title: Durham City Council June 2, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: At its June 2, 2025 regular meeting, the Durham City Council proclaimed Disaster Preparedness Week, approved the consent agenda 7-0, and confirmed eight board and commission appointments 7-0. Council passed the Revised Rules of Procedure 6-1—with Chelsea Cook dissenting over a separate 5-minute applicant rebuttal in zoning hearings—and unanimously adopted the 2025 First Quarter Crime Report 7-0 despite a sharp factual clash between Mark-Anthony Middleton and Leonardo Williams over ShotSpotter canvassing history. Following amendment negotiations over naming Amazon directly, Council unanimously adopted a resolution supporting Durham Amazon workers' right to organize (7-0 after Nate Baker corrected an initial vote mistake) and held the second public hearing on the proposed FY2025-26 Budget.

agenda_items.title: Disaster Preparedness Week Proclamation, Revaluation & Community Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman read a Disaster Preparedness Week proclamation accepted by James Chavis of PAC 1, and Council Members discussed Durham's ~71.6% property revaluation, Pride Month, federal funding cuts to the Pauli Murray Center, immigrant protections, and $305,000 in Bull City Future Fund gun-violence grants. City Manager Bo Ferguson noted an additional shooting map attachment for Item 24.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Excluding Item 24) & General Business Board Appointments (Items 4, 7, 8, 11, 12, 15)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council adopted the consent agenda (Items 1-3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 13, 16-18, 20-23, 25-34) 7-0, excluding pulled Item 24, GBA Items 19 and 38, and Budget Hearing Item 36. Council then unanimously approved General Business board appointments to DOST, Planning Commission, Sports Commission, Human Relations Commission, and Racial Equity Commission 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Revised Rules of Procedure for Durham City Council
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Speakers Pam Andrews, Donna Stainback, and Mimi Kessler opposed a 15-minute aggregate limit and presiding-officer discretion on zoning public hearings. Procedures Chair Javiera Caballero and City Attorney Kim Rehberg clarified the 15-minute provision dated to 1994 and read on-the-record apportionment language requested by Nate Baker, while Chelsea Cook objected that applicants received an extra 5-minute rebuttal atop proponent time (20 vs. 15 minutes). The revised rules passed 6-1 (Cook Nay).

agenda_items.title: 2025 First Quarter Crime Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: A Police Deputy Chief confirmed that Q1 shooting concentrations closely mirrored former ShotSpotter census tracts. Council Member Chelsea Cook noted the updated map could inform neighborhood canvassing, sparking a disagreement between Mark-Anthony Middleton and Leonardo Williams over whether Durham ever deployed HEART or unarmed responders following ShotSpotter alerts; Council adopted the report 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Resolution in Support of Durham Amazon Workers' Right to Organize
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Sponsored by Nate Baker from the Workers' Rights Commission, Item 38 drew debate after Mark-Anthony Middleton and Javiera Caballero objected to accusing Amazon of retaliation in an official resolution without a city investigation. Chelsea Cook offered an amendment—and accepted a friendly edit striking 'RDU 1'—so the clause condemned unionization retaliation generally; after accidentally voting Nay on the initial roll call, Baker immediately corrected his vote to Yes for a unanimous 7-0 adoption.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Proposed FY2025-26 Budget & FY2026-31 Capital Improvement Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Christina Rearden presented the proposed 43.71-cent property tax rate (5.48 cents above the 38.23-cent revenue-neutral rate post-revaluation). Eleven residents testified on youth programs, fare-free buses, Roxboro/Mangum and Duke/Gregson street safety, parks, eviction diversion, city pay, and 24/7 HEART expansion before Council adjourned at 8:45 PM.

votes.item_title: Adopt Consent Agenda (Items 1-3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 13, 16-18, 20-23, 25-34; Excluding Pulled Item 24)
votes.notes: Item 24 (Q1 Crime Report) pulled for discussion; Items 4, 7, 8, 11, 12, 15, 19, 38 on GBA; Item 36 on Public Hearings.
votes.discussion_detail: After Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton read the June 2 consent agenda—including the Revised Code of Ethics, 2025 Disparity Study, Non-Discrimination Ordinance regulations, GoDurham bus repowering, PFAS engineering support, and police psychological testing contracts—Item 24 (Q1 Crime Report) was confirmed as pulled while Item 19 was confirmed on the General Business Agenda. A motion to approve the consent agenda excluding Item 24 was made and seconded, and Council adopted it unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: General Business Board and Commission Appointments (Items 4, 7, 8, 11, 12, 15)
votes.notes: Appointed Maureen Quinlan & Adam T. Saulters (DOST), Anitra L. Bailey, Kimberly A. Cameron & Tai T. Huynh (Planning), Monica Brown (Sports), Zhaohui Lu, Michael L. Ross & Amanda Borer (Human Relations), and Linda E. Strong (Racial Equity).
votes.discussion_detail: The City Clerk presented Council nominations for General Business Agenda board and commission vacancies covering the Durham Open Space and Trails Commission (Item 4), Planning Commission (Item 7), Board of Adjustment (Item 8), Sports Commission (Item 11), Human Relations Commission (Item 12), and Racial Equity Commission (Item 15). Council moved and seconded confirmation of the slate as read, approving all appointments unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 19: Adopt Revised Rules of Procedure for Durham City Council
votes.notes: Rehberg confirmed the read-in language requested by Nate Baker was not voted on separately as a motion amendment but would be incorporated into the official text and redlined to Council.
votes.discussion_detail: Residents Pam Andrews, Donna Stainback, and Mimi Kessler testified against a 15-minute aggregate cap on zoning public hearing speakers and presiding-officer authority to shorten comment times. Procedures Committee Chair Javiera Caballero and City Attorney Kim Rehberg noted that the 15-minute per-side cap had existed in Durham's procedures since 1994 and read on-the-record text requested by Nate Baker restoring apportionment discretion in Section II.D.1.d. Council Member Chelsea Cook voted No because the new text granted zoning applicants an independent 5-minute rebuttal atop proponent time (20 minutes versus 15 minutes for opponents) and later flagged that Baker's text had not received a standalone amendment vote before Rehberg confirmed it would be entered in the official adopted text.

votes.item_title: Item 24: Adopt 2025 First Quarter Crime Report
votes.notes: Pulled by Mayor Leonardo Williams regarding shooting concentration maps relative to former ShotSpotter census tracts.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Leonardo Williams pulled Item 24 to review an updated shooting distribution map and ask the Police Deputy Chief whether Q1 2025 gun violence concentrated in the same census tracts previously covered by ShotSpotter, which the Deputy Chief confirmed. Council Member Chelsea Cook suggested the map could support neighborhood canvassing, prompting a disagreement between Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton and Mayor Williams over whether Durham had previously sent unarmed or HEART-style responders to canvass after ShotSpotter alerts. Following that exchange, Council adopted the First Quarter Crime Report unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 38: Adopt Resolution in Support of Durham Amazon Workers' Right to Organize (As Amended)
votes.notes: Initial roll call showed 6-1 after Nate Baker mistakenly voted Nay believing the vote was solely on the amendment; Baker immediately changed his vote to Yes on the record at [01:17:19], making final adoption 7-0.
votes.discussion_detail: Brought forward by Council Member Nate Baker on behalf of the Durham Workers' Rights Commission, the resolution drew unanimous support in spirit alongside strong objections from Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton and Council Member Javiera Caballero to naming Amazon as 'accused of retaliation' without a city investigation. Council Member Chelsea Cook drafted a substitute final Whereas clause condemning retaliation at RDU 1 and then accepted a friendly amendment removing the 'RDU 1' reference so the statement condemned anti-union retaliation generally. On the vote to adopt the resolution as amended, Baker mistakenly voted No believing only the amendment was on the floor, immediately corrected his vote to Yes on the record, and secured a final unanimous 7-0 tally.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council June 2, 2025
disagreements.issue: Zoning Public Hearing Speaker Caps & Applicant Rebuttal Time in Revised Rules of Procedure (Item 19)
disagreements.summary: Council voted 6-1 to adopt revised Council Rules of Procedure over Council Member Chelsea Cook's objection that applicants gained separate rebuttal time atop proponent limits.
disagreements.side_a_position: Adopt the updated rules clarifying 'applicant' versus 'proponent' and preserving presiding-officer discretion to apportion public comment time.
side_a_arguments: The 15-minute per-side cap had been in Council procedures since 1994 and is routinely expanded at the Mayor's discretion.

Separating applicants from community proponents prevents public commenters from consuming an applicant's legally required presentation time, while Baker's added sentence secures speaker-apportionment flexibility.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose granting applicants an extra 5-minute rebuttal on top of 15-minute proponent time while capping opponents at 15 minutes.
side_b_arguments: Former procedures deducted the 5-minute rebuttal from the proponent's 15 minutes, whereas the new rule creates a 20-minute versus 15-minute imbalance favoring applicants.
Residents speaking on complex zoning cases already face strict time constraints and no rebuttal opportunity.
disagreements.resolution: Passed 6-1 with Cook voting No; City Attorney agreed to incorporate the read-in apportionment revision and circulate a clean redline.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council June 2, 2025
disagreements.issue: History of Non-Police Post-Shooting Canvassing Under ShotSpotter (Item 24)
disagreements.summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton clashed factually during the Q1 Crime Report over whether Durham ever deployed unarmed/HEART-style personnel to canvass neighborhoods after ShotSpotter alerts.
disagreements.side_a_position: Durham previously saw social workers, EMS, and non-violent coalition volunteers canvass neighborhoods the day after shootings.
side_a_arguments: Community organizations and social worker/EMS volunteers repeatedly knocked doors in public housing neighborhoods after shootings in past years.
Day-after canvassing in high-gun-violence neighborhoods is not unprecedented and could be funded in future cycles.
disagreements.side_b_position: The City of Durham never deployed HEART or unarmed municipal responders specifically triggered by ShotSpotter gunshot detections.
side_b_arguments: Unlike peer cities using ShotSpotter alerts to dispatch HEART-type canvassers the next day, Durham only sent law enforcement assets and did not yet have HEART during earlier ShotSpotter periods.
Claiming Durham deployed ShotSpotter-triggered civilian responders is historically inaccurate.
disagreements.resolution: After trading statements on the record, Council moved on and unanimously adopted the Q1 Crime Report 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council June 2, 2025
disagreements.issue: Naming Amazon and RDU 1 Directly in Workers' Rights Resolution (Item 38)
disagreements.summary: Council debated whether to retain the Workers' Rights Commission's specific accusation of retaliation against Amazon or generalize the condemnation clause.
disagreements.side_a_position: Strike language accusing Amazon of retaliation and remove specific 'RDU 1' facility references from the official municipal resolution.
side_a_arguments: An official City Council resolution bearing the City's seal should not endorse uninvestigated accusations against a named corporate citizen.
Condemning anti-union retaliation universally without naming Amazon/RDU 1 makes the resolution stronger and avoids legal/procedural scrutiny.
disagreements.side_b_position: Retain worker-drafted condemnation of retaliation against Amazon organizing (or specify RDU 1) unless majority consensus favors removing it.
side_b_arguments: Amazon retaliation claims are widely reported and Workers' Rights Commission members organizing at Amazon drafted the language intentionally.
Targeted solidarity language matters in a state with anti-union preemption and low union density.
disagreements.resolution: Cook proposed replacing the clause to condemn retaliation at RDU 1 and then accepted a friendly edit removing 'RDU 1'; Council passed the amended resolution 7-0 after Baker corrected his initial vote.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session on Budget May 29, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council held Day 2 of its FY 2025-26 budget work sessions with all seven members present, reviewing major departmental reorganizations and service plans for Planning and Development, Environmental and Street Services, Community Safety, and Downtown Durham Incorporated. Council members debated immediate gap funding for a low-barrier day shelter versus completing a homelessness strategic plan first, as well as the absence of dedicated gun-violence intervention items and ShotSpotter in the proposed budget. At the conclusion of the two-day retreat, Council directed staff to bring additional analysis on extending the Durham Minimum Livable Wage to part-time workers at the June 5 work session and requested written updates on low-income homeowner tax relief, the Durham Affordable Housing Loan Fund, and homelessness demographics.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call and Day 2 Budget Work Session Opening
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams called the session to order with all seven seated council members present. City Manager Bo Ferguson framed Day 2 as focusing on departments undergoing significant reorganization or programmatic expansion in the proposed FY 2025-26 budget.

agenda_items.title: Planning and Development Department Reorganization and FY 2025-26 Budget
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Director Sara Young presented the consolidated Planning and Development Department expanding from 50 to 110 FTEs plus six new fee-supported engineering positions, with a budget exceeding $14 million (city-county split 50/50 after fees). Budget highlights included over $300,000 for UDO rewrite parcel mailings, $60,000 for a multimodal traffic impact analysis methodology, a city-county open space plan, and a three-year historic resources inventory update. Council members questioned private street inspections, notice procedures, UDO rewrite timing for 2026, and maintaining long-range community planning alongside development review.

agenda_items.title: Environmental and Street Services Merger, Street Maintenance PCI, and Solid Waste Changes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Marvin Williams and Wayne Fenton presented the merged Environmental and Street Services Department (307 FTEs, $57 million budget) combining Public Works, Solid Waste Management, and the NIS Impact Team. Key issues included maintaining residential street Pavement Condition Index scores in the mid-60s (~$25 million annually), high recycling contamination rates under Waste Management's hand-sort sampling, proposing a shift of yard waste collection from weekly to bi-weekly ($530,000 savings), and eliminating holiday makeup days for bulky pickups ($52,000 savings). Council members discussed per-lane-mile paving costs, peer city PCI benchmarks, regional sorting and reuse/wash facility options before the 2028 recycling contract ends, and municipal contracting limits.

agenda_items.title: Community Safety Department Expansion, HEART, Street Outreach, Survivor Care, and Homeless Services
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Director Ryan Smith outlined Community Safety's growth to 75 FTEs and an $11.2 million budget across crisis response, stabilization services, and support operations, adding 20 FTEs including four daytime HEART community response units, three positions replacing an expiring DOJ co-response grant, and five street outreach workers transitioning from Housing for New Hope. Smith also detailed the June launch of the Office of Survivor Care, the transfer of Homeless Services and Welcome Home into the department, and plans to integrate a $1 million guaranteed income carryforward for formerly incarcerated residents. Council members engaged in sharp policy debates over funding an immediate day shelter versus completing a homelessness strategic plan first, as well as the absence of ShotSpotter or a dedicated gun-violence strategy in the proposed budget.

agenda_items.title: Downtown Durham Incorporated (DDI) FY 2025-26 MSD Budget and Blueprint 2035 Preview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DDI President and CEO Nicole Thompson reviewed FY 2025 accomplishments including the Bull Ride shuttle, 307 West Main retail incubator, Wi-Fi benches, and public engagement of over 2,200 residents for the Blueprint 2035 downtown master plan. Thompson presented DDI's Business Improvement District budget proposal—maintaining the 7-cent BID rate above the 4.68-cent revenue-neutral rate—to fund a larger retail incubator, commercial land trust exploration, retail recruitment ($130,000 total), alley/parklet placekeeping, living wage increases for ambassadors, and four new unarmed safety ambassadors. Council members praised the Block by Block ambassador program and discussed downtown loop intersections, Cochran Street pedestrianization, retail ground-floor vacancies, and grocery access.

agenda_items.title: Two-Day Budget Work Session Wrap-Up and June 5 Direction
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Bo Ferguson summarized outstanding requests from the two-day budget sessions, noting no formal consensus had yet emerged to alter the proposed tax rate or base budget. Council directed staff to bring a formal analysis of part-time Durham Minimum Livable Wage options to the regular afternoon work session on June 5 rather than holding an additional morning session, while providing written updates on the low-income homeowner tax relief program, the Durham Affordable Housing Loan Fund ($2 million loan status and potential $1 million addition), and demographic homelessness data.

disagreements.meeting_title: City Council Work Session on Budget May 29, 2025
disagreements.issue: Immediate Day Shelter and Non-Congregate Shelter Funding vs. Waiting for Homelessness Strategic Plan
disagreements.summary: Council divided over whether to add immediate short-term funding for a day shelter and low-barrier non-congregate sheltering in the FY 2025-26 budget or wait for Community Safety's homelessness strategic plan before making new financial commitments.
disagreements.side_a_position: Allocate immediate short-term funding (such as ~$50,000 for a day shelter or pallet/safe-sleeping pilots) in FY 2025-26 rather than waiting a year for a strategic plan.
side_a_arguments: The 2025 point-in-time count showed chronic homelessness nearly doubled even as overall numbers dipped, and 111 individuals plus 62 families remain on shelter waitlists.
Without a day shelter, unhoused residents remain exposed to the elements and rely on public spaces like the downtown library during daytime hours.
A ~$50,000 day shelter investment was among Council's top budget retreat priorities and is small relative to a $722 million total budget.
disagreements.side_b_position: Complete the homelessness strategic plan and establish clear operational partnerships and RFPs before appropriating new shelter funds.
side_b_arguments: No clear operator, scope, or implementation plan currently exists for a $50,000 day shelter allocation, risking symbolic spending without measurable results.
Council opted against increasing the dedicated housing tax rate at the budget retreat, leaving limited capacity for unvetted pilots.
Waiting on the strategic plan allows Community Safety to align street outreach, housing unit matchmaking, and Continuum of Care investments systematically.
disagreements.resolution: No budget amendment was finalized; Council Member Cook indicated she may revisit day shelter funding at the June 5 work session pending Durham County's budget decisions.

disagreements.meeting_title: City Council Work Session on Budget May 29, 2025
disagreements.issue: Gun Violence Intervention Strategy, ShotSpotter, and Budget Priorities
disagreements.summary: A heated exchange erupted over whether the proposed FY 2025-26 budget neglects immediate gun-violence interventions following the end of ShotSpotter and Bull City United, and whether ShotSpotter should be reconsidered.
disagreements.side_a_position: Critique the absence of a dedicated gun-violence strategy and line items in the proposed budget, and urge revisiting acoustic gunfire detection (ShotSpotter) alongside a comprehensive anti-violence framework.
side_a_arguments: While Vision Zero receives dedicated staff, plans, and $200 million bond funding for traffic deaths, gun violence receives minimal dedicated operating funding after ShotSpotter and Bull City United ended.
Cities like Denver pair mental health responders and community canvassing with ShotSpotter alerts to support survivors and save gunshot victims when nobody calls 911.
Gun violence is an immediate daily threat affecting residents across Durham and requires urgent city-county coordination rather than slow-moving long-term promises.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose funding ShotSpotter as an ineffective, reactionary expense and reject claims that Council members lack urgency on gun violence, emphasizing preventative investments in housing, poverty reduction, and youth.
side_b_arguments: Council's prior quantitative and qualitative evaluation showed ShotSpotter was costly for a three-square-mile footprint without solving root causes.
Keeping families housed and addressing poverty, mental health, and basic needs are statistically proven anti-violence interventions funded heavily through Police, HEART, and Community Safety.
Members seeking policy changes such as a gun-violence strategy should bring concrete, multi-stakeholder proposals forward rather than criticizing colleagues' commitment.
disagreements.resolution: City Manager Bo Ferguson offered to organize a collaborative city-county working session reviewing national gun-violence intervention best practices and the prior Community Safety and Wellness Task Force report.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session on Budget May 28, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: Council conducted Day 1 of the FY 2025-26 budget work sessions covering overall revenues, the post-revaluation 43.71-cent property tax rate (5.48 cents above revenue neutral), employee pay and benefits, the Capital Improvement Plan, Equitable and Green Infrastructure, transit and parking, Parks and Recreation's half-penny fund and lead-remediation parks, and the new Community Engagement and Equity Department. Robust policy disagreements emerged over excluding roughly 201 non-commensurate part-time workers from the $21.90/hour Durham Minimum Livable Wage, how to sustain fare-free GoDurham buses once COVID-era fund balances deplete in FY 2026, and whether the proposed budget adequately addresses affordable housing, tax burdens, and gun violence. No formal votes were taken during the six-hour work session.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call and FY 2025-26 Budget Work Session Introduction
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams convened the session at 9:04 AM with six members present and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton en route (joining later in the session). City Manager Bo Ferguson encouraged Council to dig into key budget priorities and give timely direction ahead of June adoption, while Council Member Rist flagged the absence of dedicated housing and economic development items on the two-day agenda.

agenda_items.title: FY 2025-26 Revenue Presentation, Revaluation, Tax Rate, and Fund Balance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Christina Riordan presented post-revaluation property tax growth (real property up 71%, total tax base up 62.39%, penny value rising from $4.3M to $6.9M) and explained the proposed 43.71-cent tax rate—5.48 cents above the 38.23-cent revenue-neutral rate—alongside flat sales tax trends ($104.2M), a $1.2M occupancy tax shift to Discover Durham Next, and maintaining the 7-cent Business Improvement District tax. She highlighted using $5.3 million in fund balance (preserving the 16.7% policy floor) and shifting $4 million in recurring street maintenance funding out of General Fund balance into Debt Service, plus funding 42 new FTEs (31 tax-supported).

agenda_items.title: Employee Pay, Benefits, Structure Adjustments, and Part-Time Minimum Livable Wage
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim HR Director Montique Cleary, Jim Ryan Gruber, Althea Hardy, and Gwen Barnett presented $12.6 million in pay-for-performance merit raises (4-6% full-time, 3% part-time), a 1.45% market structure adjustment ($4.2M total), an 11.8% jump in the Durham Minimum Livable Wage to $21.90/hour, and increased employee/dependent health premium shares driven by GLP-1 drugs and high claims while keeping a $0 employee-only plan. Council sharply questioned the exclusion of 201 non-commensurate part-time workers (many in DPR youth care) from the $21.90/hour wage and requested cost scenarios, job breakdowns, and updates on HR probation, leave, and cannabis drug-testing reviews.

agenda_items.title: FY 2026-31 Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) and $200M Bond Projects
agenda_items.discussion_summary: JJ Scott reviewed the CIP scoring and multi-year debt model, highlighting $12 million over two years for park lead soil remediation, Vision Zero and $200 million bond street/sidewalk projects, facility HVAC replacements, and a joint County Emergency Operations Center / backup 911 facility. Council members requested project-by-project timelines, federal funding risk assessments for projects like the Durham Rail Trail, updates on South Ellerbe Creek stormwater bids and Carolina Theatre needs, and reserved capacity for Fire Station 21 and Mangum-Roxboro.

agenda_items.title: Equitable and Green Infrastructure (EGI) Engagement and FY 2026 Projects
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mary Grace Stoneking reported a fivefold increase in resident participation across five CEJST-selected EGI focus areas, reaching 468 residents (75% via paper surveys) to select top stormwater, park, and multimodal safety projects totaling nearly $6 million. Selected projects include ADA bus stops and CR Woods Park improvements in East End/Rowena, Bay Hargrove Park and Madison Street drainage in East Trinity/Avondale, NC 55 sidewalk gaps, Holloway/Elizabeth pedestrian safety, and a new playground at Southern Boundaries Park.

agenda_items.title: Transportation: Fare-Free GoDurham, Bus Rapid Transit, and Parking Fund
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Director Sean Egan highlighted record October 2024 ridership exceeding 650,000 trips, 13 signalized Transit Signal Priority intersections on Fayetteville Street, upcoming 10-15 minute bus expansions, and three Durham County Transit Plan-funded staff to advance the Central Durham BRT starter corridor from East Durham to Duke/VA. Egan and Manager Ferguson warned that COVID-era transit fund balance will be depleted after keeping buses fare-free through June 2026, requiring future tax increases or fare policy shifts, while the Parking Fund faces a $2.25 million deficit in FY 2026.

agenda_items.title: Durham Parks and Recreation Half-Penny Fund and Pre-Regulatory Landfill Parks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DPR Director Wade Walcott presented keeping the dedicated Parks and Trails tax at a full half penny rather than dropping to revenue neutral, adding $1.3 million and six maintenance/construction FTEs, alongside one-time funding to expand Bimbé and the sold-out senior holiday dance. Walcott also updated Council on five pre-regulatory landfill/incinerator parks awaiting final NC DEQ testing results in June, backed by $12 million in CIP funding across two cycles and court resurfacing plans including Elmira, Rock Quarry, and Morreene Road.

agenda_items.title: Community Engagement and Equity Department Reorganization and Council Closing Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy City Manager Bertha Wimbush outlined merging small engagement, equity, youth, digital inclusion, and participatory budgeting teams from six departments into a centralized Engagement Department at Golden Belt, freeing funds for a full-time ADA Coordinator and full-time Language Access position and bringing $135,000 community conversation facilitation back in-house. Council members closed with contrasting reflections on federal cut risks, housing pressures, low-income tax relief eligibility, tax base expansion, and gun violence.

disagreements.meeting_title: City Council Work Session on Budget May 28, 2025
disagreements.issue: Applying the $21.90/Hour Durham Minimum Livable Wage to Non-Commensurate Part-Time Workers
disagreements.summary: Council members clashed with staff recommendations and debated among themselves over excluding roughly 201 seasonal and non-commensurate part-time workers (earning as little as $16.85/hour) from the $21.90/hour Durham Minimum Livable Wage.
disagreements.side_a_position: Bring all part-time city workers—including seasonal youth-care and recreation staff—up to the $21.90/hour Durham Minimum Livable Wage and eliminate the 3% vs. 4-6% merit disparity.
side_a_arguments: Prior council direction in 2019 was to pay all city workers a living wage without carveouts, and paying youth-care/after-school staff $16.65-$16.85/hour undermines childcare quality.
Many part-time DPR workers are adult women of color or 10-month school employees working limited hours annually (e.g., ~366-472 hours), meaning the total budget cost is modest.
Part-time employees deserve full livable wages and equitable merit raises rather than a lower 3% cap compared to 4-6% for full-time workers.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain pay differentiation between non-commensurate seasonal roles and full-time/higher-responsibility positions to prevent severe compression and fiscal strain.
side_b_arguments: Paying gatekeepers or camp aides the same $21.90/hour as lifeguards, full-time recreation specialists, or degreed/skilled workers collapses pay hierarchies and creates severe compression—especially with DMLW projected near $25+/hour in FY 2027.
Expensive value mandates require growing the tax base or cutting elsewhere rather than eroding distinctions across the organizational chart.
disagreements.resolution: City Manager Bo Ferguson clarified the city can afford full DMLW for all part-timers if Council accepts the fairness trade-offs, and committed to returning on June 5 with demographic data, job titles, and cost options.

disagreements.meeting_title: City Council Work Session on Budget May 28, 2025
disagreements.issue: Long-Term Tax Funding Strategy for Fare-Free GoDurham Transit
disagreements.summary: Council agreed on continuing fare-free GoDurham service through FY 2026 but debated whether to rely on draining COVID-era transit fund balance now or prepare incrementally for future tax hikes or eventual fare reintroduction.
disagreements.side_a_position: Spend down existing transit fund balance to keep buses fare-free now without preemptively raising transit property taxes before needed.
side_a_arguments: 87% of GoDurham riders earn under $35,000 annually, making fare-free transit a critical equity, affordability, and ridership investment.
Reinstalling fareboxes and collecting fares from riders with senior/youth carveouts yields minimal net revenue while creating barriers.
disagreements.side_b_position: Plan incrementally for the FY 2027 fiscal cliff or revenue diversification rather than leaving a sudden tax increase or fare decision to a future council.
side_b_arguments: Waiting until fund balance reaches zero risks forcing a sharp transit tax hike during an economic downturn.
Expanding the tax base and non-property-tax revenues (and asking large regional employers for contributions) is necessary to sustain free transit without overburdening homeowners.
disagreements.resolution: Staff retained the revenue-neutral 2.4-cent transit tax rate for FY 2026 while flagging that FY 2027 will require additional tax revenue or service adjustments.

disagreements.meeting_title: City Council Work Session on Budget May 28, 2025
disagreements.issue: Proposed Property Tax Increase, Peripheral Growth Costs, and Missing Gun Violence / Housing Priorities
disagreements.summary: During Day 1 closing remarks, council members expressed diverging anxieties over the 5.48-cent rate increase above revenue neutral, infrastructure costs of peripheral development, housing affordability, and gun violence.
disagreements.side_a_position: Question the proposed tax rate increase amid economic strain and federal cuts while criticizing insufficient immediate action on housing insecurity and the cost of peripheral expansion.
side_a_arguments: Residents face job losses, federal funding cuts, and widening inequality, making a higher post-revaluation tax bill straining for middle- and low-income residents.
Outward suburban expansion carries underexamined long-term utility and service costs, while housing affordability lacks dedicated spotlight on the budget work-session agenda.
disagreements.side_b_position: Defend targeted rate investments above revenue neutral and argue expanding the tax base through development inside the Urban Growth Boundary—alongside stronger gun-violence and public-safety action—is essential.
side_b_arguments: Going solely revenue neutral would force deep service cuts; instead, Council should broaden eligibility for the joint Low-Income Homeowner Relief program.
Refusing development inside the Urban Growth Boundary undermines tax-base growth needed to fund progressive city services without constantly raising property taxes.
Mayor Williams separately criticized the lack of immediate gun-violence strategy items comparable to Vision Zero investments, noting Bull City United and ShotSpotter ended.
disagreements.resolution: No changes were directed on Day 1; members continued discussions on Day 2 and scheduled follow-ups for June 5.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session May 22, 2025 (livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: With five council members present and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton and Council Member Javiera Caballero excused, the Council reviewed pulled consent items—including a budget transfer affecting dedicated housing funds, proposed revisions to Council Rules and Procedures, HVAC maintenance, police psychological contracts, and PFAS water consulting—before hearing two major quarterly briefings. Police Chief Patrice Andrews presented the Q1 2025 Crime Report showing overall violent crime down even as homicides rose from six to nine, triggering a sharp debate between Mayor Williams and Council Members Cook, Freeman, and Baker over ShotSpotter versus preventative housing and family investments. CFO Tim Flora presented the FY 2024-25 Q3 financial report highlighting affirmed AAA bond ratings, $100 million in Connect Durham bonds sold at 3.813% interest, flat sales tax requiring $15.6 million in reserve usage, and Solid Waste reserve depletion before Council settled the June 2 agenda 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Excused Absence Approval, and Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams convened the work session with five members present (Williams, Baker, Cook, Freeman, and Rist), Council Member Javiera Caballero previously excused, and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton granted an excused absence by unanimous 5-0 voice vote. Council members shared community updates including Mayor Williams's graduation address at Hillside High School and upcoming budget sessions.

agenda_items.title: Citizen Matters
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Seven residents addressed Council during Citizen Matters on topics spanning innocent victims of gun violence and neighborhood violence (Ronnie Howard and Regina Mays following the May 4 Franklin Village/Few Gardens shooting), 18-wheeler and box-truck enforcement on Dakota Street near Shepard Middle School (Jacqueline Wagstaff and Gwen Silver), Charles Hamilton Houston Foundation updates (DeWarren Langley), PAC 1 and PAC 5 climate disaster preparedness (James Chavis), and a proposed Workers' Rights Commission resolution regarding Amazon labor practices (Italo Medelius).

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Items Review (Items 17, 19, 22, 25, 26, and 34)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council questioned staff on pulled consent items: Item 17 regarding transferring cash from the Dedicated Housing Fund to Debt Service (CFO Tim Flora and Budget Director Christina Riordan confirmed the funds remained restricted to housing debt); Item 19 on revised Council Rules and Procedures (Council Member Baker objected to routing member-initiated agenda items through the Mayor first and removing the five-vote day-of addition rule, deferring full debate to Procedures Committee Chair Caballero); Item 22 on Brady Trane HVAC maintenance; Items 25-26 on police psychological testing contracts; and Item 34 on HDR Engineering PFAS consulting amid delayed federal EPA timelines.

agenda_items.title: Item 24: Durham Police Department Q1 2025 Crime Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chief Patrice Andrews presented Q1 2025 crime statistics showing reductions across most violent and property crime categories, a 155.6% homicide clearance rate, 127 guns stolen (73% from unlocked vehicles), and 78% sworn officer staffing (388 of 533 positions). However, homicides rose from six in Q1 2024 to nine in Q1 2025 (15 year-to-date), prompting Council discussion of youth violence, locked-vehicle gun-theft campaigns, and an extended debate over gunfire detection technology versus preventative housing and family stability investments.

agenda_items.title: Item 35: FY 2024-25 Third Quarter Financial Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: CFO Tim Flora reported that Moody's, S&P, and Fitch reaffirmed Durham's AAA bond ratings—higher than the federal government following Moody's U.S. downgrade—enabling the city to sell $100 million in Connect Durham general obligation bonds at a 3.813% true interest cost. Flora noted flat sales tax collections are projected to finish $2.7 million under budget, requiring $15.6 million in General Fund reserve usage this fiscal year, while the Solid Waste fund's negative $1.7 million variance will nearly exhaust its unrestricted reserves.

agenda_items.title: Settling the June 2, 2025 City Council Meeting Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Bo Ferguson read the proposed June 2 meeting agenda separating Consent Agenda items from General Business Agenda items (including Items 19 and 38 plus public hearing Item 36), noting Item 14 was referred back to staff and Item 35 disposed of. Council approved the agenda by unanimous 5-0 voice vote and adjourned at 3:49 PM.

votes.item_title: Excused Absence for Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton
votes.notes: Mark-Anthony Middleton was absent/excused by this motion; Javiera Caballero was previously excused on May 8.
votes.discussion_detail: At the start of the May 22 work session, Mayor Leonardo Williams noted that Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton had requested an excused absence in addition to Council Member Javiera Caballero's previously approved absence. Five council members were physically present, establishing a quorum. Following a motion and second, the Council unanimously approved Middleton's excused absence by a 5-0 voice vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session May 22, 2025 (livestream)
disagreements.issue: Gunfire Detection Technology (ShotSpotter) vs. Preventative Housing and Youth Investments After Q1 Crime Report
disagreements.summary: Following Chief Patrice Andrews' Q1 2025 crime briefing showing nine Q1 homicides despite overall violent crime declines, Council clashed over whether to restore ShotSpotter/law enforcement technology or prioritize root-cause housing and poverty investments.
disagreements.side_a_position: Argue Council reacts urgently to tree protection or traffic deaths while failing to equip police with gun-violence technology like ShotSpotter.
side_a_arguments: Fifteen people had been killed year-to-date despite DPD's strong clearance rates, yet residents lack an urgent, visible gun-violence response.
Council invests aggressively in Vision Zero and environmental rules while refusing tools like ShotSpotter that Chief Andrews and officers support.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject ShotSpotter as an unproven, reactionary tool and argue that housing stability, mental health resources, and poverty reduction are true gun-violence prevention.
side_b_arguments: ShotSpotter only alerts police after shots are already fired and did not justify its cost during Durham's pilot evaluation.
Homicides stem from systemic poverty, housing instability, and inadequate mental health infrastructure, which require sustained preventative investments rather than surveillance tools.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote occurred on the Q1 report; Chief Andrews emphasized DPD's focus on community engagement, youth outreach, and stolen-gun prevention.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session May 22, 2025 (livestream)
disagreements.issue: Proposed Revisions to City Council Rules and Procedures (Item 19)
disagreements.summary: Council Member Baker raised concerns over proposed changes to Council's rules of procedure regarding how individual council members introduce agenda items and whether five votes can still add day-of items.
disagreements.side_a_position: Preserve existing avenues for council members to introduce agenda items directly and keep the five-vote mechanism to add urgent items at meetings.
side_a_arguments: Requiring council-initiated items to go through the Mayor first concentrates gatekeeping power and could delay urgent member priorities.
Removing the five-vote supermajority option eliminates flexibility when unexpected public issues arise.
disagreements.side_b_position: Streamline agenda-setting through structured committee/mayoral routing and clearer procedural rules (committee led by Javiera Caballero, who was absent).
side_b_arguments: Formal routing improves coordination and avoids ad-hoc last-minute docket additions without staff review.
disagreements.resolution: Item 19 was placed on the General Business Agenda for the June 2 meeting so absent Council Member Javiera Caballero could lead the full discussion.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting May 19, 2025 (with closed captioning)
meetings.executive_summary: With all seven members present, the Durham City Council adopted the consent agenda 7-0, approved a Legal Aid of North Carolina contract 6-0 with Council Member Chelsea Cook recused, approved conveying surplus skate park amenities to The Scrap Exchange 7-0, and unanimously passed a resolution opposing North Carolina House Bill 765's preemption of local zoning authority. City Manager Bo Ferguson formally presented the $722 million FY 2025-26 proposed budget and $537.6 million CIP following public comment on park lead soil and infrastructure needs. Council then approved the Danube Lane Townhouses rezoning (7-0) and annexation/utility agreement (6-1, Baker voting No over non-contiguous 'doughnut hole' slivers) and unanimously approved the 408-unit Brier Creek Multifamily rezoning spanning the Durham-Wake county line (7-0).

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, National Public Works Week Proclamation, Consent Agenda, and Pulled Items 4 & 18
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams called the meeting to order with all seven council members present and presented a National Public Works Week proclamation. Council adopted the consent agenda 7-0 excluding Items 4 and 18, approved Item 4 (Legal Aid of North Carolina) 6-0 with Council Member Cook recusing herself, and approved Item 18 conveying modular skate park ramps from the Wheels property to The Scrap Exchange 7-0 after public support from Mike Johnston of Manifest Skate Shop.

agenda_items.title: Resolution in Opposition to NC House Bill 765
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams and Council Member Carl Rist introduced a resolution joining North Carolina municipalities across party lines to oppose House Bill 765 ('An Act to Reform Local Government Development Regulations'), arguing Durham already leads the state on middle-housing reforms via EHC and SCAD while HB 765 undermines local planning authority and Section 160D protections.

agenda_items.title: FY 2025-26 Proposed Budget and FY 2026-31 Capital Improvement Plan Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public speakers urged faster park lead soil remediation (Mary Fontana, Molly Flow), funding for neighborhood improvements, and Vision Zero pedestrian infrastructure (Chris Perilstein), alongside comments from Gregory Williams and Sarah DeMotto. City Manager Bo Ferguson then formally presented the $722 million proposed FY 2025-26 budget and 43.71-cent tax rate, drawing initial feedback from all seven council members.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation – Danube Lane Townhouses (3824 & 3910 Danube Lane)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Peyton Burgess and Aaron Cain presented a 5.04-acre request from Brightside Ventures LLC (represented by Laura Holloman of McAdams) to annex and rezone two parcels from RS-20 to PDR 7.813 for up to 30 townhomes or duplexes, including a $10,000 Affordable Housing Fund proffer. Council questioned Durham Public Schools' zero-student generation estimate for townhomes and debated non-contiguous 'doughnut hole' parcels and trail connectivity before approving annexation 6-1 (Baker No) and rezoning/consistency 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change – Brier Creek Multifamily (Andrews Chapel Road / Cozart Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Applicant Worth Mills (Monts Ridge LLC) presented a 16.56-acre rezoning from RR and RS-10 to PDR 25.000 near the Wake County line for up to 408 units (383 apartments and 25 townhomes), proffering 5% of units at 80% AMI for 30 years, $50,000 to the Dedicated Affordable Housing Fund, $16,500 to DPS, and 100% native plantings. While Council Member Baker critiqued peripheral car-centric growth and Council Member Freeman questioned YIMBY advocacy framing by speaker Andy Lowe, Council approved all three motions unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 4: Agreement with Legal Aid of North Carolina
votes.notes: Chelsea Cook recused herself (no objection to recusal). Mayor Williams experienced a brief button issue at 00:42:32 resolved with Clerk.
votes.discussion_detail: Item 4, an agreement with Legal Aid of North Carolina (continuing eviction/expunction/restoration legal support reviewed at the May 8 work session), was pulled from consent to allow Council Member Chelsea Cook to recuse herself due to her affiliation. Hearing no objection to her recusal request, the remaining six council members voted unanimously 6-0 to approve the contract. Mayor Williams briefly verified his electronic voting button with the Clerk immediately afterward to ensure his Aye vote was properly recorded.

votes.item_title: Item 18: Resolution Approving Conveyance of Skate Park Amenities to The Scrap Exchange, Inc.
votes.notes: Conveyance pursuant to N.C.G.S. 160A-280; equipment acquired from Wheels property to be kept free and open to the public.
votes.discussion_detail: Item 18 was pulled for public comment by local skate shop owner Mike Johnston (Manifest Skate Shop), who praised the partnership between Durham Parks and Recreation and The Scrap Exchange to repurpose surplus modular skate ramps from the former Wheels property into a free, public community skate park in The Scrap Exchange's oversized Lakewood parking lot. Staff had previously confirmed at the May 8 work session that the conveyance under N.C.G.S. 160A-280 requires free public accessibility. On a motion and second, Council unanimously approved the conveyance 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 27: Resolution in Opposition to NC House Bill 765
votes.notes: Resolution opposing state preemption bill 'An Act to Reform Local Government Development Regulations'.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Williams moved Item 27 forward on the agenda and credited Council Member Carl Rist for first bringing House Bill 765 to Council's attention, explaining that the bill threatens municipal land-use authority and Section 160D protections across North Carolina. Council members noted Durham had already adopted middle-housing and parking reforms proactively via SCAD and EHC, making state preemption punitive rather than helpful. Following a motion and second, the resolution passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 25: Annexation Ordinance and Utility Extension Agreement – Danube Lane Townhouses
votes.notes: UEA with Brightside Ventures, LLC for 3824 & 3910 Danube Lane (5.04 acres). Baker opposed non-contiguous 'doughnut hole' slivers.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff presented the 5.04-acre consolidated annexation for up to 30 townhomes or duplexes along Danube Lane near US 15-501, noting Planning Commission recommended approval 12-0 and the applicant proffered $10,000 to the Dedicated Affordable Housing Fund. During questioning, Council Member Cook challenged Durham Public Schools' model projecting zero new students from 30 townhomes, while Council Member Baker objected to creating unannexed 'doughnut hole' county slivers and lacking full greenway construction on the trail easement. Baker voted No on the annexation and utility extension agreement, which passed 6-1.

votes.item_title: Item 25: UDO Zoning Map Change Ordinance (RS-20 County to PDR 7.813 City) – Danube Lane Townhouses
votes.notes: Authorizes up to 30 townhouse/duplex units with $10,000 Affordable Housing Fund proffer.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately following approval of the annexation, Council voted on the companion UDO Zoning Map Change converting 3824 and 3910 Danube Lane from RS-20 County to Planned Density Residential (PDR 7.813) City jurisdiction. Council members noted the missing-middle infill townhome scale fit the surrounding corridor near existing transit and commercial nodes. Despite voting against the annexation mechanism, Council Member Baker joined his colleagues in supporting the zoning density, passing the ordinance unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 25: Consistency Statement (N.C.G.S. 160D-605) – Danube Lane Townhouses
votes.notes: Statutory consistency finding with the Comprehensive Plan.
votes.discussion_detail: As required under North Carolina General Statutes Section 160D-605, Council considered the formal consistency statement affirming the Danube Lane PDR 7.813 rezoning aligns with Durham's Comprehensive Plan Place Type map. No additional debate occurred on the statutory finding. On a motion and second, the consistency statement was adopted unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 26: UDO Zoning Map Change Ordinance (RR & RS-10 to PDR 25.000) – Brier Creek Multifamily
votes.notes: 16.56 acres south of Andrews Chapel Rd / east of Cozart Rd; up to 408 units (383 MF, 25 TH); 5% at 80% AMI for 30 yrs; $50k housing fund; $16.5k DPS.
votes.discussion_detail: Applicant attorney Worth Mills presented the 16.56-acre Brier Creek Multifamily project straddling the Durham-Wake boundary, highlighting proffers of 5% units at 80% AMI for 30 years, $50,000 for the Dedicated Affordable Housing Fund, $16,500 for DPS, 100% native plantings, and full street/sidewalk connectivity coordinated with Raleigh. Council Member Baker critiqued the surrounding car-dependent suburban sprawl pattern while acknowledging infill proximity to existing Brier Creek amenities, and Council Member Freeman criticized pro-development speaker Andy Lowe (Center for New Liberalism) while urging deeper partnerships with Durham affordable housing providers. After Caballero, Middleton, Rist, and Williams praised the developer's responsiveness and added housing supply, Council approved the rezoning unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 26: Utility Extension Agreement with Monts Ridge LLC – Brier Creek Multifamily
votes.notes: Authorizes City Manager to enter into UEA with Monts Ridge LLC (site already inside city jurisdiction).
votes.discussion_detail: Following the zoning map approval for Brier Creek Multifamily, Council considered the companion motion authorizing the City Manager to execute a Utility Extension Agreement with Monts Ridge LLC to serve the 408-unit development. Because the Durham portion of the site was already within municipal limits, no annexation vote was required. Council approved the utility extension agreement unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 26: Consistency Statement (N.C.G.S. 160D-605) – Brier Creek Multifamily
votes.notes: Statutory consistency finding under N.C.G.S. 160D-605; meeting adjourned immediately after at 10:12 PM.
votes.discussion_detail: To finalize the Brier Creek Multifamily rezoning, Council voted on the statutory consistency statement under N.C.G.S. 160D-605 confirming the PDR 25.000 zoning aligns with Durham's Comprehensive Plan. No additional questions were raised following the earlier project discussion. The consistency statement passed unanimously 7-0, and Mayor Williams adjourned the meeting at 10:12 PM.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting May 19, 2025 (with closed captioning)
disagreements.issue: Non-Contiguous 'Doughnut Hole' Slivers and Trail Connectivity on Danube Lane Townhouses (Item 25)
disagreements.summary: Council Member Baker opposed annexing the 5.04-acre Danube Lane parcel due to unannexed county slivers and incomplete greenway construction, while six colleagues supported the project as compatible missing-middle housing.
disagreements.side_a_position: Oppose the annexation/UEA creating unannexed 'doughnut hole' county slivers and lacking full greenway trail construction.
side_a_arguments: Leave-behind county pockets complicate municipal service delivery and leave jagged jurisdictional boundaries.
Dedicating an easement without building the greenway segment misses an opportunity to connect active transportation links.
disagreements.side_b_position: Approve the consolidated annexation and rezoning for 30 missing-middle townhomes/duplexes.
side_b_arguments: The project provides needed missing-middle infill housing near major corridors alongside a $10,000 affordable housing fund contribution.
Planning Commission recommended approval 12-0 and the applicant worked within existing site constraints.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and UEA passed 6-1 (Baker No); the companion zoning map change and consistency statement passed 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting May 19, 2025 (with closed captioning)
disagreements.issue: Peripheral Car-Centric Land Use Pattern and Advocacy Critique on Brier Creek Multifamily (Item 26)
disagreements.summary: Although Council ultimately approved the 408-unit Brier Creek Multifamily project 7-0, Council Members Baker and Freeman voiced sharp criticisms of peripheral car-centric growth and outside advocacy framing.
disagreements.side_a_position: Critique the broader land-use pattern of building dense apartments in car-dependent peripheral areas without transit and question outside YIMBY advocacy rhetoric.
side_a_arguments: Approving high-density housing on the Wake County border far from frequent transit entrenches automobile dependency (Baker).
Outside groups claiming to champion affordability often rubber-stamp market-rate development without building substantive partnerships with local affordable housing organizations (Freeman).
disagreements.side_b_position: Praise the developer's responsive proffers (5% at 80% AMI for 30 years, $50,000 housing fund, $16,500 DPS, native plantings) and support adding multifamily housing supply near jobs and retail.
side_b_arguments: The parcel sits inside existing city boundaries adjacent to existing Brier Creek commercial retail and employment corridors.
The applicant increased school and housing commitments directly in response to neighborhood and Planning Commission feedback.
disagreements.resolution: Despite policy reservations expressed during debate, all seven members voted Aye on the zoning map change, UEA, and consistency statement (7-0).

development_cases.location: 3824 and 3910 Danube Lane (north and south of Carver Street)
development_cases.scale: Up to 30 dwelling units (mix of townhouses and duplexes) on 5.04 acres (2 parcels)
development_cases.zoning_change: RS-20 (County) to PDR 7.813 (City) with Falls/Jordan District B Watershed Overlay (Annexation & Utility Extension Agreement)

proffers.affordable_housing: $10,000 one-time donation to the Affordable Housing Fund (added at hearing)
proffers.environmental_tree: No construction on environmentally sensitive parcel north of Carver Street (kept permanently as open space); 100% native landscaping plants
proffers.transit_infrastructure: Dedication of greenway easement for future Cub Creek Trail; construction of bus bump-out/pad or shelter on Carver Street or Danube Lane
other_proffers: Permanent open space transition south of adjacent Danube townhomes

member_justifications.stance_summary: Cook questioned DPS's projection of zero added students from 30 townhomes and duplexes and pressed staff on how consistency with the Recreation and Open Space place type and bus pad vs. shelter decisions are made. At the hearing, she secured a formal $10,000 one-time proffer to the Affordable Housing Fund and clarified the Cub Creek greenway easement timing.
member_justifications.key_quote: To me when I see these numbers it feels ridiculous because certainly there's going to be more than zero students added.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Baker objected to remaining county 'doughnut hole' parcel slivers and right-of-way gaps left unannexed around the site, and pressed the applicant on why they committed only to a greenway easement rather than trail construction and whether units would have front-loaded garages or backyards. He voted NAY on the 6-1 annexation/UEA ordinance before voting AYE on the unanimous 7-0 zoning map change.
member_justifications.key_quote: I think we'd want to avoid as we grow and annex land keeping little remaining slivers of parcels that are county.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Caballero noted that the adjacent 400-plus-unit Cub Creek Station development had only dedicated a greenway easement rather than constructing the trail. She argued a 30-unit infill project could not reasonably be expected to fund trail construction through sensitive areas.
member_justifications.key_quote: For a development that has over 400 units, I can't imagine one that has 30 units would have the money to build a trail.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Rist praised the proposal as the exact kind of thoughtful infill project Durham wants to see, highlighting the future trail easement, Affordable Housing Fund contribution, and infrastructure commitments.
member_justifications.key_quote: This is the kind of infill project we love to see in Durham.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Middleton supported the infill development and backed the Planning Commission's recommendation, noting that council had previously approved smaller projects offering far fewer proffers.
member_justifications.key_quote: I've seen projects this size and smaller not do as much as this one that we've approved.

development_cases.location: South of Andrews Chapel Road and east of Cozart Road (crossing Durham and Wake County line)
development_cases.scale: Up to 408 dwelling units (maximum 383 multifamily apartments and 25 townhouses) on 16.56 acres
development_cases.zoning_change: RR and RS-10 to PDR 25.000 (with Utility Extension Agreement with Monts Ridge LLC)

proffers.dps_cash: $16,500 (increased at hearing from $10,000)
proffers.affordable_housing: 5% of all units at 80% AMI for 30 years plus $50,000 one-time donation to the Dedicated Affordable Housing Fund (added at hearing)
proffers.environmental_tree: 100% of street trees, vehicle use areas, and vegetative plantings to be NC native species; wooded Neuse River buffer preserved as passive open space
proffers.transit_infrastructure: 10-ft multi-use path along Andrews Chapel Road frontage; off-site 5-ft sidewalk (~175 ft) west to existing sidewalk stub toward roundabout (subject to existing right-of-way or requested easements); right-of-way dedication for ACC Boulevard
other_proffers: 30-ft wide, 0.6 opacity landscape buffer along western boundary adjacent to existing townhomes
Multifamily buildings within 250 ft of Towns at Brier Creek capped at 4 stories / 60 ft (general multifamily 5 stories / 75 ft; townhomes 3 stories / 35 ft)

member_justifications.stance_summary: Middleton secured confirmation of the 30-year affordability commitment and commended the applicant's responsiveness to Planning Commission feedback. He supported the project as appropriate multifamily density directly adjacent to major Brier Creek shopping and services.
member_justifications.key_quote: This is the type of development you would want in an area like that with these commercial developments out there.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Baker praised the development team's good-will responsiveness on proffers, while delivering a sweeping critique of auto-dependent suburban development patterns in the corridor as fundamentally broken. He argued individual developers cannot be forced to supply green buildings, public plazas, and mixed uses without systemic UDO rewrites, and ultimately joined the 7-0 approval.
member_justifications.key_quote: I find that the context of this area and the planning and development is happening out there, and this site most likely included, is fundamentally broken and flawed in the way we build our city.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Caballero agreed with Baker's urban design critique while noting Durham is reacting to Wake County's Brier Creek commercial node and constrained by North Carolina's Dillon's Rule limits on municipal mandates. She praised the applicant for meeting Planning Commission requests on DPS, affordable housing, and native trees.
member_justifications.key_quote: We cannot demand sustainability best practices, we have to ask for them.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Rist supported the rezoning because it meets Mixed Residential Neighborhood density goals, connects sidewalks toward a bus route 0.6 miles away, and delivers 5% affordable housing alongside added cash proffers.
member_justifications.key_quote: The way I see this, you certainly are meeting the density we seek in a Mixed Residential Neighborhood.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Williams echoed Dillon's Rule constraints and warned that excessive proffer demands can get passed on to future renters and buyers. He voted yes because the improved package was closer to good than bad.
member_justifications.key_quote: I'll be supporting it because I think it's closer to good than bad.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Freeman appreciated the 0.6 opacity buffer, 100% native plantings, and added DPS/housing proffers, though she voiced lingering concerns about the lack of a binding commitment dispersing open space across the site. She encouraged the applicant to partner with local affordable housing providers at buildout.
member_justifications.key_quote: I do have some concerns about the open space protections, and I do have some concerns about where those open spaces will be, but do feel comfortable.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session for May 8, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: At the May 8, 2025 work session with six members present and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton previously excused, Council granted an excused absence for Council Member Javiera Caballero for May 22, accepted the City Manager's priority items, and voted 6-0 to hold a closed session on *Town of Chapel Hill v. City of Durham*. Council reviewed pulled consent items covering the FY 2026 Planning Work Program, Legal Aid DEAR contract, Hillandale Golf Course driving range expansion, the Cultural Roadmap timeline, and conveying surplus skate park equipment to The Scrap Exchange, and heard the Durham Racial Equity Commission's 2024 Annual Report highlighting wealth, traffic-stop, jury, and housing disparities. Council then discussed and placed Mayor Williams's resolution opposing NC House Bill 765 onto the May 19 General Business Agenda and settled the May 19 agenda 6-0 before entering closed session.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Excused Absence Request, Priority Items, and Closed Session Motion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams convened the session with six members present and Mark-Anthony Middleton previously excused. Council approved an excused absence for Javiera Caballero for May 22 (6-0), received the City Manager's priority items—Item 5 DREC Annual Report and Item 24 FY 2025-26 Budget presentation (6-0)—and approved holding a closed session at the end of the meeting regarding *Town of Chapel Hill v. City of Durham*, 85 CVS 3108 (6-0).

agenda_items.title: Citizen Matters
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Two speakers addressed Council during Citizen Matters: Robin raised concerns about OEWD delayed grant disbursements via MFA for small business/workforce services, and DeWarren Langley of the Charles Hamilton Houston Foundation discussed community initiatives.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Items 3 and 4 (FY26 Planning Work Program & Legal Aid DEAR Contract)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Members Baker and Rist questioned planning staff on Item 3 (FY 2026 Planning Work Program) regarding UDO rewrite sequencing and staffing bandwidth, while Council Member Rist asked questions on Item 4 regarding the Legal Aid of North Carolina / Durham Expunction and Restoration (DEAR) contract.

agenda_items.title: Durham Racial Equity Commission (DREC) 2024 Annual Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DREC representatives Nisha Williams and Elena Snavely presented the commission's 2024 report examining disparities across criminal legal systems (traffic stops and jury inclusivity with Duke Sanford/Clerk of Court), housing, health, and wealth, recommending bold policies such as rent stabilization, guaranteed income expansion, and livable wages. Council members engaged in substantive discussion over local wealth data sources, Duke University contributions, bold policymaking without fear of state backlash, and whether future reports should include resident-facing recommendations alongside institutional reforms.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Items 13, 15, and 18 (Hillandale Golf, Cultural Roadmap, Scrap Exchange Skate Park)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council questioned staff on Item 13 (design-build renovation of Hillandale Golf Course's driving range and putting area benefiting youth programs like Swing Pals and First Tee), Item 15 (extending Phase 3 of the Cultural Roadmap into late fall 2025/spring 2026 after a four-year process), and Item 18 (donating surplus Wheels modular skate park ramps under N.C.G.S. 160A-280 to The Scrap Exchange for a free public skate park).

agenda_items.title: Resolution Opposing NC House Bill 765 and Settling May 19, 2025 Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams introduced Item 27 opposing North Carolina House Bill 765 alongside bipartisan I-85 Corridor mayors and the NC League of Municipalities, with Council Members Freeman and Caballero strongly endorsing the defense of Section 160D local land-use powers. Council then settled the May 19 meeting agenda (Consent Items 1-23; GBA Items 24 & 27; GBA Public Hearings 25 & 26) by 6-0 voice vote and recessed into closed session at 3:00 PM.

votes.item_title: Excused Absence for Council Member Javiera Caballero for May 22, 2025 Work Session
votes.notes: Mark-Anthony Middleton was absent (previously excused on May 5).
votes.discussion_detail: Near the opening of the May 8 work session, Council Member Javiera Caballero requested an excused absence in advance for the upcoming May 22, 2025 work session. With Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton absent on a previously approved excuse, six council members were present. Following a motion and second, Council unanimously granted Caballero's excused absence by a 6-0 voice vote.

votes.item_title: Motion to Receive City Manager's Priority Items (Items 5 and 24)
votes.notes: Priority Items: Item 5 (DREC 2024 Annual Report) at May 8 work session; Item 24 (FY25-26 Proposed Budget & CIP) at May 19 Council meeting.
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager Bo Ferguson presented two priority items for Council's schedule: Item 5, the Durham Racial Equity Commission's 2024 Annual Report for immediate presentation at the work session, and Item 24, the FY 2025-26 Proposed Budget and FY 2026-31 CIP presentation scheduled for the May 19 regular meeting. No objections or modifications were raised by members. Council unanimously voted 6-0 by voice vote to receive the priority items.

votes.item_title: Motion to Hold Closed Session (Town of Chapel Hill v. City of Durham, 85 CVS 3108)
votes.notes: Pursuant to N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3) for attorney-client consultation; held at end of meeting at 3:00 PM.
votes.discussion_detail: City Attorney staff requested a closed session at the conclusion of the May 8 work session pursuant to N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3) to consult with the City Attorney and preserve attorney-client privilege regarding pending litigation in *Town of Chapel Hill v. City of Durham*, Wake/Orange/Durham Superior Court file 85 CVS 3108. Council voted unanimously 6-0 by voice vote to authorize the closed session. After completing the public agenda, Mayor Williams confirmed the earlier vote and moved members into the Council conference room at 3:00 PM, adjourning afterward.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session for May 8, 2025
disagreements.issue: Scope of Durham Racial Equity Commission Recommendations: Institutional Change vs. Individual Action & Backlash Risk
disagreements.summary: Following DREC's 2024 Annual Report, Council members differed in emphasis between pushing bold structural policies regardless of state backlash, investigating Duke's tax/resource equity, and adding individual resident-level action steps.
disagreements.side_a_position: Focus squarely on bold institutional, wealth-disparity, rent-stabilization, and livable-wage reforms rather than legislating out of fear of state pushback or shifting responsibility onto individuals.
side_a_arguments: Racial equity work is fundamentally systemic because residents do not control government purse strings or macroeconomic structures.

Durham should lead boldly on policies like rent stabilization, wealth data tracking, and equitable contributions from major institutions like Duke rather than self-censoring over potential state backlash.
disagreements.side_b_position: Include parallel recommendations for individual residents alongside institutional reforms so residents also see steps to position themselves to access opportunities.
side_b_arguments: While government bears primary responsibility, having a complete picture requires empowering individuals with actionable steps to connect to programs and services.
disagreements.resolution: DREC presenters agreed to consider resident-facing guidance while reiterating that DREC's core charge is evaluating government institutions and policies.
