meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting February 17, 2025 with closed captioning
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council approved its Consent Agenda (excluding pulled Items 11 and 12), accepted the Homeless Services Advisory Committee Annual Report, appointed Tasha D. Melvin to the Homeless Services Advisory Committee, and unanimously approved two major land-use cases: the Polanco Residence annexation and the 23.2-acre Hoover Road Assemblage rezoning for up to 402 residential units. Council referred Item 12 (an amendment to the UMCNC MWBE/Section 3 compliance contract) back to staff after a motion by Mayor Pro Tem Middleton to approve it immediately died for lack of a second. Members and the City Manager also addressed community anxiety following recent targeted federal ICE operations in Durham and welcomed local youth advocates from POOF and Haven 360 Project.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Proclamation for EPIC Day & Council Comments on ICE Operations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams called the roll with all seven Council members present and issued a proclamation declaring February 17, 2025 as Empowered Parents in Community (EPIC) Day. Mayor Williams and City Manager Bo Ferguson addressed recent federal ICE enforcement activity in Durham, affirming that the Durham Police Department does not act as an extension of federal immigration enforcement. Council members also discussed eviction court hardship, federal funding uncertainties, employee retention gains following budget pay increases, and heard from youth speakers affiliated with POOF and Haven 360 Project.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1, 3-10, 13-32; excluding pulled Items 11 and 12)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager noted supplemental information on Item 12 and the earlier HOPWA presentation under Item 35, and the City Clerk read the Consent Agenda. Items 11 and 12 were pulled for public comment and separate discussion, while Item 25 was briefly mentioned by Council Member Baker before being left on consent. Council adopted the remaining Consent Agenda items unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Homeless Services Advisory Committee (HSAC) Annual Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Item 11 was pulled for public speaker Sarah D'Amato of Legal Aid of North Carolina's Eviction Diversion Program, who urged Council to sustain investments in eviction prevention and homeless services amid rising demand. Council members thanked HSAC and community partners for their work across the Continuum of Care. Council voted unanimously to accept the annual report.

agenda_items.title: Amendment No. 1 to Contract #18421 with United Minority Contractors of North Carolina, Inc. (UMCNC)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Carl Rist requested additional firm-level details and contract dollar data regarding MWBE, Workforce, Section 3, and Davis-Bacon compliance monitoring before voting on Amendment No. 1, and Community Development Director Reginald Johnson offered to supply the breakdown. Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton argued there was no valid reason to delay the contract amendment and moved to approve it, but the motion received no second. Mayor Williams referred Item 12 back to staff to return with the requested firm-level information.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Referred back to staff (motion died for lack of second)

agenda_items.title: Appointment to the Durham Homeless Services Advisory Committee (Non-Profit Organization Category)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a tie between Tasha D. Melvin and Drew Wooten at the February 6 work session when two Council members were absent, the City Clerk polled the full Council and reported a majority in favor of Tasha D. Melvin. Council voted unanimously to appoint Tasha D. Melvin to the Durham Homeless Services Advisory Committee.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation - Polanco Residence (4873 Stanley Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a voluntary non-contiguous annexation petition for 0.529 acres at 4873 Stanley Road owned by Rodrigo Polanco and Yenis Carolina Morales, with direct translational zoning to RS-20 in the Falls/Jordan Watershed District B. The applicants' surveyor Mary Elizabeth and contractor Bryan Sawyer explained the request was driven by septic system failure and the need for city sewer service. After the public hearing closed with no opposition, Council unanimously approved the annexation/utility extension agreement, zoning map change, and consistency statement.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change - Hoover Road Assemblage
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff and attorney Patrick Byker presented a rezoning of 63 parcels totaling 23.204 acres west of Miami Boulevard and Hoover Road from RU-5, RU-5(2), and CN to PDR 17.325 for up to 402 residential units, including at least 25% townhomes and dedicated affordable housing with Durham Habitat for Humanity participation. Council members questioned native tree preservation, green infrastructure, the 20-year versus 30-year affordability commitment split between apartments and townhomes, and the removal of four Neighborhood Services Place Type parcels along Miami Boulevard. Following discussion, Council unanimously approved the utility extension agreement, rezoning ordinance, and plan consistency statement.

agenda_items.title: Bull City Futures Fund Clarification & Mayor Excused Absence Request
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman clarified funding distinctions between city resources and the privately raised Bull City Futures Fund for youth-serving nonprofits like POOF. Mayor Williams requested an excused absence for the February 20 work session due to scheduling and expected winter weather, passing the gavel briefly to Mayor Pro Tem Middleton for the vote. Council approved the excused absence by voice vote and adjourned at 8:41 p.m.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Excused absence approved by voice vote

votes.item_title: Adoption of Consent Agenda (Items 1, 3-10, 13-32; excluding Items 11 and 12)
votes.notes: Items 11 and 12 were pulled for separate consideration; Item 2 was previously placed on the General Business Agenda.
votes.discussion_detail: Following priority item updates from the City Manager and reading of the agenda by the City Clerk, Council members pulled Items 11 and 12 for public comment and additional scrutiny. Council Member Nate Baker initially inquired about Item 25 before retracting the pull so it remained on consent. With all seven seated Council members present, the motion to adopt the remaining Consent Agenda passed unanimously 7-0 via electronic voting.

votes.item_title: Item 11: Acceptance of the Homeless Services Advisory Committee Annual Report
votes.notes: Pulled from consent for public comment.
votes.discussion_detail: Item 11 was pulled from the Consent Agenda to hear registered speaker Sarah D'Amato from Legal Aid's Eviction Diversion Program. D'Amato highlighted eviction pressure facing Durham tenants and urged continued city support for eviction prevention and homeless services coordination. Council members thanked the committee and service providers for their annual reporting and unanimously voted 7-0 to accept the report.

votes.item_title: Item 2: Appointment of Tasha D. Melvin to the Durham Homeless Services Advisory Committee (Non-Profit Organization Category)
votes.notes: Resolved earlier February 6 work session tie after full Council polling by the City Clerk.
votes.discussion_detail: This General Business Agenda appointment had been placed on the voting agenda after the February 6 work session ended in a split decision between Tasha D. Melvin and Drew Wooten while two Council members were absent. The City Clerk reported that after polling Council Member Javiera Caballero and tallying full Council preferences, Tasha D. Melvin held the majority support. Council then formally voted 7-0 to appoint Melvin to the Non-Profit Organization seat on HSAC.

votes.item_title: Item 33 (Part 1): Consolidated Annexation Ordinance and Utility Extension Agreement - Polanco Residence (4873 Stanley Road)
votes.notes: 0.529-acre non-contiguous satellite annexation for single-family home experiencing septic failure.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff presented the voluntary annexation and utility extension agreement for a 0.529-acre single-family parcel at 4873 Stanley Road contiguous to existing satellite city limits. Representative Mary Elizabeth and contractor Bryan Sawyer testified that property owners Rodrigo Polanco and Yenis Carolina Morales needed municipal sewer access due to septic system issues. With no speakers in opposition during the public hearing, Council voted unanimously 7-0 to adopt the annexation ordinance and utility extension agreement.

votes.item_title: Item 33 (Part 2): UDO Zoning Map Change to RS-20 - Polanco Residence (4873 Stanley Road)
votes.notes: Direct translational zoning from County RS-20 to City RS-20 (Falls/Jordan Watershed District B); Mayor confirmed Council Member Cook's clicker registered.
votes.discussion_detail: Following approval of the annexation, Council considered the accompanying translational zoning map amendment to establish City RS-20 zoning in the Falls/Jordan District B watershed overlay. No modifications to density or permitted residential uses were sought beyond existing county zoning. After confirming all electronic voting clickers recorded properly, the clerk announced the motion passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 33 (Part 3): Plan Consistency Statement - Polanco Residence (4873 Stanley Road)
votes.notes: Statutory consistency finding accompanying RS-20 zoning adoption.
votes.discussion_detail: Staff confirmed the translational RS-20 designation aligned with applicable comprehensive plan policies for existing single-family residential parcels near satellite municipal services. Council moved and seconded the required statutory plan consistency statement without further debate. The consistency statement passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 34 (Part 1): Utility Extension Agreement with Hoover-Damn Investment, LLC - Hoover Road Assemblage
votes.notes: Utility extension agreement covering 23.204-acre assemblage for up to 402 units including Habitat for Humanity townhomes.
votes.discussion_detail: Attorney Patrick Byker presented the Hoover Road Assemblage on behalf of local owners including Durham Habitat for Humanity, detailing commitments for at least 25% townhomes, a $13,000 proffer to Durham Public Schools, and 20-year apartment and 30-year townhome affordability terms. PAC District 5 voiced support, while Council members questioned native tree preservation (Cook), 20-year vs. 30-year affordability duration (Baker), and the loss of Neighborhood Services commercial frontage along Miami Boulevard (Rist). Satisfied that the project provided substantial attainable housing within the urban growth boundary, Council approved the utility extension agreement 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 34 (Part 2): UDO Zoning Map Change (RU-5/RU-5(2)/CN to PDR 17.325) - Hoover Road Assemblage
votes.notes: Covers 63 parcels totaling 23.204 acres west of Miami Boulevard and Hoover Road for up to 402 residential units.
votes.discussion_detail: Council voted on the zoning map amendment to rezone the 63-parcel assemblage to Planned Development Residential 17.325 with a development plan capping density at 402 units. While Council Member Rist noted regret over converting four parcels designated Neighborhood Services on the Place Type map into strictly residential zoning, he and the rest of Council weighed the affordable homeownership and multifamily supply positively. The rezoning passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 34 (Part 3): Plan Consistency Statement - Hoover Road Assemblage
votes.notes: Adopted comprehensive plan consistency finding for PDR 17.325 rezoning.
votes.discussion_detail: Council considered the statutory plan consistency statement acknowledging the residential transition of four Neighborhood Services Place Type parcels along Miami Boulevard in favor of broader housing affordability and transit-adjacent infill goals. Members had completed policy questions on environmental commitments and retail frontage prior to closing the hearing. The consistency statement passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Excused Absence Request for Mayor Leonardo Williams (February 20, 2025 Work Session)
votes.notes: Mayor Williams yielded the gavel to Mayor Pro Tem Middleton to facilitate the vote on his own excused absence request.
votes.discussion_detail: At the close of Other Matters, Mayor Leonardo Williams requested an excused absence for the upcoming Thursday, February 20, 2025 Council work session due to scheduling constraints and anticipated inclement weather. Mayor Williams yielded facilitation briefly to Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton so the body could act cleanly on the request. A motion was moved, seconded, and approved unanimously by voice vote with no opposition.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting February 17, 2025 with closed captioning
disagreements.issue: Item 12 (UMCNC MWBE/Section 3 Consulting Contract Amendment #1) Readiness vs. Referral Back to Staff
disagreements.summary: Mayor Pro Tem Middleton moved to approve Amendment No. 1 to Contract #18421 immediately, whereas Council Member Rist sought firm-level subcontractor and dollar breakdowns first; Middleton's motion died for lack of a second and Mayor Williams referred the item back to staff.
disagreements.side_a_position: Hold the contract amendment and refer back to Community Development staff until firm-level MWBE, Workforce, Section 3, and Davis-Bacon contract data are provided in writing.
side_a_arguments: Following concerns raised at the February 6 work session, Council still lacked firm-specific names and dollar figures showing exact subcontractor participation and compliance deliverables.
Community Development Director Reginald Johnson indicated staff could compile and provide the firm-level amounts if referred back.
disagreements.side_b_position: Approve Amendment No. 1 immediately without further delay.
side_b_arguments: There was no substantive flaw demonstrated with UMCNC's compliance monitoring work or the contract amendment itself.
Delaying approval unnecessarily slows down active compliance oversight on federally and locally funded housing projects.
disagreements.resolution: Middleton's motion to approve received no second, and Mayor Williams referred Item 12 back to staff to bring back additional firm-level data.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting February 17, 2025 with closed captioning
disagreements.issue: Loss of Neighborhood Services Commercial Frontage on Miami Boulevard in Hoover Road Assemblage (Item 34)
disagreements.summary: Council Member Rist expressed concern over converting four Miami Boulevard frontage parcels designated Neighborhood Services on the Place Type map into purely residential PDR zoning, while the applicant and full Council ultimately prioritized the 402-unit housing and Habitat townhome package.
disagreements.side_a_position: Preserve Neighborhood Services commercial/walkable retail nodes along major corridors rather than allowing exclusively residential development to consume commercial Place Type frontage.
side_a_arguments: Four parcels along Miami Boulevard were designated Neighborhood Services to support neighborhood-scale commercial amenities and walkable services.
Replacing designated commercial frontage solely with apartments reduces future retail access for surrounding East Durham residents.
disagreements.side_b_position: Approve the residential PDR 17.325 rezoning to maximize housing units and support Durham Habitat for Humanity homeownership.
side_b_arguments: The 23.2-acre assemblage delivers up to 402 units including at least 25% townhomes and dedicated long-term affordable units in partnership with Habitat for Humanity.
Residential density and attainable housing within the urban growth boundary outweigh retaining commercial zoning on those four frontage parcels.
disagreements.resolution: Passed unanimously 7-0 after debate.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Acknowledged the Durham Public Schools proffer and pressed the applicant on whether they could commit to Comprehensive Plan Policies 101 and 108 regarding native trees, plants, and green infrastructure. Accepted the ownership team's explanation that committing to specific green infrastructure parameters was difficult before selecting a builder.
member_justifications.key_quote: I was wondering if there were any proffers you could make around that.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Welcomed the Sedge/Saider street grid connection and agreed that closing a northern stub was reasonable due to high-tension power line easements, as well as removing the Neighborhood Services designation given heavy commercial and industrial uses directly east across Miami Boulevard. Pressed the applicant to extend apartment affordability from 20 years to 30 years as Planning Commissioners suggested, though he accepted their explanation of multifamily financing constraints.
member_justifications.key_quote: I'm comfortable with us being able to change that. ... A lot of Planning Commissioners commented that 20 years, it'd be better if it was 30 years. Is that something interested in proffering?

member_justifications.stance_summary: Praised the local ownership group, community engagement, infill location, and DPS proffer, while raising concerns about removing the Neighborhood Services place type along Miami Boulevard given long-term 15-minute city goals and nearby projects like Brickworks. Was reassured that Brickworks and Wellons Village will provide walkable commercial options nearby.
member_justifications.key_quote: What I'm concerned about is if we take away the Neighborhood Services now, are we going to say 10 years from now, now we've got housing to the street there, we'd really appreciate having neighborhood services right there on that frontage?

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supported the rezoning as strong infill development inside the Urban Growth Boundary that cleans up a chronic illegal dumping ground and diversifies East Durham housing with mixed ownership and rental units. Noted that local owners lack the financial ledger of multinational developers, so he accepted the 20-year apartment affordability horizon alongside the 30-year townhome commitment.
member_justifications.key_quote: This is infill development which in my quest to keep fidelity with what I voted for the Urban Growth Boundary I place fidelity on good infill development. Not perfect but good.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Strongly supported the project and highlighted the value of having local Durham residents—rather than a Wall Street public company—invest in housing that meets community needs.
member_justifications.key_quote: It feels good to see folks that I see on a daily basis in the coffee shops or grocery store ... making an investment that responds to the needs we have in Durham as well, so, I am grateful for this project.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat - Feb 14, 2025 (livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council held Day 1 of its FY26 Budget Retreat, receiving comprehensive presentations on the preliminary $6.4M general fund baseline gap, statewide economic trends from EDPNC CEO Christopher Chung, the 2024 ETC Resident Satisfaction Survey, ETR Community Conversations, Strategic Plan alignment, the 2025 countywide property tax reappraisal (+74% projected city real property base increase), CIP debt capacity limits, and the FY26 Equitable Green Infrastructure (EGI) redesign. In the afternoon, Council members introduced 37 individual budget requests totaling roughly $36M alongside $32.4M in departmental requests, withdrawing or consolidating several overlapping asks. No formal votes were held, though members actively debated the preliminary prioritization ranking process, survey framing on policing versus deterrence, and equity/fiscal terminology.

agenda_items.title: Opening Remarks & FY26 Budget Outlook / Multi-Year Forecast
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Bo Ferguson framed the FY26 budget cycle around balancing immediate operational needs against long-term strategy using a chess-versus-checkers analogy. Budget and Management Services Director Christina Riordan reported FY25 property tax collections at roughly 94% of budget, slowing sales tax projected $2.6M under budget, phase-out of occupancy tax beginning FY26 (-$1.1M), personnel costs at 79% of the general fund with lower vacancies, and a $6.4M baseline gap before 135 departmental requests ($32.4M) and 37 Council requests.

agenda_items.title: Statewide Economic Development & Macro Workforce Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Economic Development Partnership of North Carolina CEO Christopher Chung presented statewide corporate recruitment trends, noting 95% of active pipelines are industrial/manufacturing rather than pre-pandemic office headquarters and highlighting workforce bottlenecks such as child care, housing affordability, power demand from AI data centers, and remote-work office vacancies. Council members engaged Chung on worker-rights rankings, managing rapid in-migration (~500 new residents monthly in Durham), and potential impacts of federal immigration tightening on construction, health care, and hospitality.

agenda_items.title: 2024 Resident Satisfaction Survey Results (ETC Institute)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: ETC Institute Vice President Jason Morado presented results from 600 city respondents, showing 79% rate Durham an excellent or good place to live and customer service from city staff exceeding the U.S. average by 27 percentage points. Top community priorities remained public schools, affordable housing, police protection, street maintenance, and sidewalks, while public school ratings and Hispanic respondents' perceptions of safety and race relations declined. Council members asked for 10-year longitudinal trends, transit ridership cross-tabs, and separate survey metrics distinguishing HEART/community safety from traditional policing.

agenda_items.title: FY26 Community Conversations Qualitative Engagement Report (ETR Services)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dr. Jen Gaffin and Kesha Martin of ETR Services reported findings from seven facilitated community conversations involving 359 attendees across libraries, Holton Center, Boys and Girls Club, and a Spanish-language session at El Futuro (over 75% people of color and 26% youth). Top qualitative themes were safe youth programming and employment above age 13, community-centered decision-making, crime deterrence and expanding HEART to youth, housing affordability, and park maintenance/remediation. Council praised improved data quality while debating whether sample sizes adequately represent Durham's 317,000 residents and how to better align quantitative and qualitative safety metrics.

agenda_items.title: Strategic Plan Alignment & Performance Measurement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Strategy and Initiatives Manager Sherri Mehta linked the ETC survey and Community Conversations to the FY24-26 Strategic Plan's five goals, 15 objectives, and 41 initiatives, while City Manager Ferguson explained that staff defaults to Council-sanctioned plan and engagement priorities unless Council specifies adjustments. Council members requested clearer outcome tracking showing where the city is meeting or falling short on strategic objectives alongside objective crime, housing-stock, and park-usage metrics.

agenda_items.title: 2025 Property Tax Reappraisal Preview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Durham County Tax Administrator Keyar Doyle previewed the 2025 six-year statutory reappraisal of ~127,000 parcels, showing Durham's median home sale price rose from $240,000 in 2019 to $416,000 in late 2024 and total city real property assessed value is projected to jump roughly 74% from $36B to $63B-$65B+. Doyle explained appeal deadlines tied to upcoming value notices, high commercial/office vacancy pressures expected to drive appeals, and how residential values outpacing commercial properties shift relative tax burden ahead of revenue-neutral tax rate calculations.

agenda_items.title: FY26 Capital Improvement Program (CIP) & Debt Capacity Preview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Assistant Budget Director JJ Scott reported 89 general capital project requests totaling $178M for FY26 against limited debt service fund capacity ($17M baseline capacity for FY26 under the existing 11.5-cent debt allocation) after honoring existing project commitments and asset maintenance. Scott also showed how the 2024 voter-approved bond expands annual street paving from $15M to $25M and adds $10M in sidewalk repair capacity while freeing some general CIP capacity.

agenda_items.title: FY26 Equitable Green Infrastructure (EGI) Program Redesign
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Business Services Administrator Mary Grace Stoneking outlined lessons from FY24 EGI ($17M across seven neighborhoods) and presented the redesigned biennial FY26 EGI model ($6M available from a dedicated half-penny tax plus modeled debt), narrowing focus areas to five smaller census-block-group clusters with paid community ambassadors. Mayor Pro Tem Middleton praised the substance but suggested considering less politically exposed terminology such as empowerment zones or focus areas, which staff noted they were already evaluating alongside Mayor Williams' call to reduce engagement silos.

agenda_items.title: Council Member FY26 Budget Requests Introduction & Prioritization Framework
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Innovation Manager Lindsay Gavin and City Manager Ferguson facilitated one-minute introductions of 37 Council budget requests, including Baby Bonds ($300k), Immigrant Legal Defense Fund expansion, firefighter cancer screenings ($60k), Economic Development Plan ($150k), Small Business Support Fund ($100k), recurring Guaranteed/Basic Income ($1M), 24/7 HEART expansion (Cook and Caballero consolidated), alternative and day shelters, Dolph affordable housing loan fund ($2M), living wage adjustments for seasonal/part-time workers (~$1.3M) and blended-average ordinance updates, fare-free buses (Cook and Baker consolidated), downtown loop/parking-deck redevelopment studies, Ujamaa Market, World University Games ($55k/yr), Carolina Theatre HVAC ($6-8M CIP), Lead in Parks remediation ($7M CIP), Solid Waste wash station, and Street Design Manual ($250k-$300k). Baker withdrew his comprehensive housing plan and Southeast Durham land use strategy, and Mayor Williams rescinded several crime/ShotSpotter items in favor of $100k Bull City Future Fund, $100k Task Force on Black Men and Boys, and $5k Youth Advisory Council; Council agreed to submit follow-up questions to staff before ranking.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat - Feb 14, 2025 (livestream)
disagreements.issue: Methodology and Timing of Ranking $36M in Council Budget Requests
disagreements.summary: Council members and the City Manager differed over whether to rank all 37 Council requests immediately after one-minute introductions before seeing tax revaluation numbers, departmental requests, and inter-member Q&A.
disagreements.side_a_position: Hold a deeper work-session deliberation and clarify double-counting, total fiscal impact, and staff overlap before ranking requests.
side_a_arguments: Putting forward $36M in Council asks alongside $32.4M in departmental requests risks triggering unrealistic public expectations or major tax hikes without prior trade-off discussions.
Members cannot score proposals accurately from one-minute snippets without questioning colleagues and confirming which items departments already submitted.
disagreements.side_b_position: Complete the online ranking exercise promptly as non-binding conceptual guidance to inform the manager ahead of Retreat Day 2.
side_b_arguments: The preliminary ranking helps the City Manager understand relative Council priorities conceptually while actual cost vetting and balanced-budget cuts happen later.
Further deliberation is already built into the February 28 second retreat after revaluation and departmental updates arrive.
disagreements.resolution: Manager Bo Ferguson agreed to collect Council questions over the weekend and add requested clarifications to the Thursday work session agenda, confirming rankings remain non-binding advisory guidance.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat - Feb 14, 2025 (livestream)
disagreements.issue: Interpreting Resident Priorities on Policing vs. Non-Police Crime Deterrence
disagreements.summary: Council members clashed over whether ETC survey and Community Conversations data indicate support primarily for policing or for non-police prevention/deterrence investments.
disagreements.side_a_position: Community engagement shows residents prioritize crime prevention, economic opportunity, youth spaces, and alternative responders like HEART rather than expanding traditional policing.
side_a_arguments: Survey framing conflates broad feelings about safety with police protection and omits dedicated evaluation of Community Safety / HEART services.
Qualitative Community Conversations explicitly called for expanding HEART to youth and funding root-cause economic and community-engagement deterrents.
disagreements.side_b_position: Both traditional policing response to lethal gun violence and non-police tools remain critical priorities backed by residents.
side_b_arguments: ETC data demonstrate Black residents do not support defunding the police, and youth/neighborhood fatalities require immediate law-enforcement and violence-intervention capacity.
With 317,000+ residents, samples of 359 to 600 participants must be weighed alongside objective crime statistics and broader constituent outreach.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote; staff noted separate ETC police-survey results would be presented at the next work session.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat - Feb 14, 2025 (livestream)
disagreements.issue: Fiscal Terminology ('Deficit' vs. 'Budget Gap') and Equity Program Nomenclature
disagreements.summary: Mayor Pro Tem Middleton urged staff to stop describing the early-stage budget baseline projection as a 'deficit' and suggested reframing 'Equitable Green Infrastructure' nomenclature to protect equity investments from external political scrutiny.
disagreements.side_a_position: Retire alarmist or politically vulnerable labels ('deficit', 'Equitable Green Infrastructure') while preserving balanced-budget discipline and underlying equity criteria.
side_a_arguments: Because North Carolina cities must legally adopt balanced budgets, calling an early revenue-expenditure delta a 'deficit' misleads the public into thinking the city is running in the red.
Renaming EGI to 'empowerment zones' or 'areas of focus' protects essential infrastructure investments in underserved neighborhoods amid heightened statewide and federal scrutiny.
disagreements.side_b_position: Staff agreed to adjust 'deficit' to 'budget gap' and confirmed internal discussions are underway on making EGI's name more relatable, while Freeman and Baker emphasized maintaining transparency and accessibility.
side_b_arguments: Technical terms should communicate accurately to residents without obscuring how equity criteria target underserved census block groups.
disagreements.resolution: City Manager Ferguson adopted 'budget gap' and staff confirmed EGI rebranding options are under review.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session February 6, 2025
meetings.executive_summary: With five Council members present and Council Members Freeman and Caballero excused by unanimous 5-0 votes, the Durham City Council reviewed consent items ahead of the February 17 meeting and settled its agenda by a 5-0 vote. Residents used Citizens Matters to press for East Durham youth violence intervention, drug-activity enforcement near East Main and Laurel, and delayed $20,000 Momentum Financial Academy grants—prompting Deputy City Manager Chadwell and OEWD leadership to commit to a March 24, 2025 deadline to issue ~$260,000 using ARPA funds. Council pulled six items for questioning—highlighting debate over Item 12 (UMCNC compliance contract funding)—and held an extensive review of the HOPWA housing program following the abrupt collapse of subrecipient Central Piedmont Community Action.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Excused Absences & Tribute to Building Inspector Julian Arroyo
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams called the session to order with Middleton, Baker, Cook, and Rist present, and Council voted 5-0 to grant excused absences to DeDreana Freeman and Javiera Caballero (illness). Council members recounted a tour of the Durham Police Department Forensics Lab and mourned recent youth homicides, while Deputy City Manager Garland Keith Chadwell paid tribute to deceased Inspections building inspector Julian Arroyo.

agenda_items.title: Manager Priority Item (HOPWA Presentation) & Clerk BCC Appointment Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy City Manager Chadwell requested adding Item 35 (supplemental HOPWA presentation), which Council accepted 5-0. The City Clerk reported consensus appointments for the Recreation Advisory Commission (Michael Johnston) and DPAC Oversight Committee (Don Moffett, Alice L. Sharp), while a tie for the Durham Homeless Services Advisory Committee non-profit seat between Tasha D. Melvin and Drew Wooten moved the appointment to the General Business Agenda by a 5-0 vote.

agenda_items.title: Reading of Consent Agenda & Pulling of Items 12, 18, 19, 22, 25, 27, 28
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk read Items 1 through 35 for the upcoming February 17 Council meeting agenda. Council members pulled Items 12, 18, 19, 22, 25, and 27 (with Baker requesting Item 28 alongside Item 27) for discussion during the work session.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Items pulled for discussion / No vote

agenda_items.title: Youth Violence, East Durham Safety & Momentum Financial Academy Grant Delays
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Speakers Adwin Langley, Pastor Burris, and Ree Smith urged urgent intervention on East Durham gun violence and neighborhood drug activity near East Main and Laurel Streets. Business owner Shay Ramos protested a five-month delay in $20,000 Momentum Financial Academy grants; Acting OEWD Director Nixon and DCM Chadwell explained HUD CDBG environmental-review hurdles and committed to issuing ~$260,000 in checks to up to 13 cohort graduates via ARPA funds by a 45-day deadline of March 24, 2025.

agenda_items.title: Review of Pulled Consent Agenda Contracts
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council examined seven pulled items, notably debating Item 12 (UMCNC Amendment #1 for MWBE/Section 3 compliance) over using Dedicated Housing Funds and missing original contract backup, with staff asked to attach prior data before February 17. Members also questioned Item 18 (Turner & Townsend Heery Parks bond management), Item 19 (retroactive ratification of five FY25 festivals contracts), Item 22 (Bimbé Festival booking contract, clean-lyrics policies, and collections against prior defaulting contractor Mr. Weeks), Item 25 (stormwater PDAP cost-share), and Items 27-28 (ePlus Technology fiber network upgrades).
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational review prior to Feb 17 meeting

agenda_items.title: HOPWA (Housing Opportunities for Persons With AIDS) Program Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson and Homeless System Manager Colin Davis presented on the five-county HOPWA Emergency Services Metropolitan Statistical Area grant, explaining that subrecipient Central Piedmont Community Action abruptly closed operations, leaving landlords unpaid and forcing CDD to bring Tenant-Based Rental Assistance in-house ahead of a July 1 RFP. Council members criticized underutilization, landlord late fees paid from CDD general funds, and inadequate lived-experience input in designing the upcoming RFP.

agenda_items.title: Settling the February 17, 2025 City Council Meeting Agenda & USAID Resolution Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk settled the February 17 agenda with Consent Items 1 and 3-32, General Business Agenda Item 2, and Public Hearings Items 33-34 (noting Item 35 was completed). Council voted 5-0 to settle the agenda, and Mayor Williams noted ongoing regional collaboration on a joint resolution responding to federal USAID funding freezes affecting Triangle employers such as RTI before adjourning at 3:56 p.m.

votes.item_title: Motion to Grant Excused Absence for Council Member DeDreana Freeman
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman and Javiera Caballero absent at roll call.
votes.discussion_detail: At the start of the February 6, 2025 work session following roll call, the City Clerk noted that Council Member DeDreana Freeman had requested an excused absence. With five members seated in the chamber, a motion to excuse Freeman was moved and properly seconded. The motion passed unanimously 5-0 by roll call.

votes.item_title: Motion to Grant Excused Absence for Council Member Javiera Caballero
votes.notes: Clerk read Caballero's email requesting excused absence due to illness.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately following the vote on Council Member Freeman's absence, Council took up an email request from Council Member Javiera Caballero seeking an excused absence due to illness. No objections were raised by the five seated members. Council voted 5-0 via roll call to excuse Caballero.

votes.item_title: Acceptance of City Manager Priority Item (Supplemental Item 35 HOPWA Presentation)
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman and Javiera Caballero absent (excused).
votes.discussion_detail: Deputy City Manager Garland Keith Chadwell presented the City Manager's priority item adding a supplemental presentation on the Housing Opportunities for Persons With AIDS (HOPWA) program as Item 35. Council had requested the HOPWA briefing during its January 23 work session to inspect funding administration and partner performance. A motion to accept the Manager's priority item passed 5-0 on roll call.

votes.item_title: Acceptance of City Clerk Boards, Committees & Commissions Report (Placing Tied HSAC Appointment on GBA)
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman and Javiera Caballero absent (excused). Confirmed consensus nominees to Recreation Advisory Commission and DPAC Oversight Committee while sending tied HSAC seat to GBA.
votes.discussion_detail: The City Clerk reported board and commission polling results, confirming consensus for Michael Johnston on the Recreation Advisory Commission and Don Moffett and Alice L. Sharp on the DPAC Oversight Committee. However, the five members present split into a tie on the Homeless Services Advisory Committee non-profit representative between Tasha D. Melvin and Drew Wooten, requiring the item to move to the February 17 General Business Agenda as Item 2. Council voted 5-0 to receive the Clerk's report.

votes.item_title: Motion to Settle the February 17, 2025 City Council Meeting Agenda
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman and Javiera Caballero absent (excused). Settled Consent Items 1 and 3-32, GBA Item 2, and Public Hearings Items 33-34.
votes.discussion_detail: At the conclusion of the work session following pulled-item questioning and the HOPWA briefing, the City Clerk outlined the final placement of items for the February 17, 2025 City Council meeting. Consent items were set as Items 1 and 3 through 32, Item 2 (HSAC appointment) was placed on the General Business Agenda, and Items 33 and 34 were set as Public Hearings. Council voted 5-0 to settle the agenda.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session February 6, 2025
disagreements.issue: Item 12 (UMCNC Compliance Contract Amendment #1) Use of Dedicated Housing Funds & Backup Transparency
disagreements.summary: Council Member Cook questioned using Forever Home Durham / Dedicated Housing Fund dollars and lacking original contract backup for UMCNC compliance monitoring, while Mayor Pro Tem Middleton defended external compliance oversight.
disagreements.side_a_position: Scrutinize dedicating housing program funds to external compliance consulting and require full original contract documentation and MWBE attainment metrics before final approval.
side_a_arguments: Dedicated Housing Fund / Forever Home Durham dollars are scarce affordable housing capital, and Council needs to see the original contract scope and results before expanding it.
Staff had not attached the original contract or firm-level outcome breakdown to the agenda packet.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain independent third-party monitoring of MWBE, Workforce, Section 3, and Davis-Bacon obligations so the city does not grade its own compliance.
side_b_arguments: External oversight ensures independent verification of labor and minority/women business participation rather than relying solely on internal departmental self-reporting.
Reginald Johnson reported the project exceeded citywide MWBE targets (13% minority and 12% women participation versus 11%/7% goals).
disagreements.resolution: Staff agreed to attach the original contract and supporting compliance figures ahead of the February 17 Council meeting.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session February 6, 2025
disagreements.issue: Durham Homeless Services Advisory Committee (HSAC) Non-Profit Appointment Split
disagreements.summary: Council tied on the HSAC non-profit seat between Tasha D. Melvin and Drew Wooten with two members absent, sending the appointment to the General Business Agenda.
disagreements.side_a_position: Appoint Tasha D. Melvin to the HSAC Non-Profit Organization seat.
side_a_arguments: Supporters cited Melvin's qualifications and community background for the non-profit seat.
disagreements.side_b_position: Support Drew Wooten for the HSAC Non-Profit Organization seat (with remaining absent votes uncast).
side_b_arguments: Remaining votes favored Drew Wooten, creating an impasse with Freeman and Caballero absent.
disagreements.resolution: Placed on the February 17 General Business Agenda as Item 2; Clerk subsequently polled full Council and Melvin won a majority.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session February 6, 2025
disagreements.issue: HOPWA Program Oversight, Eviction Risks & Community Engagement Following Subrecipient Collapse
disagreements.summary: Council members pressed Community Development leadership over underutilization, landlord late fees, eviction filings, and lack of lived-experience input after Central Piedmont Community Action abruptly folded.
disagreements.side_a_position: CDD must embed client/lived-experience engagement into RFP design, improve grant utilization, and institute early-warning financial checks before subrecipients collapse.
side_a_arguments: Abrupt agency failure left clients facing unpaid rent, late fees covered out of CDD's general operating budget, and eviction filings.
Community partners and clients were not adequately engaged in shaping the upcoming July 1 RFP.
disagreements.side_b_position: CDD took emergency in-house stewardship of TBRA payments to prevent client displacement while preparing a competitive July 1 RFP.
side_b_arguments: Central Piedmont Community Action ceased operations abruptly with little advance notice, forcing rapid emergency transition in-house.
CDD staff committed to incorporating oversight lessons and communicating transitions more proactively.
disagreements.resolution: Informational briefing concluded with Council direction to tighten early-warning monitoring and stakeholder outreach for the July 1 RFP.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting February 3, 2025 (audio synched with closed captioning)
meetings.executive_summary: With five members present and Council Members Cook and Freeman previously excused, the Durham City Council adopted its Consent Agenda 5-0, approved the Gradient PLLC Algal Floway site-evaluation contract 5-0, and approved the 2613 Carpenter Road annexation and rezoning for up to 98 townhomes 5-0 after securing a greenway-construction proffer. Facing 89 registered speakers on two controversial land-use cases, Council reduced public comment time to one minute per speaker. After lengthy hearings, Council continued the Picket Apartments rezoning by consensus to March 17, 2025 for further work on bird-friendly design and trail connectivity, and voted 0-5 to reject the 168.37-acre Moriah Ridge annexation and rezoning across the Durham-Orange county line.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call & Council Comments on Immigration Enforcement, Refugee Funding & Public Safety
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams called the roll with Middleton, Baker, Caballero, and Rist present (Cook and Freeman excused at the January 23 work session). Council members commented on federal refugee-resettlement cuts, immigrant fear and Day Without Immigrants observances, the RDU1 Amazon union vote, recent shooting of a two-year-old in Durham, and Durham native Rebecca Lobach's death in the Washington, D.C. aviation crash.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1-7, 9, 14; excluding pulled Item 8)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager noted additional backup attached to Item 8 and the City Clerk read Consent Agenda Items 1 through 9 and 14 (Item 10 having been presented at the work session). Item 8 was pulled for public speakers, and Council unanimously adopted the remaining Consent Agenda 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Contract with Gradient PLLC for Site Evaluation and Identification for the Algal Floway Project
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Speakers Pamela Andrews and Robin Barefoot questioned whether the previous 2021 site study would be discarded and whether algae scrubbers perform effectively in North Carolina's climate. Public Works staff Jonathan Baker cited Durham's 2017 Falls Lake pilot results and explained the study builds on earlier data within Durham County, while Mayor Pro Tem Middleton stressed this contract funds site evaluation rather than construction. Council approved the contract, contingency, and amendment authorization 5-0 across three votes.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation - 2613 Carpenter Road
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Taken out of order prior to the longer hearings, staff and attorney Thomas H. Johnson Jr. presented a 18.29-acre contiguous annexation and rezoning from RR to PDR 5.587 for up to 98 townhomes (5% affordable) for SVK Carpenter Road LLC. Public speakers raised Panther Creek floodplain, traffic, and greenway trail concerns, prompting the applicant to accept Council Member Baker's request to proffer building the greenway trail inside the easement. Council unanimously approved the annexation/UEA, zoning map change, and consistency statement 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change - Picket Apartments (3117-3127 Picket Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Preceded by a five-minute recess and reduction of speaker time to one minute per person due to 89 cards across Items 11 and 13, attorney Neil Ghosh presented Ascension's proposal for up to 140 apartments (10% affordable) on 6.12 acres rezoned from RS-20 to PDR 36.176, adding $300,000 toward a Sandy Creek Trail connection, Energy Star certification, and bird-friendly window glass. Roughly 20 neighbors and bird conservationists opposed the scale, traffic near Durham Academy, flooding, and bird-strike risks. Despite Mayor Williams wanting to vote immediately, Caballero, Rist, and Middleton backed continuing the hearing; Mayor Williams reopened and continued the public hearing to March 17, 2025 by consensus.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Continued to March 17, 2025 by consensus (no roll-call vote)

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation - Moriah Ridge (Erwin Rd & Mt. Moriah Rd)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented M/I Homes of Raleigh LLC's 168.37-acre annexation and rezoning (PDR 7.34 for up to 1,000 residences and 2,500 sq ft office plus two RS-20 parcels) spanning the Durham-Orange County line, noting a corrected Fiscal Impact Analysis cut projected FY34 net fiscal gain from ~$27M to $5,363,462. Roughly 25 speakers opposed breaching the Urban Growth Boundary, cross-county school/tax mismatches with Orange County, unmapped streams, and land-acquisition conduct toward neighboring 'donut hole' owners. All five Council members voiced objections to approving the petition, and the motion to adopt the annexation and utility extension agreement failed 0-5; the meeting adjourned at 11:55 p.m.

votes.item_title: Adoption of Consent Agenda (Items 1-7, 9, 14; excluding pulled Item 8)
votes.notes: Chelsea Cook and DeDreana Freeman absent (excused at Jan 23 work session). Item 8 pulled for public comment.
votes.discussion_detail: Following manager priority item remarks noting supplemental materials on Item 8, the City Clerk read Consent Agenda Items 1 through 9 and 14. Item 8 was pulled to hear registered public speakers, while no other consent items were pulled by Council. With five seated members present and two excused absences, the remaining Consent Agenda passed unanimously 5-0.

votes.item_title: Item 8 (Motion 1): Authorize Contract with Gradient PLLC for Algal Floway Site Evaluation and Identification
votes.notes: Chelsea Cook and DeDreana Freeman absent (excused). Transcript ASR obscured exact dollar figures on this vote; January 23 briefing cited ~$1.2M total including optional tasks and contingency.
votes.discussion_detail: Public speakers Pamela Andrews and Robin Barefoot questioned whether the city was discarding a 2021 study of 35 sites and doubted whether an algal floway technology designed in Florida would work effectively in North Carolina's climate. Public Works engineer Jonathan Baker responded that Gradient PLLC would build upon the 2021 site screening within Durham County's Falls Lake watershed and cited successful 2017 local pilot nutrient-removal results. Mayor Pro Tem Middleton emphasized the contract authorizes only site identification rather than construction or land purchase, and Council voted 5-0 to approve the contract.

votes.item_title: Item 8 (Motion 2): Establish Contingency Fund for Gradient PLLC Algal Floway Contract
votes.notes: Chelsea Cook and DeDreana Freeman absent (excused). Companion motion establishing 15% contract contingency fund.
votes.discussion_detail: As the second of three standard motions accompanying the Gradient PLLC Professional Services contract, Council considered establishing the project's contingency fund. Staff had previously explained at the January 23 work session that optional tasks (including a 30% site plan, solar feasibility, and multi-site evaluation) and a 15% contingency were built into the CIP budget to manage site uncertainties. The motion passed unanimously 5-0.

votes.item_title: Item 8 (Motion 3): Authorize City Manager to Execute Amendments Within Approved Algal Floway Total Contract Cap
votes.notes: Chelsea Cook and DeDreana Freeman absent (excused). Companion motion granting amendment authority up to the approved cap.
votes.discussion_detail: Council took up the final companion authorization allowing the City Manager to negotiate and execute contract amendments provided the combined total contract and contingency costs remain within the approved cap. No further objections were raised after staff confirmed the public would have opportunities to weigh in on any eventual selected site. The motion passed unanimously 5-0.

votes.item_title: Item 12 (Part 1): Voluntary Annexation Ordinance and Utility Extension Agreement - 2613 Carpenter Road (SVK Carpenter Road LLC)
votes.notes: Chelsea Cook and DeDreana Freeman absent (excused). 18.29-acre contiguous expansion of corporate limits.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff presented a 18.29-acre contiguous annexation and UEA at 2613 Carpenter Road for up to 98 townhomes, noting Planning Commission recommended approval 9-1 and the applicant included a 5% affordable housing commitment. Residents raised concerns about 100-year floodplain buffers along Panther Creek, Carpenter Road traffic, and greenway trail connectivity. After applicant attorney Thomas H. Johnson Jr. agreed to Council Member Nate Baker's request to proffer constructing the greenway trail within the easement, Council voted 5-0 to adopt the annexation ordinance and UEA.

votes.item_title: Item 12 (Part 2): UDO Zoning Map Change (RR County to PDR 5.587 City) - 2613 Carpenter Road
votes.notes: Chelsea Cook and DeDreana Freeman absent (excused). Falls/Jordan District B watershed overlay.
votes.discussion_detail: Following adoption of the annexation ordinance, Council voted on the companion UDO zoning map change from Residential Rural (County) to Planned Development Residential 5.587 (City) with a textual development plan. Staff confirmed the PDR density and layout complied with mixed residential neighborhood and recreation/open space Place Type designations. The rezoning passed unanimously 5-0.

votes.item_title: Item 12 (Part 3): Plan Consistency Statement - 2613 Carpenter Road
votes.notes: Chelsea Cook and DeDreana Freeman absent (excused).
votes.discussion_detail: Council considered the required statutory consistency statement finding the PDR 5.587 zoning consistent with the Comprehensive Plan's Mixed Residential Neighborhood and Recreation/Open Space designations. The added greenway construction proffer further reinforced active-transportation connectivity goals. The consistency statement passed unanimously 5-0.

votes.item_title: Item 13: Consolidated Annexation Ordinance and Utility Extension Agreement - Moriah Ridge (M/I Homes of Raleigh LLC)
votes.notes: Chelsea Cook and DeDreana Freeman absent (excused). Vote failed 0-5 (announcer misspoke '5-0' before correcting 'motion fails'); companion rezoning and consistency motions were not called following failure of annexation.
votes.discussion_detail: M/I Homes sought voluntary annexation and utility extension for 15 parcels totaling 168.37 acres across the Durham-Orange county line for up to 1,000 residential units and 2,500 sq ft of office space, while staff disclosed a corrected FIA reducing projected FY34 net fiscal benefit from ~$27M to $5.36M. Roughly 25 speakers strongly opposed the development for breaching the Urban Growth Boundary, splitting Orange County property taxes/schools (CHCCS) from Durham municipal infrastructure, alleging aggressive acquisition tactics toward remaining 'donut hole' homeowners, and relying on incomplete stream surveys. All five Council members agreed the project was premature and inconsistent with the UGB and comprehensive plan (though Mayor Pro Tem Middleton cautioned external state development pressures could return), and the annexation motion failed unanimously 0-5.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting February 3, 2025 (audio synched with closed captioning)
disagreements.issue: Item 11 (Picket Apartments) Immediate Vote vs. Continuance for Bird-Friendly Design & Sidewalk Connectivity
disagreements.summary: Council debated whether to vote immediately on Picket Apartments (140 units, 10% affordable adjacent to Sandy Creek Park) or continue the public hearing to pursue bird-safe glazing/lighting and a multi-agency Durham Academy sidewalk partnership.
disagreements.side_a_position: Continue the public hearing to March 17, 2025 to refine bird-friendly building/lighting commitments and explore sidewalk funding coordination with Durham Academy.
side_a_arguments: Neighbors and bird conservationists documented 185 bird species at Sandy Creek Park and requested clearer window-treatment and dark-sky lighting commitments rather than ambiguous menus.
Continuing gives Ascension time to meet good-faith community stakeholders and explore off-site sidewalk partnership options alongside LEED/green building inquiries.
disagreements.side_b_position: Vote on the rezoning immediately rather than continuing when the developer already stated it cannot commit to building the full sidewalk culvert connection.
side_b_arguments: Applicant attorney Neil Ghosh clearly stated the project cannot financially absorb or timeline-guarantee triple-culvert wetland sidewalk construction beyond its $300,000 contribution.
With 10% affordable apartments near transit and services, the project's benefits already outweighed its drawbacks without risking moved goalposts.
disagreements.resolution: Mayor Williams yielded to Council consensus, reopened the public hearing, and continued it to a date certain of March 17, 2025.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting February 3, 2025 (audio synched with closed captioning)
disagreements.issue: Item 13 (Moriah Ridge) Urban Growth Boundary Enforcement & Cross-County Annexation Policy
disagreements.summary: While all five seated Council members voted against Moriah Ridge over UGB inconsistency, cross-county school/tax impacts, stream mapping gaps, and landowner treatment, members differed slightly on the broader risk of rejecting large-scale housing outside the UGB.
disagreements.side_a_position: Strictly enforce the adopted Urban Growth Boundary and reject cross-county greenfield annexation lacking full stream protections and Durham County tax/school alignment.
side_a_arguments: Allowing 1,000 units outside the UGB in Orange County undermines the Comprehensive Plan's core infill-first commitment and creates fractured school/tax responsibilities.
Revised fiscal math dropped projected net gains from ~$27M to $5.36M, and unmapped streams plus aggressive 'donut hole' owner impacts require denial.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject this application based on UGB fidelity and landowner acquisition concerns, while warning that rejecting housing near Durham-Chapel Hill could invite higher-impact outcomes or state intervention.
side_b_arguments: Mayor Williams cited the need for consistency on the UGB while emphasizing dissatisfaction with aggressive land acquisition pressure on neighboring homeowners.
Mayor Pro Tem Middleton noted Durham still needs substantial housing tax base and cautioned that, as with 751 South, outside forces or state rules could force development without local conditions.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and UEA motion failed unanimously 0-5.

development_cases.location: 2613 Carpenter Rd
development_cases.scale: Up to 98 townhouse units on 18.29 acres
development_cases.zoning_change: RR (County) to PDR 5.587 (City, Falls/Jordan District B Overlay) with Textual Development Plan

proffers.affordable_housing: 5% of units set aside as affordable housing (~5 townhomes)
proffers.environmental_tree: Extra 5% tree preservation (25% total = 4.57 acres, clustered around Panther Creek floodplain/wetlands); 50-ft frontage buffer along Carpenter Rd; contiguous open space around floodplain
proffers.transit_infrastructure: 10-ft multi-use path along Carpenter Rd; donating greenway corridor easement along abandoned railroad ROW and committed at hearing to construct the Greenway Trail within that easement
other_proffers: Utility Extension Agreement with SVK Carpenter Road LLC

member_justifications.stance_summary: Asked the applicant to commit to constructing the Greenway Trail within the donated easement rather than only dedicating the land, securing that binding commitment before voting aye.
member_justifications.key_quote: Just one question: would you consider constructing the Greenway Trail within the easement?

development_cases.scale: Up to 140 apartments on 6.12 acres (3.42-acre building/parking envelope outside floodplain)
development_cases.zoning_change: RS-20 to PDR 36.176

proffers.affordable_housing: 10% income-restricted affordable units (split evenly across 60%, 80%, and 100% AMI)
proffers.environmental_tree: 24.5% tree preservation (above 20% required); tree preservation within floodway/fringe and all buildings/parking outside floodplain; ~55% impervious; Energy Star Multifamily New Construction certification (added at hearing); bird-friendly window treatment commitment (added at hearing)
proffers.transit_infrastructure: 10-ft multi-use path along Pickett Rd frontage; securing off-site easement/ROW over parcel REID 236562 plus $300,000 toward payment-in-lieu / sidewalk connection to Sandy Creek Trail (added at hearing)
other_proffers: Elevators in all multi-story residential buildings for accessibility (added at hearing)

member_justifications.stance_summary: Praised the project as consistent with the Place Type map, Urban Growth Boundary, and 15-minute city goals, and refused to backtrack on reduced parking minimums, while proposing a continuance to March 17, 2025 to refine bird-friendly glass/lighting standards and explore a financing partnership with Durham Academy for the Sandy Creek Trail sidewalk connection.
member_justifications.key_quote: Sometimes when there is spaces where I think the applicant and community can continue conversations, there's a win for everyone, and we ask the applicant if they are interested in a continuance.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Probed the full culvert engineering cost of the Sandy Creek Trail connection beyond the $300,000 proffer, compared Energy Star to LEED, and asked whether additional stormwater or green-building commitments could be added. Supported continuing the hearing to March 17, stating at [03:10:48] that his review would focus on LEED compliance/green architecture and bird-friendly design.
member_justifications.key_quote: Are there any additional stormwater, green building, site mitigation commitments you have pondered or could make?

member_justifications.stance_summary: Pushed back against exclusionary rhetoric regarding apartment 'strangers' near Durham Academy and Sandy Creek Park, affirming apartment residents deserve access to parks. Supported continuing the item to explore a joint funding solution with Durham Academy for the trail connection and clarify bird-friendly design, while noting by-right development remains an alternative.
member_justifications.key_quote: People that live in apartments deserve to live near parks... When we say no as a council, it's yes to something else.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Highlighted the 10% affordable units across 60%/80%/100% AMI, strong stormwater controls, and road capacity (56%), while supporting a continuance to finalize specific bird-friendly window standards and pedestrian connectivity to Sandy Creek Park.
member_justifications.key_quote: The two pieces to me that are of concern are this connectivity piece... [and] I want to make sure we have the right set of things that we're listing [for bird-friendly design].

member_justifications.stance_summary: Found the project objectively satisfied Place Type map, Urban Growth Boundary, and housing diversity criteria without worsening flooding under city stormwater rules, and while ready to vote yes, concurred in continuing the public hearing to March 17 to strengthen bird-friendly design and connectivity.
member_justifications.key_quote: I look at this project individually; despite how I feel about it, the pros outweigh the cons and I would be prepared to move tonight.

development_cases.project_name: Moriah Ridge (M/I Homes of Raleigh LLC)
development_cases.location: Between Erwin Rd and Mt. Moriah Rd, crossing the Orange County / Durham County line
development_cases.scale: Up to 1,000 apartments, townhomes, and single-family units plus 2,500 sq ft office on 155.04 acres (plus 12.327 acres RS-20 = 168.37 acres total across 15 parcels)
development_cases.zoning_change: Rural Transition (Orange County) / RS-20 (Durham County) to PDR 7.34 and RS-20 (City of Durham)

proffers.affordable_housing: 5% affordable units (~50 units) planned via 9% LIHTC
proffers.environmental_tree: Amended Condition 10 to convey ecologically sensitive New Hope Creek Corridor land east of Mt. Moriah Rd to a governmental conservation entity; native plant species; reduced floodplain impacts; 100-year storm event stormwater handling; Green Building standards for all housing types
proffers.transit_infrastructure: 10-ft multi-use paths along both sides of Mt. Moriah Rd; flashing-beacon pedestrian crossing across Mt. Moriah Rd; connected walking/biking trails linking New Hope Creek Corridor, Mt. Moriah Rd, and Erwin Rd; EV charging spaces in common areas; 0.25 miles from transit
other_proffers: Maximum-height opaque fencing around McGregor, Roden, and Garcia 'donut-hole' properties (added at hearing); Utility Extension Agreement with M/I Homes of Raleigh LLC

member_justifications.stance_summary: Voted no because the project lies outside Durham's Urban Growth Boundary, which took nearly five years of community planning to establish, without a joint-jurisdictional community-driven area plan. Warned approval would set a damaging precedent for every edge of the Urban Growth Boundary across Durham County.
member_justifications.key_quote: It is beyond the urban growth boundary... I think that if we approved [it], it would set a precedent for every single other part of the urban growth boundary in the entire county of Durham.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Acknowledged strong open space conservation, sidewalk connectivity, and proximity to commercial and transit, but voted no because the community worked hard to establish the Urban Growth Boundary to focus density inward and he was unwilling to expand outside it at this time.
member_justifications.key_quote: In creating the urban growth boundary, we work a lot here to make sure that we get denser inside that urban growth boundary, and so I'm not comfortable going outside the urban boundary at this point on this case.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Recognized the site is near the 15-501 corridor and future BRT and appreciated the 9% LIHTC affordable housing plan, but voted no because the 1,000-unit project is premature amid unresolved NCDOT disputes over 15-501 BRT and pedestrian/bike design and does not advance Comprehensive Plan goals today.
member_justifications.key_quote: You can see what's coming, I don't think that day is today... It has to be in a way that does actually move the goals forward in the comp plan, and this project as it stands today does not do that.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Noted that Council's prior vote to amend the Durham-Chapel Hill consent judgment had signaled potential development and warned residents that rejecting the case could invite state forces to impose a worse outcome later. Nevertheless voted no to stay faithful to his long-standing advocacy for the Urban Growth Boundary as Durham's footprint expanded into Orange County.
member_justifications.key_quote: Because I have been a big proponent of the urban growth boundary... I'm not prepared to go forward with this case tonight.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Reaffirmed his generally pro-development, pro-infill approach, but voted no because the site is clearly outside the Urban Growth Boundary, left too many unresolved questions about streams across the Chapel Hill/Orange County line, and raised serious concerns about aggressive land-acquisition treatment of neighbors.
member_justifications.key_quote: In this case, we're clearly out [of the urban growth boundary], and part of this is also just being consistent for the sake of trust.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session January 23, 2025 (livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council excused Council Members Cook and Freeman for the upcoming February 3 meeting, accepted City Manager priority items, and settled the February 3 Council agenda by voice votes. During Citizens Matters, speakers urged immediate winter warming-shelter access, protection of the Urban Growth Boundary, and youth gun-violence intervention, while Council questioned Community Development Director Reginald Johnson on Item 14's $100,000 Corporate Facts federal-grant reconciliation contract. Extended policy debates erupted during briefings on Item 8 (Algal Floway site evaluation), Item 10 (Participatory Budgeting Cycle 4 equity targets), and Transportation Director Sean Egan's Vision Zero Action Plan update regarding engagement spending, equity weighting scrutiny, and gun-violence response.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Council Announcements & Excused Absences for Feb 3 Meeting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams convened the session with Middleton, Baker, Freeman, and Rist present, while Cook and Caballero arrived during announcements. Council Member Cook requested a future briefing on HOPWA and ending-the-HIV-epidemic funding (while Mayor Williams noted a federal-funding risk assessment with Ice Miller and the African-American Mayors Association), Middleton reaffirmed DEI and language access commitments, and Council voted by voice to excuse Cook and Freeman from the February 3 meeting.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Cook & Freeman excused by voice votes (2 votes)

agenda_items.title: Priority Items, BCC Report & Reading of Feb 3 Consent Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Bo Ferguson presented priority items adding Item 8 (Algal Floway presentation), Item 14 (Corporate Facts contract), and a supplemental Vision Zero update, which Council accepted by voice vote. The City Clerk presented nominations to the Workers' Rights Commission and Housing Appeals Board, and Council read Consent Items 1-14, pulling Item 14 for immediate questions.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Manager priority items accepted by voice vote

agenda_items.title: Warming Shelters, Urban Growth Boundary & Youth Gun Violence
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Speakers Mary Molina, former Council Member Lisa Scheidel, and Angela Vick-Lewis urged opening daytime warming spaces earlier during freezing weather when shelters discharge residents at 9:00 a.m. and libraries open delayed. Ken Pugh urged defending the Urban Growth Boundary against 'broken window' sprawl exemptions, and Dennis Garrett offered to serve as a community street translator to curb youth gun violence.

agenda_items.title: Contract with Corporate Facts to Reconcile CDBG, HOPWA & ESG Allocations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson explained the ~$100,000 operating-budget contract with Corporate Facts to reconcile federal IDIS balances with city general ledgers for CDBG, HOPWA, and ESG grants by a February HUD deadline after previously reconciling HOME funds. Cook, Middleton, and Rist questioned why internal staff lacked bandwidth and whether training and staffing vacancies from COVID had now been resolved to prevent recurring outside consulting fees.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational review prior to Feb 3 meeting

agenda_items.title: Presentation: Algal Floway Site Evaluation Contract (Gradient PLLC) & Community Engagement Debate
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works staff Jonathan Baker and Water Quality Manager Michelle Woolfolk presented the ~$1.2M (with optional tasks and 15% contingency) Gradient PLLC site-search contract across Durham County's Falls Lake watershed to meet costly State Stage II nutrient rules (previously estimated near $1B for water management). Council questioned odor/environmental justice impacts, solar options, algae compost outlets, and real-estate speculation confidentiality, and sparked an extended policy debate over spending ~$80k-$100k per project on outsourced community engagement.

agenda_items.title: Participatory Budgeting (PB) Cycle 4 Launch Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Carmen Ortiz and Fallon Thompson presented plans for PB Cycle 4's $2.4M capital budget and 14,000-vote goal following 12,000+ Cycle 3 votes (including 2,800 DPS students) and a Duke Center for Advanced Hindsight study showing PB boosts civic trust and election participation. Mayor Pro Tem Middleton praised PB while pressing staff on the exact scoring and paper-ballot outreach methodology behind the 60% geographic equity target so it can withstand heightened legal and political scrutiny.

agenda_items.title: Vision Zero Action Plan Interim Update & Gun Violence 'Vision Zero' Debate
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Director Sean Egan reported High Injury Network findings showing 11% of non-highway Durham streets account for 74% of traffic deaths and serious injuries (55,000 crashes 2017-2023; 170 fatalities) ahead of the final action plan set for March 20, 2025. Council Member Rist backed quick-build treatments and intersection daylighting, while Mayor Williams, Middleton, Cook, and Baker debated establishing equivalent dedicated staffing and urgency for a 'Vision Zero for gun violence' and whether PB security cameras deter shootings.

agenda_items.title: Settling the February 3, 2025 City Council Meeting Agenda

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session January 23, 2025 (livestream)
disagreements.issue: Cost, Duration, and Outsourcing of City Community Engagement Under the 2018 Equitable Engagement Blueprint
disagreements.summary: Debate sparked by the ~$80,000 public-outreach component of the Algal Floway contract pitted Council members criticizing expensive, multi-year third-party consulting against members defending deep, culturally responsive outreach.
disagreements.side_a_position: Audit and curb outsourced community engagement contracts (~$80k-$100k per project) and return closer to the original 90-day timeline or build internal city capacity.
side_a_arguments: Paying private consultants $80,000-$100,000 per project has spawned an expensive 'cottage industry' where engagement drags on for years while residents still complain they were not reached.
Elected officials and internal NIS staff should lead engagement while directing scarce public dollars toward housing and core delivery.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain multi-round, linguistically accessible, community-centered outreach even if it costs ~10% of project budgets and adapts as sites evolve.
side_b_arguments: The 2018 Equitable Engagement Blueprint was created because projects like the Durham Beltline and Third Fork Creek proceeded without reaching renters and marginalized residents.
Ten percent of a $1M project is reasonable for mailings to renters, translation, and iterative outreach whenever project locations change over multi-year timelines.
disagreements.resolution: Council agreed to schedule a dedicated future work-session policy review of the 2018 Equitable Engagement Blueprint.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session January 23, 2025 (livestream)
disagreements.issue: Gun Violence Priority Parity with Vision Zero & Surveillance Cameras in Participatory Budgeting
disagreements.summary: Council members debated dedicating salaried 'Gun Violence Zero' capacity equal to traffic Vision Zero and clashed over whether resident-chosen PB security cameras represent meaningful safety or passive surveillance.
disagreements.side_a_position: Prioritize gun-violence prevention with dedicated salaried coordination and acknowledge that residents repeatedly vote for security cameras via PB.
side_a_arguments: The city pays a full-time Vision Zero coordinator for traffic deaths while lacking an equivalent dedicated coordinator to receive proposals like Dennis Garrett's or Advance Peace for gun violence.
Middleton noted residents in high-violence areas chose security cameras via democratic PB ballots when given the choice.
disagreements.side_b_position: Address systemic street-design and state-road causes of traffic deaths and prioritize active intervention (such as Advance Peace) over passive surveillance cameras.
side_b_arguments: Baker argued surveillance cameras neither call police nor dispatch ambulances, merely producing high-resolution footage after someone is already shot.
Cook emphasized winning state DOT/legislative support on multi-lane state highways (where most high-injury traffic crashes occur) and reviewing Advance Peace holistically.
disagreements.resolution: Informational discussion concluded with Mayor Williams signaling an upcoming proposal for a 'Vision Zero for gun violence' initiative.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session January 23, 2025 (livestream)
disagreements.issue: Participatory Budgeting (PB) 60% Geographic Equity Target Methodology
disagreements.summary: Mayor Pro Tem Middleton praised PB's outcomes while questioning how its 60% underserved-area project goal is operationalized in a one-person, one-vote election so staff can defend it against rising external scrutiny.
disagreements.side_a_position: Clarify and rigorously document how delegate equity scoring and targeted paper-ballot outreach drive the 60% outcome without creating legal vulnerabilities akin to quotas.
side_a_arguments: Concentrating physical polling/boots-on-the-ground paper outreach in selected areas alongside delegate scoring weights produces different demographic pools than online voting.
Amid shifting state and national legal scrutiny of municipal equity programs, Durham must be able to defend its methodology with complete precision.
disagreements.side_b_position: Defend PB's geographic equity scoring as a vital tool to include low-income, transit-dependent, and unhoused/incarcerated residents lacking digital access.
side_b_arguments: Every resident can submit ideas and vote once, while paper ballots at bus stations, convenience stores, and the jail ensure populations without cell phones or emails participate.
disagreements.resolution: Informational briefing; Middleton thanked staff for transparent demographic and survey-methodology breakdowns.
