meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting January 21, 2025 (audio synched with closed captioning)
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams presided over a full-attendance Durham City Council meeting ahead of worsening snow and freezing temperatures, opening with a National Mentoring Month proclamation and announcements on White Flag shelters, eviction court, the Gaza ceasefire, and federal immigration enforcement preparedness. Council unanimously approved the consent agenda (7-0), appointed Cory Pantic to the Durham Planning Commission (7-0) after a multi-round nomination shift, and approved the PROUD reentry workforce grant agreement with Eckerd Connects (7-0) following staff data clarifications requested by Carl Rist. Council also unanimously approved three zoning map changes—3112 South Alston Avenue (7-0), the 95.4-acre Brickworks mixed-use development up to 1,880 units (7-0) after securing NGBS Bronze+ and doubled $120,000 DPS commitments, and Davis Park West's development plan amendment (7-0)—and held the first FY25–30 Consolidated Plan / FY25–26 Annual Action Plan public needs hearing. On the final item, Council debated the quantitative return on investment versus racial equity rationale for a $250,000 Durham Legacy economic development grant to Ellis D. Jones & Sons, Inc., passing the agreement 6-1 with Carl Rist voting no before Manager Bo Ferguson announced delayed City Hall opening and suspended solid waste collection for the winter storm.

agenda_items.title: National Mentoring Month Proclamation and Council Member Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton presented a National Mentoring Month proclamation to Drew Langley of the Charles Hamilton Houston Foundation. During announcements, Council members highlighted White Flag cold-weather shelters and NIS emergency heating inspections, eviction court pressures, a request from Chelsea Cook for a briefing on HOPWA HIV housing funds, the Garner Amazon RDU1 union vote, the Gaza ceasefire, local immigrant rights preparedness, the January 27 Point-in-Time count, and Mayor Williams's U.S. Conference of Mayors meetings.

agenda_items.title: Priority Items, Agenda Adjustment, and Consent Agenda Adoption
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager attached requested information on Item 5 (PROUD grant) and deferred the Vision Zero update to the January 23 work session. Council approved the consent agenda covering FY25 CIP 2024 GO Bond amendments, Fire Department breathing apparatus and air/light truck purchases, Made in Durham career funding, Hillandale Road bike/pedestrian and sidewalk contracts, FTA Section 5310 transit grant, ERP and OnBase IT contracts, and candidate filing fees, while Mayor Williams moved Item 17 to be heard first.

agenda_items.title: FY2025-2030 Consolidated Plan and FY2025-2026 Annual Action Plan Public Needs Hearing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald J. Johnson outlined projected FY25–26 HUD entitlement grants—approximately $2.2 million CDBG, $1.4 million HOME, $179,000 ESG, and $1.13 million HOPWA—and the public comment timeline toward July 25 submission. Virtually, Dr. Haley Cunningham testified on behalf of the Coalition to End the HIV Epidemic in Durham, citing underutilized HOPWA vouchers (20 of 45 used) and urging the City to partner on a $2.5 million coordinated care system.

agenda_items.title: Durham Planning Commission Appointment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Because prior work-session nominations yielded no majority (Caitlin Kempsey 2, Cory Pantic 2, Ramsey Richie 1, Michael J. Young 1, with DeDreana Freeman's form unsubmitted), Council conducted open nomination updates on the dais. After Freeman recorded her vote for Kempsey (3) and Nate Baker shifted his vote because his prior nominee was ineligible, Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Leonardo Williams, and Carl Rist formed a 4-vote majority for Cory Pantic, followed by a unanimous ratification vote.

agenda_items.title: PROUD Grant Cooperative Agreement with Eckerd Youth Alternatives, Inc. (Eckerd Connects)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Carl Rist pulled Item 5 to review year-two evaluation data for the DOJ/DOL PROUD federal reentry workforce grant administered across three regional Workforce Development Boards. Staff reported 68 regional enrollees in forklift certification and 15 in ServSafe, with 18 served locally toward Durham's three-year goal of 90—noting limits because the grant only serves federal Butner releases and Durham lacks a federal halfway house, necessitating Greensboro partnerships. Rist praised the program and asked for future job-placement and wage outcome data.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change — 3112 South Alston Avenue
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and applicant Mike Klein (MRK Planning Consulting) presented a 0.75-acre split-zoned parcel rezoning to Office and Institutional with a textual development plan restricting uses to up to seven townhouses or detached rowhouses, including a northbound left-turn lane, 10-foot shared path, and 30-foot rail-corridor tree buffer. Chelsea Cook questioned choosing O&I zoning for residential-only units and DPS's zero-student generation estimate, which staff attributed to updated DPS townhome generation ratios. Council approved the rezoning and consistency statement unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change — Brickworks (95.4 Acres, Hoover Road / Angier Avenue / East End Avenue)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and attorney Nil Ghosh (on behalf of Space Craft and Thomas & Hutton) presented a 95.4-acre former Borden Brick industrial infill rezoning to PDR 19.81 for up to 1,880 residential units and 49,500 square feet of non-residential space, clustering development on roughly 23 acres with 5,000 linear feet of trails, Route 12 transit access, and 5% of apartments at 60% AMI for 30 years. Neighbor Ian Kipp urged Phase I and Phase II environmental testing of the borrow pit pond, while Council members questioned apartment-minimum guarantees, pedestrian/transit design commitments, stormwater, recycling transfer-station buffering, and school impacts—prompting the developer to commit to NGBS Bronze+ green building standards and double its DPS contribution to $120,000.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change — Davis Park West Development Plan Amendment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and attorney Patrick Byker (for Craig Davis Properties) presented an amendment to Design Commitments 4 and 5 of the 2019 Mixed Use with Development Plan approval at 350/362 Davis Drive and 900 Marin Avenue. The changes allow ground-floor structured parking (with architectural screening) and office uses, and allow retail frontages to face internal pedestrian-oriented streets rather than Davis Drive (a 50 mph thoroughfare), similar to Meadowmont. Council approved the ordinance and consistency statement unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing and Economic Development Incentive Agreement — Ellis D. Jones & Sons, Inc.
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chris Dickie (Office of Economic and Workforce Development) presented a $250,000 Neighborhood Revitalization Grant / Durham Legacy Business agreement to help fourth-generation Black-owned Ellis D. Jones & Sons Funeral Home renovate its 4,732-square-foot second floor at 419 Dowd Street as part of an $859,000 investment with five years of guaranteed community space access. Carl Rist challenged the lack of quantitative tax-revenue ROI and noted only three of five projected jobs met living-wage thresholds, while Mark-Anthony Middleton, DeDreana Freeman, Javiera Caballero, Chelsea Cook, and Mayor Leonardo Williams defended the deal as an equity-driven capital revitalization investment addressing historic disinvestment. The agreement passed 6-1 with Rist dissenting, after which City Manager Bo Ferguson announced delayed City Hall opening and closed solid waste collection due to snow and ice.

votes.item_title: Durham Planning Commission Appointment (Cory Pantic)
votes.notes: Final ratification vote was unanimous (7-0) following a 4-3 open nomination preference round; mover and seconder were not named in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: After the Clerk reported an inconclusive work-session tally, DeDreana Freeman announced her vote for Caitlin Kempsey (giving Kempsey 3 votes) and Nate Baker shifted his vote due to his prior nominee's ineligibility, yielding a four-member majority (Javiera Caballero, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Leonardo Williams, and Carl Rist) for Cory Pantic. Council then moved, seconded, and unanimously ratified the appointment to fill the Planning Commission vacancy.

votes.item_title: PROUD Grant Cooperative Agreement with Eckerd Youth Alternatives, Inc. (dba Eckerd Connects) (Item 5)
votes.notes: Mover and seconder were not named in the transcript; Clerk announced the motion passed unanimously.
votes.discussion_detail: Carl Rist pulled Item 5 from the consent agenda to obtain year-two performance metrics on the DOJ/DOL PROUD federal reentry workforce grant. Durham Workforce Development Board staff Adriel Graham-Scott and Michael London reported 68 forklift and 15 ServSafe regional enrollees and 18 Durham participants served toward a 90-person goal (limited by federal Butner eligibility and lack of a local halfway house), after which Council unanimously approved the agreement as published.

votes.item_title: Zoning Ordinance Amending the UDO — 3112 South Alston Avenue (Item 14)
votes.notes: Mover and seconder were not named in the transcript; Planning Commission had unanimously recommended approval on November 12, 2024.
votes.discussion_detail: Council considered a rezoning of 0.75 acres at 3112 South Alston Avenue (transcribed as South Austin Avenue) from Office & Institutional and Residential Rural to Office & Institutional with a textual development plan restricting development to up to seven townhouses or detached rowhouses. Following brief questions from Chelsea Cook regarding O&I zoning choice and DPS student-generation formulas and a public hearing with only applicant Mike Klein speaking, Council unanimously adopted the ordinance.

votes.item_title: Consistency Statement (NCGS 160D-605) — 3112 South Alston Avenue (Item 14)
votes.notes: Mover and seconder were not named in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately following adoption of the 3112 South Alston Avenue rezoning ordinance, Council moved, seconded, and approved the statutory consistency statement under NCGS Section 160D-605 by a 7-0 vote.

votes.item_title: Utility Extension Agreement with Brick Works Land LLC (Item 15)
votes.notes: Mover and seconder were not named in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Following an extensive public hearing and Council deliberation on the 95.4-acre Brickworks infill project, Council authorized the City Manager to enter into a utility extension agreement with Brick Works Land LLC on a unanimous 7-0 vote.

votes.item_title: Zoning Ordinance Amending the UDO — Brickworks PDR 19.81 (Item 15)
votes.notes: Includes 5% of apartments affordable at 60% AMI for 30 years; mover and seconder were not named in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Before the vote, staff confirmed two additional proffered commitments offered during the hearing: all apartment and mixed-use buildings will meet at least National Green Building Standard Bronze, and the developer's Durham Public Schools contribution will double from $60,000 to $120,000 at Chelsea Cook's request. Council then unanimously adopted the ordinance rezoning 95.4 acres from IL and RU-5 to PDR 19.81 (Falls/Jordan Lake Watershed Overlay District B) for up to 1,880 residential units and 49,500 square feet of non-residential space.

votes.item_title: Consistency Statement (NCGS 160D-605) — Brickworks (Item 15)
votes.notes: Mover and seconder were not named in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately following the Brickworks rezoning ordinance vote, Council moved, seconded, and unanimously adopted the required NCGS Section 160D-605 consistency statement.

votes.item_title: Zoning Ordinance Amending the UDO — Davis Park West MU(D) Amendment (Item 16)
votes.notes: Mover and seconder were not named in the transcript; Planning Commission had unanimously recommended approval on November 12, 2024.
votes.discussion_detail: Council considered Craig Davis Properties' amendment to Design Commitments 4 and 5 of the 2019 Davis Park West development plan (10.847 acres at 350/362 Davis Drive and 900 Marin Avenue) to permit ground-floor structured parking and office uses and orient retail frontages toward internal pedestrian streets rather than Davis Drive. Following brief clarifying questions from Carl Rist, Council unanimously adopted the ordinance.

votes.item_title: Consistency Statement (NCGS 160D-605) — Davis Park West (Item 16)
votes.notes: Mover and seconder were not named in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately following the Davis Park West rezoning vote, Council moved, seconded, and passed the required NCGS Section 160D-605 consistency statement on a 7-0 vote.

votes.item_title: Authorize Economic Development Agreement with Ellis D. Jones & Sons, Inc. ($250,000, 419 Dowd Street) (Item 18)
votes.notes: Mover and seconder were not named in the transcript; Clerk announced 'the motion passes 6 to 1 with Council Member Rist voting no.'
votes.discussion_detail: Council debated a $250,000 Neighborhood Revitalization Grant / Durham Legacy Business agreement supporting an $859,000 second-floor renovation at Ellis D. Jones & Sons Funeral Home at 419 Dowd Street in Northeast Central Durham, requiring at least five years of public community-space availability. Carl Rist questioned the lack of quantitative tax-revenue ROI and noted only three of five projected positions met living-wage thresholds, while Mark-Anthony Middleton, DeDreana Freeman, Javiera Caballero, Chelsea Cook, and Mayor Leonardo Williams supported the grant as an equity-centered Legacy Business capital investment. The motion passed 6-1 with Carl Rist voting no.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting January 21, 2025 (audio synched with closed captioning)
disagreements.issue: Return on Investment and Living-Wage Metrics for $250,000 Ellis D. Jones & Sons Economic Development Incentive
disagreements.summary: Council split 6-1 over whether a $250,000 Neighborhood Revitalization / Durham Legacy Business grant to Ellis D. Jones & Sons Funeral Home required stronger quantitative ROI and living-wage job justification or was warranted as an equity-centered capital preservation investment.
disagreements.side_a_position: Support the $250,000 grant as a performance-based equity and neighborhood revitalization investment in a fourth-generation Black-owned legacy institution.
side_a_arguments: Unlike corporate recruitment deals (such as Apple or Google), Neighborhood Revitalization Grants leverage roughly 3:1 private capital to preserve Black-owned legacy businesses harmed by historic systemic inequities and gentrification.
The performance-based agreement helps unlock bank lending for capital improvements and requires the renovated second floor to host community events and meetings for at least five years.
disagreements.side_b_position: Question the $250,000 public expenditure without a quantitative 'but-for' or tax-revenue ROI analysis and fuller living-wage job creation.
side_b_arguments: According to the staff jobs table, only three of five projected jobs over five years meet the city's living-wage threshold.

Staff did not perform a quantitative tax-revenue or public ROI analysis (only qualitative arguments) or a formal 'but-for' calculation demonstrating the project could not proceed without the $250,000 grant.
disagreements.resolution: Passed 6-1 (Carl Rist voting No) after Mayor Leonardo Williams noted he texted Carl Rist to continue discussing legacy-business incentive evaluation in future policy conversations.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Praised the proposal as much closer to Comprehensive Plan consistency than typical large rezonings—highlighting its infill location, mix of uses, density, clustering, 60% AMI affordable housing, walking trails, and new NGBS Bronze commitment. Urged stronger site-design commitments (pedestrian/transit orientation, rear-alley/porch townhomes) since the current UDO does not require them, and reiterated that request to the architect at [01:58:19].
member_justifications.key_quote: We have here the density and we have the diversity of uses, which again we don't always see as proposed, and then it's that design piece that I just want it to get to be right because this is such a large transformative site.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supported the redevelopment of a challenging former industrial site for its affordability, transit access, mix of uses, and trail network, while questioning buffering against the adjacent recycling transfer station and anticipated market-rate rents.
member_justifications.key_quote: This is an exciting redevelopment project for all the reasons we talked about: the affordability, the infill, access to transit, the mix of uses, the pathways.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supported converting a former brickyard industrial site into a dense mixed-use infill neighborhood and cautioned against overly prescriptive facade mandates in the UDO.
member_justifications.key_quote: These larger infill sites where there was not anything particularly attractive—case in point, light industrial site—and it's going to get redone into something better.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Previously verified at [01:32:06] how the 5% affordable apartment set-aside operates under UDO buildout rules, and then pressed the developer on the low per-student DPS contribution—successfully securing a doubling of the DPS cash proffer from $60,000 to $120,000.
member_justifications.key_quote: What has been committed is less than half of [$500 per student], so I was wondering if there is any interest in increasing that commitment to Durham Public Schools.

proffers.transit_infrastructure: Retail oriented onto internal pedestrian-friendly, traffic-calmed streets rather than 50 mph Davis Dr

member_justifications.stance_summary: Questioned how allowing ground-floor retail to face internal streets instead of Davis Drive aligns with Comprehensive Plan street-frontage preferences, and accepted the rationale that pedestrian-oriented internal streets (modeled on Meadowmont) are far safer and more viable than fronting a 50-mph thoroughfare.
member_justifications.key_quote: So you don't want to face Davis Drive... that's why you're being asked to face externally.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Praised the four-generation Black-owned funeral home's community service during COVID and gun violence crises, arguing the grant is essential equity support for Legacy businesses facing historic property-ownership barriers even though broader reparative work remains undone.
member_justifications.key_quote: This is like the least that we could do... it's important that we do this around our Legacy businesses, especially Black-owned businesses.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Strongly endorsed the performance-based grant as an equity investment to keep a foundational Black-owned Durham institution from being displaced by gentrification, pushing back on Rist's job-creation metric as mismatched to a Legacy business stabilization grant.
member_justifications.key_quote: You should read that as equity. This is part of our equity program... This isn't Apple, this isn't Google; this is part of the DNA of Durham.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supported investing in Legacy businesses in Northeast Central Durham in principle, but dissented over insufficient quantitative ROI and job-creation metrics—noting only 3 of 5 projected jobs met the city's living wage threshold for $250,000 in public funds and questioning the 'but-for' analysis.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supported the grant as an intentional, out-of-the-box shared economic prosperity tool to sustain Black-owned Legacy businesses in Durham.
member_justifications.key_quote: When we talk about shared economic prosperity, there's lots of tools at our disposal to make that a reality in Durham.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session January 9, 2025 (livestream)
meetings.executive_summary: Opened and chaired by Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton (with Mayor Williams arriving shortly after roll call and asking Middleton to continue presiding, and Council Member DeDreana Freeman excused 5-0), the Durham City Council prepared the January 21, 2025 regular meeting agenda and settled it 6-0. Members paid tribute to deceased General Services inspector Bruce Mabery and civic leader Dr. Lavonia Allison, received priority additions including a fire truck purchase and election filing fee ordinance, and sent a split Planning Commission nomination to the General Business Agenda. Pulled consent discussions focused on Eckerd Connects' PROWD workforce grant evaluation (Item 5), utility-locate contracts (Item 7), sidewalk repair backlog equity (Item 8), and Mayor Williams' proposal to apply a Vision Zero framework to gun violence.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Excused Absence for Freeman & Council Tributes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton convened the work session with Baker, Caballero, Cook, and Rist present, and Council passed a 5-0 voice vote excusing DeDreana Freeman before Mayor Leonardo Williams arrived at 00:06:57. Council members commented on winter-weather shelter rights, mourned city employee Bruce Mabery, civic leader Dr. Lavonia Allison, and President Jimmy Carter, and requested upcoming briefings on HOPWA/Continuum of Care funding (Caballero) and Vision Zero (Rist).

agenda_items.title: Manager/Attorney Priority Items, Winter Storm Readiness & Planning Commission Deadlock
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Bo Ferguson added supplemental Item 19 (heavy-duty mobile air and light support truck purchase), General Services recognized Bruce Mabery's service, Deputy City Manager Winbush outlined winter storm preparedness and HEART hours, and the City Attorney added Item 20 (municipal election filing fees). The City Clerk reported no majority consensus for the Planning Commission vacancy (with Caitlin Kempsey receiving two votes and three members voting separately), prompting referral to the General Business Agenda.
agenda_items.vote_summary: No vote (Planning Commission seat moved to GBA)

agenda_items.title: Agenda Reading & Review of Pulled Items (PROWD Grant, Utility Locate, Sidewalk Repairs)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After reading Items 1-20, Council pulled Item 5 (PROWD Grant agreement with Eckerd Connects) at Baker's request to review Year 1 evaluation outcomes on the GBA, Item 7 (Contract ST-334C Utility Locate Services) for Middleton's questions on subsurface sensors, and Item 8 (Contract SW-97 Sidewalk Repairs 2025). On Item 8, Cook and Rist questioned equity and risk prioritization across the $1.9M-$2.25M contract (~12,000 linear feet), while Mayor Williams asked about in-house versus contracted costs given staff's reported $80M sidewalk backlog.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Item 5 placed on GBA; Items 7 & 8 retained on Consent

agenda_items.title: Non-CIP Spending Assessment, 'Vision Zero for Gun Violence' & Settling Jan 21 Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Williams urged reviewing non-CIP spending effectiveness and proposed adopting a data-driven 'Vision Zero for gun violence' strategy, with Council Member Cook offering to collaborate. The City Manager settled the January 21 agenda (Consent 2-4, 6-13, 19-20; GBA 1, 5; Public Hearings 14-18), which Council approved 6-0 by voice vote before adjourning at 1:51 p.m.

votes.item_title: Motion to Grant Excused Absence to Council Member DeDreana Freeman
votes.notes: Mayor Leonardo Williams arrived at 00:06:57 after this vote; DeDreana Freeman absent (excused).
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton opened the January 9, 2025 work session as acting chair while Mayor Leonardo Williams was en route. Following roll call showing five members present, Council entertained a motion to grant an excused absence to Council Member DeDreana Freeman. The motion was moved, seconded, and approved unanimously 5-0 by voice vote.

votes.item_title: Motion to Settle the January 21, 2025 City Council Meeting Agenda
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman absent (excused). Placed Consent Items 2-4, 6-13, 19-20; GBA Items 1 (Planning Commission) and 5 (PROWD Grant); Public Hearings Items 14-18.
votes.discussion_detail: At the close of the work session, City Manager Bo Ferguson summarized final agenda assignments for the January 21, 2025 City Council meeting, retaining pulled Items 7 and 8 on Consent while moving Item 5 (Eckerd Connects PROWD grant) alongside Item 1 (Planning Commission appointment) to the General Business Agenda. A motion to settle the agenda was moved and seconded by the six seated members. Mayor Pro Tem Middleton called the voice vote and the motion passed unanimously 6-0.

disagreements.issue: Planning Commission Appointment Split & Lack of Work-Session Consensus

disagreements.resolution: Mayor Pro Tem Middleton directed the appointment to the January 21 General Business Agenda (Item 1) for a formal recorded vote.

meetings.title: Durham City Council January 6, 2025 (audio synched with closed captioning)
meetings.executive_summary: With all seven members present and electronic voting clickers malfunctioning, the Durham City Council conducted votes by a show of hands, adopting its Consent Agenda 7-0 and voting 0-7 to reject proposed revisions to City Code Section 6-3 lowering minimum acreage and setback buffers for deer bow hunting. Before formal business, Council honored Durham Public Schools students with proclamations and awards for the Bull City Mayor's Veganuary Challenge and officially swore in William 'Bo' Ferguson as Durham's new City Manager. On the bow-hunting ordinance, Mayor Williams ruled Council Member Freeman's substitute motion to refer to the Environmental Affairs Board out of order until after acting on the already-seconded main motion, with members citing state preemption against neighborhood-only rules.

agenda_items.title: Veganuary Challenge Proclamation, DPS Student Awards & Swearing-In of City Manager Bo Ferguson
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following roll call (all seven present), Mayor Williams and Council Member Rist presented a Veganuary 2025 proclamation with Dr. Van Vorhees and recognized Durham Public Schools art and Northern High School culinary challenge winners. Council then held a formal oath-of-office ceremony swearing in William 'Bo' Ferguson as City Manager, followed by warm Council remarks praising former Mayor Bill Bell's street renaming, mourning President Jimmy Carter and former Salisbury Mayor Karen Alexander, and highlighting eviction court struggles and Vision Zero traffic fatalities.

agenda_items.title: Priority Items & Consent Agenda (Items 1-4, 6-10)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Ferguson reported one priority item disposing of December 19 Citizens Matters, and Mayor Williams announced voting devices were inoperable so votes would proceed by show of hands. After the Clerk read Consent Items 1-4 and 6-10 (including RDU Airport Authority and Racial Equity Commission appointments, HEART and ADA Title II performance audits, and WIOA grant amendments), Council adopted the Consent Agenda 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Revisions to Deer Bow Hunting Ordinance (City Code Section 6-3)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Ten Treyburn residents testified on opposing sides of an HOA-backed request to reduce bow-hunting minimums citywide from 5 acres to 2 acres and from a 250-foot buffer to 60 feet, citing deer overpopulation, tickborne disease, and vehicle collisions versus safety hazards to children and pets and rapid deer repopulation. Council members expressed concern that state preemption prevents restricting the relaxed rules solely to Treyburn, and Mayor Williams ruled DeDreana Freeman's substitute referral motion out of order behind an active seconded main motion. Council voted down the ordinance revisions 0-7 by show of hands and adjourned at 8:46 p.m.

votes.item_title: Item 5: Proposed Revisions to City Code Section 6-3 (Deer Bow Hunting Acreage and Setback Reduction)
votes.notes: Vote conducted by show of hands due to clicker malfunction. Preceded by DeDreana Freeman's ruled-out-of-order substitute motion to refer to the Environmental Affairs Board.
votes.discussion_detail: Council considered proposed amendments to City Code Section 6-3 reducing the minimum parcel size for bow hunting from five acres to two acres and the safety setback from 250 feet to 60 feet following sharply divided testimony from Treyburn homeowners. Every Council member voiced reluctance to relax bow-hunting buffers citywide because the City Attorney advised state law preempts geographic overlays, timeframes, or neighborhood-specific restrictions, while Cook and Caballero noted wildlife-feeding ordinances and Environmental Affairs Board study as alternatives. After Mayor Williams declined to entertain DeDreana Freeman's substitute referral motion ahead of the seconded main motion (and Middleton and Cook kept their motion on the floor to establish a clean vote before any later referral), the ordinance failed unanimously 0-7 by show of hands.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council January 6, 2025 (audio synched with closed captioning)
disagreements.issue: Procedural Handling of Item 5: Vote Down Bow-Hunting Ordinance First vs. Substitute Motion to Refer to Environmental Affairs Board (EAB)
disagreements.summary: While all seven Council members agreed against adopting the citywide Section 6-3 bow-hunting reduction as written, Council Member Freeman attempted a substitute motion/friendly amendment to refer the matter to the EAB rather than voting it down, whereas Mayor Williams, Mayor Pro Tem Middleton, and Council Member Cook insisted on voting on the active main motion first.
disagreements.side_a_position: Vote directly on the already-seconded main motion to defeat the proposed Section 6-3 ordinance and decide independently afterward whether and where to refer wildlife-management alternatives.
side_a_arguments: Once a main motion is moved and seconded, Council must act on that motion to establish a clear legislative record.
It is not yet clear whether EAB is the right body to study broader wildlife, feeding, or non-lethal policies across other Durham neighborhoods.
disagreements.side_b_position: Offer a substitute motion/friendly amendment referring the item to the Environmental Affairs Board instead of delivering an outright rejection.
side_b_arguments: Referring the issue to EAB provides a constructive, collaborative pathway for Treyburn and other neighborhoods experiencing deer or wildlife conflicts rather than leaving residents empty-handed.
disagreements.resolution: Middleton declined to withdraw his main motion and Cook maintained her second; the main motion was voted down 0-7, leaving future referral to EAB or staff alternatives open.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session December 19, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: The December 19, 2024 Work Session featured farewell tributes to retiring City Manager Wanda Page after 37 years of city service and an intense debate over lifting an administrative pause on HEART staff distributing tents to unsheltered residents during winter weather. Council also heard a citizen presentation opposing water fluoridation and performance audits on the Community Safety Department's HEART program and the City's ADA Title II compliance, before questioning proposed reductions to deer bow hunting acreage and setback buffers.

agenda_items.title: Council Announcements and Tribute to Retiring City Manager Wanda Page
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members recognized retiring City Manager Wanda Page on her 37-year career in Durham local government and welcomed incoming City Manager Bo Ferguson. Javiera Caballero noted she would need to depart around 2:00 PM.

agenda_items.title: Board and Commission Nominations (RDU Airport Authority & Racial Equity Commission)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk announced council nominations for Tammy E. Hall to the Raleigh-Durham Airport Authority and Shannon M. Jones to the Racial Equity Commission ahead of formal consent confirmation.

agenda_items.title: Citizen Matter: Suspension of Community Water Fluoridation (Jared Rist)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident Jared Rist urged Council to temporarily suspend municipal water fluoridation at 0.7 mg/L following a September 24, 2024 federal court ruling in the Northern District of California by Judge Edward Chen regarding developmental neurotoxicity risk.

agenda_items.title: General Public Comment on Youth Violence, Housing Infrastructure, and Eviction Diversion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Speakers addressed youth gun violence and federal Tiahrt Amendment restrictions (Minister Paul Scott), youth workforce investment (Dwor Langley), water pressure and alleged code retaliation on Ardmore Drive (Mr. Woods), water and fire-door safety concerns at the Whitted Building senior apartments (Regina Mace), and the depletion of Entry Point Durham's $475,000 funding 8 months early (Emily Wilks).

agenda_items.title: Unsheltered Residents Winter Tent Distribution Policy Debate
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chelsea Cook raised an unagendized discussion requesting an immediate lift of the City's administrative pause barring HEART and staff from distributing tents until HSAC adopts a formal policy. Nate Baker and DeDreana Freeman supported protecting workers from disciplinary risk during cold rain, while Mark-Anthony Middleton and Mayor Leonardo Williams opposed issuing ad hoc work-session directives and asked staff to return with urgent winter shelter options and cost estimates.

agenda_items.title: HEART Program Performance Audit (November 2024)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Audit Director Germaine Brewington and Community Safety Director Ryan Smith presented two audit findings: FY25's 52% eligible call-response goal vs. 25% actual in FY24 (held down by 12% co-response coverage compared to 53.5% for CRT and 75% for CCD), and 128 records (1.1%) closed after the 24-hour target.

agenda_items.title: ADA Title II Governance Performance Audit (November 2024)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Audit Services and Equity & Inclusion Director Sharon Williams reviewed three audit findings showing an unclear ADA Coordinator structure, unresolved permanent departmental placement, and misalignment with the City's transition plan, with target remediation milestones running through January 2026.

agenda_items.title: Revisions to City Deer Bow Hunting Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Treyburn HOA representative Quincy Hutto spoke in favor of reducing minimum parcel acreage and setback buffers for bow hunting. Council members Chelsea Cook, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Carl Rist, and DeDreana Freeman raised safety, data, non-lethal alternative, and equity concerns regarding the proposed 250-to-60 foot buffer reduction and 5-to-2 acre drop, resulting in the item moving to January General Business.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Agenda for Next Regular City Council Meeting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page presented the final docket for the upcoming January regular meeting, placing Items 1-4 and 6-10 on Consent and Item 5 (Deer Bow Hunting) on the General Business Agenda.

votes.item_title: Set the Agenda for Next Regular City Council Meeting (Consent: Items 1-4, 6-10; GBA: Item 5)
votes.notes: Javiera Caballero departed around 2:00 PM prior to the afternoon audit items and agenda vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Following presentations on the HEART Program and ADA Title II performance audits and substantive council reservations regarding the proposed deer bow hunting ordinance revisions, City Manager Wanda Page read the recommended agenda placement for the upcoming regular meeting. Items 1 through 4 and 6 through 10 were assigned to the Consent Agenda, while Item 5 on the deer bow hunting ordinance was routed to the General Business Agenda for fuller public consideration. Council moved and seconded the motion without further amendment, approving the slate by unanimous 6-0 voice vote among the six members remaining present.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session December 19, 2024
disagreements.issue: Authority and Safety of Lifting the Administrative Pause on City Tent Distribution to Unsheltered Residents
disagreements.summary: Council members clashed over whether to direct staff during a work session to lift an administrative pause prohibiting HEART and other city staff from distributing tents while HSAC finalizes a countywide policy.
disagreements.side_a_position: Lift the administrative pause immediately so outreach workers can distribute tents during freezing rain without risking disciplinary retaliation.
side_a_arguments: Freezing rain and cold winter nights pose immediate danger to unsheltered residents before a formal HSAC policy is finished.
Staff such as HEART responders should not face write-ups or uncertainty for providing emergency shelter gear.
disagreements.side_b_position: Do not issue unagendized work-session directives or endorse tents as winter shelter in below-freezing weather; defer to formal policy channels and indoor shelter options.
side_b_arguments: Council cannot govern by ad hoc work-session fiat without an agendized item, staff cost data, or formal vote.
Tents are unsafe in sub-freezing temperatures; the City should explore indoor facilities such as vacant City real estate or Durham Public Schools gyms and align with HSAC.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Mayor Williams declined to suspend the rules and instructed City Manager Wanda Page, incoming Manager Bo Ferguson, Deputy Manager Keith Chadwell, and Community Safety Director Ryan Smith to develop an urgent response.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session December 19, 2024
disagreements.issue: Proposed Citywide Reductions to Deer Bow Hunting Acreage and Setback Buffers (Item 5)
disagreements.summary: Multiple council members pushed back on lowering the minimum parcel size from 5 to 2 acres and shrinking the dwelling setback from 250 to 60 feet citywide in response to Treyburn HOA requests.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve relaxed citywide acreage and buffer limits so neighborhoods like Treyburn can manage severe deer overpopulation and tick-borne disease risk.
side_a_arguments: Treyburn has roughly 70 deer per square mile and cannot physically satisfy the 250-foot buffer requirement even on combined 5-acre parcels.
Certified bow hunters shooting downward from elevated 10-foot stands pose minimal risk and already operate safely in neighboring jurisdictions.
disagreements.side_b_position: Require stronger citywide safety data, daytime/signage restrictions, non-lethal alternatives, and consideration of neighborhood equity before weakening weapon discharge buffers.
side_b_arguments: A citywide ordinance change opens bow hunting in denser neighborhoods outside Treyburn with fewer notice protections for residents and pets.

Council lacked empirical deer-count data, exploration of sterilization options, and justification for prioritizing suburban deer culling relative to gun violence in communities like McDougald Terrace.
disagreements.resolution: Item 5 was placed on the January General Business Agenda rather than Consent for further deliberation and public hearing.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Dec 16 2024
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council celebrated retiring City Manager Wanda Sims Page with a proclamation, Key to the City, and Order of the Long Leaf Pine after 37 years of local government service, alongside a 60th-anniversary proclamation for Sam Cooke's 'A Change Is Gonna Come.' Council approved the Consent Agenda (7-0), certified the November 2024 $200 million General Obligation Bond referendum, authorized $4.94 million across two contracts for 77 hybrid police patrol SUVs and vehicle upfitting (7-0 each) amid public pushback over November 12 encampment sweeps at Long Meadow Park, and approved a $1.75 million ARPA home-repair contract with Hayti Promise CDC and Rebuilding Together of the Triangle (7-0). Council also unanimously approved a $7,250 Spanish translation amendment with WSP USA Inc. after contentious debate over dropping contractor Idealisms LLC, and renamed Vivian Street to William V. 'Bill' Bell Way (7-0). Following closed session, Council voted to appoint Deputy City Manager William Bowman 'Bo' Ferguson as City Manager, triggering sharp objections from Council Members Chelsea Cook, DeDreana Freeman, and Javiera Caballero over the un-agendized motion, rushed vote during which Cook stated she did not cast a vote, and lack of an open national search.

agenda_items.title: Proclamation: 60th Anniversary of Sam Cooke's 'A Change Is Gonna Come'
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton read a proclamation honoring the 60th anniversary of Sam Cooke's 'A Change Is Gonna Come,' highlighting Cooke's May 1963 visit to Durham and interaction with North Carolina Central University sit-in activists prior to writing the song. Guests Andrea Lee, Nikia Davis, Levi Wiggins, Ruth Montia, Jason Perlmutter, and Ian Mance joined Council for remarks.

agenda_items.title: Retirement Proclamation, Key to the City, and Order of the Long Leaf Pine for City Manager Wanda Sims Page
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams presented retiring City Manager Wanda Sims Page with a proclamation, the Key to the City, and North Carolina's Order of the Long Leaf Pine recognizing her 37 years of local government service and four-year tenure leading Durham through $200 million in voter-approved bonds and post-pandemic growth. Council members, the City Clerk, and City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg praised her steady leadership before Page thanked employees and residents ahead of her December 31, 2024 retirement.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Excluding Items 4, 5, 6, 10, and 14; Item 19 GBA; Item 21 Public Hearing)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council pulled Items 4, 5, 6, 10, and 14 for comment or separate action while noting General Business Agenda Item 19 and Public Hearing Item 21. Council Member Chelsea Cook and Mayor Leonardo Williams offered brief supportive remarks on Item 10 (Durham Symphony funding) before Council adopted the remaining Consent Agenda.

agenda_items.title: GBA: First Amendment to Supplemental Agreement #3 with WSP USA Inc. (Durham Freeway Study Translation)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council considered a $7,250 contract amendment (bringing the total contract to $438,500) for WSP USA Inc. to translate Durham Freeway Study reports into Spanish after Item 18 with Idealisms LLC was referred back. Council Member DeDreana Freeman opposed relying on internal staff instead of community-based engagement practitioners, arguing it undermined relationships built by Idealisms LLC, while Council Member Carl Rist, City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg, and others countered that municipal consultant work product belongs to the City and translating existing reports improves bilingual access.

agenda_items.title: Certification of November 5, 2024 $200 Million General Obligation Bond Referendum Results
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council opened Item 4 to certify the November 2024 $200 million GO bond election results for streets, sidewalks, and parks. Four public commenters—Virginia Workman, Ripley Thornton, Samuel Scarboro, and Thomas Crowell-Albritton—protested the November 12 Durham Police Department sweep of the Long Meadow Park homeless encampment and urged Council to expand supportive housing, storage, and winter warming shelters before Mayor Williams opened the vote and proceeded to Item 5.

agenda_items.title: Contract with Clinton Automotive LLC dba Deacon Jones Ford for 77 Hybrid Police Patrol SUVs ($3,662,325.59)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council considered a $3,662,325.59 fleet contract with Clinton Automotive LLC dba Deacon Jones Ford to purchase 77 hybrid police patrol SUVs. Public speaker Samuel Scarboro opposed police fleet expansion and called for redirecting funds toward housing and eviction prevention prior to Council's unanimous approval.

agenda_items.title: Contract with Dana Safety Supply Inc. for Upfitting 77 Police Patrol Vehicles ($1,274,306)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council considered a $1,274,306 upfitting contract with Dana Safety Supply Inc. for the 77 patrol SUVs. Speaker Elizabeth Avant criticized spending nearly $5 million total on police vehicles amid homelessness and utility needs; Mayor Williams defended Durham's investments including the $95 million housing bond, ~$4 million in homeless response grants, and Legal Aid eviction funding while citing state preemptions, and Council Member Freeman challenged critics to identify specific $3.7 million budget offsets before voting unanimously to approve.

agenda_items.title: ARPA Contract with Hayti Promise CDC and Rebuilding Together of the Triangle ($1,750,000)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed a $1,750,000 ARPA-funded home repair and neighborhood preservation contract along the Fayetteville Street Corridor. Speaker Victoria Peterson urged upgrades for the W.D. Hill Recreation Center, while City Manager Page and Interim Neighborhood Improvement Services Director Alexis John clarified upfront nonprofit disbursement rules and confirmed more than 20 vacant properties had active code-enforcement cases before Council approved the contract.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing SN2400001: Street Renaming from Vivian Street to William V. 'Bill' Bell Way
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council held a public hearing on street-renaming request SN2400001 honoring former Durham Mayor William V. 'Bill' Bell along Vivian Street at a signage cost of $365. Kristen Adair, Bell's daughter, thanked Council on behalf of her family before Council unanimously adopted the renaming.

agenda_items.title: Appointment of William Bowman 'Bo' Ferguson as City Manager
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Returning from closed session, Council moved to appoint Deputy City Manager William Bowman 'Bo' Ferguson as Durham's next City Manager following Wanda Page's retirement. Mayor Williams declared the vote unanimous at 02:34:12, prompting immediate objection from Council Member Chelsea Cook that she had her hand raised, believed discussion was still underway, and never cast a vote, followed by criticism from Cook, DeDreana Freeman, and Javiera Caballero regarding closed-door decision-making, omission of a public search, and procedural haste.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed (declared unanimous; Cook stated she did not vote)

votes.notes: Brings total WSP Supplemental Agreement #3 contract to $438,500.
votes.discussion_detail: After debate between Freeman and other council members/City Attorney over consultant relationship ownership following Idealisms LLC's removal from Item 18, all seven members voted to translate the existing WSP reports into Spanish.

votes.item_title: Item 4: Certification of November 5, 2024 $200M General Obligation Bond Referendum Results

votes.notes: Motion called at 01:49:09 and carried unanimously at 01:49:45.
votes.discussion_detail: Approved after public comment from Samuel Scarboro opposing police vehicle spending.

votes.item_title: Item 6: Contract with Dana Safety Supply Inc. (Upfitting 77 Police Vehicles, $1,274,306)
votes.notes: Motion called at 02:00:05 and passed unanimously at 02:02:03.
votes.discussion_detail: Approved unanimously after public comment questioning nearly $5M in total police vehicle costs and Council responses detailing Durham's affordable housing and homelessness spending.

votes.item_title: Item 14: ARPA Contract with Hayti Promise CDC & Rebuilding Together of the Triangle ($1,750,000)
votes.notes: Mayor announced 7-0 passage at 02:23:02.
votes.discussion_detail: Approved after staff clarified upfront CDC disbursement mechanics and code enforcement on vacant properties along Fayetteville Street.

votes.item_title: Item 21: Street Renaming SN2400001 (Vivian Street to William V. 'Bill' Bell Way)
votes.notes: Motion made at 02:32:06 and carried unanimously at 02:32:27.
votes.discussion_detail: Public hearing held with remarks from former Mayor Bell's daughter Kristen Adair; passed unanimously.

votes.item_title: Appointment of William Bowman 'Bo' Ferguson as City Manager
votes.tally: Declared unanimous (Cook stated she did not vote)
votes.notes: Individual roll-call votes were not read aloud; Cook's non-vote and dissent on process were entered on the record.
votes.discussion_detail: Motion made immediately after closed session without prior public agenda notice. Mayor Williams declared passage unanimous at 02:34:12, though Council Member Chelsea Cook objected at 02:34:54 and 02:45:27 that she had her hand raised to continue debate and did not vote (noting she would have voted yes had discussion proceeded properly).

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Dec 16 2024
disagreements.issue: Community Engagement Consultant Transition and Intellectual Property (Item 19 - WSP USA Translation)
disagreements.summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman challenged relying on City staff and WSP USA Inc. after removing Idealisms LLC (Item 18), arguing it unfairly appropriated relationships built by community practitioners; other members and the City Attorney countered that municipal consultant work product belongs to the City and Spanish translation should proceed.
disagreements.side_a_position: Concerned that cutting Idealisms LLC while continuing staff-led engagement exploits community-based practitioners' relationships
side_a_arguments: Community engagement firms build years of local trust that City staff should not bypass or repurpose
Questioned continuing the study scope without the originally partnered community engagement firm
disagreements.side_b_position: Support approving the $7,250 WSP amendment to translate already-completed Durham Freeway Study reports into Spanish
side_b_arguments: City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg advised that deliverables produced under City contracts are work for hire owned by the City
Spanish-speaking residents need immediate translated access to existing technical reports
disagreements.resolution: Passed 7-0 after Council Member Freeman voted Aye while maintaining her process critique on the record.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Dec 16 2024
disagreements.issue: City Manager Appointment Process, Transparency, and Vote Timing (Bo Ferguson)
disagreements.summary: Following a closed session, a surprise open-session motion to appoint Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson was declared unanimously passed, sparking sharp disagreement over procedural fairness, lack of an open national search, closed-session division, and Chelsea Cook not having a chance to cast her vote.
disagreements.side_a_position: Objected to the un-agendized motion, rushed vote without discussion, and closed-door hiring process lacking a public search
side_a_arguments: Cook stated she had her hand raised to speak, did not know a final vote was closing, and never cast a ballot
Freeman cited prior closed-session disagreement (4-3 or 5-2) and criticized skipping an open search for Durham's highest-paid executive
Caballero emphasized public transparency expectations for major executive appointments and voicemail/communication delays
disagreements.side_b_position: Defended appointing internal Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson through the same council appointment mechanism used previously
side_b_arguments: Williams and Middleton highlighted Ferguson's institutional continuity and leadership during major crises such as the 2019 gas explosion
Asserted the appointment followed the same precedent used to appoint outgoing City Manager Wanda Page
disagreements.resolution: Appointment stood as declared at 02:34:12 without a revote; Cook stated for the record she did not vote during the tally though she supported Ferguson personally.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Dec 5, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: With Mayor Leonardo Williams absent on City business in Wilmington, Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton chaired the December 5, 2024 Work Session where Council accepted City Manager Priority Items (6-0), removing Idealisms LLC (Item 18) back to Transportation and canceling Item 22. During review of pulled consent items for the December 16 regular meeting, Council Members Carl Rist, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, and Chelsea Cook successfully polled to refer Item 13 (FY24-25 Pay Plan Amendment for ~196 bypassed Fire and Police employees) back to staff to recalculate retroactive implementation to July 1, 2024 rather than January 11, 2025. Council also heard public protest from Thomas Crowell-Albritton over the November 12 Long Meadow Park homeless encampment sweeps during discussion of Item 4 ($200M GO Bond certification), scrutinized a $1.4 million rock-excavation cost overrun on Duke/MCNC fiber construction (Item 16) and transit capital plans including a $200,000 BRT feasibility study (Item 20), and voted 6-0 to settle the December 16 agenda without Item 13.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Items and Board/Commission Nominations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented Priority Items referring Item 18 (Idealisms LLC Durham Freeway engagement) back to the Transportation Department, canceling Item 22 (Jacobs Engineering contract), and adding Item 23 (Chapman transportation response). The City Clerk also read nominations for Hispanic/Latino affairs and Planning Commission appointments before Council accepted Priority Items.

agenda_items.title: GO Bond Referendum Certification ($200M) and 77 Hybrid Police SUVs ($3.66M)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: During discussion of Item 4 certifying the $200 million GO bond vote, resident Thomas Crowell-Albritton protested the November 12 DPD sweeps at Long Meadow Park and criticized City surplus spending versus homelessness aid. On Item 5, staff member Michael Boyd answered Council Member Nate Baker's questions regarding the 77 hybrid patrol SUV purchase.

agenda_items.title: FY24-25 Pay Plan Amendment for Bypassed Public Safety Employees (~196 Fire & Police Staff)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff proposed a pay-plan correction costing $95,000 for the remainder of FY25 ($188,000 annualized) effective January 11, 2025 to address compression affecting roughly 196 Fire and Police employees bypassed during prior adjustments. Council Members Carl Rist, Javiera Caballero, DeDreana Freeman, and Chelsea Cook objected to delaying parity until January despite City Manager Wanda Page citing tight sales tax growth and complex overtime recalculations, leading Middleton to poll four-plus hands to refer Item 13 back to staff for a July 1, 2024 retroactive calculation.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Referred back to staff (excluded from Dec 16 agenda)

agenda_items.title: Hayti Promise ARPA Contract ($1.75M), Duke/MCNC Fiber Overrun ($1.4M), WSP Translation ($7,250), and Transit CIP
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed Hayti Promise CDC's $1.75 million ARPA corridor repair contract (Item 14), questioned a $1.4 million subsurface rock cost overrun on the Duke/MCNC dark-fiber project (Item 16), moved WSP USA's $7,250 Spanish translation amendment (Item 19) to GBA for final decision, and examined Item 20's Transit Capital Improvement Program updates covering GoDurham Access paratransit facilities and a $200,000 Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) feasibility study.

agenda_items.title: Proposed Urban Bow Hunting Ordinance Scheduling
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Carl Rist and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton confirmed that a revised draft of the urban bow hunting ordinance would be scheduled for further review at the December 19, 2024 work session before advancing to a regular council vote.

agenda_items.title: Settle Agenda for December 16, 2024 Regular City Council Meeting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council settled the December 16, 2024 agenda placing Items 1–12, 14–17, and 20 on Consent, Item 19 on General Business Agenda, and Item 21 under Public Hearings while omitting Item 13 pending staff recalculation.

votes.item_title: Accept City Manager Priority Items (Referring Item 18 to Transportation, Canceling Item 22, Adding Item 23)
votes.notes: Mayor Leonardo Williams was absent (in Wilmington).
votes.discussion_detail: Accepted priority agenda adjustments ahead of pulled-item review.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Dec 5, 2024
disagreements.issue: Retroactive Effective Date for FY24-25 Public Safety Pay Plan Correction (Item 13)
disagreements.summary: Council debated whether pay-compression adjustments for roughly 196 bypassed Fire and Police employees should take effect January 11, 2025 as proposed by staff or retroactively to the start of the fiscal year on July 1, 2024.
disagreements.side_a_position: Make the public safety pay correction retroactive to July 1, 2024
side_a_arguments: Affected Fire and Police employees missed parity increases implemented in the FY25 budget at the start of the fiscal year
Delaying implementation until January 11, 2025 shortchanges employees who were bypassed by administrative structure
disagreements.side_b_position: Staff cautioned against mid-year retroactivity due to budget tightness and payroll calculation complexity
side_b_arguments: City Manager Wanda Page cited sluggish sales tax revenue growth (~13 months into tighter post-ARPA budgeting)
Retroactively recalculating 6 months of variable public safety overtime shifts poses heavy payroll and financial uncertainty
disagreements.resolution: Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton polled at least four supporting members and referred Item 13 back to staff to recalculate costs effective July 1, 2024; Item 13 was omitted from the December 16 agenda.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Dec 2 2024
meetings.executive_summary: The December 2, 2024 Regular City Council meeting resulted in nine unanimous 7-0 votes, including a $1,000,000 ARPA award for the Fayetteville Street Corridor initiative, two rezonings, a five-year statutory vested rights extension for Davis Park Pod G, and a Victory Lane cul-de-sac closure. Council probed the Vivo Living Ivy Creek adaptive hotel reuse project closely over mold remediation, affordable voucher access, and pedestrian connectivity to MLK Parkway before approving its 128 apartments with 25 income-restricted units.

agenda_items.title: World AIDS Day Proclamation and HOPWA Grant Criticism
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chelsea Cook read the World AIDS Day proclamation recognizing December 1, 2024. Coalition representative Dr. Haley Cunningham thanked the City while criticizing the denial of a support letter for a $2.5M federal HOPWA HINT grant and unspent HOPWA allocations.

agenda_items.title: Excused Absence for Mayor Leonardo Williams (December 5 Work Session)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council considered and unanimously approved Mayor Leonardo Williams's excused absence request for the upcoming December 5, 2024 work session.

agenda_items.title: Adoption of Consent Agenda (Items 1, 3, 5, 7-19, 21-26, 32)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council adopted the consent docket excluding Item 6 (pulled as a resource/ARPA item), Item 20 (referred back), and Public Hearing Items 28-31.

agenda_items.title: ARPA Fayetteville Street Corridor Planning and Infrastructure Community Assistance Initiative
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted separately on the pulled ARPA grant of up to $1,000,000 with Fayetteville Street Planning Group Inc. and United Way of the Greater Triangle.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public hearing on rezoning 3.59 acres from CG(D) and OI(D) to PDR 35.654 to convert a former hotel into 128 studio and one-bedroom apartments, with 25 units (20%) committed at 60% AMI for 30 years plus $10,000 each to the Affordable Housing Fund and DPS.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public hearing to rezone 0.50 acres from CD-S2 to CI(D) to expand an existing Chapel Hill Tire facility from 6 to 8 service bays, accompanied by five text commitments including Rose Hill sidewalk construction and a Hillsboro Road bus shelter (Planning Commission recommended approval 6-3).

Nate Baker and Carl Rist questioned density and pedestrian design tradeoffs relative to the newer district standards.

agenda_items.title: Permanent Street Closing - Portion of Victory Lane Cul-de-Sac Bulb (SC2300005)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public hearing on permanently closing 2,899 square feet of the Victory Lane cul-de-sac bulb for the Fletcher Ridge/Phillips Valley development by D.R. Horton.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: DeDreana Freeman reminded homeowners in pre-1988 properties who received federal lead-pipe inventory notices to contact Durham One Call at 919-560-1200 for inspection assistance.

No objections were raised by council colleagues regarding the scheduling conflict. A motion was made and seconded and passed unanimously 7-0 on the electronic board at 00:29:46.

votes.item_title: Item 6: ARPA Fayetteville Street Corridor Planning and Infrastructure Community Assistance Initiative (NTE $1,000,000)
votes.notes: Agreement with Fayetteville Street Planning Group Inc. and fiscal partner United Way of the Greater Triangle.
votes.discussion_detail: Pulled from the Consent Agenda for separate action, Item 6 authorized up to $1,000,000 in American Rescue Plan Act funding for the Fayetteville Street Corridor Planning and Infrastructure Community Assistance Initiative administered with Fayetteville Street Planning Group Inc. and United Way of the Greater Triangle. Having reviewed the revised scope after its earlier October referral back to staff, council members raised no further objections at the table. The motion passed unanimously 7-0 at 00:36:23.

votes.item_title: Item 28: Vivo Living Ivy Creek UDO Zoning Map Amendment (CG(D)/OI(D) to PDR 35.654, 1920 Ivy Creek Blvd)
votes.notes: Adaptive hotel reuse into 128 apartments with 25 units (20%) at 60% AMI for 30 years, $10k Housing Fund, $10k DPS, and a 12-ft shared-use path connection.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff presented the 3.59-acre adaptive reuse proposal by Vivo Living to convert the vacant hotel at 1920 Ivy Creek Boulevard into 128 efficiency and one-bedroom apartments with 25 affordable units at 60% AMI for 30 years. Council members probed the developer intensively: Chelsea Cook challenged an inaccuracy in the staff report listing the site as vacant and questioned mold remediation, reduced application fees, and Durham Housing Authority voucher acceptance; Nate Baker pressed on Planning Commission concerns and written fee commitments; Carl Rist secured focus on a 12-foot shared-use path to MLK Parkway; Mark-Anthony Middleton stressed parity between affordable and market units and inspection rigor; and DeDreana Freeman questioned mold inspection methods. Satisfied with the applicant's proffers and commitments, Council approved the rezoning unanimously 7-0 at 01:19:04.

votes.item_title: Item 28: Consistency Statement under NCGS 160D-605 (Vivo Living Ivy Creek)
votes.notes: Statutory consistency finding with the Comprehensive Plan.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately following approval of the Vivo Living Ivy Creek zoning map amendment, Council considered the mandatory statutory consistency statement pursuant to NCGS 160D-605. The statement affirmed that the PDR 35.654 adaptive-reuse residential project aligns with the Comprehensive Plan's goals for infill housing and transit-accessible affordability. Council adopted the consistency statement 7-0 at 01:19:38.

votes.item_title: Item 29: Hillsboro Road Commercial / Chapel Hill Tire UDO Zoning Map Amendment (CD-S2 to CI(D), 2504 Hillsboro Rd)
votes.notes: Allows expansion from 6 to 8 service bays with 5 text commitments including Rose Hill sidewalk and a Hillsboro Rd bus shelter; Planning Commission voted 6-3 in favor.
votes.discussion_detail: Staff and representatives for Chapel Hill Tire presented the 0.50-acre rezoning from CD-S2 to Commercial Infill with Development Plan (CI(D)) to expand from six to eight automotive service bays at 2504 Hillsboro Road, noting the Planning Commission's 6-3 recommendation of approval. Speakers and council members examined neighborhood pedestrian safety along Rose Hill Avenue, noise/hours buffers, and how the five text commitments address stormwater and a Hillsboro Road transit shelter. Council members commended the transit and sidewalk investments on an older suburban commercial parcel and approved the rezoning unanimously 7-0 at 01:48:46.

votes.item_title: Item 29: Consistency Statement under NCGS 160D-605 (Hillsboro Road Commercial)
votes.discussion_detail: Following the Hillsboro Road Commercial rezoning approval, Council voted on the companion NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement. Council affirmed that the CI(D) expansion with committed sidewalk and bus-shelter improvements was consistent and reasonable under the Comprehensive Plan. The motion passed unanimously 7-0 at 01:49:14.

votes.item_title: Item 30: Ordinance Approving Statutory Vested Rights Determination for Davis Park Pod G (1400 Maran Ave)
votes.notes: Extends site plan D2200108 on 2.83 acres until December 2, 2029.
votes.discussion_detail: Attorney Patrick Byker and developer Lance Chernow requested a statutory vested rights extension through December 2, 2029 for site plan D2200108 on 2.83 acres at Davis Park Pod G (1400 Maran Avenue). Nate Baker and Carl Rist closely questioned why the 2023 site plan should remain vested rather than adapting to newly enacted Page-Miami Design District urban-form and density standards, while applicants cited infrastructure investments and financing delays. After weighing prior site-plan approvals and RTP market timing, Council unanimously approved the vested rights ordinance 7-0 at 02:17:38.

votes.item_title: Item 31: Permanent Closing of Portion (2,899 sq ft) of Victory Lane Cul-de-Sac Bulb (SC2300005)
votes.notes: Fletcher Ridge / Phillips Valley development by D.R. Horton.
votes.discussion_detail: Staff presented street-closing case SC2300005 to permanently close 2,899 square feet of the temporary Victory Lane cul-de-sac bulb so through-street connectivity could be completed for D.R. Horton's Fletcher Ridge/Phillips Valley development. No public objections were raised during the public hearing, and staff confirmed required public utility easements and access continuity were protected. Council adopted the street-closing order unanimously 7-0 at 02:23:54.

development_cases.location: 1920 Ivy Creek Blvd
development_cases.scale: 128 apartments on 3.59 acres
development_cases.zoning_change: CG(D) / OI(D) to PDR 35.654

proffers.dps_cash: $10,000 one-time contribution
proffers.affordable_housing: 20% of units (25 units) deed-restricted as affordable housing for 30 years (60% AMI, evenly distributed across building), plus $10,000 one-time contribution to Durham Dedicated Housing Fund; reduced application fee equal to actual credit report cost (waived if not qualified) for affordable units
proffers.environmental_tree: Adaptive reuse of existing hotel structure avoiding ground-up construction and reducing carbon footprint; mold mitigation required prior to certificate of occupancy
proffers.transit_infrastructure: Bike racks on site; located near MLK Pkwy and Transit Opportunity Area (declined 12-ft shared-use path to MLK Pkwy due to NCDOT ROW and detention basin retaining wall constraints)
other_proffers: On-site professional management, lobby, clubhouse, fitness center, and laundry facilities

member_justifications.stance_summary: Probed Planning Commission concerns regarding mold/habitability and partial ongoing hotel occupancy, and welcomed Vivo's policy change waiving application fees for disqualified affordable-unit applicants. Urged the developer to examine whether high fees and screening rules still create racial equity barriers for market-rate tenants.
member_justifications.key_quote: I'm glad that they've changed for the affordable units, but I would love for your folks to think about how that application might deter or might racially bias the folks coming to live there even in the market-rate units.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Praised the case as 'on the better side of many of the rezoning cases' because it adaptively reuses an existing building, delivers a deep 60% AMI affordable housing commitment, and responded constructively to prior council feedback. Questioned the developer on mold mitigation and whether the reduced application fee could be bound to the zoning (the applicant said operational rules could not be tied to the land).
member_justifications.key_quote: There on paper there are a lot of very positive things about this rezoning case: it's an adaptive reuse of an existing structure, there's a deep commitment to 60% area median income affordable housing.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supported the adaptive reuse, 20% at 60% AMI affordability, and contributions to the housing fund and DPS, and pressed the developer to build a 12-ft shared-use path connecting the site to MLK Parkway. Accepted that NCDOT ROW and stormwater basin retaining wall obstacles would threaten the project's affordability.
member_justifications.key_quote: I really appreciate the adaptive reuse... I appreciate the 20% affordable at 60% AMI... and also the contributions both to the dedicated Durham housing fund and DPS.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supported the adaptive reuse and affordable housing while putting the broader development community on notice that Durham expects affordable units to be indistinguishable in quality, upkeep, and habitability from market-rate housing.
member_justifications.key_quote: For us in Durham, affordable housing does not mean substandard housing... we don't want you to be able to tell the difference outside between the market-rate apartments and affordable units.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supported converting an older hotel into permanent housing near major employers like Blue Cross Blue Shield, grocery stores, and retail.
member_justifications.key_quote: I'm glad that we're actually making it into permanent housing because it's going to provide a very good quality of life for folks that will live there.

development_cases.location: 2504 Hillsboro Rd
development_cases.scale: 0.50 acres; interior conversion expanding from 6 to 8 service bays (no building footprint or height increase)
development_cases.zoning_change: CD-S2 to CI(D) (Commercial Infill with Textual Development Plan)

proffers.environmental_tree: Removing small amount of impervious surface to install UDO-compliant vehicle-use-area landscaping along Hillsboro Rd and Rose Hill Ave; prior owner pollution remediated
proffers.transit_infrastructure: City-standard sidewalk in Rose Hill Ave ROW; bus shelter along Hillsboro Rd (subject to NCDOT and GoDurham approval); removal of middle curb cut on Rose Hill Ave
other_proffers: Prohibits nightclub, bar, and payday lender uses; replaces copy sign with UDO-compliant sign; two new bays limited to technical repair rather than tire work to limit noise

member_justifications.stance_summary: Called it a 'feel-good rezoning case' for a beloved local business and noted that while he prefers design districts, the discretionary review produced a 'happy middle ground' securing a sidewalk and bus stop. Asked planning staff whether the UDO rewrite could ease non-conforming use conversions within existing buildings.
member_justifications.key_quote: It's a beloved local business and in some ways we get to keep all of that and we get a bus stop and sidewalk, so I think in many ways this discretionary review allows for us to find that happy middle ground.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supported the rezoning and praised Chapel Hill Tire's mechanic internship and mentoring program for high school students.
member_justifications.key_quote: I'll be supporting this; thank you for everything you do, especially your mentoring of mechanics for high school students.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Praised the Old West Durham community engagement and landscaping/bus shelter proffers, and asked whether green building techniques such as solar panels were feasible on the 39-year-old building.
member_justifications.key_quote: Appreciate the community engagement that you've described there, very impressive, appreciate the additional proffers.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Criticized over-regulation that required a rezoning for an interior storage-to-service-bay conversion and praised the company's apprenticeship program as his primary reason for support.
member_justifications.key_quote: Sometimes I feel like we are so over-regulated that it just becomes overly complex... I'm really impressed with this mentoring program, the apprenticeship program.

development_cases.location: 1400 Maran Ave (Davis Park East)
development_cases.scale: 250 multifamily units on 2.83 acres (extending approved site plan validity from March 29, 2027 to December 2, 2029)
development_cases.zoning_change: No zoning change (5-year Statutory Vested Rights extension for Site Plan D220108)

proffers.transit_infrastructure: Part of 107-acre Davis Park East master plan connected by pedestrian paths near planned Hopson Rd / Davis Dr commercial nodes
other_proffers: Preserves approved 250-unit site plan against potential density reduction and design changes under proposed Page-Miami Design District

member_justifications.stance_summary: Clarified that the proposed Page-Miami Design District prompted the vesting request to avoid density reductions and new street-frontage/fenestration rules. Acknowledged valid fairness reasons for vesting law given substantial engineering investments and phased construction, and supported the extension after confirming the approved site plan already builds toward the sidewalk.
member_justifications.key_quote: There are very good reasons and fair reasons for vesting law; you've invested quite a bit into a property and it would be unfair to change the regulations that apply.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Asked why a 5-year rather than 2-year statutory vesting period was warranted and praised Davis Park as a high-quality walkable and bikeable mixed-use model after touring the site.
member_justifications.key_quote: I did drive the site today and you're absolutely right: high-quality development, absolutely walkable, bikeable, yeah a good model.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supported the 5-year vesting extension as a reasonable remedy for COVID-era construction delays, noting the site plan matches the established character of Davis Park.
member_justifications.key_quote: I think this is a pretty reasonable ask; I think the remedy that's being proposed here for whatever happened in COVID and other unforeseeable circumstances is reasonable.
