meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Nov 21, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: At the November 21, 2024 Work Session, Council suspended the rules to pass an NCDOT-required resolution closing streets for the December Durham Holiday Parade and reviewed the clean FY24 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report alongside the FY25 Q1 financial update. Police Chief Patrice Andrews delivered the Q3 2024 crime report amid council questions on stolen guns, ShotSpotter, police staffing at 73%, and U-Visas, followed by a split in tone as Council reluctantly voted 7-0 to enter closed session on a personnel matter.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Items, Rules Suspension & Item 20 Holiday Parade Street Closures
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page introduced priority additions including the ACFR presentation (Item 4), referral back of Item 13, Q3 crime report (Item 21), supplemental Sandy Ridge Villas loan assignment (Item 32), and immediate action on Item 20 for 2024 Holiday Parade NCDOT street closures.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Priority items, rules suspension, and Item 20 all approved 7-0

agenda_items.title: Board and Commission Nominations and Civilian Police Review Board Appointments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Clerk reported nominations for BPAC Youth (Rosalia M. Edmonds), readvertisement of the Workers' Rights Commission seat, and Civilian Police Review Board confirmations (Shan Allen, Cassandra Johnson, Shawana Lindsey, Michael Cam, and Alexander Williams).

agenda_items.title: ARPA Durham Community Land Trustees (DCLT) Modular Homeownership Amendment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pulled for discussion with DCLT Director Sherry Taylor regarding contract revisions enabling modular affordable homeownership delivery under ARPA timelines.

agenda_items.title: FY25 Domestic Violence and Gang Reduction Agreement with NC AOC / District Attorney
agenda_items.discussion_summary: District Attorney Satana Deberry and Community Safety Director Ryan Smith answered council questions on renewed city funding supporting domestic violence prosecution and gang-reduction coordination.

agenda_items.title: DWSRF $500,000 Emerging Contaminants (PFAS) Study Grant
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Water Management staff Lori Montgomery detailed the state Drinking Water State Revolving Fund $500,000 grant to study PFAS and emerging contaminants.

agenda_items.title: FY24 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR) and FY25 Q1 Financial Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Auditors from Cherry Bekaert issued an unmodified clean audit opinion on FY24 financials, followed at 01:04:42 by Budget Director Christina Riordan presenting FY25 Q1 sales and property tax performance.

agenda_items.title: Q3 2024 Durham Police Department Crime Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief Patrice Andrews and Deputy Chief Walter Tate presented Q3 crime statistics, prompting council inquiries on stolen firearms from unlocked cars, federal Tiahrt Amendment restrictions, ShotSpotter outcomes, sworn staffing levels (73%), and U-Visa certifications.

agenda_items.title: Closed Session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6) (Personnel) & Lead Pipe Notice Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted 7-0 to enter closed session for personnel matters, though Cook and Freeman objected to handling major leadership-transition discussions without broader public engagement. Afterward at 02:19:51, Freeman raised resident confusion over pre-1988 lead service line letters.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Closed Session approved 7-0; Set Agenda approved 7-0

votes.item_title: Accept City Manager's Priority Items
votes.notes: Nate Baker arrived during council announcements at 00:03:21 prior to all votes.
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager Wanda Page presented her priority updates for the November 21 work session, including moving the ACFR presentation (Item 4), referring Item 13 back to staff, presenting the Q3 Crime Report (Item 21), requesting immediate action on Holiday Parade street closures (Item 20), and adding supplemental Item 32 for Sandy Ridge Villas. Council had no objections to incorporating these priority adjustments into the afternoon's schedule. A motion to accept the priority items was moved, seconded, and approved 7-0 by voice vote.

votes.item_title: Suspend the Rules to Vote on Item 20 (Durham Holiday Parade Street Closures)
votes.notes: Required to take final action during a Work Session due to new NCDOT timing requirements.
votes.discussion_detail: Because new North Carolina Department of Transportation permitting requirements required formal Council approval before the December regular meeting in order for the annual Durham Holiday Parade to proceed on state-maintained downtown roadways, the administration asked Council to suspend its work-session rules. No council member opposed expediting the procedural authorization given the upcoming event date. Council moved, seconded, and unanimously passed the rules suspension 7-0 by voice vote.

votes.item_title: Item 20: Resolution Approving Street Closures for the 2024 Durham Holiday Parade
votes.notes: Satisfies NCDOT requirement for temporary state-roadway closures.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately following the rules suspension, Mayor Leonardo Williams entertained a motion to adopt the resolution authorizing temporary street closures for the 2024 Durham Holiday Parade. Staff noted that NCDOT newly required an explicit governing-body resolution ahead of the parade date rather than standard administrative permitting alone. Council expressed support for keeping the community tradition on schedule and passed the resolution unanimously 7-0 by voice vote at 00:14:00.

votes.item_title: Motion to Enter Closed Session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6) (Personnel)
votes.notes: Chelsea Cook and DeDreana Freeman voted Aye reluctantly while objecting to insufficient public/stakeholder process.
votes.discussion_detail: Council considered a motion to enter closed session pursuant to NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6) for confidential personnel deliberations ahead of City Manager Wanda Page's upcoming retirement. Before voting, Chelsea Cook and DeDreana Freeman voiced frustration that sensitive decisions surrounding top leadership and interim planning were being handled privately without public or stakeholder engagement. Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton defended closed-session confidentiality as standard and legally necessary for personnel matters. After registering those objections on the record, Council approved entering closed session 7-0 at 02:19:19.

votes.item_title: Set the Agenda for Next Regular City Council Meeting (Consent: 1, 3-12, 14-19, 21-26, 32; GBA Public Hearings: 28-31)
votes.notes: Item 13 referred back; Item 20 already acted upon.
votes.discussion_detail: Prior to convening in closed session, City Manager Wanda Page read the recommended agenda placement for the December 2, 2024 regular Council meeting, assigning Items 1, 3 through 12, 14 through 19, 21 through 26, and supplemental Item 32 to the Consent Agenda while placing Items 28 through 31 on the General Business Public Hearings docket. Item 13 remained referred back to Engineering and Infrastructure, and Item 20 had already been resolved at the work session. Council moved, seconded, and unanimously adopted the schedule 7-0 by voice vote at 02:25:39.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Nov 21, 2024
disagreements.issue: Public and Stakeholder Transparency in Executive Personnel Discussions (Closed Session NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6))
disagreements.summary: Although all seven members voted to enter closed session, members disagreed sharply on whether executive transition deliberations were overly shielded from community input.
disagreements.side_a_position: Executive transition and key leadership-role discussions require structured public and stakeholder engagement rather than being handled primarily behind closed doors.
side_a_arguments: Major community-facing leadership roles affect residents directly and merit public input on priorities and expectations.
Supporting the statutory closed-session vote should not be mistaken for endorsing a closed-off transition process.
disagreements.side_b_position: Personnel evaluations, candidate discussions, and contractual deliberations must remain confidential in closed session to comply with North Carolina law and protect candor.
side_b_arguments: NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6) specifically authorizes confidential personnel deliberation when evaluating individuals or terms.
disagreements.resolution: Council unanimously voted 7-0 to enter closed session at 02:19:19 after Cook and Freeman placed their process objections on the public record.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Nov 18 2024
meetings.executive_summary: At the November 18, 2024 regular meeting, all seven Council members unanimously adopted Consent Agenda Items 1–20 (7-0) and approved transitional annexation/zoning for Constitution Drive right-of-way (7-0 across three votes), the 126-unit Vivo Living hotel-conversion apartment rezoning at 4515 NC 55 including 25 units at 60% AMI (7-0), and the Caring House expansion at 2625 Pickett Road (7-0). However, Council split 4-3 on two rural-edge residential annexations and rezonings—Doc Nichols Townes (25 townhomes on Doc Nichols Road) and Tri Creek (6017–6023 Leesville Road)—with Mayor Williams, Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton, and Council Members Caballero and Rist voting Aye while Council Members Baker, Cook, and Freeman dissented over suburban sprawl, Lick/Hurricane Creek sediment and stream-buffer impacts, blasting wells, and the Davidson Rural Area Plan (though consistency statements passed 7-0). During the Doc Nichols Townes debate, Middleton clashed sharply with Baker and invoked a procedural point of order against Freeman over comments referencing developer representatives.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Items 1–20
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed and passed Consent Agenda Items 1 through 20 together without items pulled for separate floor debate.

agenda_items.title: Constitution Drive Right-of-Way Annexation and Initial Zoning (RS-20)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council held a public hearing on Southland Associates' transitional annexation and RS-20 city zoning application for Constitution Drive right-of-way. No opposition emerged and Council unanimously passed the annexation, zoning map change, and consistency statement.

agenda_items.title: Vivo Living Durham (4515 NC 55) Zoning Map Change (OI to PDR 53.390)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council considered rezoning 4515 NC 55 from OI to PDR 53.390 to convert an existing hotel into 126 studio/multifamily apartments, including 25 affordable units at 60% AMI plus proffers of $10,000 to Durham Public Schools and $10,000 to the Dedicated Housing Fund. Council Member Chelsea Cook questioned $150–$200 nonrefundable application fees and background screening policies before Council unanimously approved the rezoning and consistency statement.

agenda_items.title: Doc Nichols Townes (1321 Doc Nichols Rd) Annexation and Zoning Map Change (RR to PDR 5.55)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council considered annexing and rezoning 1321 Doc Nichols Road from RR to PDR 5.55 for 25 townhomes with proffers of $10,000 to DPS, $25,000 to the Housing Fund, and a conditional 10-foot multiuse path. Surrounding residents cited traffic, Lick/Hurricane Creek sediment runoff, blasting, and reduced 30-foot stream buffers, igniting heated Council debate between supporters emphasizing housing supply and dissenters citing rural preservation and environmental protection.

agenda_items.title: Tri Creek (6017 & 6023 Leesville Rd) Annexation and Zoning Map Change (RR to PDR 3.768)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed annexation and rezoning of 6017 and 6023 Leesville Road from RR to PDR 3.768 with proffers of $5,000 to DPS and $20,000 to the Housing Fund. Council split 4-3 along the same urban-perimeter fault lines seen on Doc Nichols Townes before adopting the consistency statement unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Caring House Expansion (2625 Pickett Rd) Zoning Map Change (PDR 0.000 Amendment)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council held a public hearing on an amended PDR 0.000 development plan to allow expansion of the Caring House cancer-patient lodging facility at 2625 Pickett Road. Council praised the nonprofit mission and unanimously approved both the zoning change and consistency statement.

disagreements.issue: Rural-Perimeter Annexation, Watershed Buffers, and Rural Area Plan Precedent (Item 23: Doc Nichols Townes)
disagreements.summary: Council divided 4-3 and engaged in sharp debate—including a point of order called by Middleton during Freeman's remarks—over extending municipal utilities and townhome density into the Doc Nichols Road rural periphery amid resident warnings on Lick/Hurricane Creek sediment, well blasting, and stream-buffer reductions.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve annexation and PDR 5.55 rezoning with housing/school/trail proffers
side_a_arguments: Parcel lies adjacent to existing urban growth patterns and provides needed townhome housing supply
Includes $25,000 Dedicated Housing Fund and $10,000 DPS proffers plus conditional 10-foot multiuse path
Middleton argued Baker's invocation of external Davidson Rural Area Plan standards conflicted with Durham's Comprehensive Plan framework
disagreements.side_b_position: Deny annexation and rezoning to protect watershed buffers and curb peripheral suburban sprawl
side_b_arguments: Opposed extending City sewer outside core infrastructure into rural neighborhoods lacking nearby transit or services
Cited Lick/Hurricane Creek sediment impacts, blasting impacts on neighboring wells, and loss of 30-foot stream buffers
Baker referenced regional rural-preservation tools such as the Davidson Rural Area Plan
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and zoning passed 4-3; consistency statement adopted 7-0.

proffers.dps_cash: $10,000 one-time contribution
proffers.affordable_housing: 20% of units (25 units) deed-restricted at 60% AMI for 30 years (privately funded without LIHTC), plus $10,000 one-time contribution to Durham Dedicated Housing Fund

member_justifications.stance_summary: Strongly supported the adaptive reuse of a vacant hotel, praising the 20% affordable housing commitment, cash contributions to the Dedicated Housing Fund and DPS, and the GoDurham bus shelter proffer.
member_justifications.key_quote: This is the kind of thing we want in Durham, right? You're reusing a vacant hotel, the commitment of 20% affordable is awesome.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supported the adaptive reuse and 20% affordable housing commitment, but warned that Vivo Living's nonrefundable $150-$200 application fees and strict criminal/rental screening criteria create severe barriers for low-income applicants. Urged the operator to reform those policies so low-income residents can actually access the units.
member_justifications.key_quote: I think that the reuse is awesome, I love the affordable housing commitment... [but] the application process is extremely burdensome, and we're missing out on a lot of people that could live there.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Echoed Cook's tenant-screening concerns and offered to connect Vivo Living with local community-rooted affordable housing organizations such as Housing for New Hope, Families Moving Forward, and Durham Community Land Trustees.
member_justifications.key_quote: Housing for New Hope, Families Moving Forward, and DCLT are all community-rooted organizations that do affordable housing work.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supported the project and highlighted that privately funding 20% affordable units without LIHTC tax credits or public dollars frees scarce public subsidies for other projects.
member_justifications.key_quote: Whenever we have applicants who aren't asking for public dollars, it helps those public dollars go to other projects that may need them.

development_cases.location: 1321 Doc Nichols Rd
development_cases.scale: Up to 25 townhouse units on 4.5 acres
development_cases.zoning_change: RR to PDR 5.55

proffers.affordable_housing: $25,000 to Durham Dedicated Housing Fund ($1,000/unit)
proffers.environmental_tree: Mass grading prohibited on site; maximum impervious surface capped at 50%; native plant species
proffers.transit_infrastructure: 10-ft shared-use path along frontage; required turn lane on Doc Nichols Rd
other_proffers: Conveyed encroachment strip to resolve boundary issue with southern neighbor (Knight property)

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supported the 25-unit townhouse infill proposal as consistent with surrounding residential development, arguing neighborhood opposition targeted area growth in general rather than the merits of this small site. Emphasized that no zip code in a growing city is exempt from change.
member_justifications.key_quote: The case against this is being more made against development in general in the area as opposed to this particular case.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supported the infill project and praised the trade-off of capping impervious cover at 50% and prohibiting mass grading on a 4.5-acre site rather than requiring a larger 100-year stormwater pond. Later at [02:07:30] pushed back on Baker's Davidson example, noting Durham protects northern watersheds and channels growth inside its Urban Growth Boundary.
member_justifications.key_quote: I appreciate the tradeoff I'm seeing is okay, we're not doing 100-year stormwater... but then the counter is to just do 50% impervious and there's a commitment for not doing mass grading.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Argued Council must judge projects in their cumulative context within the heavily cleared Hurricane Creek watershed rather than in isolation, criticizing the proposal for offering only minimum open space and tree coverage. Preferred growing outward from the urban core rather than clear-cutting cheaper outskirts parcels.
member_justifications.key_quote: To me, this is not the right spot for this, given the context of the area and the environmental concerns.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Stated he pushes developers for strong proffers but will not penalize proposals that meet UDO standards, arguing additional housing supply is needed to support schools and transit.
member_justifications.key_quote: I won't penalize if someone didn't go above what is required.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Criticized piecemeal Southeast Durham suburban subdivisions as 100% auto-oriented, climate-catastrophic sprawl rather than opposing growth itself. Urged Durham to adopt proactive small-area planning modeled on Davidson's Rural Area Plan to convene landowners, protect environmental corridors, and cluster development with the 3Ds and affordable housing.
member_justifications.key_quote: We're looking at some of the most unsustainable kinds of development on the planet, which is American-style suburban planning, which is completely 100% auto-oriented... It's one of Durham's most critical environmental crises, and it's self-inflicted.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Argued the city is concentrating environmental and traffic impacts on South/Southeast Durham residents while protecting Northern Durham. Criticized the 'micro vs. macro' defense as disrespectful to residents bearing cumulative impacts.
member_justifications.key_quote: Just acknowledge that you're pushing for more development at the expense of certain people... to try and make it as if there's no other way to do it is what's so disrespectful.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Nov 7, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: Convening two days after the November 5 general election, Council celebrated Durham voters overwhelmingly passing $200 million in Parks and Streets/Sidewalks general obligation bonds (75% and 71% approval). In a concise work session with Mark-Anthony Middleton on an excused absence, Council reviewed transit center CMAR costs (~$26M), GoDurham Access property acquisition, ParkMobile payment equity for unbanked residents, and resolved a DOST appointment tie before unanimously setting the upcoming agenda 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Post-Election Reflections and Celebration of $200 Million General Obligation Bonds
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reflected on the November 5, 2024 election and celebrated voter passage of the $200 million Parks & Recreation and Streets & Sidewalks bond referendums by 75% and 71% margins respectively. Mark-Anthony Middleton's excused absence (attending an NCLM hurricane relief meeting in Morganton) was noted at 00:00:22.

agenda_items.title: Public Comments on Wildlife Feeding, Eviction Diversion, and East Main Safety
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Speakers requested a Treyburn wildlife-feeding ordinance to deter deer habituation (Stephen Harris), urged emergency funding for Entry Point Durham's depleted eviction diversion program and tenant protections (Grace Wakeman and Emily Wilks), and raised drug activity and safety concerns near East Main and Stokes Streets (Regina Frazier, PAC 5).

agenda_items.title: FY25-26 Budget Development Schedule and Non-Digital Outreach
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed the upcoming FY25-26 budget calendar and stressed ensuring non-digital engagement options for residents without reliable internet access.

agenda_items.title: Durham Station Transit Center CMAR GMP Amendment and GoDurham Access Property Acquisition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation staff reviewed the Durham Station Transit Center CMAR guaranteed maximum price amendment (~$26 million total project cost) and property acquisition plans at 00:49:20 for a dedicated GoDurham Access paratransit facility.

agenda_items.title: ParkMobile Pay-by-Phone Parking Equity for Unbanked and Elderly Residents
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council questioned ParkMobile convenience-fee structures and accessibility for unbanked, cash-reliant, and elderly downtown parkers.

agenda_items.title: Board and Commission Nominations (DOST Tie Resolution, Appearance Commission, HRC, PB Steering)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Clerk reported nominations for Appearance Commission (Allison P. Steele, Caitlin Wheeler), Human Relations Commission (Scott Brummel, Shandra M. Jones), and Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee (Samuel F. Thomas III), while a tie on the Durham Open Space and Trails Commission (DOST) was resolved when Chelsea Cook shifted her vote from Alexis Steele to Lindsay S. Biersbach.

agenda_items.title: Set the Agenda for Next Regular City Council Meeting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council set the November regular meeting agenda placing Items 1-20 on Consent and Public Hearing Items 21-25 on the General Business Agenda.

votes.item_title: Set the Agenda for Next Regular City Council Meeting (Consent: Items 1-20; GBA Public Hearings: Items 21-25)
votes.notes: Mark-Anthony Middleton had an excused absence attending a North Carolina League of Municipalities hurricane relief meeting in Morganton.
votes.discussion_detail: Having reviewed the pulled budget schedule, transit capital projects, and parking items as well as resolving the DOST board nomination tie in open session, Council took up the recommended regular-meeting docket. Items 1 through 20 were placed on the Consent Agenda and public hearings 21 through 25 were assigned to the General Business Agenda. With Mark-Anthony Middleton absent on an approved excused absence, the six present council members moved, seconded, and approved the agenda unanimously 6-0 by voice vote.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Nov 4, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: In a marathon four-hour regular session on November 4, 2024, Council took 12 formal votes highlighted by two sharp 4-3 zoning splits over suburban greenfield projects opposed by the Planning Commission. Mayor Leonardo Williams, Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, and Carl Rist overcame objections from Nate Baker, Chelsea Cook, and DeDreana Freeman to approve the 102-unit Lindley Townhouses rezoning (over a 10-3 Planning Commission denial) and Drees Homes' 120-unit Sharon Grove annexation and rezoning (over a 12-1 Planning Commission denial) after mid-meeting proffer increases.

agenda_items.title: Family Homelessness Awareness Week Proclamation, Hispanic Heritage Honorees, and Closed Session Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council issued a proclamation for Family Homelessness Awareness Week accepted by Atasha Melvin of Families Moving Forward, read Hispanic Heritage Month honoree names (00:16:23), excused Mark-Anthony Middleton for November 7 (00:42:14), and reported out from its pre-meeting closed session on annual evaluations and salary adjustments for Clerk Diana Schreiber, City Attorney Kim Rehberg, and City Manager Wanda Page (00:49:05).

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Adoption (Items 1, 4-8)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved routine consent items 1 and 4 through 8 while pulling Item 3 (Kunshan Sister Cities agreement) for amendment and reserving Items 11-13 for public hearings.

agenda_items.title: Sister Cities Agreement with Kunshan, China
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council amended the draft Sister Cities agreement with Kunshan, China to strike the final 60-day termination sentence of Section 5 and then authorized Mayor Williams to sign the amended agreement.

agenda_items.title: Lindley Townhouses UDO Zoning Map Amendment (1343 Ellis Rd & 1326 Clinton Rd)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Lengthy public hearing on rezoning 12.25 acres from RR to PDR 8.326 for 102 townhomes (5% at 80% AMI for 30 years, 100-year stormwater standard, and a 10-ft path commitment added at 01:56:43). Facing a 10-3 Planning Commission denial recommendation and heavy resident opposition over Ellis Road traffic and flooding, Council split 4-3 to approve.

agenda_items.title: Sharon Grove Consolidated Annexation and Rezoning (803, 901, 903 Sharon Rd)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public hearing on annexing and rezoning 24.2 acres for 120 single-family units (+57 new lots on parcel 803) by Drees Homes with zero on-site affordable units, which the Planning Commission recommended denying 12-1. After a recess, Drees increased proffers to $120,000 for the Housing Fund, $21,000 for DPS, and 100-year stormwater detention; Council still split 4-3 on annexation and zoning.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Annexation & Zoning passed 4-3; Consistency statement passed 7-0

agenda_items.title: Winsford at the Park Consolidated Annexation and Rezoning (103 Zante Currant Rd)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Uncontested public hearing to annex and rezone a 1.79-acre open-space cleanup parcel into RS-M(D) for Winsford at the Park.

votes.item_title: Excuse Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton from November 7, 2024 Work Session
votes.notes: Excused to attend an NCLM hurricane recovery meeting in Morganton.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton requested an excused absence for the November 7, 2024 City Council Work Session in order to travel to Morganton for a North Carolina League of Municipalities hurricane relief gathering. Council colleagues raised no objections to the civic travel request. A motion was made and seconded and passed unanimously 7-0 at 00:42:35.

votes.item_title: Item 3 Amendment: Strike Final Sentence of Section 5 (60-Day Termination Clause) in Kunshan Sister Cities Agreement
votes.notes: Clarified termination notice terms before final execution.
votes.discussion_detail: After pulling Item 3 from Consent, Council reviewed the proposed Sister Cities agreement establishing a partnership with Kunshan, China. Following a brief discussion with staff and legal counsel regarding contract termination phrasing in Section 5, a motion was made to amend the agreement by striking the final sentence governing 60-day termination notice. Council unanimously adopted the amendment 7-0 at 01:02:20.

votes.item_title: Item 3 Main Motion: Authorize Execution of Sister Cities Agreement with Kunshan, China as Amended
votes.discussion_detail: With Section 5 amended to Council's satisfaction, Mayor Leonardo Williams entertained the main motion authorizing execution of the Sister Cities agreement with Kunshan, China. Council members voiced general support for expanding Durham's international civic and cultural partnerships alongside existing ties with Xi'an. The main motion as amended passed unanimously 7-0 at 01:03:04.

votes.item_title: Item 11: Lindley Townhouses UDO Zoning Map Amendment (RR to PDR 8.326, 1343 Ellis Rd & 1326 Clinton Rd)
votes.notes: Planning Commission recommended denial 10-3; developer committed 5% units at 80% AMI for 30 yrs, 100-yr stormwater standard, and a 10-ft path added during hearing.
votes.discussion_detail: Applicant representatives sought to rezone 12.25 acres from Rural Residential to Planned Development Residential 8.326 for 102 townhomes, adding a 10-foot pedestrian path proffer during the hearing alongside 5% units at 80% AMI for 30 years and 100-year stormwater detention. Nearby residents strongly opposed the project citing narrow Ellis Road access, flooding, and a 10-3 Planning Commission denial recommendation. Opponents Nate Baker, Chelsea Cook, and DeDreana Freeman argued the suburban site lacked transit, pedestrian infrastructure, and deep affordability while overriding community and Planning Commission opposition; supporters Williams, Middleton, Caballero, and Rist argued Durham urgently needs homeownership townhome supply near major job corridors and praised the stormwater and path upgrades. The rezoning narrowly passed 4-3 at 03:14:54.

votes.item_title: Item 11: Consistency Statement under NCGS 160D-605 (Lindley Townhouses)
votes.notes: Statutory consistency finding following split 4-3 zoning approval.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the contentious 4-3 vote approving the Lindley Townhouses rezoning, Council voted on the companion NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement. Even the three council members who had opposed the rezoning joined the majority on the procedural consistency finding acknowledging the Urban Growth Boundary and Place Type alignment in the adopted map. The consistency statement passed 7-0 at 03:15:24.

votes.item_title: Item 12: Sharon Grove Consolidated Annexation and Utility Extension Agreement (803, 901, 903 Sharon Rd)
votes.notes: Initially misread as 5-2 before immediately being corrected to 4-3 to include Nate Baker's Nay vote; Drees Homes increased Housing Fund proffer to $120k and DPS to $21k after a break.
votes.discussion_detail: Drees Homes sought annexation and rezoning of 24.2 acres along Sharon Road for 120 total single-family detached homes (57 additional lots on parcel 803), carrying a 12-1 Planning Commission denial recommendation and zero on-site affordable units. After a council break, the developer raised its proffers to $120,000 for the Affordable Housing Fund, $21,000 for Durham Public Schools, and 100-year stormwater detention. Baker, Cook, and Freeman objected to single-family-only greenfield expansion without walkable urban form or on-site affordability, while Williams, Middleton, Caballero, and Rist argued the site sits inside the Urban Growth Boundary, replaces worse county-jurisdiction outcomes, and delivers housing supply plus cash proffers. The annexation passed 4-3 at 04:09:24 after the clerk corrected an initial 5-2 readout to reflect Baker's No vote.

votes.item_title: Item 12: Sharon Grove UDO Zoning Map Amendment (RR/RS-20/RS-10(D) to RS-8(D))
votes.notes: Companion zoning map change for 120-unit Sharon Grove single-family subdivision.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the 4-3 annexation vote, Council voted on the companion UDO zoning map amendment rezoning 803, 901, and 903 Sharon Road from RR, RS-20, and RS-10(D) to RS-8(D). Council members maintained the exact positions debated during the annexation hearing regarding greenfield infrastructure costs, car-dependent single-family sprawl, and housing supply versus cash affordable-housing contributions. The zoning map amendment passed along the same 4-3 divide at 04:10:19.

votes.item_title: Item 12: Consistency Statement under NCGS 160D-605 (Sharon Grove)
votes.discussion_detail: Council next took up the statutory NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement for the Sharon Grove RS-8(D) rezoning. Consistent with Durham practice separating policy opposition from statutory Place Type findings, all seven members voted in favor of adopting the consistency statement. The vote passed 7-0 at 04:10:53.

votes.item_title: Item 13: Winsford at the Park Consolidated Annexation (103 Zante Currant Rd)
votes.notes: 1.79-acre open-space cleanup annexation.
votes.discussion_detail: Staff presented Item 13 as a technical open-space annexation cleanup covering 1.79 acres at 103 Zante Currant Road adjacent to the existing Winsford at the Park development. No residents spoke against the boundary cleanup during the public hearing. Council approved the annexation and utility extension order unanimously 7-0 at 04:14:52.

votes.item_title: Item 13: Winsford at the Park UDO Zoning Map Amendment to RS-M(D)
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately after annexing 103 Zante Currant Road, Council voted on zoning the 1.79-acre open-space parcel to Residential Suburban Multifamily with Development Plan (RS-M(D)) to match the parent development. No additional debate occurred. The zoning map amendment passed unanimously 7-0 at 04:15:17.

votes.item_title: Item 13: Consistency Statement under NCGS 160D-605 (Winsford at the Park)
votes.discussion_detail: To complete the Winsford at the Park boundary cleanup, Council considered the statutory NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement. Having confirmed the parcel merely brings open space into city jurisdiction under matching zoning, Council adopted the statement 7-0 at 04:15:44.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Nov 4, 2024
disagreements.issue: Lindley Townhouses Suburban Greenfield Rezoning over Planning Commission 10-3 Denial (Item 11)
disagreements.summary: Council divided 4-3 over rezoning 12.25 rural residential acres on Ellis and Clinton Roads for 102 townhomes amid resident flooding/traffic objections and a 10-3 Planning Commission denial.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the PDR 8.326 townhome rezoning based on housing supply needs, 5% homeownership affordability, and enhanced stormwater and path commitments.
side_a_arguments: Durham urgently needs missing-middle townhomes and entry-level homeownership opportunities near jobs.
The developer added a 10-foot pedestrian path and 100-year stormwater detention exceeding baseline rules, and 5% of units at 80% AMI for 30 years provides meaningful workforce housing.
disagreements.side_b_position: Deny the rezoning in deference to the Planning Commission's 10-3 vote, neighborhood safety concerns, and inadequate transit/pedestrian context.
side_b_arguments: Ellis Road and surrounding rural roads lack sidewalks, transit, and infrastructure for higher townhome density.
Overriding a 10-3 Planning Commission denial for only 5% affordability at 80% AMI sets a weak standard for greenfield development.
disagreements.resolution: Approved 4-3 at 03:14:54.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Nov 4, 2024
disagreements.issue: Sharon Grove Single-Family Annexation and Rezoning without On-Site Affordability (Item 12)
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-3 on annexing and rezoning 24.2 acres along Sharon Road for Drees Homes' 120-unit single-family project despite a 12-1 Planning Commission denial.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the annexation and RS-8(D) rezoning after Drees Homes increased cash proffers to $120,000 for housing and $21,000 for schools.
side_a_arguments: The site lies inside the Urban Growth Boundary and annexing it yields city water/sewer oversight, 100-year stormwater standards, and $141,000 in combined Housing Fund and DPS contributions.
Denying annexation leaves the property open to lower-standard county development without affordable housing proffers.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject single-family-only suburban sprawl inside the UGB lacking mixed housing types, walkability, and on-site affordable units.
side_b_arguments: The Planning Commission overwhelmingly recommended denial 12-1.
Zero on-site affordable units and a car-oriented single-family layout run counter to Durham's Comprehensive Plan Place Type principles.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and zoning both passed 4-3 at 04:08:35 and 04:09:41 (following correction of Baker's Nay vote).

development_cases.location: 1343 Ellis Rd & 1326 Clinton Rd
development_cases.scale: Up to 102 townhouses on 12.25 acres (two parcels)
development_cases.zoning_change: RR to PDR 8.326

proffers.dps_cash: Commitment to Durham Public Schools (exact dollar amount unstated in transcript)
proffers.affordable_housing: 5% of units at 80% AMI for 30 years
proffers.environmental_tree: Committed to handling the 100-year storm event; maximum impervious surface capped at 80%; 50-ft stream buffers and 10-ft no-build buffer required at site plan
proffers.transit_infrastructure: 10-ft shared-use path along Ellis Rd frontage (proffered at hearing, subject to NCDOT approval); bring Lindley Rd (gravel) up to 60-ft city standard; interior sidewalks on both sides; vehicular access via Carywood Dr and Lindley Rd only (no direct Ellis Rd access per NCDOT)
other_proffers: Textual development plan capping density at 102 units (30% fewer than prior denied 147-unit proposal)

member_justifications.stance_summary: Argued the Ellis Rd area is transitioning and that Council's Comprehensive Plan and Urban Growth Boundary require denser infill housing inside city limits where water and sewer already exist. Contended 102 townhomes (~$380k-$400k) are preferable to by-right $700k single-family homes on 1-acre lots that would not include the 100-year stormwater proffer.
member_justifications.key_quote: When we made that decision quite frankly what we decided is everything on the inside of the line is going to have to get upzoned if we're going to protect the things that we say we want to protect.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Criticized the applicant's community engagement for leaving neighbors feeling unheard and argued the car-centric townhouse project fails to advance 15-minute walkable neighborhoods or access to amenities. Contended Council should demand higher-quality infill projects that prioritize affordability and natural resource protection.
member_justifications.key_quote: This is another example of car-centric urban sprawl; we're getting townhouses that aren't accessible to needed amenities, they're not bringing us closer to our 15-minute walking neighborhoods goal.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Acknowledged the site is infill within city limits with water and sewer and that RR is not the best zoning, but argued simply adding housing stock is too low a bar on an auto-centric parcel disconnected from transit and walkable amenities. Used zoning leverage to call for a revised proposal aligned with community input and the Comprehensive Plan, later noting at [03:10:48] that a 15-minute city requires all '3 Ds' (density, diversity of uses, and design).
member_justifications.key_quote: To me, the argument of adding housing stock, that is an argument that I care about; it is also a low bar and it is not a bar that is high enough for me.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supported the project as necessary infill inside the Urban Growth Boundary to address housing affordability and gradually retrofit car-dependent corridors with sidewalks toward a 15-minute city. Pressed the applicant to increase affordable units from 5% to 8%, though the applicant declined.
member_justifications.key_quote: This is an infill project; we've got an urban growth boundary and we've got to get more dense within our urban core.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Criticized the Council majority for repeatedly dismissing neighborhood traffic and runoff concerns as 'micro' issues and accepting minimal developer proffers. Argued the city should prioritize existing residents' quality of life over developers.
member_justifications.key_quote: It's really just been a frustration of doing as little as possible to actually meet the need of the people in our community.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Argued that infill development inside city limits and the Urban Growth Boundary is the exact opposite of urban sprawl and noted stormwater rules prohibit worsening pre-development runoff. Maintained that 102 townhomes with 5% affordable units at 80% AMI is a better use along an urban corridor than large-lot single-family homes.
member_justifications.key_quote: This is not an example of car-centered urban sprawl; this is the exact opposite of urban sprawl—this is within the city limits, within an urban growth boundary.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Sympathized with residents' flooding and traffic concerns but emphasized existing flooding predates this unbuilt project and that Council must balance environmental rules, affordability, and infill density. Argued Council should stay consistent with the Urban Growth Boundary rather than moving the goalposts against infill projects.
member_justifications.key_quote: If we're going to do this, then we have to actually have infill and we need to be consistent with that, but now I feel like we are continuously moving the goalposts.

development_cases.location: 803, 901, 903 Sharon Rd
development_cases.scale: Up to 120 single-family and townhouse units on 24.2 acres (adding 57 townhomes on 6.43-acre parcel 803 Sharon Rd to 63 previously zoned units)
development_cases.zoning_change: RR / RS-20 / RS-10(D) to RS-8(D) (Falls/Jordan Watershed Protection Overlay District B)

proffers.dps_cash: $21,000 total (increased from $18,500)
proffers.affordable_housing: $120,000 to Durham Dedicated Housing Fund (increased from $40,000 to $80,000, then to $120,000 during break; 0 on-site affordable units)
proffers.environmental_tree: 100-year storm event stormwater control commitment (added at hearing); 25% open space; minimum 20% tree preservation (no extra canopy proffer)
proffers.transit_infrastructure: 10-ft multi-use path along Sharon Rd frontage; required street stub-outs via Poplar and Foxboro
other_proffers: Shared stormwater infrastructure redirecting 803 Sharon Rd drainage south to 901/903 to address eastern neighbor flooding

member_justifications.stance_summary: Questioned the absence of tree canopy commitments beyond code minimums and challenged why no on-site affordable housing units were offered in a 120-unit rezoning. Rejected the applicant's explanation that financing two 60-unit phases separately prevented underwriting on-site affordable units.
member_justifications.key_quote: So we have the same developer building multiple units... and you're telling me that there's no way to underwrite the cost because we did it at different times?

member_justifications.stance_summary: Examined the affordable housing cash proffer relative to staff's $100-$1,000 per-unit range and asked about BPAC comments on the 10-ft Sharon Rd path and future Lick Creek Greenway connectivity. Supported the project after the cash proffers were raised during the break.
member_justifications.key_quote: This is obviously... complicated with these two phases, right? So again, when you were referring to the proffers, that was based on 120 units across all three parcels.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Challenged the packaging of the rezoning as 120 units on paper while treating it as two separate 60-unit projects when asked for on-site affordable housing units. Voted yes after the applicant increased the Affordable Housing Fund contribution to $120,000.
member_justifications.key_quote: This is appearing to me as a proposal that wants to be viewed... as 120 single-family townhouse dwelling units, but we don't get to treat it as such... when it comes to things like affordable housing.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Accepted that 803 Sharon Rd is treeless and separate in financing from 901/903, and urged the developer to increase monetary proffers to the Affordable Housing Fund and DPS given DPS's higher per-pupil capital and operating costs. Her questioning prompted a recess during which the applicant raised proffers to $120,000 for housing and $21,000 for DPS.
member_justifications.key_quote: I would encourage you to speak to your applicant and see... how much more is the applicant potentially willing to proffer either for the affordable housing fund or for DPS.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session October 24, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: The October 24, 2024 Work Session—opened by Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton before Mayor Leonardo Williams arrived—centered on three policy debates without formal action: testing the Environmental Affairs Board's Sustainable Decision-Making Tool, reallocating $249,000 in unobligated ARPA funds (with Council rejecting internal salary use in favor of kindergarten baby bonds or existing youth nonprofits), and HR Director Robin Wynn's 30-day recruitment timeline for a new City Manager. Council passed five procedural votes 6-0 with DeDreana Freeman on an excused absence.

agenda_items.title: Opening Remarks, Excused Absences (Cook & Williams), and Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Middleton called the meeting to order with DeDreana Freeman on an excused absence; Mayor Williams arrived at 00:06:21. Council excused Cook for November 7 and Williams for December 5, approved an attorney-client closed session, accepted priority items (referring back Item 2 Fayetteville St ARPA and adding Item 14 CM Recruitment), and moved the Clerk's B&C report to Priority Items (Mary Ellen Green nominated to BPAC).

agenda_items.title: Sister Cities Agreement with Kunshan, China
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Carl Rist asked about Durham maintaining two Sister City partnerships in China (joining Xi'an), and staff confirmed no policy bars multiple sister cities in a large nation.

agenda_items.title: Environmental Affairs Board (EAB) Sustainable Decision-Making Tool Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The EAB chair presented a standardized sustainability impact checklist for cross-departmental budget and policy decisions. Caballero, Cook, and Rist backed running a collaborative staff test case, while Mayor Williams objected to bypassing City staff and Middleton questioned extra bureaucracy.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / Direction to work with staff

agenda_items.title: ARPA Update and Reallocation Options for Remaining $249,000
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DCM Bertha Johnson-Winbush and Victoria Samayoa recommended retaining $249,000 in unobligated ARPA interest/funds to cover admin salaries and software. Council members unanimously preferred community deployment before December 31, debating Mayor Williams and Carl Rist's kindergarten baby bonds concept versus existing vetted nonprofits like El Futuro, Book Harvest, or Knox Street.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / Staff directed to explore options

agenda_items.title: Supplemental: City Manager Executive Recruitment Plan & Interim Planning
agenda_items.discussion_summary: HR Director Robin Wynn outlined an internal HR-led recruitment plan featuring a 30-day national posting (Nov 10-Dec 10), SharePoint screening, and Jan/Feb interviews. Cook urged assessment centers and community finalist panels, while Middleton warned the schedule leaves a post-December vacancy requiring a November 4 6:00 PM closed session on interim leadership and alternatives.

agenda_items.title: Set the Agenda for November 4 Regular City Council Meeting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page presented the November 4 agenda placing Item 1 and Items 3-8 on Consent and Items 11-13 on General Business Public Hearings (following staff recognition of Erin Miles winning IMLA's Young Public Lawyer Award).

votes.item_title: Excuse Council Member Chelsea Cook from November 7, 2024 Work Session
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman had an excused absence; Mayor Williams arrived in chamber just prior at 00:06:21 while Middleton temporarily presided.
votes.discussion_detail: Before turning the gavel over to Mayor Leonardo Williams upon his arrival at 00:06:21, Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton entertained a motion to approve Chelsea Cook's requested excused absence for the November 7, 2024 Work Session. No objections were raised by the six members present (with DeDreana Freeman on an excused absence). The motion was moved, seconded, and carried unanimously 6-0 by voice vote at 00:06:51.

votes.item_title: Excuse Mayor Leonardo Williams from December 5, 2024 Work Session
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman excused absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Upon assuming the chair, Mayor Leonardo Williams requested an excused absence for the December 5, 2024 City Council Work Session. Council colleagues raised no concerns with the advance notice. A motion was moved, seconded, and approved unanimously 6-0 by voice vote at 00:07:22.

votes.item_title: Closed Session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3) (Attorney-Client Consultation)
votes.notes: Requested by Senior Deputy City Attorney Fred Lamar; held at the conclusion of the work session.
votes.discussion_detail: Senior Deputy City Attorney Fred Lamar requested a closed session pursuant to North Carolina General Statute 143-318.11(a)(3) to consult with legal counsel on privileged matters. Mayor Williams asked to take the vote immediately so Council could transition directly into closed session after finishing public work-session business. The motion was moved, seconded, and approved 6-0 by voice vote at 00:13:47.

votes.item_title: Approve City Manager's Priority Items (Item 2 Refer-Back and Item 14 Supplemental CM Recruitment Plan)
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman excused absent.
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager Wanda Page presented two priority modifications: referring Item 2 (the Fayetteville Street Corridor ARPA agreement) back to the City Manager's office for further review and adding supplemental Item 14, a 20-minute HR presentation on the City Manager executive recruitment plan. Council voiced no objections to either adjustment. A motion to approve the Manager's priority items passed unanimously 6-0 at 00:14:05.

votes.item_title: Set the Agenda for November 4, 2024 Regular City Council Meeting (Consent: 1, 3-8; GBA PH: 11-13)
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman excused absent; Council also informally agreed to a 6:00 PM pre-meeting closed session on November 4.
votes.discussion_detail: At the close of the work session, City Manager Wanda Page presented the final docket for the November 4, 2024 regular meeting, recommending Item 1 and Items 3 through 8 for Consent and public hearing Items 11 through 13 for the General Business Agenda (with Item 2 remaining referred back). Council members also gave consensus thumbs-up to convene a 6:00 PM closed session prior to the November 4 meeting to discuss interim manager options. The motion to set the agenda was moved, seconded, and approved 6-0 by voice vote at 02:49:36.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 24, 2024
disagreements.issue: Process and Utility of Testing the EAB Sustainable Decision-Making Tool (Item 9)
disagreements.summary: Council divided over advancing an Environmental Affairs Board sustainability assessment checklist directly to a Council test case versus requiring staff vetting first and limiting bureaucratic layers.
disagreements.side_a_position: Run a collaborative test case with staff to standardize sustainability and equity metrics across all City departments.
side_a_arguments: A single standardized rubric gives non-expert policymakers consistent data instead of piecemeal departmental reports.
Piloting one item with staff will quickly show whether the tool helps or burdens workflows.
disagreements.side_b_position: Require advisory boards to collaborate directly with City staff experts before asking Council to approve or pilot an operational tool.
side_b_arguments: Bypassing department staff demoralizes professional staff and creates out-of-order policy proposals.
Existing staff already incorporate sustainability and racial equity considerations without needing extra bureaucratic checklists.
disagreements.resolution: Caballero and Cook clarified the test case meant EAB working directly with appropriate staff first; no formal vote was taken.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 24, 2024
disagreements.issue: Deployment of Remaining $249,000 in Unobligated ARPA Funds (Item 10)
disagreements.summary: While Council rejected staff's recommendation to keep $249,000 internally for administrative salaries, members differed on whether to seed universal kindergarten baby bonds or fund existing nonprofits.
disagreements.side_a_position: Use the $249,000 as seed money—paired with corporate matches and Latino Credit Union/DPS Foundation partnerships—to launch kindergarten baby bonds / youth savings accounts.
side_a_arguments: Starting accounts (~$25 per student for ~2,000 kindergarteners born during the pandemic) creates long-term generational wealth and leverages corporate matching from firms like Wells Fargo.
Means-testing City revenue-replacement dollars complies with state law while private funds cover universal access.
disagreements.side_b_position: Prioritize already-vetted nonprofits or existing ARPA partners (such as El Futuro, Book Harvest, or Knox Street) due to extreme December 31 contracting and legal constraints.
side_b_arguments: Legal and staff capacity constraints make negotiating a brand-new subrecipient agreement and means-tested bond structure by December 31 high risk.
Existing nonprofits such as El Futuro or homelessness/food organizations already have vetted scopes ready to deploy funds without risking federal clawback.
disagreements.resolution: Council directed staff to pursue baby bonds feasibility via existing partners such as United Way/LCCCU/DPS Foundation while preparing fallback options among existing youth-serving ARPA grantees.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 24, 2024
disagreements.issue: City Manager Recruitment Timeline, Interview Format, and Interim Governance (Item 14)
disagreements.summary: Members agreed on HR leading the search but differed on moving straight into the proposed timeline versus pausing for closed-session deliberation over interim leadership and alternative paths.
disagreements.side_a_position: Proceed briskly with the HR-led national posting, adding virtual screening, in-person finalist visits with community/stakeholder roundtables, and assessment center exercises.
side_a_arguments: Time is tight and an aggressive 30-day holiday posting window captures qualified candidates cleanly.
Bringing at least two finalists in person and using EQI/assessment centers ensures rigorous vetting.
disagreements.side_b_position: Flag that the proposed timeline extends past December 31 without a manager, necessitating closed-session discussion of an interim manager and alternative options.
side_b_arguments: Full endorsement of the posted timeline should wait until Council holds a personnel closed session to weigh interim appointment and alternative recruitment options.
disagreements.resolution: Council agreed by consensus to hold a closed session on November 4 at 6:00 PM prior to the regular meeting while HR drafts the recruitment brochure for November 7 review.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Oct 21, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: With Council Member DeDreana Freeman absent with an excused absence, the six present Council members unanimously approved every item on the October 21, 2024 agenda (6-0 across 13 formal votes). Following Consent Agenda adoption, Council confirmed Gonzalo to the Durham Affordable Housing Implementation Committee, endorsed a state NC EMC Falls/Jordan watershed overlay removal request at Patterson Place, and adopted a revised General Business Agenda resolution endorsing the NACTO Urban Street and Bikeway Design Guides. In four consecutive land-use public hearings, Council unanimously approved the 58-unit Mineral Springs Townhomes development (including 5 units at 80% AMI, 100-year stormwater controls, and a clarified south sidepath condition), a general RSM rezoning at 302 Morrene Road, the 58.7-acre Oxford Ridge development (up to 300 units with Catsburg cleanup commitments and senior affordability), and the permanent street closing of 165 feet of Hamlin Street.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled GBA Items 3, 10, and 31)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council adopted the Consent Agenda unanimously (6-0) while holding General Business Agenda Items 3, 10, and 31 for separate discussion and votes.

agenda_items.title: GBA: Appointment to Durham Affordable Housing Implementation Committee (Gonzalo)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council considered and unanimously confirmed the appointment of Gonzalo to the Durham Affordable Housing Implementation Committee.

agenda_items.title: GBA: Request to NC Environmental Management Commission for Falls/Jordan Watershed Overlay Removal (Patterson Place)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed a resolution requesting NC EMC removal of an overlapping Falls/Jordan watershed overlay designation affecting Patterson Place and approved it unanimously.

agenda_items.title: GBA: Resolution Endorsing NACTO Urban Street and Bikeway Design Guides
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following prior work-session revisions softening directive language, Council discussed and unanimously adopted the resolution endorsing NACTO urban street and bikeway design guidelines as a planning reference.

agenda_items.title: Mineral Springs Townhomes Annexation and Zoning Map Change (PDR 5.349)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council held a public hearing on Mineral Springs Townhomes proposing 58 townhomes under PDR 5.349, featuring 5 units restricted at 80% AMI, 100-year storm stormwater retention, and a negotiated textual adjustment ensuring a conditional south sidepath commitment. All six present members approved the annexation, zoning, and consistency statement.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council considered a general rezoning of 302 Morrene Road to Residential Suburban Multifamily (RSM) and unanimously approved both the zoning change and consistency statement.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed a 58.7-acre mixed residential proposal at Oxford Ridge zoned PDR 5.174 allowing up to 300 units with commitments for Catsburg site cleanup and senior affordable housing. All three motions passed unanimously.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Caballero noted she had pulled the item from consent to conduct additional research and gather community input, and after receiving that input moved approval.
member_justifications.key_quote: I pulled that one just to do a little bit more research, but having gotten some input from the community I'm good to go on that one.

proffers.dps_cash: Commitment to Durham Public Schools stated (exact dollar amount unstated in transcript)
proffers.affordable_housing: Minimum 5 income-restricted townhomes (>8% of units) sold at 80% AMI for 30 years
proffers.environmental_tree: Tree canopy coverage increased from 20% to 25% completely from preserved trees; maximum impervious surface reduced from 70% to 50%; native plant species; detention of 100-year storm event
proffers.transit_infrastructure: 10-foot multi-use path along site frontage; conditional commitment added on floor to investigate and build up to a 10-foot multi-use path (or sidewalk if space allows) across 3 southern parcels if sufficient ROW exists; raised crosswalks across car entrances (subject to City/NCDOT approval); Mineral Springs Rd improvements if accessed from Mineral Springs
other_proffers: Open space broken into at least 3 distinct areas

member_justifications.stance_summary: Caballero explored whether an off-site sidewalk across three southern parcels could be proffered conditionally if adequate public right-of-way exists, prompting the developer to obtain client approval on the floor for an up-to-10-foot multi-use path.
member_justifications.key_quote: Is there a way to structure a proffer based on that information? So if then...

member_justifications.stance_summary: Cook questioned why Transportation lacked ROW survey data, probed blasting alternatives and creek erosion controls, and discussed DPS Grow Together school capacity before supporting the infill townhomes to house residents.
member_justifications.key_quote: I am ultimately trying to put a roof over anyone's head that lives in this area. So I'll be supporting this tonight as well.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Rist secured a proffer for raised crosswalks at vehicular entrances and praised the affordability, 100-year stormwater detention, lower relative price point, and conditional off-site 10-foot path proffer.
member_justifications.key_quote: These sidewalk gaps are expensive. So I appreciate that proffer. And then overall this is a really good project.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Middleton supported the case as contiguous infill within the Urban Growth Boundary and rejected neighborhood opposition that amounted to a de facto moratorium on all development in Southeast Durham.
member_justifications.key_quote: Given our really fervent desire to keep faith with our urban growth boundary, infill just takes on a new meaning for me.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Baker supported the rezoning, acknowledging the area is currently auto-dependent and imperfect, but emphasizing the City's responsibility to build infrastructure out to new communities and praising the applicant's willingness to collaborate on proffers.
member_justifications.key_quote: There's no perfect case... I think our challenge in the city of Durham is to build our infrastructure out to meet these new communities that we're building.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Cook praised the developer-funded benzene remediation at no cost to impacted neighbors and strong Braggtown community consensus, concluding those benefits outweigh the Place Type Map inconsistency.
member_justifications.key_quote: The cleanup at no cost to the neighbors is such a valuable thing... I know that it doesn't quite fit our place type map, but I think that all of those aspects are really important.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Baker recalled playing baseball at Catsburg field and praised Braggtown residents whose sustained organizing turned past opposition into a deeply supported project. He confirmed with the developer that the homes will feature front porches.
member_justifications.key_quote: Sometimes you have to say no a few times to get to a really good yes. And I think that this shows that.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Caballero lauded Oxford Ridge as 'the happy project' and a collaborative template between neighbors and developers, noting future city investment in sidewalks and transit will connect homeowners to nearby industrial jobs.
member_justifications.key_quote: I'm glad that the neighbors who have had not safe drinking water are going to get safe drinking water.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Rist praised the benzene cleanup, community engagement, 80% AMI affordable homeownership, and Carver Street bike/pedestrian connectivity, while probing B-PAC requests for crosswalks and East Carver connections.
member_justifications.key_quote: I love the cleanup piece, the deep engagement you've done in the community, the affordability, both the specific affordability at 80% AMI, but also the price point of the for sale units.

member_justifications.stance_summary: After earlier disclosing that his nonprofit owns nearby land with zero financial interest, Middleton celebrated the project's approval as one of the high moments of his council tenure.
member_justifications.key_quote: When I'm out of the seat and I look back, this will be one of the times I look back on and say that was one of the high moments.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Williams praised the transformation from adversarial hearings to community-developer partnership and noted the housing density alongside Welcome Venture Park creates demand for future bus service.
member_justifications.key_quote: We now have actual demand to put a bus line out there because we're going to have the residential demand.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session October 10, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: During a wide-ranging nearly four-hour October 10, 2024 Work Session, Council discussed Durham County's 2025 property tax reappraisal (highlighting residential median prices rising from $239,500 in 2019 to $431,000 in 2024), low-income downtown worker parking discounts, 60 replacement bus shelters, and a rare Jordan Lake watershed boundary interpretation. Council deferred proposed deer bow hunting revisions for one cycle over safety concerns, sent the NACTO street-design guides resolution to General Business for legal review, and polled 6-1 in favor of an internal HR-led City Manager search over Mark-Anthony Middleton's preference for a closed-session direct-appointment discussion.

agenda_items.title: Hurricanes Helene/Milton Remarks, Oct 7 Meeting Apologies, and Freeman Excused Absences
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Javiera Caballero apologized for testy exchanges at the October 7 meeting and urged early voting and Western NC/Florida storm aid; Nate Baker requested adding City Manager search discussion to the agenda, which Mayor Williams routed to Other Matters. Council approved DeDreana Freeman's excused absences for Oct 21 and 24.

agenda_items.title: Public Comments on Senior Safety, Cultural Event Funding, and NACTO Street Standards
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Speakers raised 911 response delays and senior bus-stop seating on Hollowell Street (Susan Purvis), event-grant critiques from Slingshot/Moogfest (Kedra), and support for adopting NACTO street design guidelines for safer sidewalks and bike lanes (Chris Perin).

agenda_items.title: Updates to Low-Income Monthly Parking Discounted Voucher Program & Evening Parking Rate
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DDI CEO Nicole Thompson praised the General Fund-supported discounted monthly parking program for downtown hourly restaurant and service workers. Council commended staff for balancing worker access with transit goals.

agenda_items.title: Revisions to City Deer Bow Hunting Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chelsea Cook, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and DeDreana Freeman raised concerns over lowering bow hunting restrictions citywide in response to Treyburn HOA, prompting a one-cycle deferral for NC Wildlife input and legal review of time/notice restrictions.

agenda_items.title: Forest Hills Sprayground Design Contract & 60 GoDurham Bus Shelters
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff clarified MWBE/HUB utilization on the Forest Hills Sprayground design contract with With Architecture PA, and Transportation Director Sean Egan clarified at 01:16:18 that City Transit property-tax funds (not the ~$130M County Transit fund) provide the local match for replacing 60 older metal bus shelters.

agenda_items.title: Durham County 2025 Property Reappraisal Update and Tax Relief Programs
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Tax Administrator Keyar Doyle, Deputy Assessor Starlin Beatty, James Roberts, and ACM Dwayne Brinson briefed Council on the 2025 reappraisal (residential median jumping from $239,500 to $431,000, commercial sales ratio at 0.53) and the four state/local relief programs, fielding sharp council questions on gentrification displacement, appeal equity, and LOHRP grant scaling.

agenda_items.title: Watershed Protection Overlay Interpretation Request at Patterson Place
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Aaron Cain explained the rare request (first in 9 years) to forward sealed survey evidence on 14 parcels at Patterson Place—showing they lie over 5 miles from Jordan Lake normal pool—to the NC Environmental Management Commission, removing the 70% impervious limit. Cook moved the item to GBA for review.

agenda_items.title: Supplemental Resolution Adopting NACTO Urban Street & Bikeway Design Guides
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council debated whether adopting NACTO guides by resolution creates binding legal mandates before the UDO rewrite. Following City Attorney clarification that the latest draft lacked final legal review, Item 31 moved to General Business.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Search Process Poll (HR-Led vs Search Firm vs Direct Appointment)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: HR Director Robin Wynn outlined three recruitment options; six members favored an HR-led search while Middleton preferred direct appointment and objected to polling without prior closed-session deliberation. Wynn was directed to draft an HR-led timeline.

agenda_items.title: Clerk B&C Report, Set the Agenda, and City Clerk Evaluation Closed Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Clerk reported nominations (Discover Durham: Sean Umstead; REC: Elena Snavely; Planning: Khalila Karim; HRC: Christina Crosby; MHLC: Crystal Alvarez & Africa Dornera) plus a 3-3-1 DHAIC tie moved to GBA. Council then voted 7-0 to settle the agenda and enter closed session for Clerk Diana Schreiber's evaluation.

votes.item_title: Excuse Council Member DeDreana Freeman for October 21 and October 24, 2024 Meetings
votes.notes: Mark-Anthony Middleton joked about voting no before all members voted Aye.
votes.discussion_detail: During council announcements, DeDreana Freeman requested excused absences for the upcoming October 21 regular meeting and October 24 work session. Following brief remarks and good-natured banter from Mark-Anthony Middleton, Mayor Leonardo Williams entertained a motion to approve the absences. The motion was moved, seconded, and passed unanimously 7-0 by voice vote at 00:17:18.

votes.item_title: Set the Agenda for October 21, 2024 Regular City Council Meeting
votes.notes: Consent: Items 1-2, 4-8, 11-25; GBA: Items 3 (DHAIC tie), 10 (Patterson Place watershed), and 31 (NACTO guides); GBA Public Hearings: Items 27-30.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the Clerk's report showing a 3-3-1 tie on the Durham Affordable Housing Implementation Committee nomination (Item 3), City Manager Wanda Page set the October 21 regular meeting docket. Items 1-2, 4-8, and 11-25 were assigned to Consent; Items 3, 10 (Patterson Place watershed interpretation), and 31 (NACTO design guides) were placed on the General Business Agenda; and Items 27 and following (public hearings) were placed under General Business Public Hearings. Council moved, seconded, and unanimously adopted the agenda 7-0 at 03:57:22.

votes.item_title: Closed Session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(6) (Annual Performance Evaluation of City Clerk Diana Schreiber)
votes.discussion_detail: After settling the October 21 meeting agenda, Mayor Leonardo Williams read a motion to convene in closed session pursuant to North Carolina General Statute 143-318.11(a)(6) to conduct the annual performance evaluation of City Clerk Diana Schreiber. No member objected to entering executive session, though staff needed a few minutes to halt the public livestream. The motion was seconded and passed unanimously 7-0 by voice vote at 03:57:48.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 10, 2024
disagreements.issue: Citywide Scope and Safety Protections in Proposed Deer Bow Hunting Ordinance Revisions (Item 9)
disagreements.summary: Council members questioned whether loosening bow hunting acreage and setback rules citywide for Treyburn HOA introduces safety and equity risks without sufficient data or time limits.
disagreements.side_a_position: Note existing 2013 ordinance safeguards (10-ft elevated stand requirement) and address Treyburn residents' documented deer overpopulation concerns promptly.
side_a_arguments: Treyburn cannot meet existing buffer limits even after consulting NC Wildlife and NC State.
Shooting downward from an elevated 10-foot stand is viewed by NC Wildlife officials as the primary safety protection, and no injuries have occurred under the 2013 ordinance.
disagreements.side_b_position: Defer the ordinance amendment by at least one cycle to investigate tighter calendar/daylight time limits, public notice, population thresholds, and citywide implications.
side_b_arguments: Ordinances apply the force of law citywide rather than solely to Treyburn, creating unforeseen risks for pets and pedestrians in denser areas.
Council must avoid rushing code changes for suburban deer complaints compared with gun-violence challenges elsewhere in Durham.
disagreements.resolution: Deferred one work-session cycle so DCM Bo Ferguson and the City Attorney's Office could consult NC Wildlife officials and research potential limits.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 10, 2024
disagreements.issue: 2025 Property Reappraisal Equity, Appeal Disparities, and LOHRP Grant Scaling (Item 26)
disagreements.summary: Council members pressed Durham County tax officials over whether rapid gentrification increases and unequal appeal access worsen racial tax burdens and whether local relief grants scale with post-reappraisal tax bills.
disagreements.side_a_position: Examine demographic appeal disparities, communicate relief programs more simply, and explore scaling LOHRP assistance when gentrifying home values jump above the countywide average.
side_a_arguments: Fixed-income homeowners in rapidly gentrifying neighborhoods face above-average assessment spikes, yet LOHRP grants remain tied to income rather than bill jumps.
National research documents racial disparities in effective sales ratios due to unequal access to appeals, and residents struggle to find clear guidance on County webpages.
disagreements.side_b_position: Emphasize that tax assessors follow market sales under strict state statute without demographic data and highlight Durham's 2021 UNC School of Government equity study and online evaluator.
side_b_arguments: Tax offices do not create property values and Durham's 2021 UNC SOG study found no consistent demographic bias in appeal outcomes, prompting expanded community outreach.
LOHRP is nearly unique in the South (funded $750K County / $500K City), while statutory fixes such as lifting the $36,700 state homestead cap require General Assembly action.
disagreements.resolution: Informational briefing; County staff agreed to share the UNC SOG audit and work with City Communications on clearer water-bill and web tax-relief messaging.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 10, 2024
disagreements.issue: Legal Effect of Adopting NACTO Urban Street and Bikeway Design Guides by Resolution (Item 31)
disagreements.summary: Council debated whether adopting NACTO design guides as 'official' guidelines via resolution prematurely locks staff into inflexible legal standards prior to the UDO rewrite.
disagreements.side_a_position: Adopt NACTO and ITE guides now as official reference guidelines to unlock federal Bipartisan Infrastructure Law flexibility and inform the UDO and Reference Guide updates.
side_a_arguments: Guidelines remain flexible reference documents rather than rigid cross-section construction standards.
Official adoption empowers Durham under the federal Bipartisan Infrastructure Law on federally funded city street projects.
disagreements.side_b_position: Avoid resolution language with mandatory legal force ahead of the UDO rewrite and require City Attorney review of the revised draft before any vote.
side_b_arguments: Using words like 'official' and 'adopt' in a resolution creates quasi-legal force that can cause disputes when field exceptions are warranted.
Staff had not finalized City Attorney review of the second draft and must ensure the UDO rewrite schedule is not delayed.
disagreements.resolution: Cook requested moving Item 31 to the General Business Agenda so the City Attorney's Office could complete review of the revised resolution before the October 21 vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 10, 2024
disagreements.issue: City Manager Search Process and Public Polling vs. Closed-Session Deliberation (Other Matters)
disagreements.summary: Mayor Williams polled members publicly on three City Manager selection paths, revealing a 6-1 preference for an internal HR-led search over Mark-Anthony Middleton's objection to the unannounced poll.
disagreements.side_a_position: Conduct an internal HR-led national posting process quickly and transparently rather than paying a 35% search-firm fee or waiting longer.
side_a_arguments: HR Director Robin Wynn confirmed internal capacity to post nationally on ICMA, NCLM, and diversity boards within a 30-day window without a ~35% search-firm fee.
Debating process transparently in public reassures residents the transition is moving promptly.
disagreements.side_b_position: Discuss leadership succession—including directly appointing from Durham's internal bench—in confidential closed session rather than an unannounced public poll.
side_b_arguments: Members had no prior notice that HR would queue up a live public poll during Other Matters.
Publicly stating preferences risks telegraphing personnel evaluations; Durham has an exceptional internal bench capable of direct appointment or interim service without rushing.
disagreements.resolution: Mayor Williams directed HR Director Robin Wynn to prepare an HR-led recruitment plan for Council review at the October 24 Work Session, noting no formal binding decision had yet been made.
