meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session August 8, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: The marathon four-hour August 8, 2024 Work Session—with Nate Baker on an excused absence—was dominated by nearly three hours of analysis, public advocacy, and Council debate over Item 7: selecting The Peebles Corporation as preferred developer for the City-owned 505 West Chapel Hill Street site. While Council members largely favored Peebles' Base Proposal (reusing the historic Milton Small building into a hotel alongside residential and lab/office space), Rist, Cook, and Baker insisted staff first model a long-term ground lease and expanded affordable housing before voting, prompting staff to revise the August 19 General Business motions.

agenda_items.title: Severe Weather Remarks, Priority Items (6-0), and Quincy Hutto on Treyburn Deer Culling
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council urged storm safety ahead of Tropical Storm Debby rainfall, approved City Manager Priority Items 6-0 (with Nate Baker excused absent), and heard Treyburn HOA President Quincy Hutto request a variance or city ordinance amendment lowering Durham's 5-acre and 250-ft bow-hunting limits where NC Wildlife estimates 70 deer per square mile.

agenda_items.title: Board/Commission Attendance Reports and 2025 City Council Meeting Schedule
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DeDreana Freeman asked the Clerk's office to review discrepancies in board/council attendance logs, and Council debated moving the July 24, 2025 work session to preserve a full July break (moving Item 5 to GBA over Cook's concern about 15-hour combined meeting days and Attorney Rehberg's July 31 conference conflict).
agenda_items.vote_summary: Item 5 moved to General Business Agenda

agenda_items.title: American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) Update & DHA Resident Arrears Relief Proposal
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DCM Bertha Johnson-Winbush and Victoria Samayoa reported 35 executed contracts ($5.6M spent) and proposed directing ~$305,000-$314,756 in unobligated funds toward one-time COVID-era rent-arrears relief for low-income Durham Housing Authority residents below 30% AMI.

agenda_items.title: Update on Redevelopment of 505 West Chapel Hill Street (Preferred Developer Selection)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Services Director Stacy Poston and HR&A Advisors consultant Mark Kashi compared five proposals from Acreage, Conifer, and The Peebles Corporation ($57M subordinate loan, 92 affordable units, 255k sq ft commercial, hotel reuse of Milton Small, NPV $22.6M under 6% taxable LOBs), followed by a 6-organization coalition (Durham CAN, CAHT, NAACP, People's Alliance, DCABP, Duke Memorial) urging >=175 affordable units and a ground lease, and Preservation Durham backing hotel reuse. Council divided over voting Peebles preferred now versus pre-modeling a ground lease and more units.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Moved to General Business Agenda with revised motion language

agenda_items.title: Clerk B&C Nominations (Barbara Lau, Monica Brown, Philip Sakalis) and Council Furniture Opt-Outs
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Clerk reported nominations for Cultural Advisory Board (Barbara Lau), Sports Commission (Monica Brown), and BPAC Youth (Philip L. Sakalis). Mayor Williams invited opt-outs on Council Suite furniture updates; Cook and Freeman questioned the high cost during a tax-increase year, while five members publicly opted out.

agenda_items.title: Set the Agenda for Next Regular City Council Meeting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page presented the regular docket placing Items 1-4, 6, and 8-15 on Consent; Items 5 and 7 on GBA; and Items 17-18 on GBA Public Hearings.

votes.item_title: Accept City Manager's Priority Items (Item 7 Financial Model & Item 19 Quincy Hutto Info)
votes.notes: Nate Baker had an excused absence approved the previous Monday; recorded by show of hands.
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager Wanda Page introduced two priority updates for the August 8 work session: a revised financial model presentation for Item 7 (the redevelopment of 505 West Chapel Hill Street) and supplemental presentation materials submitted by Treyburn HOA President Quincy Hutto for Item 19. No council member objected to adding the revised materials ahead of discussion. With Nate Baker on an excused absence, the six present members moved, seconded, and approved the priority items 6-0 by show of hands at 00:10:17.

votes.item_title: Set the Agenda for Next Regular City Council Meeting (Consent: 1-4, 6, 8-15; GBA: 5, 7; GBA PH: 17-18)
votes.notes: Nate Baker excused absent; Item 4 flagged for potential attendance-record update prior to regular meeting.
votes.discussion_detail: Concluding the four-hour work session, City Manager Wanda Page read the agenda placement for the upcoming regular City Council meeting: Items 1 through 4, Item 6, and Items 8 through 15 on Consent (noting Item 4's attendance log might be updated); Items 5 (2025 council schedule) and 7 (505 West Chapel Hill Street) on General Business; and Items 17 and 18 on General Business Public Hearings. Following extensive negotiation over how the 505 motions would be drafted for that regular meeting, Council moved and unanimously approved setting the agenda 6-0 by voice vote at 04:16:08.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session August 8, 2024
disagreements.issue: 505 West Chapel Hill Street Preferred Developer Terms: Land Sale vs. Ground Lease and Affordable Unit Count (Item 7)
disagreements.summary: While all present members expressed positive views toward The Peebles Corporation's team, Council divided over voting Peebles preferred under the Base Proposal's $7.5M fee-simple sale and 92 affordable units versus requiring pre-vote modeling of a long-term ground lease and significantly more affordable units.
disagreements.side_a_position: Advance Peebles' Base Proposal largely as submitted to respect RFP fidelity, avoid stalling a third time after Fallon's collapse, and preserve historic hotel/commercial revenue.
side_a_arguments: The RFP specifically authorized land sale with restrictive covenants and set 250,000 sq ft commercial and 92-unit thresholds that Peebles met; changing core terms mid-stream risks a de facto RFP reopening and developer distrust.

Middleton argued it is legally and ethically unfair to lock in one preferred developer while altering terms that other proposers might also bid better on, while Freeman stressed getting units built after seven years of delay.
disagreements.side_b_position: Require staff and Peebles to model retaining City land ownership via long-term ground lease and increasing affordable units (toward the consortium's 175-unit ask) before locking into a binding term sheet.
side_b_arguments: Selling the City's last large downtown parcel for $7.5M surrenders long-term public wealth and leverage; a 50-99 year ground lease protects permanent affordability.

Council members should see concrete financial tradeoffs upfront (and Baker requested voluntary 5% market-rent caps, affordable retail, geothermal/solar, and protected bikeways) rather than repeating Fallon-style surprises a year later.
disagreements.resolution: City Attorney Fred Lamar confirmed no re-bid is legally required; General Services Director Stacy Poston agreed to return on August 19 with revised GBA motions adding an interim step to explore expanded affordable units and a ground-lease option alongside the base proposal.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session August 8, 2024
disagreements.issue: Canceling or Rescheduling the July 2025 Work Session in the Annual Meeting Calendar (Item 5)
disagreements.summary: Council debated whether to eliminate the late-July 2025 work session upfront or adjust closer to summer to avoid exhausting combined meeting days.
disagreements.side_a_position: Eliminate the July 24, 2025 work session now (or move it to July 31) to protect a full July Council recess.
side_a_arguments: The original policy goal was keeping all of July meeting-free, and Mayor Williams noted planned international travel in July 2025.
disagreements.side_b_position: Wait until June 2025 to assess conflicts and avoid scheduling two full meetings on a single 14-to-15-hour Monday.
side_b_arguments: Working council members struggle with back-to-back 15-hour combined meeting days, Local Progress conference dates are not yet set, and City Attorney Kim Rehberg noted July 31 conflicts with the Municipal Attorneys Conference.
disagreements.resolution: Item 5 was moved to the General Business Agenda for final resolution.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session August 8, 2024
disagreements.issue: Council Suite Furniture Replacement Cost During a Tax-Increase Year (Other Matters)
disagreements.summary: Following Mayor Williams's request for opt-outs on budgeted Council Suite furniture replacements, multiple members objected to the overall price tag during a high-tax year.
disagreements.side_a_position: Proceed with budgeted furniture and audiovisual upgrades for the Mayor's office and common conference room while allowing individual members to opt out.
side_a_arguments: Existing furniture is outdated and funds were already budgeted; individual opt-outs substantially reduce total expenditure.
disagreements.side_b_position: Opt out of personal office furniture spending and question the overall price tag given resident tax pressures.
side_b_arguments: Spending large sums on Council furniture sends the wrong message in a year when residents face steep property-tax bills; upgrades should be narrowed to shared AV/conference needs.
disagreements.resolution: Five members publicly stated they opted out of individual office furniture; no formal vote was taken.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Aug 5 2024
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams presided over the August 5, 2024 regular City Council meeting—Council's first regular session back from summer break and its return to broadcast on government Channel 8—with all seven members present. Opening remarks honored retiring City Manager Wanda Page, celebrated the newly enacted FY 2024-25 budget and guaranteed income funding, and recognized community partner 'My Durham' for contributing $60,000 alongside a $500,000 city allocation. In the visible portion of General Business after middle truncation, Council debated the Alcott Tract consolidated annexation and rezoning (M/I Homes of Raleigh, LLC), splitting over clear-cutting, blasting, creek runoff, Comprehensive Plan consistency, and an unresolved homeowner water issue versus infill context, a 5% commitment, reduced impervious surface, and North Carolina's by-right zoning constraints. Council approved the annexation and utility extension 4-3 (Chelsea Cook, Nate Baker, and DeDreana Freeman voting no), approved the UDO rezoning 5-2 (Freeman and Cook voting no), and adopted the consistency statement unanimously (7-0).

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, Channel 8 Broadcast Return, and Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams called the meeting to order following the three-to-four-week summer break, celebrating the return of Council meetings to government Channel 8 alongside online streaming, with all seven members answering roll call. Members praised retiring City Manager Wanda Page, Mark-Anthony Middleton highlighted the new budget and guaranteed income initiative, and Mayor Williams recognized community organization partners for adding $60,000 to a $500,000 city allocation and noted his upcoming Bloomberg mayors travel.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Farewell Remarks and Consent Agenda Reading
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page delivered brief farewell remarks thanking current and former Mayors and Council members for their trust across her tenure. Mayor Williams began reading the Consent Agenda (appointing members to commissions and reviewing software contracts) before the transcript digest truncates through the middle of the meeting.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Consolidated Annexation and Rezoning — Alcott Tract (M/I Homes of Raleigh, LLC)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: In the resumed digest segment, Council members debated the Alcott Tract development surrounded on three sides by annexed city land and on the north by county development. Supporters highlighted improved proffers (including a 5% commitment and decreased impervious surface), Mark-Anthony Middleton stressed that the Comprehensive Plan is an aspirational guide rather than a governance document, and speakers noted denying rezoning would leave existing by-right zoning in place. Opponents cited clear-cutting, blasting, stormwater impacts to the creek, and an unresolved homeowner water issue before Council passed annexation 4-3, UDO zoning 5-2, and the consistency statement 7-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Annexation passed 4-3; UDO rezoning passed 5-2; consistency statement passed 7-0

votes.item_title: Item 26 (Motion 1): Adopt Annexation Ordinance for Alcott Tract and Authorize Utility Extension Agreement with M/I Homes of Raleigh, LLC
votes.notes: Show-of-hands vote with all 7 seated members present.
votes.discussion_detail: Council voted by show of hands to annex the Alcott Tract into the City of Durham and authorize a utility extension agreement with M/I Homes of Raleigh, LLC; the Clerk reported the motion passed 4-3 with Chelsea Cook, Nate Baker, and DeDreana Freeman voting no.

votes.item_title: Item 26 (Motion 2): Adopt UDO Zoning Map Amendment for Alcott Tract (County RR/RS-20 & Falls/Jordan Watershed Protection District B to City Jurisdiction)
votes.notes: Show-of-hands vote; Nate Baker shifted to an aye vote on the zoning ordinance after voting no on annexation.
votes.discussion_detail: Council voted by show of hands to adopt the UDO zoning map amendment shifting the Alcott Tract from county jurisdiction to city jurisdiction; the Clerk reported the motion passed 5-2 with DeDreana Freeman and Chelsea Cook voting no.

votes.item_title: Item 26 (Motion 3): Adopt Consistency Statement Pursuant to N.C.G.S. 160D-605 (Alcott Tract)
votes.notes: All 7 seated members present.
votes.discussion_detail: Council unanimously approved the statutory consistency statement required under N.C.G.S. 160D-605 by show of hands.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Aug 5 2024
disagreements.issue: Alcott Tract Annexation, Environmental Impacts, and Comprehensive Plan Alignment
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-3 on annexing the Alcott Tract and 5-2 on rezoning it, balancing environmental, blasting, and Comprehensive Plan objections against improved developer proffers, surrounding infill context, and North Carolina by-right zoning rules.
disagreements.side_a_position: Support annexation and/or rezoning based on infill context, improved proffers, and North Carolina land-use constraints.
side_a_arguments: The site is smaller and surrounded on three sides by annexed land and on the fourth by existing county development.
The applicant added substantive proffers including a 5% commitment and decreased impervious surface.
The Comprehensive Plan is an aspirational guide passed on a split vote rather than a binding governance document, and under North Carolina law voting no leaves existing by-right zoning in place.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose annexation (Cook, Baker, Freeman) and/or rezoning (Freeman, Cook) over environmental impacts, blasting, and unresolved neighborhood water issues.
side_b_arguments: Clear-cutting and blasting on the site risk sending soil and stormwater runoff into nearby creeks.
A nearby homeowner's water issue remained unresolved after two years.
Projects should be held to higher environmental, climate, and Comprehensive Plan standards.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation passed 4-3 (Cook, Baker, Freeman voting no); UDO rezoning passed 5-2 (Freeman, Cook voting no); consistency statement passed 7-0.

development_cases.scale: Up to 35 townhouse units on 5.075 acres (5 parcels)
development_cases.zoning_change: RS-20 County to PDR 6.897 (read as PDR 6.27 in motion), Falls/Jordan Lake Watershed Protection District B, Textual Development Plan

proffers.affordable_housing: $35,000 to Dedicated Affordable Housing Fund (no on-site income-restricted units)
proffers.environmental_tree: Oversized erosion-control sediment basins; preservation of northern parcel cemetery
proffers.transit_infrastructure: 10-foot multi-use path along Clayton Road frontage plus entrance road improvements
other_proffers: Design commitments
Anticipated for-sale starting price point around $299,000

member_justifications.stance_summary: Criticizes replacing on-site affordable units with a $35,000 cash payment when building one affordable unit costs $200,000-$300,000, objects to the inability to commit against rock blasting near neighbors, and faults minimal community engagement and lack of dedicated active open space.
member_justifications.key_quote: Thirty-five thousand dollars doesn't build a single unit when affordability takes $200,000 to $300,000, and neighbors still have unanswered blasting concerns.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Examines economies-of-scale constraints for affordable units on a 35-unit site and questions why BPAC requests for off-site sidewalk gaps and bollard bike lanes were not included, ultimately accepting the 10-foot shared-use path explanation and voting aye.
member_justifications.key_quote: On a 35-unit project, I understand the scale constraints, though I wanted to make sure the 10-foot multi-use path addresses BPAC's connectivity concerns.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Highlights the $35,000 housing fund contribution, $5,000 DPS cash proffer, ~$299,000 attainable for-sale price point, small-footprint townhome design, and unanimous Planning Commission endorsement.
member_justifications.key_quote: With an expected price point near $299,000 and unanimous Planning Commission support, this small townhome infill helps entry-level homeownership.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supports the sub-50-unit local project, noting that cash contributions to the Dedicated Affordable Housing Fund follow established precedent for small townhome developments.
member_justifications.key_quote: For a local project under 50 units, a cash contribution to the Affordable Housing Fund fits our precedent.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Compares the projected ~$299,000 townhome prices favorably against Durham's $416,000+ average home price as a needed option for residents.
member_justifications.key_quote: When average home prices in Durham are over $416,000, townhomes around $299,000 give working families an entry point.

development_cases.location: 1414 NC Highway 54 (corner of NC 54 and Dresden Drive)
development_cases.scale: Up to 6,000 sq ft non-residential office space on 0.582 acres (1 parcel)
development_cases.zoning_change: RS-20 to OI (Office and Institutional) with Textual Development Plan (Falls/Jordan Watershed Protection District B)

proffers.environmental_tree: Enhanced stormwater management to the 25-year storm standard (applicant declined 100-year control due to 0.582-acre site constraints)
proffers.transit_infrastructure: 5-ft right-of-way dedication along NC 54; vehicular access restricted to Dresden Drive only (no driveway onto NC 54)
other_proffers: Prohibited residential and drive-through uses; limited to office uses

member_justifications.stance_summary: Probes why the half-acre parcel stopped at 25-year rather than 100-year stormwater controls, why BPAC pedestrian crosswalk and bike requests on Dresden Drive were declined, and flags discrepancies in LLC manager addresses on Secretary of State filings before joining the unanimous approval.
member_justifications.key_quote: Why couldn't the 100-year stormwater standard or the BPAC Dresden crosswalk request be accommodated on this corner parcel?

member_justifications.stance_summary: Criticizes repeatedly seeing BPAC recommendations dismissed as 'no commitment' on rezoning reports and calls for clearer City-BPAC priority alignment plus stronger LLC ownership transparency, while supporting this small office rezoning backed unanimously by the Planning Commission.
member_justifications.key_quote: I really don't like seeing our rezoning map change reports with lots of B-PAC recommendations and responses to them that say no commitment has been made to address this request.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Echoes Baker's frustration and affirms the vital role BPAC plays in pushing multimodal safety and connectivity on rezonings.
member_justifications.key_quote: I agree with Council Member Baker—BPAC does crucial work pushing us on multimodal connectivity and shouldn't just be brushed aside.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Cautions against layering heavy off-site infrastructure mandates onto small commercial parcels because those costs ultimately get passed along to tenants and customers.
member_justifications.key_quote: When we heap big infrastructure costs onto a tiny half-acre commercial project, those costs end up passed on to the end users.

development_cases.location: 433 Sherron Road (transcribed '433 Sharon road'), Southeast Durham near Lick Creek
development_cases.scale: Up to 100 townhouses on 13.22 acres (1 parcel)
development_cases.zoning_change: RR / RS-20 County (Falls/Jordan Watershed Protection District B) to PDR 7.698 City

proffers.affordable_housing: 5% of housing stock at 80% AMI for 30 years (upgraded on the dais to replace a prior $120,000 cash proffer)
proffers.environmental_tree: 20.5% tree cover (20% existing tree preservation saving all trees outside road connections plus 0.5% new plantings); 100% native plant species for required landscaping; maximum impervious surface lowered from 70% to 60%; 100-year storm controls; NGBS Bronze+ or Energy Star 75+ green building certification
proffers.transit_infrastructure: 3 street access points (Sherron Rd, Pembroke Dr, and stub to 509 Sherron Rd) with sidewalks; 10-ft multi-use path; 25-ft Sherron Road right-of-way dedication; raised crosswalk across Sherron Road access subject to City/NCDOT approval
other_proffers: Partnering with an external affordable housing developer to deliver the 5% on-site units

member_justifications.stance_summary: Commends the applicant for converting its $120,000 cash proffer into 5% on-site 30-year affordable units following a split Planning Commission vote, argues North Carolina preempts municipal blasting bans, and characterizes the comprehensive plan as aspirational guidance rather than binding law.
member_justifications.key_quote: Shifting from $120,000 cash to 5% on-site affordable units for 30 years is a meaningful improvement on a site surrounded by existing development.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Calls rapid auto-oriented Southeast Durham sprawl the Triangle's greatest environmental and climate crisis. Notes Alcott Tract is a tougher borderline infill case surrounded on four sides with strong tree-preservation (20.5%), 60% impervious cap, NGBS, and 5% affordable unit proffers, so he votes NAY on the decisive 4-3 annexation motion (at 03:30:03) for comprehensive plan non-consistency on fringe growth, then votes AYE on the subsequent 5-2 UDO zoning motion (at 03:30:49) because once annexed the proffered zoning outperforms county by-right rules.
member_justifications.key_quote: The development that's happening in Southeast Durham is Durham's and probably the Triangle's greatest environmental crisis, the Triangle's greatest climate crisis.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Draws on California and Oakland's housing shortage to warn against starving supply, arguing 100 compact townhomes with 5% on-site affordability and lower 60% impervious limits outperform county by-right sprawl on surrounded Southeast Durham acreage.
member_justifications.key_quote: Blocking infill townhomes that are surrounded on four sides only pushes growth into worse by-right county sprawl.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Explains that the dais upgrade to 5% on-site affordability moved him from undecided to yes, citing Triangle-wide housing supply additions helping push rents slightly down.
member_justifications.key_quote: Moving to 5% on-site affordable units on the dais got me off the fence, alongside real evidence that new supply cools housing costs.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Rejects a simplistic housing supply narrative and opposes both motions, citing clear-cutting and Lick Creek stormwater runoff, missing 15-minute walkability/transit/public infrastructure, D-grade (69%) comprehensive plan metrics, and chaotic piecemeal development across Southeast Durham.
member_justifications.key_quote: Instead, we're seeing this sort of just haphazard, one developer at a time... completely disoriented and chaotic.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Maintains that the comprehensive plan is advisory rather than statutory and warns that voting down rezonings leaves underlying by-right county zoning intact without any affordability, tree, or stormwater proffers.
member_justifications.key_quote: Voting no doesn't stop development; it just leaves by-right zoning without any of these tree, stormwater, or affordability commitments.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Votes nay on both annexation and zoning over clear-cutting, blasting, erosion into Lick Creek, and unresolved Junction Road groundwater/well impacts from unchecked Southeast Durham growth.
member_justifications.key_quote: Until we address clear-cutting, erosion into Lick Creek, and neighbors' well-water concerns in Southeast Durham, I cannot support expanding here.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session August 5, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams presided over the August 5, 2024 City Council work session following the summer recess, during which Council approved excused absences for Nate Baker (for the Thursday work session) and Mayor Williams (for upcoming Bloomberg and leadership travel), adopted a motion to hold a closed session under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5) regarding employment contract negotiation terms, and accepted the City Manager's priority items (Items 27 and 28). During Citizens Matters, D'Warren Langley urged dedicated funding for boys and young men of color, including the Charles Hamilton Houston Foundation. Council pulled Items 10, 11, 16, and 18 for discussion—reviewing Audit Services reports on fictitious employees and a March 2025 target waste diversion rate, questioning Habitat for Humanity and Durham Community Land Trust long-term affordable homeownership terms on Item 16, and reviewing an HR item on Item 18—before settling the evening's regular agenda and recessing to closed session.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Summer Break Announcements, Excused Absences, and Closed Session Request
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams opened the work session after the summer break, with Council passing voice motions to excuse Nate Baker from the upcoming Thursday work session and to approve Mayor Williams's requested absences for Bloomberg mayors and North Carolina leadership engagements (confirming Mark-Anthony Middleton would preside in September). Members praised retiring City Manager Wanda Page and thanked staff for publishing road repaving schedules. The City Attorney requested and Council approved a closed session after regular business under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5) to instruct negotiators on employment contract terms.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed by voice votes (absences and closed session)

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Items (27-28), Consent Agenda Reading, and Citizens Matters
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page presented Item 27 (Alisa Johnson update with Planning and Police attachments) and supplemental Item 28 (Southside Revitalization Phase III and IV ground lease agreement), which Council accepted by voice vote. Mayor Williams read Consent Items 1-28, pulling Items 10, 11, 16, and 18 for discussion. Under Citizens Matters (00:36:19), D'Warren Langley called on Council to prioritize funding and strategy for boys and young men of color, including the Charles Hamilton Houston Foundation.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed by voice vote (accept priority items)

agenda_items.title: Audit Services Performance Audits: Fictitious Employees and Solid Waste Diversion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Audit Services Director Germaine Brewington addressed Council questions on the fictitious employees payroll audit—explaining legacy paper check accommodations and the discontinuation of payroll debit cards—and confirmed a March 2025 implementation target for staff to recommend a target waste diversion rate. A council member noted the full audit report was missing from the public Granicus packet, and City Manager Page committed to checking and ensuring it was uploaded.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Forwarded to Consent Agenda (no work session vote)

agenda_items.title: Affordable Homeownership Development RFP / Habitat for Humanity & DCLT Partnership
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pulled by Chelsea Cook, Council discussed building generational wealth through low-income homeownership at 80% AMI, transit accessibility so residents do not need a car, and resale formulas to preserve long-term affordability. Staff and Habitat representatives discussed extending affordability covenants to 50 years or longer and ongoing discussions between Habitat for Humanity and Durham Community Land Trust (DCLT) leadership on a land-trust partnership.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Forwarded to Consent Agenda (no work session vote)

agenda_items.title: Human Resources Item Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pulled by Carl Rist, Assistant HR Director Jim Reiner answered questions from Rist regarding Item 18 before Council moved to settle the evening's regular meeting agenda.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Forwarded to Consent Agenda (no work session vote)

agenda_items.title: Settle August 5, 2024 Evening Regular Meeting Agenda and Recess to Closed Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager presented the settled agenda for the evening's regular meeting—Consent Items 1-23 and Item 28, and GBA Public Hearings Items 24-26—which Council approved by voice vote before taking a five-minute break to lock down the chamber for closed session.

votes.item_title: Excuse Council Member Nate Baker for Thursday Work Session
votes.notes: No roll-call tally announced; Nate Baker and DeDreana Freeman did not answer initial roll call in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: A council member moved and seconded excusing Nate Baker from the upcoming Thursday work session; Mayor Williams called the voice vote and approved the motion.

votes.item_title: Approve Excused Absences for Mayor Leonardo Williams
votes.notes: Transcript captures 'Opposed' when the chair asked 'Those opposed?' before 'Thank you. Motion carries.' without a roll-call tally.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Williams requested excused absences for upcoming official Bloomberg mayors and leadership program travel, with Mark-Anthony Middleton confirming he would preside in September; Mayor Williams declared the motion carried after a voice vote.

votes.item_title: Hold Closed Session Pursuant to N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5) Regarding Employment Contract Negotiation Terms
votes.notes: Voice vote; no roll-call tally announced.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the City Attorney's request for formal direction, Council moved, seconded, and approved by voice vote a motion to hold a closed session under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5) after regular work session business to instruct negotiating agents on material terms of an employment contract.

votes.item_title: Accept City Manager's Priority Items (Items 27 and 28)
votes.notes: Voice vote; no roll-call tally announced.
votes.discussion_detail: Council approved by voice vote accepting the City Manager's priority items: updated attachments for Item 27 (Alisa Johnson) and supplemental Item 28 (Southside Revitalization ground lease agreement).

votes.item_title: Settle the August 5, 2024 Regular City Council Meeting Agenda
votes.notes: Voice vote; no roll-call tally announced.
votes.discussion_detail: Council moved, seconded, and approved by voice vote settling the evening regular meeting agenda with Consent Items 1-23 and 28 and GBA Public Hearings Items 24-26.

meetings.title: Durham City Council June 17, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams presided over the June 17, 2024 regular City Council meeting with all seven members present, opening with proclamations for Cleft and Craniofacial Awareness and Durham's fifth annual Refugee and Immigrant recognition. During announcements, Chelsea Cook praised Juneteenth celebrations and 911 call center staff while criticizing Council for repeatedly approving late-night rezonings—including a 200-acre Southeast Durham case—that depart from the newly adopted Comprehensive Plan, and Mark-Anthony Middleton honored late community leader Richard Morgan. After the truncated middle section (which included Item 16 budget adoption, covered in UCfjiR1zVoA), Council concluded the Item 38 public hearing on the $200 million 2024 General Obligation Bond referendum—hearing Bike Durham, Durham Parks Foundation, and Braggtown speakers—and voted unanimously (7-0) across three motions to adopt the $85M Parks and Recreation bond order, the $115M Streets and Sidewalks bond order, and the November 5, 2024 special referendum resolution.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, Proclamations, and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Williams called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. with all seven members present and presented proclamations for Cleft and Craniofacial Awareness (Duke Cleft and Craniofacial Center) and Refugee and Immigrant recognition. In announcements, Chelsea Cook reflected on Braggtown/Merrick Moore Juneteenth events and a 911 call center tour before delivering an extended critique of Council disregarding the October 2023 Comprehensive Plan in late-night zoning decisions, including a 200-acre Southeast Durham rezoning. Mayor Williams recognized student and community achievements, and Mark-Anthony Middleton highlighted PAC 2 budget outreach, Housing for New Hope's homelessness count, and the passing of Morgan Imports owner Richard Morgan.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing (Continued) & Adoption: 2024 General Obligation Bond Referendum ($200M)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resuming after the truncated middle portion of the meeting, Council heard public comments from Bike Durham representatives (John Talmadge with a 186-signature petition and Gregory Williams), a Durham Parks Foundation representative supporting the 'Splash and Play' parks bond, and Braggtown resident Donna asking how much of the $115M sidewalk bond would reach East Club Boulevard. Following the close of the public hearing at 02:15:02, Council unanimously passed (7-0) three separate votes authorizing the $85M Parks and Recreation bond order, the $115M Streets and Sidewalks bond order, and the November 5, 2024 special bond referendum. Council and Communications Director Beverly Thompson then clarified that staff can share factual information while outside groups such as the Chamber Foundation, Parks Foundation, and Bike Durham lead campaign advocacy.

votes.item_title: Item 38 (Motion 1): Adopt Bond Order Authorizing Issuance of $85 Million General Obligation Parks and Recreation Bonds

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session June 6, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman presided over the opening of the June 6, 2024 Work Session until Mayor Leonardo Williams arrived at 00:20:48, with Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton having an excused absence. Council reviewed pulled consent items ahead of the June 17 meeting—including budget/CIP transparency, nonprofit reporting, affordable housing technical assistance, Moss + Ross communications contracting, police applicant polygraphs, and Little River Dam seepage engineering—and received major project presentations on the Durham Rail Trail 65%-100% design and the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) rewrite audit. Substantive policy debates emerged around contractor livable-wage compliance, Rail Trail anti-displacement and delivery speed, and UDO audit transparency, skewed online survey demographics, and density vs. unit-size assumptions. Council concluded by settling the June 17, 2024 meeting agenda 6-0, shifting two contested board/commission appointment items to General Business Agenda.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman presided initially while Mayor Leonardo Williams was ~15 minutes late and Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton had an excused absence. Nate Baker noted Durham Cooperative Extension may partner on an out-of-school time study, Chelsea Cook noted Pride Month, and Freeman suggested non-recurring budget asks under $2M could be routed to Participatory Budgeting (PB), though Javiera Caballero clarified PB has focused on capital improvements on public property.

agenda_items.title: Priority Items from City Manager, City Attorney, and City Clerk
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager introduced supplemental items including the Durham Rail Trail design presentation (Item 28), two FAA Airport Improvement Program grants (Items 39–40), an ARPA subrecipient agreement for the Fitz Powell affordable housing project (Item 41), and an on-call executive recruitment list (Item 42). The City Attorney introduced three summer legal interns (Alice Barkley, Brindavani Mudati, Caroline Pettit), and the City Clerk reported no priority items.
agenda_items.vote_summary: City Manager priority items received 5-0 (Williams not yet present, Middleton excused)

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Pulls and Public Comments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council pulled Items 10, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 34, and 36 for discussion (plus presentations 28 and 37, and Item 22 later addressed). Jacqueline Wagstaff challenged virtual speaker sign-up deadlines relative to written 2012 Council procedures; Delorean Langley requested $25,000 for the Charles Hamilton Houston Foundation; and Dan Nunn and John Warasila urged urgent action on overflow, sanitation, and a June fire at the Orange Street downtown waste enclosure.

agenda_items.title: Durham Homeless Services Advisory Committee Appointments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chelsea Cook questioned how Council could select appointees for a faith-community seat and a formerly-homeless seat when the application form did not ask candidates to identify those categories. Assistant Clerk Javon Pratt and Lola Roland proposed having staff contact the four existing applicants to confirm their categories before the June 17 meeting rather than re-advertising for 30 days, and Council agreed to keep the item on GBA.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Referred to June 17 GBA during agenda settlement

agenda_items.title: FY2024-25 Budget and FY2025-30 Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Carl Rist and Javiera Caballero requested an itemized side-by-side comparison showing which projects changed between the spring budget retreat CIP list and the proposed one-year CIP ordinance, including projects shifted to the proposed GO bond. Budget Director Christina Riordan and staff agreed to provide the guide, while Jacqueline Wagstaff spoke against the proposed property tax increase and $200M bond referendum.

agenda_items.title: Contract with El Centro Hispano for Salary and Operating Support
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Javiera Caballero requested a consolidated list of City-funded nonprofits, and Carl Rist asked for annual high-level performance visibility on nonprofit contracts. El Futuro Director Luke Smith urged Durham to adopt an equitable, competitive funding process for Latino-serving organizations similar to neighboring municipalities.

agenda_items.title: Contract Amendment No. 2 with Moss + Ross LLC for Communications Consulting Services
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chelsea Cook and DeDreana Freeman questioned why Forever Home Durham communications ($6,000/month) were outsourced rather than staffed in-house and whether contractors met MWBE tracking and City livable-wage standards. Staff explained outsourcing stemmed from initial 2019 bond capacity decisions, while City Attorney staff confirmed state preemption prohibits mandating contractor wages despite voluntary contract language.

agenda_items.title: Contract Amendment with Corporate Facts (CFACTS) for Affordable Housing Technical Assistance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson explained to Chelsea Cook that HUD's Greensboro field office advised specialized technical assistance because the $8M Commerce Street project layers RAD, Choice Neighborhoods, and HOME compliance rules, creating recapture risk if underwriting or documentation falls short.

agenda_items.title: First Amendment to Contract with Volunteers of America of the Carolinas for Coordinated Entry
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Homeless System Manager Colin Davis explained how Volunteers of America staffs Durham's Coordinated Entry system inside Durham County DSS offices under a City-funded contract. Mayor Williams and Davis also announced a $1.66M HUD regional youth homelessness grant secured via Central Pines Regional Council for Durham, Wake, Orange, and Chatham counties.

agenda_items.title: Contract for Pre-Employment Polygraph Examinations of Police Applicants
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy Chief Melissa Bishop clarified for Chelsea Cook that DPD uses polygraphs solely as a checks-and-balances background supplement—never as an automatic disqualifier—noting Raleigh, Greensboro, and Charlotte-Mecklenburg use similar practices.

agenda_items.title: Amendment 1 with Schnabel Engineering South PC for Little River Dam Settlement and Seepage Improvements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Water Management staff explained that a construction flaw in Little River Dam's east wing wall requires an eventual $40M-$50M repair involving lowering the reservoir. The design amendment prepares shovel-ready plans immediately in case quarterly monitoring detects accelerated degradation before Jordan Lake supply comes online in 2031.

agenda_items.title: Durham Rail Trail Project Design Update and Contract Amendment with John R. McAdams Company, Inc.
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Services and McAdams presented the 65%-100% design supplement and a 3D fly-through video showing the $16.3M base trail (funded within the $9M RAISE grant and existing budget), $2.5M amenity enhancements, and $8.2M Gateway Park (total $36.4M including prior acquisition), targeting fall 2027 opening. Council discussed delivery speed, edge zoning/UDO coordination, value capture, and anti-displacement/property tax relief for nearby residents.

agenda_items.title: Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) Rewrite Audit Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff, Code Studio (Colin Scarf), and Equitable Engagement consultant Dr. Tuwana Allen presented the UDO audit, proposing consolidating 17 articles into 10, merging residential districts (RU-5/RU-5(2), RS-8/RS-10 into RN, RS-20/RR), and replacing units-per-acre density caps with form/height standards. Council debated the absence of a written audit report, dropped short-term amendments, unrepresentative online survey demographics (82% white, 51% over $100k income), and housing size vs. affordability tradeoffs.

agenda_items.title: Board/Commission Nominations Report, Budget Follow-Ups, and Agenda Settlement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk reported board/commission nominations, including re-advertising a BPAC marginalized-groups seat, resolving a split Environmental Affairs Board vote (recommending Jonathan Chan and Karina Barnett-Loro, though Item 8 was moved to GBA to verify Sandra De Howell's reapplication), and placing Item 10 (Homeless Services) on GBA. DeDreana Freeman reported Legal Aid has $350k rolling over to remain whole at $1M for FY24-25 (with a $650k base) and flagged DCAB and StepUp Durham funding asks for Monday's budget meeting.

votes.item_title: Receive City Manager's Priority Items (Work Session Supplemental Additions)
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman presided; Leonardo Williams had not yet arrived (arrived at 00:20:48) and Mark-Anthony Middleton had an excused absence. Vote taken by raising right hand.
votes.discussion_detail: The City Manager presented five priority items for the June 6 work session: a presentation on Item 28 (Durham Rail Trail design update and McAdams contract amendment) plus four supplemental agenda items—Items 39 and 40 (USDOT FAA Airport Improvement Program grant offers), Item 41 (ARPA subrecipient agreement with Affordable Community Residents Association for the Fitz Powell affordable housing project), and Item 42 (on-call executive recruitment services list). Council Member Freeman initially asked whether approval was required and then called for a motion, which was moved and seconded without verbal opposition. All five members present raised their right hands in favor.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session June 6, 2024
disagreements.issue: Outsourced Consulting Contracts, In-House Capacity, and Contractor Living-Wage Compliance (Items 18 & 19)
disagreements.summary: Council members clashed over whether the City should continue outsourcing communications and technical work (such as Moss + Ross LLC at $6,000/month for Forever Home Durham) instead of hiring in-house staff, and how the City enforces livable wages and MWBE equity among contractors.
disagreements.side_a_position: Scrutinize outsourcing vs. in-house FTEs and track contractor wages and MWBE pay equity.
side_a_arguments: Paying $6,000/month over multi-year bond cycles raises questions about why communications are not brought in-house.
Council should ensure the City is not cutting costs via contracting at lower wages and should track MWBE and contractor pay against the City's minimum livable wage.
disagreements.side_b_position: Trust City Manager operational make-or-buy decisions and avoid micromanaging staffing amid tax pressures.
side_b_arguments: With a proposed 3.85-cent City tax increase and 4.5-cent County increase, Council sets policy and should trust the manager to make cost-effective operational choices.
North Carolina state law preempts municipalities from mandating contractor wages, so City contracts rely on voluntary livable-wage expectation clauses and lowest-bidder rules where applicable.
disagreements.resolution: Items 18 and 19 remained on the June 17 Consent Agenda; staff committed to checking whether Moss + Ross counted toward MWBE tracking and providing the City's contract living-wage clause.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session June 6, 2024
disagreements.issue: Durham Rail Trail Delivery Acceleration vs. Community Engagement and Anti-Displacement Policies (Item 28)
disagreements.summary: Council members differed on whether to push staff to accelerate the Durham Rail Trail timeline (currently targeting fall 2027 opening) and how urgently the City must pair the project with anti-displacement and value-capture measures.
disagreements.side_a_position: Push to accelerate infrastructure delivery timelines while pursuing value-capture overlay/tax tools.
side_a_arguments: Voters supporting a tax increase and $200M bond want to know what staffing or funding would deliver funded projects like the Rail Trail a year earlier.
Rising property values along the corridor should be paired with value capture or overlay mechanisms and stay-in-place policies.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain realistic schedules that honor equitable engagement and recognize market realities around major amenities.
side_b_arguments: Rushing project delivery risks excluding East Durham residents from equitable engagement and causing construction flaws.

High-value amenities inevitably raise surrounding market prices, and anti-displacement programming carries ongoing tax costs; Durham already replaced neighborhood-specific pilots with the County's low-income homeowner relief program.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote; Council requested an update from Durham County on the Low-Income Homeowner Relief Program at a future Joint City-County Committee meeting.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session June 6, 2024
disagreements.issue: UDO Rewrite Audit Transparency, Survey Demographics, and Density vs. Unit-Size Assumptions (Item 37)
disagreements.summary: Council members sharply questioned Code Studio and Planning staff over missing written audit deliverables, dropped short-term code amendments, heavily skewed online survey demographics, and whether eliminating density caps guarantees affordable family housing.
disagreements.side_a_position: Audit deliverables and survey framing are inadequate/unrepresentative, and density alone does not ensure family-sized affordability.
side_a_arguments: Council was led to expect short-term targeted UDO recommendations and a full written audit report rather than only a slide deck.
Presenting online survey results that are 82% white and >51% over $100k income as a baseline before qualitative community engagement undermines equitable engagement.

Code Studio's affordability chart relies on shrinking units to 800 sq ft for a family of four; density should be paired with affordable housing density bonuses, and inner-core lot caps of 8 units may be overly conservative vs. 12-plexes or cottage courts.
disagreements.side_b_position: Eliminating units-per-acre density caps is vital to lower rents and support transit, and early online data is only an incomplete baseline.
side_b_arguments: Removing density caps and regulating by form/height aligns land use with the Comprehensive Plan, Urban Growth Boundary, and regional transit goals.

Online surveys historically skew white and affluent nationwide, which is why Dr. Tuwana Allen's parallel in-person ambassador outreach is underway; incomplete survey numbers (214 responses) should simply be held or framed clearly.
disagreements.resolution: Informational presentation only; Planning staff confirmed the first full draft UDO will return in late fall 2024 ahead of early 2025 public review.

meetings.title: Durham City Council June 3, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: With all seven members present, the Durham City Council recognized Juneteenth Week, approved an excused absence for Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton's upcoming Thursday work session, and passed the Consent Agenda 7-0. Council unanimously approved a $3 million grant agreement for the Dillard Street Apartments (Item 9) despite resident concerns about DHA/DVI management accountability, introduced $85 million Parks & Recreation and $115 million Streets & Sidewalks General Obligation bond orders for a June 17 public hearing (Item 12), and adopted a 20% Fire Department inspection and permit fee increase (Item 38). The meeting concluded with a lengthy public hearing on the proposed FY2024-25 Budget and FY2025-30 CIP (Item 37), where dozens of residents debated property taxes, police vs. HEART funding, $25-$27/hr livable wages and CDL reclassification for Solid Waste workers, $200,000 in added operating funds for StepUp Durham's guaranteed income program, Vision Zero street safety, and eviction diversion.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, Juneteenth Proclamation, and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: All seven Council members answered roll call. Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton read a proclamation declaring June 15–22, 2024 as Juneteenth Week alongside Sister Ashabu, who urged adding $100,000 to fully fund the Durham Cultural Advisory Board's $400,000 request. Council members celebrated Pride Month, DPS graduates, and Vision Zero; Council approved Middleton's excused absence for June 6; and Mayor Williams warned that youth gun violence in Durham has reached a crisis level requiring top priority.

agenda_items.title: Priority Items from City Manager, City Attorney, and City Clerk
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager noted supplemental responses attached for Items 21 (NCWorks), 26 (Q1 Crime Report), 27 (Vision Zero Resolution), and 41 (Virgil Road annexation), and reported Item 25 (USTA Southern Build It Forward Grant) was referred back to Parks and Recreation. The City Attorney and City Clerk had no priority items.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Adoption (Items 1–8, 13–24, 26–32)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council read the Consent Agenda, pulling Items 9, 11, and 12 (with Item 25 referred back to staff). Notable consent items included board/commission appointments, Hope VI and Fayette Place predevelopment grants, ARPA cultural and business equity awards, Roxboro Rail Trail cost-sharing, USTA grants, the Q1 Crime Report, and the revised Vision Zero resolution.

agenda_items.title: Grant Agreement with Development Ventures Incorporated (DVI) for Dillard Street Apartments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pulled by resident Regina Maze, who spoke on Items 9–11 and criticized poor property management, unresponsive out-of-state developers, rapid manager turnover, maintenance backlogs, and eviction filings tied to DHA recertification delays. Mayor Williams directed staff to obtain Ms. Maze's contact information for follow-up, and Council authorized the grant up to $3,000,000.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Approved unanimously (no dissent; tally omitted in ASR)

agenda_items.title: 2024 General Obligation Bond Referendum Orders ($85M Parks & Recreation, $115M Streets & Sidewalks)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pulled by Walltown Community Association resident Danielle Dogan, who urged prioritizing remediation of lead and soil contamination in East Durham Park and four other contaminated parks before disturbing soil with capital improvements. Council introduced the $85M Parks & Recreation bond order, the $115M Streets & Sidewalks bond order, and a resolution setting the public hearing for June 17, 2024.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Proposed Durham Fire Department Permit and Inspection Fee Increase for FY2024-25
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Fire Chief Bob Zoldos and Fire Marshal Jody Morton presented a ~20% fee increase—the first since July 2019—averaging $21 per routine inspection to generate ~$187,000 in added cost recovery toward state-mandated inspections. No public speakers signed up, and Council adopted the ordinance amending Chapter 8 of the fee schedule.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Proposed FY2024-25 Budget and FY2025-30 Capital Improvement Plan (CIP)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Assistant Budget Director J.J. Scott opened the public hearing on the FY24-25 budget and FY25-30 CIP. Over 20 online and in-person speakers testified on property tax burden, police vs. Community Safety/HEART funding, $25-$27/hr livable wages and CDL reclassification for Solid Waste workers, firefighter pay raises, $200,000 in added operating funds for StepUp Durham's guaranteed income program, Vision Zero and fare-free transit, Legal Aid eviction diversion, and $25,000 for Charles Hamilton Houston Foundation youth mentorship.

votes.item_title: Approve Excused Absence for Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton (June 6, 2024 Work Session)
votes.notes: Electronic voting system used after City Clerk reminded Council it was a regular meeting rather than a work session. Middleton requested the excuse to host the NC League of Municipalities Board of Directors meeting in Durham as its new president.
votes.discussion_detail: During Council announcements, Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton requested an excused absence for the June 6, 2024 work session and Friday commitments because, as incoming president of the North Carolina League of Municipalities, he would be hosting the NCLM Board of Directors in Durham. Mayor Williams noted he would briefly greet the NCLM board on Thursday before returning to chair the work session. After a motion and second were made, the City Clerk reminded Council that an electronic vote was required rather than a hand vote, and the motion passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 9: Authorize Grant Agreement with Development Ventures Incorporated for Dillard Street Apartments ($3,000,000 Cap)
votes.notes: Electronic vote opened at 00:37:04 and passed with no dissent before moving directly to Item 12 at 00:37:38 (Clerk's verbal tally announcement not captured in ASR). Mayor directed staff to obtain speaker Regina Maze's contact info.
votes.discussion_detail: Resident Regina Maze pulled Item 9 to raise accountability concerns about private-developer partnerships with Durham Housing Authority and Development Ventures Incorporated (DVI). She testified to experiencing maintenance backlogs, rapid property manager turnover within 30 days, unresponsive out-of-state corporate offices in Boston and Maryland, and evictions filed due to incomplete DHA recertifications. Mayor Williams asked staff to get Ms. Maze's contact information for follow-up, and a Council member moved to authorize the grant agreement with DVI for the Dillard Street Apartments in an amount not to exceed $3,000,000. The motion was seconded and passed without dissent.

votes.item_title: Item 12a: Introduce Bond Order Authorizing $85,000,000 General Obligation Parks and Recreation Bonds
votes.notes: First of three statutory actions on the 2024 GO Bond Referendum; subject to June 17 public hearing and November voter approval.
votes.discussion_detail: Walltown Community Association resident Danielle Dogan pulled Item 12 to express concern that the proposed $85 million Parks and Recreation bond includes improvements at East Durham Park, one of five Durham parks with severe lead and soil contamination. She urged Council to avoid disturbing soil before remediation and to expand bond funds to help remediate contaminated parklands. Following her remarks, Council moved, seconded, and unanimously passed 7-0 the introduction of the $85,000,000 General Obligation Parks and Recreation bond order.

votes.item_title: Item 12b: Introduce Bond Order Authorizing $115,000,000 General Obligation Streets and Sidewalks Bonds
votes.notes: Second of three statutory actions on the 2024 GO Bond Referendum; electronic vote opened at 00:41:05 and proceeded directly to Item 12c at 00:41:26 with no dissent (Clerk's verbal tally announcement not captured in ASR).
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately following introduction of the Parks and Recreation bond order, Mayor Williams entertained a motion to introduce the companion bond order authorizing the issuance of $115,000,000 in General Obligation Streets and Sidewalks bonds for the November 2024 referendum. No separate debate occurred on this motion beyond the earlier public comment on Item 12. The motion was seconded and passed without dissent via electronic vote.

votes.item_title: Item 12c: Adopt Resolution Setting Public Hearing on 2024 GO Bond Orders for June 17, 2024
votes.notes: Sets statutory public hearing for June 17, 2024 on both the $85M Parks & Recreation and $115M Streets & Sidewalks bond orders.
votes.discussion_detail: As the final required statutory step on Item 12 for the evening, Mayor Williams entertained a motion to adopt the resolution setting a public hearing on both the $85 million Parks and Recreation and $115 million Streets and Sidewalks bond orders for June 17, 2024. The motion was moved, seconded, and approved unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 38: Adopt Ordinance Amending Fire Inspection and Permit Fees in Chapter 8 of City Fee Schedule
votes.notes: Approx. 20% fee increase (average $21 per routine inspection), generating ~$187,000/year toward cost recovery; first increase since July 2019.
votes.discussion_detail: Fire Chief Bob Zoldos and Fire Marshal Jody Morton presented Durham Fire Department's request to raise state-mandated fire permit and inspection fees by approximately 20% for FY2024-25—averaging $21 per routine inspection and adding roughly $187,000 in revenue above the $935,736 projected for FY23-24. They noted fees had not increased since July 1, 2019 and the adjustment moves DFD closer to cost recovery. With no public speakers signed up and no Council questions, the Mayor opened and closed the public hearing, and Council unanimously adopted the Chapter 8 fee schedule amendment 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council June 3, 2024
disagreements.issue: FY2024-25 Budget Priorities: Police vs. HEART Funding and City/Solid Waste Worker Compensation (Item 37)
disagreements.summary: During the FY2024-25 budget public hearing, residents, labor advocates, and public employees presented sharply competing visions over tax increases, police vs. Community Safety (HEART) spending, and whether the City's pay plan adequately serves its lowest-paid and Solid Waste workers.
disagreements.side_a_position: Cut or halt police budget growth in favor of HEART/guaranteed income, raise the minimum wage to $25-$27/hr, and reclassify CDL Solid Waste workers.
side_a_arguments: Triangle DSA criticized increasing DPD's budget by $4M (to $82M) while increasing Community Safety/HEART by only $1M (to $7.5M).

Solid Waste workers and labor advocates argued the proposed $19.58/hr minimum falls far short of Durham's cost of living (urging $25-$27/hr) and demanded CDL-holding Solid Waste drivers be reclassified as Maintenance Specialist Seniors or Heavy Equipment Operators.
StepUp Durham and Durham for All urged adding $200,000 so the $1M guaranteed income allocation goes 100% to direct payments.
disagreements.side_b_position: Prioritize sworn Police and Fire compensation/staffing, protect taxpayers from high property tax hikes, or support the City Manager's balanced package.
side_b_arguments: Public safety advocates and city staff (John Wacka, Wilma Oliver) stressed DPD staffing shortages, rising property tax burdens, and the vital daily work of police, firefighters, and code enforcement officers.

Local 668 firefighters thanked Council for substantial raises cutting sub-livable-wage firefighters from over 100 to 31, while safe-streets and eviction-diversion advocates urged passing the proposed CIP, Vision Zero, fare-free transit, and Legal Aid items.
disagreements.resolution: Public hearing only; Council received testimony ahead of final budget deliberations and adoption later in June.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council June 3, 2024
disagreements.issue: Use of $85M Parks Bond Funds vs. Lead and Soil Contamination Remediation (Item 12)
disagreements.summary: A Walltown resident challenged the proposed $85M Parks and Recreation GO bond for funding park improvements at East Durham Park without first remediating lead and soil contamination, while Council advanced the bond orders to a June 17 public hearing.
disagreements.side_a_position: Halt soil-disturbing improvements and expand the bond to fund lead and contamination remediation in the five affected parks.
side_a_arguments: East Durham Park is one of five City parks deeply affected by lead and serious contamination, and disturbing soil could put toxic particles into the air.
Bond funds should remediate known environmental hazards rather than fund routine maintenance or improvements over contaminated ground.
disagreements.side_b_position: Advance the $85M Parks & Recreation and $115M Streets & Sidewalks bond orders to the statutory public hearing.
side_b_arguments: Introducing the bond orders sets the required June 17 public hearing and preserves voter consideration on the November ballot.
disagreements.resolution: Council unanimously (7-0) introduced both bond orders and set the public hearing for June 17, 2024.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council June 3, 2024
disagreements.issue: Private-Developer Accountability in City-Funded Affordable Housing Grants (Item 9)
disagreements.summary: A resident living in a DHA/DVI-partnered development urged Council not to hand over housing grant funds without enforceable resident protections and management accountability, while Council approved the $3M Dillard Street grant and ordered staff follow-up.
disagreements.side_a_position: Withhold or condition DVI/DHA grant funds on stronger tenant accountability and management oversight.
side_a_arguments: Residents face chronic manager turnover within 30 days, ignored maintenance requests, unresponsive out-of-state corporate owners, and wrongful eviction filings stemming from DHA recertification delays.
disagreements.side_b_position: Approve the $3M Dillard Street Apartments grant agreement while directing staff to investigate the resident's complaints.
side_b_arguments: The grant advances needed affordable housing units while City staff can follow up directly with the resident on management issues.
disagreements.resolution: Council approved the $3M grant agreement without dissent, and Mayor Williams instructed staff to collect the speaker's contact information for follow-up.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Budget Work Session May 30, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: Day 2 of the Durham City Council FY 2024-25 Budget Work Session was opened by Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton (with Mayor Leonardo Williams arriving later) and featured departmental budget reviews, beginning with City-County Planning Director Sara Young's presentation on staffing, permit review backlogs, and fee updates. Council members inquired about non-departmental items including the $1 million Guaranteed Income allocation and a proposed $100,000 addition to the festival grant pool. In closing deliberations, Council reached informal consensus not to add unfunded items that would unbalance the proposed budget—citing Durham's tight fund balance, the County's $550 million bond, and the need to protect the City's AAA credit rating—and canceled the optional June 6 morning budget meeting.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Questions on Unpresented Budget Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton opened the May 30 budget work session while Mayor Leonardo Williams was en route, and Budget Director Christina Reardon outlined presentations from Planning, Community Development, Community Safety, Police, and Fire. A council member asked when non-departmental items—specifically the $1,000,000 Guaranteed Income program and an additional $100,000 for festivals (bringing the General Services grant pool from $200,000 to $300,000)—would be discussed, and City Manager Wanda Page confirmed she could address those items.

agenda_items.title: City-County Planning Department Proposed FY 2024-25 Budget
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning Director Sara Young presented an approximately 10% budget increase driven by personnel costs, adding two new FTEs (a building permit review planner to address doubled review volumes and a senior community planner for small-area planning, comprehensive plan implementation, and historic preservation) to bring staffing from 51 to 53 FTEs. She also highlighted ~800 annual public records requests, restored zoning enforcement staffing, modest fee adjustments across roughly 30 application types generating $617,000 in new revenue (~$3.1M total, covering ~50% of department costs with a 25%/25% City-County split), and restoration of pre-pandemic travel and training funds.

agenda_items.title: Budget Balancing, Festival Funding, Fund Balance, AAA Rating, and June 6 Session Decision
agenda_items.discussion_summary: In wrap-up deliberations following departmental presentations (middle segment truncated in transcript), council members confirmed there was no majority direction to unbalance the budget or add taxpayer-funded festival subsidies, emphasizing corporate sponsorships, fund balance constraints, and preserving Durham's AAA credit rating ahead of limited obligation bond issuances. Council agreed to cancel the tentative June 6 morning budget session ahead of the June 3 public hearing and June 17 adoption, and asked staff to pair strategic-goal performance metrics with the Popular Annual Financial Report for community outreach.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Budget Work Session May 29, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: On Day 1 of the FY 2024-25 Budget Work Session, Mayor Leonardo Williams convened Council for a full-day review of revenues, employee pay and benefits, the Capital Improvement Plan, and infrastructure departments. Budget Director Christina Reardon detailed the ~$669 million proposed budget ($305 million General Fund, up 8.7%) anchored by a proposed 3.85-cent property tax increase dedicated to the General Fund, 5% projected sales tax growth ($104.9 million), and a projected $76.2 million year-end FY24 fund balance. Later deliberations examined transportation project delivery timelines for the Mangum/Roxboro two-way reversion (ahead of Duke/Gregson), federal grant reliance, mobility hub phasing, and the long-term sustainability of fare-free GoDurham transit.

agenda_items.title: FY 2024-25 Revenue Forecast, Proposed 3.85-Cent Tax Increase, and Fund Balance Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams called the session to order at 9:00 AM (noting Chelsea Cook was delayed), and Budget Director Christina Reardon presented the ~$669M proposed FY25 budget ($305M General Fund), including a 3.85-cent property tax rate increase (one penny generating $4.27M in FY25). Reardon reviewed $21M (+16%) in property tax growth, $104.9M (+5%) in sales tax under the 44.5%/55.5% City-County interlocal split, $3.3M (+51%) in occupancy tax, $8.5M in Powell Bill revenue, $5.7M for county fire consolidation, and a $76.2M projected FY24 year-end fund balance ($14.4M above the 16.7% policy reserve).

agenda_items.title: Transportation Project Delivery, Mangum/Roxboro Two-Way Reversion, and Fare-Free Transit
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following truncated middle department presentations, Council and staff discussed accelerating multimodal infrastructure ahead of the fall $200M bond referendum, noting procurement and NCDOT coordination require FY25 for Mangum and Roxboro two-way design before FY26 construction (which precedes Duke and Gregson conversions). Members also discussed ongoing resurfacing, parking/lighting safety equity, $10.8M in federal funding for Durham Station, phased improvements at the city's second-highest transit boarding hub, and sustaining fare-free GoDurham service.

agenda_items.title: Manager's Wrap-Up and Guidance Request for June 17 Budget Adoption
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page thanked staff and the budget team and asked Council to provide clear majority direction by Day 2 on any dollar changes needed to maintain a balanced $670M budget ahead of the June 3 public hearing and June 17 adoption vote. Mayor Williams adjourned the session at 2:30 PM.
