meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session May 23, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: In a nearly five-hour work session (with Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton absent and Council Member DeDreana Freeman departing around 3:00 PM), Council received priority items from the City Manager and City Attorney, heard public comments on public records and youth mentorship, and reviewed nine pulled consent items ahead of the June 3 meeting. Major presentations covered the Downtown Durham Municipal Service District (MSD) annual report—featuring an urgent letter from 260 small businesses on construction disruptions, parking rates, and small business grants—the Q1 2024 Crime Report, Parks & Recreation summer camps and aquatics, the FY23-24 Q3 Financial Report, and a Vision Zero update proposing 2035 and 2045 fatality-reduction targets. Council settled the June 3 agenda 5-0 and entered closed session 5-0 for attorney-client consultation on a pending liability settlement demand.

agenda_items.title: Council Announcements and Manager/Attorney/Clerk Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council continued announcements (Freeman noted her 3:00 PM departure and shared the Durham Crisis Response helpline; Rist previewed Vision Zero following the NC Transportation conference). Mayor Williams moved Item 34 up first. Council voted 6-0 to receive the City Manager's priority items (Item 26 presentation and supplemental responses for Items 20–21) and 6-0 to accept the City Attorney's request for a closed session at meeting's end.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review and Public Comment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council read Items 1–38 and pulled Items 7, 10, 11, 12, 15, 18, 19, 20, and 21 for discussion. In public comment, Jacqueline Wagstaff demanded restoration of deleted May 17 Mayor social media videos as public records, and Delorean Langley requested $25,000 for Charles Hamilton Houston Foundation mentorship to curb youth gun violence.

agenda_items.title: Downtown Durham Municipal Service District (MSD) Annual Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DDI CEO Nicole Thompson presented the MSD report and read a letter on behalf of 260 downtown businesses citing 82 lost businesses since COVID and demanding action on construction notifications/penalties, lower hourly/employee parking rates ($2.25–$2.50/hr, $140/mo), outdoor dining rules, and restoring BIG/facade grants. Four downtown workers and business owners testified to lost clientele and blocked access; Council debated UDO fixes vs. administrative action and citywide small-business equity.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Presentation only / Directed City Manager to report back with timeline

agenda_items.title: FY2023-24 Budget and Capital Project Ordinances Amendment (Legal Aid Comment)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Former Council Member Laura Capel spoke on Item 7 on behalf of Legal Aid's eviction diversion program, reporting 66–100 eviction cases on daily dockets and 85% judgment-avoidance success, and urged Council not to cut funding that would halve attorney staffing.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Grants: DHA HOPE VI & Fayette Place Redevelopment and Made in Durham
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chelsea Cook inquired about long-term management for HOPE VI properties and praised mixed-income integration on Fayette Place/Forest Hills Heights (Item 11). DeDreana Freeman urged Parks & Rec partnerships to keep community centers open at DHA/Community Builders sites (Anthony Snell responded). On Item 20 (Made in Durham), Freeman requested demographic tracking and Carl Rist praised the contract's clear benchmarks.

agenda_items.title: 2024 First Quarter Crime Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chief Patrice Andrews and Deputy Chief Melissa Bishop reported Q1 violent crime up 3.7% (homicides down 53.9% to 6, 18 YTD; robberies up 18% with 49% Hispanic victims), shootings down 34.1%, and property crime up 15.6% driven by a 53.2% surge in auto thefts (Kia/Hyundai). Sworn staffing stood at 74% (397 of 535 filled) and Priority 1 response times averaged 6m37s. Council questioned staffing metrics, U-Visa denials, ICE cooperation impacts on immigrant trust, and Mayor Williams urged treating youth gun violence (~1,500 shell casings YTD) as Durham's top crisis.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Items: GO Bonds, Garage Banners, Cornerstone Software, ARPA Equity, and NCWorks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Jacqueline Wagstaff opposed the $200M GO bond referendum (Item 12) and tax hike while Cook and staff (Tim Flora) highlighted the City's AAA rating (~3.6% projected interest) and requested a side-by-side CIP comparison. Staff clarified City insurance covers only ~$6k of the $100k Corcoran garage banner repair (Item 15), corrected missing attachments on Item 18, explained the $1M ARPA cap reduced OEWD's equity/employee-ownership grant to $400k on Fayetteville St (Item 19), and agreed to return outcome metrics for the $100k NCWorks management contract (Item 21).
agenda_items.vote_summary: Items 15, 18–21 on June 3 Consent; Item 12 pulled for June 3

agenda_items.title: Summer Camp, Aquatics, and Teen Programming Presentation and Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DPR presented 1,261 summer camp slots (adding half-day and STEM camps amid staffing and year-round school lunch shifts), Teen Connect, MyDurham, DPR-PAL basketball, and opening Forest Hills and Hillside pools daily with 62 newly certified lifeguards ($18.90/hr). Council explored waitlists (147 at Edison Johnson), a countywide out-of-school time study, and free camps (~$162k full-fee offset); Lee Bailey (Swim for Charlie) urged simplifying DPR's 112-question hiring portal to staff pools for 7 East Durham elementary schools.

agenda_items.title: FY2023-24 Third Quarter Financial Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Finance Director Tim Floyd reported General Fund expenditures tracking $6.4M under budget (due to vacancy savings), revenues $779K over budget despite sales tax trailing target by $749K, and planned use of $3.58M fund balance without large prior-year surpluses. Enterprise funds (Water/Sewer, Solid Waste, Stormwater, DPAC, Ballpark, County Inspections) are healthy, though the Parking Fund carries a $1.5M deficit/loan due to remote work.

agenda_items.title: Vision Zero Update Presentation and Revised Resolution
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Vision Zero Coordinator Lauren Grove reviewed crash data (28 deaths in 2023; 80% on surface streets; 30% of fatal crashes in low-income/POC communities vs. 16% of all crashes), explained the Safe Systems pyramid, and requested adopting Item 27 setting targets of 50% reduction by 2035 and zero deaths/serious injuries by 2045 to qualify for federal SS4A grants. Council discussed street design speeds, UDO width standards, and delivery bottlenecks.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Resolution (Item 27) placed on June 3 Consent Agenda

agenda_items.title: Agenda Settlement, Clerk's Nominations Report, and Closed Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted 5-0 (Freeman departed around 3:00 PM; Middleton absent) to settle the June 3 agenda (Consent Items 1–32; GBA Public Hearings Items 37–38). The City Clerk read board/commission nominations, including re-advertising a second Planning Commission seat. Council then voted 5-0 to enter closed session under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3) for attorney-client consultation on a liability settlement demand.

votes.item_title: Receive City Manager's Priority Items
votes.notes: Mark-Anthony Middleton absent. Vote taken by show of hands.
votes.discussion_detail: Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson presented the City Manager's priority items: a work session presentation on Item 26 (2024 First Quarter Crime Report) and supplemental written responses attached for Items 20 and 21 (ARPA Fayetteville Street corridor improvement items) following questions from the May 20 meeting. After being prompted by the City Attorney, Mayor Williams entertained a motion to receive the priority items. The motion was moved, seconded, and approved unanimously by show of hands among the six members present.

votes.item_title: Receive City Attorney's Priority Item (Request for Closed Session)
votes.notes: Mark-Anthony Middleton absent. Agreed to hold closed session at end of meeting; Freeman noted she was leaving at 3:00 PM and Mayor Williams asked that both Freeman and Middleton be briefed afterward.
votes.discussion_detail: The City Attorney requested a closed session at the conclusion of regular business for attorney-client consultation, noting the City needed to enter into an agreement by June 1 and required briefing and final approval. Mayor Williams noted Council Member Freeman's planned 3:00 PM departure and Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton's absence, requesting that both absent members receive the closed-session briefing materials afterward. Council then moved, seconded, and unanimously voted by show of hands (6-0) to accept the priority item and schedule the closed session for the end of the meeting.

votes.item_title: Enter Closed Session Pursuant to N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3) (Liability Settlement Demand)
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman departed earlier; Mark-Anthony Middleton absent. Vote taken by raising hands; transcript ASR rendered statute as '143 38183'.
votes.discussion_detail: After the City Clerk delivered the report on board and commission nominations, the City Attorney read the formal closed-session motion under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3) for attorney-client consultation concerning the handling of a settlement demand for a yet-to-be-filed liability claim. A motion was made and seconded, and the five Council members remaining present voted unanimously by raising their hands to recess into closed session.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session May 23, 2024
disagreements.issue: Addressing Downtown Business Disruptions: UDO Rewrite vs. Administrative Action and Citywide Equity (Item 34)
disagreements.summary: Following DDI's urgent letter from 260 downtown businesses, Council members and DDI diverged over whether construction/streetscape reforms belong in the UDO rewrite or immediate administrative operations, and whether grants and support should extend citywide beyond downtown.
disagreements.side_a_position: Address construction communication, ADA compliance, and public goods through UDO standards, and ensure small-business support extends beyond downtown.
side_a_arguments: Large out-of-town corporate developers should have communication, sidewalk, and utility/trash allocation standards baked into the UDO rewrite and targeted amendments.
Small businesses in neighborhoods outside downtown—such as Ninth Street and Driver Street—also suffer from utility shutoffs and lack a DDI-style organization to advocate for them.
disagreements.side_b_position: Focus on immediate City operational fixes (employee parking, alert systems, fines for bad actors) without tying them to the UDO.
side_b_arguments: DDI's letter seeks pre-development meetings, enforcement of existing closure plans, employee parking relief by September, and administrative coordination rather than waiting on the UDO.
Council should stay focused on actionable operational fixes and activating the existing small business fund rather than letting out-of-town developer critiques hijack the discussion.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote; Council asked Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson to consult City Manager Wanda Page and return with a timeline of immediate vs. FY26 budgetary actions.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session May 23, 2024
disagreements.issue: Youth Gun Violence Response, ShotSpotter Termination, and Police Staffing Realism (Item 26)
disagreements.summary: During the Q1 Crime Report discussion, Mayor Williams sharply criticized Council's handling of gun violence after ending ShotSpotter without an alternative response, while Council members also questioned whether DPD's 535 sworn staffing target is realistic.
disagreements.side_a_position: Treat youth gun violence as Durham's top crisis and provide concrete alternatives after ending ShotSpotter.
side_a_arguments: Neighborhoods are enduring heavy gunfire (~1,500 shell casings collected YTD) and Council ended ShotSpotter without putting a response in place.
Council shut down City Hall for a Gaza ceasefire resolution while staying quiet on gun violence in Durham; public safety must be prioritized alongside bike lanes and sidewalks.
disagreements.side_b_position: Question whether filling 535 sworn positions is realistic and pair pay raises with holistic investments.
side_b_arguments: With sworn staffing at 74% (397 of 535) and modest academy class sizes, reaching 100% of authorized slots may be unrealistic without reassessing workload and vacancy metrics.
Higher pay in the FY24-25 budget (moving everyone to July raises) alongside investments in youth, Survivor Care, and community trust—including protecting immigrant reporting—are key responses.
disagreements.resolution: Item 26 remained on the June 3 Consent Agenda; staff committed to providing shooting demographics and tracking Latino youth crime trends.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session May 23, 2024
disagreements.issue: UDO Street Widths, Autocentrism, and Vision Zero Target Timelines (Item 36)
disagreements.summary: Council members debated whether Durham's street width standards and greenfield rezonings undermine Vision Zero, how quickly fatalities can be eliminated, and how to balance narrower streets with emergency and service vehicle needs.
disagreements.side_a_position: Reform UDO street standards to prevent auto-centric sprawl and accelerate Vision Zero delivery timelines.
side_a_arguments: Approving auto-centric single-family sprawl on annexed land contradicts Comprehensive Plan walkability and Vision Zero goals, and current UDO street widths may be excessive.
Setting 10-year (50% by 2035) and 20-year (0% by 2045) targets feels slow given recent traffic deaths; accelerating project delivery is vital to win federal SS4A grants.
disagreements.side_b_position: Adopt realistic timelines and coordinate street narrowing delicately with Fire, Solid Waste, and transit buses.
side_b_arguments: Setting hard target dates creates anxiety given current project-delivery capacity and NCDOT constraints, and narrow streets require testing with fire trucks, school buses, and solid waste vehicles.
disagreements.resolution: Council expressed consensus support for advancing the revised Vision Zero resolution (Item 27) onto the June 3 Consent Agenda.

meetings.title: Durham City Council May 20, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: At its May 20, 2024 regular meeting, Durham City Council excused Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton's upcoming May 23 work-session absence, heard priority updates and Item 35's FY 2024-25 budget introduction, and took pivotal ARPA funding votes for the Fayetteville Street / Hayti corridor. On Item 20, Council approved a $6,755,000 grant agreement with Hayti Promise CDC and St. Joseph's Historic Foundation by a 6-1 vote after Council Member DeDreana Freeman voted no over missing maps, minutes, and anti-displacement assurances. After passing companion Item 21 ($3,245,000) unanimously 7-0 following public transparency testimony from Larry and Denise Hester, Council approved a formal motion allowing Freeman to change her Item 20 vote from no to yes so the full $10 million package passed unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Council Announcements and Excused Absence for Mayor Pro Tem Middleton
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members recognized the Citizens Advisory Board retreat (Chelsea Cook), Bike Durham's Ride of Silence and the Planning Academy (Javiera Caballero), Malcolm X's 99th birthday and formerly incarcerated reentry support (DeDreana Freeman), Rotary Flags for Heroes and budget outreach (Carl Rist), and Mayor Williams's visit to Dallas's Klyde Warren freeway cap park. Council also voted to excuse Mark-Anthony Middleton's absence from the May 23 work session.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Additions and Consent Agenda Reading
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Williams noted Item 35 (the Manager's FY 2024-25 budget presentation) and upcoming June 3 public hearing, while City Manager Wanda Page added supplemental attachments for Item 41 (annexation utility extension), Item 44 (HOME grant project ordinances), and Item 45 (2024 meeting schedule revision). Reading of the Consent Agenda began at 00:20:33 before middle segments were truncated in the digest.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / Consent vote truncated in digest

agenda_items.title: ARPA Grant Agreement with Hayti Promise CDC and St. Joseph's Historic Foundation ($6,755,000)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DeDreana Freeman objected to voting without project maps, approved board minutes, or binding protections keeping existing businesses on the Fayetteville Street corridor, while supporting colleagues argued St. Joseph's/Hayti Heritage Foundation serves as fiscal agent for Hayti Promise CDC and that detailed plans would follow funding approval. The motion initially passed 6-1 with Freeman voting no.

agenda_items.title: ARPA Subrecipient Grant Agreement with Hayti Promise CDC and St. Joseph's Historic Foundation ($3,245,000)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Longtime Fayetteville Street business owners Larry and Denise Hester welcomed the $10M corridor investment but pressed for transparency regarding Hayti Promise CDC's board composition, accountability, and work program. Staff acknowledged missing background information had not been prepared for the meeting and promised to supply it; Council then approved the $3,245,000 agreement unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Motion to Accept Council Member Freeman's Vote Change on Item 20 from No to Yes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After Item 21's discussion clarified details, DeDreana Freeman asked to change her Item 20 vote from no to yes; Mark-Anthony Middleton raised a point of order regarding procedural limits on changing a legally cast vote, and the City Attorney cited UNC School of Government guidance. Following colleague support for unanimity, Council adopted a motion accepting Freeman's vote change from no to yes on Item 20 before adjourning at 1:06 AM.

votes.item_title: Excuse Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton's Absence for Thursday's Work Session
votes.notes: Exact electronic tally was not read aloud after closing the vote; no dissent announced.
votes.discussion_detail: Mark-Anthony Middleton requested an excused absence for the May 23 work session to attend graduation celebrations; Council moved, seconded, and approved the electronic vote.

votes.notes: Clerk announced: 'The motion passes six to one with Council Member Freeman voting no.'
votes.discussion_detail: Passed 6-1 after DeDreana Freeman raised transparency and anti-displacement concerns; subsequently changed to unanimous 7-0 via procedural motion at 06:07:35.

votes.item_title: Authorize City Manager to Execute ARPA Subrecipient Grant Agreement with Hayti Promise CDC and St. Joseph's Historic Foundation, Inc. (Not to Exceed $3,245,000) — Item 21
votes.notes: Clerk announced motion passed unanimously.
votes.discussion_detail: Council approved the companion $3,245,000 ARPA subrecipient grant agreement after public speakers Larry and Denise Hester called for board and program transparency and staff agreed to provide missing documentation.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council May 20, 2024
disagreements.issue: Transparency and Governance Requirements for $6.755M Hayti Promise CDC / Fayetteville Street Corridor Grant (Item 20)
disagreements.summary: Council initially split 6-1 on Item 20 over whether sufficient project maps, approved board minutes, and business-retention guarantees had been provided prior to releasing $6,755,000 to Hayti Promise CDC and fiscal agent St. Joseph's Historic Foundation.
disagreements.side_a_position: Require transparent documentation, approved board minutes, project mapping, and anti-displacement assurances for existing Fayetteville Street businesses before approving the grant.
side_a_arguments: No map, approved board minutes, or clear commitment ensuring existing corridor businesses remain in place had been provided to Council.
Staff acknowledged during Item 21 that certain requested background information was not prepared for presentation.
disagreements.side_b_position: Approve the grant immediately so long-delayed funding for the historic Hayti / Fayetteville Street corridor can begin flowing while detailed operational specifics are developed in later phases.
side_b_arguments: St. Joseph's Historic Foundation / Hayti Heritage Foundation serves only as fiscal agent while Hayti Promise CDC was unanimously selected by Hayti community groups.
Fayetteville Street corridor stakeholders have waited decades for investment and should not be delayed while administrative details are finalized.
disagreements.resolution: Item 20 initially passed 6-1 at 05:48:09, and after additional discussion during Item 21, Council voted unanimously at 06:08:07 to accept DeDreana Freeman's vote change from no to yes, making passage unanimous.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session May 9, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council held a wide-ranging work session reviewing ARPA spending progress, affordable housing investments, surplus land disposal, and major corridor projects ahead of the May 20 Council meeting. Council suspended rules to approve $1.08M in emergency Carolina Theater roof repairs using surplus ballpark funds and heard detailed presentations on the $28M Sankofa Landing bond deal, the Durham Immigrant Legal Assistance Program, and the $10M ARPA Fayetteville Street Corridor package. Members also scrutinized permanent affordability mechanisms for surplus city lots, the Hayti Promise CDC governance structure, and a contested Discover Durham board nomination before settling the May 20 agenda.

agenda_items.title: Council Announcements and Upcoming Events
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams noted a recent DOST trails bus tour, while Carl Rist highlighted National Bike Month, the Ride of Silence memorializing cyclists, and active transportation efforts. DeDreana Freeman requested that staff present options on May 23 for utilizing Durham Parks and Recreation summer camp funding for additional community camps. Chelsea Cook announced she needed to depart by 5:00 PM due to a prior conflict.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Items and Item 18 Suspension Request
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page presented priority additions and adjustments, including adding Item 42 (NCDOT East Club Boulevard/I-85 lighting agreement) and Item 43 (Mythics Oracle Fusion contract), referring Item 38 (Sheffield Farms annexation/zoning) back to Planning, and requesting rule suspension to vote immediately on Item 18 for urgent Carolina Theater roof structural repairs. Council approved accepting the priority items, suspended the rules, and passed all five Item 18 sub-motions.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Priority items accepted 7-0; rules suspended 7-0; Item 18 sub-votes passed 6-0 (1 recusal)

agenda_items.title: Public Comments on Fluoridation, 911/Police Staffing, and Youth Programs
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident Jared Rist urged Council to end municipal water fluoridation, citing neurotoxicity and dental fluorosis research, while Anita Keith-Foust raised alarms over 911 response delays, police staffing shortages, and gunfire near elderly housing. Later in the meeting, Darrell Langley requested $250,000 for Charles Hamilton Houston Foundation mentorship programming, and Jacqueline Wagstaff advocated for summer camp funding and a $1M grant to support domestic workers.

agenda_items.title: Durham Immigrant Legal Assistance Program (ILAP) Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Justice Matters attorneys presented outcomes from the City's $250,000-per-year ILAP grant, reporting that more than 4,900 Durham residents currently have cases pending in Charlotte Immigration Court, where roughly 82% of immigrants lack legal counsel. Presenters noted the program has screened hundreds of residents and achieved 100% court appearance rates for represented clients while urging sustained municipal funding alongside Orange County.

agenda_items.title: March 18 City Council Minutes Correction
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman requested a correction to the draft March 18 regular meeting minutes to accurately reflect remarks and exchanges during the meeting. Staff noted the requested edit for the May 20 consent agenda.

agenda_items.title: ARPA Performance Audit Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Audit Services Director Dr. Germaine Brewington reviewed an audit of the City's American Rescue Plan Act portfolio, reporting that 42% of funds were obligated and 23% expended ahead of the December 31, 2024 federal obligation deadline. Council members questioned how quickly remaining balances and unspent allocations could be redeployed if partner projects stall.

agenda_items.title: Planning Department FY25 Work Program
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning Director Sara Young outlined the FY25 work program priorities, including completing the comprehensive UDO rewrite, advancing the Walltown/Northgate small area plan, and updating Miami-Page Design District rules. Nate Baker and other members pressed for alignment between transit-oriented area expectations, small area planning capacity, and ongoing rezoning reviews.

agenda_items.title: Sankofa Landing Multifamily Housing Revenue Bonds
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development staff presented a $28M conduit multifamily housing revenue bond issuance through the Durham Housing Authority paired with a $9.7M City ARPA loan for Sankofa Landing. Council examined debt service structure, timeline urgency, and how deep affordability commitments are locked into the DHA-affiliated project.

agenda_items.title: Durham Community Land Trust (DCLT) Forgivable Loan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DCLT Executive Director Sherry Taylor and City staff detailed a forgivable loan supporting home rehabilitations and preservation in Northeast Central Durham with a 30-year plus 20-year affordability framework tied to the community land trust model. Council praised the permanent stewardship approach while clarifying income eligibility thresholds.

agenda_items.title: 2022 Continuum of Care Planning Grant
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff briefly reviewed the Continuum of Care planning grant renewal supporting homelessness coordination, data systems, and regional housing provider planning. No objections were raised ahead of placement on the May 20 consent agenda.

agenda_items.title: ARPA Fayetteville Street Corridor Improvements and Hayti Promise CDC
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and Hayti stakeholders presented a $10M corridor package split between direct ARPA grant funds and revenue replacement, naming St. Joseph's Historic Foundation as fiscal agent while seeding a 7-member Hayti Promise Community Development Corporation board alongside $6.7M for Reimagine Durham Freeway transit/corridor work. Council probed governance transparency, fiscal safeguards, conflict-of-interest rules, and community selection of the CDC board.

agenda_items.title: Shared Active Transportation / Micromobility Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation staff reviewed minor updates to the shared active transportation ordinance governing e-scooters and shared micromobility permitting and right-of-way parking enforcement. Council raised no objections to placing the ordinance on consent.

agenda_items.title: Mythics LLC Contract for Oracle Fusion ERP Replacement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chief Information Officer Frederick Raven briefed Council on the Mythics LLC implementation contract to migrate the City from legacy Munis financial and HR systems to Oracle Fusion ERP. Council asked about implementation timeline, staff training, and total cost controls.

agenda_items.title: Intent to Declare Surplus City-Owned Properties for Affordable Housing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Alicia Bass presented an HR&A study evaluating 1,134 city-owned parcels and identifying 10 high-scoring surplus sites capable of yielding an estimated 46 to 106 affordable units. Council members debated upset-bid statutory requirements versus RFP disposition, and several members urged pairing surplus transfers with permanent affordability or community land trust covenants rather than expiring deed restrictions.

agenda_items.title: Resolution Supporting Upper Neuse River Basin Association (UNRBA) FY25 Budget
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Michelle Woolfolk explained the annual resolution backing the UNRBA FY25 budget under $1M, noting that updated Falls Lake nutrient management rules have been pushed to 2027-2028 while modeling and monitoring continue. Council supported advancing the item to consent.

agenda_items.title: Summer Schedule Change and Mayor's Remark Retraction
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council agreed to reschedule the July 25 work session to August 5, 2024 at 1:00 PM due to previously approved summer absences. Mayor Williams also publicly retracted a prior 'don't do that again' remark toward a Spectrum News reporter, affirming respect for local journalism and First Amendment press access.

agenda_items.title: Board Nominations and May 20 Council Agenda Settling
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Members placed nominations on the ballot for Tammera H. Schlett (Environmental Affairs Board), Tavan Ricks (Affordable Housing Implementation Committee), and Sean Umstead and Crystal E. Taylor (Discover Durham), though Javiera Caballero flagged concern over bypassing Discover Durham's recommended candidate Sydney Cove. Council then formally settled the May 20 meeting agenda.

votes.item_title: Accept City Manager's Priority Items (May 9, 2024)
votes.notes: Accepted additions of Items 42 and 43, referral of Item 38 back to Planning, and priority scheduling of Item 18.
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager Wanda Page presented priority updates to the May 9 work session agenda, explaining that Item 38 (Sheffield Farms) needed to be referred back to the Planning Department while Items 42 (NCDOT East Club Blvd lighting) and 43 (Mythics Oracle ERP contract) required late addition. She also flagged Item 18 concerning urgent structural roof repairs at the Carolina Theater. Council asked no objections regarding accepting the priority items onto the work session docket. A motion to accept the City Manager's priority items passed unanimously by voice vote.

votes.item_title: Suspend Council Rules for Immediate Action on Item 18 (Carolina Theater Repairs)
votes.notes: Required to take binding financial and contract votes during a work session.
votes.discussion_detail: Staff explained that waiting until the May 20 regular meeting to approve roofing and structural stabilization at the Carolina Theater would risk further water intrusion and scheduling delays with the contractor. Because Durham City Council rules normally restrict work sessions to agenda setting and briefings rather than binding contract approvals, a suspension of the rules was necessary. Council expressed consensus on addressing the emergency preservation need immediately. All seven members voted aye by voice vote to suspend the rules for Item 18.

votes.item_title: Item 18a: Amend General Capital Improvements Project Ordinance (#16163) for CC46 Carolina Theater
ayes: All present voting members (6-0; 1 unnamed member on Carolina Theater board recused)
abstentions: Unnamed council member serving on Carolina Theater board (recused)
votes.notes: Reallocated $224,420 for Carolina Theater roof and structural project CC46; one member announced board service at 00:18:22 and abstained/did not vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Staff presented the budget ordinance amendment increasing project funding for Carolina Theater structural and roofing repairs by $224,420 under General CIP Ordinance #16163. Before any vote occurred, one Council member explicitly stated on the record that they serve on the Carolina Theater board and requested recusal from voting on all Item 18 sub-motions. City staff confirmed the structural deterioration required prompt action to protect the historic municipal facility and maintain planned programming. With the board-affiliated member abstaining, the six remaining Council members approved the CIP ordinance amendment 6-0 by voice vote.

votes.item_title: Item 18b: Amend Ballpark Capital Improvements Project Ordinance (#16170) to Reallocate Surplus Funds to Carolina Theater
ayes: All present voting members (6-0; 1 unnamed member on Carolina Theater board recused)
abstentions: Unnamed council member serving on Carolina Theater board (recused)
votes.notes: Transferred $224,800 from completed/surplus Durham Bulls Athletic Park capital accounts to Carolina Theater.
votes.discussion_detail: Budget and General Services staff detailed the reallocation of $224,800 in surplus funds from Durham Bulls Athletic Park capital ordinance #16170 to help cover the Carolina Theater roof replacement budget gap. Council noted that repurposing leftover ballpark capital capacity avoided tapping General Fund operating reserves or delaying urgent building maintenance. The unnamed Council member sitting on the Carolina Theater board reiterated their recusal prior to the vote. The motion passed 6-0 among the six voting members.

votes.item_title: Item 18c: Approve Construction Contract with Simon Roofing and Sheet Metal Corp. for Carolina Theater Roof
ayes: All present voting members (6-0; 1 unnamed member on Carolina Theater board recused)
abstentions: Unnamed council member serving on Carolina Theater board (recused)
votes.notes: Contract not to exceed $938,297.76.
votes.discussion_detail: Staff recommended awarding the Carolina Theater roof replacement and associated structural construction contract to Simon Roofing and Sheet Metal Corp. in an amount not to exceed $938,297.76. General Services officials explained the procurement used cooperative purchasing/competitive pricing to lock in immediate mobilization before peak summer storms. No members raised technical or vendor objections during the brief review. With one board member recused, the contract passed 6-0 by voice vote.

votes.item_title: Item 18d: Establish Project Contingency Fund for Carolina Theater Roof Replacement
ayes: All present voting members (6-0; 1 unnamed member on Carolina Theater board recused)
abstentions: Unnamed council member serving on Carolina Theater board (recused)
votes.notes: Contingency fund of $140,744.24 (15%).
votes.discussion_detail: Staff requested a dedicated project contingency of $140,744.24 to address unforeseen structural decking or historic masonry conditions uncovered once roof tear-off begins. Given the age of the downtown theater building, staff advised that standard contingency headroom prevents mid-construction work stoppages. Council raised no objections to establishing the reserve within the overall project cap. The six non-recused members voted aye to approve the contingency 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 18e: Authorize City Manager to Execute Carolina Theater Contract Modifications
ayes: All present voting members (6-0; 1 unnamed member on Carolina Theater board recused)
abstentions: Unnamed council member serving on Carolina Theater board (recused)
votes.notes: Modification authority capped at total project cost not to exceed $1,079,042.
votes.discussion_detail: The final Item 18 authorization empowered the City Manager to negotiate and execute necessary contract amendments or change orders up to a combined ceiling of $1,079,042, encompassing both the base Simon Roofing contract and approved contingency. This administrative authority ensures field conditions discovered during construction can be resolved promptly without returning to Council mid-project. With the Carolina Theater board member remaining recused, Council approved the delegation 6-0 by voice vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session May 9, 2024
disagreements.issue: Discover Durham Board Nomination Bypassing Organization Recommendation
disagreements.summary: Council debated whether to respect Discover Durham's internal nominating recommendation (Sydney Cove) or advance alternative Council nominations for two board seats.
disagreements.side_a_position: Honor Discover Durham's submitted slate recommendation alongside Sean Umstead rather than bypassing its vetted nominee.
side_a_arguments: Partner tourism organizations vet candidates for operational fit and conflict-free representation.
Passing over Discover Durham's recommended nominee Sydney Cove breaks typical deference without clear rationale.
disagreements.side_b_position: Exercise Council's independent appointment authority by nominating Crystal E. Taylor and Sean Umstead to the ballot.
side_b_arguments: Council members retain discretion to nominate qualified community and hospitality leaders directly.
Nomination to the ballot still allows all Council members to vote at the regular meeting.
disagreements.resolution: Both Sean Umstead and Crystal E. Taylor were placed on the nomination slate for formal voting at the May 20 meeting, with Caballero's objection noted on the record.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session May 9, 2024
disagreements.issue: Surplus City Land Disposition and Permanent Affordability Terms
disagreements.summary: Members differed on how aggressively the City should mandate permanent affordability covenants and community land trust transfers versus flexible RFP/upset-bid disposition on 10 surplus city-owned sites.
disagreements.side_a_position: Prioritize permanent affordability and community land trust stewardship over time-limited deed restrictions or open market upset bids.
side_a_arguments: Publicly owned land represents an irreplaceable asset that should stay permanently affordable beyond 30-year windows.
Conveyances to nonprofits or land trusts avoid speculative turnover on small infill lots.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain flexible disposition pathways including upset-bid and negotiated RFP authority under NC law so parcels actually get developed quickly.
side_b_arguments: State disposition statutes constrain direct transfers unless specific statutory affordable housing or nonprofit channels apply.
Overly rigid requirements can stall small, scattered-site projects identified in the HR&A inventory.
disagreements.resolution: Staff advanced Item 19 to the May 20 Consent Agenda as an initial intent-to-declare-surplus step while committing to return with disposition structure details for each parcel.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting May 6, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: At its May 6, 2024 regular meeting, the Durham City Council approved 19 consent items, annexed and zoned Kates Estate (7-0), and adopted FY25 stormwater rate increases (7-0), while splitting sharply over mid-year summer camp funding and the Fox Crossing 2 rezoning. A motion by DeDreana Freeman to allocate $41,000 in FY24 funds for the Heart of a Champion summer camp failed 3-4 as a four-member majority insisted on routing camp requests through the upcoming competitive FY25 Youth Fund. Following extensive resident opposition over Spring Street traffic and Lick Creek watershed impacts—and an unusual parliamentary recall vote when two members misheard the initial motion order—Council narrowly approved Fox Crossing 2's Utility Extension Agreement and PDR 12.75 rezoning 4-3.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations, Key to the City for NCCU Chancellor Akinleye, and Duke Fellows Recognition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Williams presented a Key to the City and proclamation honoring retiring NCCU Chancellor Dr. Johnson O. Akinleye, alongside proclamations for Year of the Aerial Insectivore (presented with Carl Rist), Police Week/Peace Officers Memorial Day, Drinking Water Week, and NPHC Day (presented with Mark-Anthony Middleton). Council also recognized visiting Duke Sanford LDF Middle East fellows.

agenda_items.title: Council Member Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members commented on a wide range of local, state, and international issues: Chelsea Cook spoke on NCCU graduation, UNC campus protest policing, Holocaust Remembrance Day, and Gaza/Rafah; Javiera Caballero and DeDreana Freeman condemned NC House Bill 10 on ICE detainers, with Freeman also recognizing retiring DPS Superintendent Dr. Pascal Mubenga; Carl Rist highlighted Book Harvest and Vision Zero; and Mark-Anthony Middleton and Mayor Williams addressed recent gun violence, wounded Officer Briana Jones, and establishing a dedicated Youth Fund.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Informational Updates (Items 6, 20, 21)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page noted informational priority items on Lofts at Southside Phase 3 (Item 6), the 2024 GO Bond referendum (Item 20), and the Classification and Compensation Study (Item 21). Because the priority list contained only informational adjustments already addressed at the work session, Mayor Williams confirmed at 01:34:33 that no separate priority-item vote was required.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1 through 19)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With no items pulled from the consent docket, Council moved directly to adopt Items 1 through 19 en bloc.

agenda_items.title: Summer Camp Funding Request ($41,000 for Heart of a Champion / Cornwallis)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman championed a $41,000 mid-year allocation for Education 360 / Heart of a Champion at Cornwallis, while multiple community youth providers—including Built2Last, Durham Freedom Schools, Believers United for Progress ($200k ask + Hope Center), Bull City Best, and Campaign for Change ($500k partnership)—also urged immediate camp funding. A four-member majority argued that selective mid-year awards bypass equitable procurement and committed instead to launching a competitive Youth/Camp Fund in the FY25 budget.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Initial Zoning: Kates Estate (2625 Ferrell Rd)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a voluntary annexation and direct RS-20 initial zoning translation for a 2.8-acre parcel at 2625 Ferrell Road for single-family residential use, which had received unanimous 10-0 Planning Commission approval. Nate Baker and Javiera Caballero voiced general reservations about satellite annexations stretching municipal utility boundaries, though Council approved all three motions unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Zoning Map Change & UEA: Fox Crossing 2 (734 S Miami Blvd, 1220 Lynn Rd, 101 Spring St)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and applicant representatives presented a 25.565-acre rezoning from RU-5 to PDR 12.750 for up to 320 apartments and 2,000-7,000 sq ft of commercial/civic space, which the Planning Commission had voted 7-4 (with 2 absent) to recommend denying. Following heavy neighborhood opposition over narrow Spring Street safety, Lick Creek watershed impacts, and 7% tree preservation, the applicant expanded income-restricted commitments (5% at 80% AMI) from 20 to 30 years and added 100-year stormwater ponds, native landscaping, Energy Star residential certification, and crosswalk commitments; after an initial confusion required a 6-1 recall vote on the zoning motion, Council approved the UEA and rezoning 4-3.
agenda_items.vote_summary: UEA Passed 4-3; Initial Rezoning 6-1 Recalled (6-1); Final Rezoning Passed 4-3; Consistency Passed 7-0

agenda_items.title: FY25 Stormwater Utility Fee Schedule
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works Director Marvin Williams presented FY25 stormwater rate increases effective July 1, 2024: Tier 1 rising $0.75 to $5.70/month, Tier 2 rising $1.55 to $11.80/month, Tier 3 rising $3.11 to $23.60/month, and non-residential rising $1.55 per 2,400 sq ft ERU. DeDreana Freeman and Chelsea Cook noted the lack of a stormwater hardship assistance program and rent pass-through impacts on apartment tenants before joining a unanimous vote.

votes.item_title: Item 25: Allocate FY24 Funds ($41,000) for Heart of a Champion Summer Camp and FY25 July/August Funding
votes.notes: Hand/roll-call vote; majority favored competitive FY25 Youth/Camp Fund instead of direct mid-year allocation.
votes.discussion_detail: Council Member DeDreana Freeman moved to immediately allocate $41,000 from FY24 funds for Education 360 / Heart of a Champion at Cornwallis along with bridging support into July and August of FY25, citing urgent gun violence prevention needs for public housing youth. Multiple competing nonprofit youth operators spoke during the hearing requesting substantial summer allocations ranging from $200,000 to $500,000, underscoring demand across the city. Opponents of the motion—Williams, Middleton, Caballero, and Rist—argued that awarding an unbid mid-year earmark to one organization while other groups awaited process was inequitable and bypassed budget discipline, committing instead to create a larger competitive Youth Fund in FY25. Supporters Baker, Cook, and Freeman contended the modest sum was needed immediately for summer 2024 rather than waiting another year, but the motion failed 3-4.

votes.item_title: Item 22a (Kates Estate): Approve Utility Extension Agreement and Annexation Ordinance
votes.notes: 2.8 acres at 2625 Ferrell Rd with applicants Patrick and Rebecca Kates.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff presented the voluntary contiguous/satellite annexation and Utility Extension Agreement for Patrick and Rebecca Kates covering a 2.8-acre single-family parcel at 2625 Ferrell Road, noting 10-0 Planning Commission endorsement. Council members Nate Baker and Javiera Caballero questioned whether extending utility infrastructure to peripheral single-lot tracts aligns with long-term fiscal sustainability, while staff clarified the existing adjacent municipal line and limited service demand. Following public hearing closure with no neighbor opposition, Council voted 7-0 to approve the annexation ordinance and UEA.

votes.item_title: Item 22b (Kates Estate): Approve Initial Zoning Map Change (RS-20 County to RS-20 City)
votes.notes: Direct translation of existing County RS-20 zoning upon municipal annexation.
votes.discussion_detail: Companion to the Ferrell Road annexation, staff proposed translating the parcel's Durham County RS-20 residential zoning directly into the City's equivalent RS-20 designation without increasing density. Staff confirmed the direct translation matches adjacent residential patterns and raised no environmental or transportation flags. Council raised no further debate after the preceding annexation discussion and adopted the initial zoning ordinance 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 22c (Kates Estate): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Zoning Consistency Statement
votes.notes: Statutory consistency finding for Kates Estate initial zoning.
votes.discussion_detail: Pursuant to North Carolina General Statute 160D-605, Council considered the formal statement affirming that the direct RS-20 translation for 2625 Ferrell Road is consistent with the Durham Comprehensive Plan and reasonable in the public interest. Staff confirmed the statutory text was included in the agenda packet. Council adopted the consistency statement 7-0 without further discussion.

votes.item_title: Item 23a (Fox Crossing 2): Approve Utility Extension Agreement with Burnham Fee Acquisition LLC
votes.notes: Hand vote taken due to voting machine malfunction; approved UEA for 25.565-acre site.
votes.discussion_detail: Fox Crossing 2 generated nearly two hours of testimony and debate regarding up to 320 multifamily apartments and 2,000-7,000 sq ft of commercial space near South Miami Boulevard, Lynn Road, and Spring Street. Seven neighborhood residents opposed the project, citing hazardous two-lane traffic on Spring Street, Lick Creek headwater flooding, low tree preservation (7%), and dissatisfaction with Planning Commission's 7-4 denial vote. Proponents on Council pointed out the infill parcel sits inside the Urban Growth Boundary near jobs and transit, while the applicant increased its 5% at 80% AMI affordability commitment from 20 to 30 years and added 100-year stormwater ponds, native landscaping, Energy Star buildings, and crosswalk commitments. Conducted by raised hands due to a voting clicker issue, the Utility Extension Agreement passed 4-3 with Baker, Cook, and Freeman dissenting.

votes.item_title: Item 23b (Fox Crossing 2 — Initial Vote, Subsequently Recalled): Adopt UDO Zoning Map Change RU-5 to PDR 12.75
votes.notes: Initially recorded as 6-1, then recalled at 04:45:34 because Nate Baker and Chelsea Cook misheard the item being called (thinking it was consistency).
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately after the 4-3 vote on the Fox Crossing 2 Utility Extension Agreement, the chair called the question on the companion rezoning ordinance from RU-5 to PDR 12.75 incorporating the textual development plan and five added commitments. Because the voting system was malfunctioning and members were voting by hand in rapid sequence, Nate Baker and Chelsea Cook both raised their hands believing the body had moved to the statutory consistency statement rather than the zoning map change itself. As a result, the initial tally was announced as 6-1 with only DeDreana Freeman voting nay. Minutes later, Baker and Cook alerted the chair to the misunderstanding, prompting a formal recall motion to re-take the rezoning vote accurately.

votes.item_title: Item 23c (Fox Crossing 2): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Zoning Consistency Statement
votes.notes: All seven members voted aye on the consistency statement.
votes.discussion_detail: Council voted on the formal NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement accompanying the Fox Crossing 2 rezoning ordinance. Consistent with Council practice of adopting the statutory consistency finding once the underlying land-use vote is taken, all seven members raised their hands in favor. Immediately following this vote, members realized the previous rezoning hand count had been misunderstood by Baker and Cook, triggering the recall motion.

votes.item_title: Recall Initial Vote on Item 23b (Fox Crossing 2 Rezoning Ordinance)
votes.notes: City Attorney advised a recall motion to re-vote Item 23b accurately; Clerk initially misspoke 5-2 before Mayor confirmed 6-1.
votes.discussion_detail: Council Member Chelsea Cook raised a point of order noting that she and Nate Baker had voted on the initial Item 23b rezoning motion believing it was the consistency statement, and requested to correct their votes to reflect their opposition to Fox Crossing 2. After consulting the City Attorney on parliamentary procedure under Robert's Rules and Council rules, the chair entertained a motion by Cook to recall the previous vote on Item 23b. When the Clerk initially misread the hand count as 5-2, Mayor Williams corrected the record to confirm the recall passed 6-1.

votes.item_title: Item 23b (Fox Crossing 2 — Final Re-Vote): Adopt UDO Zoning Map Change RU-5 to PDR 12.75 with Added Commitments
votes.notes: Re-vote following 6-1 recall; recorded exact split aligned with UEA vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the successful recall motion, Mayor Williams re-read the Item 23b rezoning motion to amend the zoning map from RU-5 to PDR 12.75 with the textual development plan and the five commitments added during the public hearing. Supporters Williams, Middleton, Caballero, and Rist emphasized the need for housing inside the Urban Growth Boundary, improved affordability duration, stormwater upgrades, and commercial space along South Miami Boulevard. Dissenters Baker, Cook, and Freeman maintained that Spring Street lacked safe pedestrian infrastructure, a private-parking connectivity clause undermined street design, and Lick Creek headwaters and residents deserved stronger protection. The re-vote passed 4-3 by raised hands.

votes.item_title: Item 24: Adopt Ordinance Amending Fee Schedule for FY25 Stormwater Rates
votes.notes: Effective July 1, 2024; Tier 1 to $5.70/mo (+$0.75), Tier 2 to $11.80/mo (+$1.55), Tier 3 to $23.60/mo (+$3.11), non-residential +$1.55 per ERU.
votes.discussion_detail: Public Works Director Marvin Williams presented the FY25 stormwater utility fee ordinance required to fund watershed maintenance, green stormwater infrastructure, and regulatory compliance starting July 1, 2024. The adjustment raises monthly residential bills by $0.75 in Tier 1, $1.55 in Tier 2, and $3.11 in Tier 3, alongside $1.55 per equivalent residential unit for non-residential parcels. DeDreana Freeman and Chelsea Cook voiced concern that stormwater billing lacks a low-income affordability relief program and noted apartment landlords often pass fee hikes directly to renters, urging future exploration of assistance mechanisms. All seven Council members nevertheless voted to adopt the fee schedule 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting May 6, 2024
disagreements.issue: Mid-Year FY24 Direct Allocation vs. Competitive FY25 Youth Fund for Summer Camps
disagreements.summary: Council divided 3-4 over approving an immediate $41,000 FY24 allocation for the Heart of a Champion camp at Cornwallis versus routing all youth summer programming through a competitive FY25 process.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve $41,000 immediately so Cornwallis youth have structured summer programming in June 2024 rather than waiting a year.
side_a_arguments: Youth in Cornwallis and public housing communities face immediate summer safety and enrichment gaps.
The $41,000 request was previously vetted with Council awareness and is modest relative to overall youth-violence costs.
Waiting for FY25 RFPs leaves families without programming during Summer 2024.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject ad hoc single-organization mid-year earmarks and establish an open, competitive FY25 Youth/Camp Fund.
side_b_arguments: Multiple deserving youth groups testified requesting hundreds of thousands of dollars, making single-group mid-year awards unfair.
Allocating funds without a competitive solicitation or budget review sets an unsustainable precedent.
Establishing a broader FY25 Youth Fund allows transparent criteria and equitable distribution.
disagreements.resolution: Motion failed 3-4; majority directed summer camp proposals toward the FY25 budget Youth Fund process.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting May 6, 2024
disagreements.issue: Fox Crossing 2 Rezoning Density, Spring Street Safety, and Lick Creek Protection
disagreements.summary: Following Planning Commission's 7-4 denial recommendation and substantial resident opposition, Council split 4-3 over approving up to 320 apartments and commercial space off South Miami Boulevard and Spring Street.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the infill rezoning inside the Urban Growth Boundary with added 30-year affordability, 100-year stormwater ponds, native trees, and crosswalk commitments.
side_a_arguments: Site lies inside the Urban Growth Boundary near East End Connector and jobs, advancing housing supply.
Applicant expanded affordability term from 20 to 30 years (reaching 6% total income-restricted units including commercial/mixed-use provisions) and committed to 100-year storm ponds.
Incremental housing projects are necessary 'puzzle pieces' while broader UDO reforms proceed.
disagreements.side_b_position: Deny the rezoning due to unsafe Spring Street access, environmental risks to Lick Creek, minimal tree save (7%), and connectivity loopholes.
side_b_arguments: Spring Street is an unimproved narrow road lacking sidewalks, threatening Vision Zero pedestrian safety.
Only 7% tree preservation near Lick Creek headwaters exacerbates downstream erosion and neighbor flooding.
Parking-lot connectivity language circumvents true multimodal public street integration, and residents felt dismissed.
disagreements.resolution: After a 6-1 parliamentary recall to fix misheard initial hand votes, both the UEA and the PDR 12.75 rezoning passed 4-3.

development_cases.location: 2625 Ferrell Road
development_cases.scale: 1 single-family home on 2.8 acres
development_cases.zoning_change: RS-20 County to RS-20 City (Falls/Jordan Lake Watershed Overlay District B) — non-contiguous satellite annexation

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supports a small family-owned one-to-one county-to-city zoning translation to obtain utility service and preserve generational homeownership.
member_justifications.key_quote: Supporting a direct zoning translation for a single family home is straightforward and builds generational stability.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Notes general caution toward satellite annexations, but votes aye because adjacent municipal water and sewer lines already exist and the city gains tax revenue.
member_justifications.key_quote: While I'm usually hesitant on satellite annexations, utility lines are already adjacent here and it brings in city tax base.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Emphasizes the water-quality benefit of connecting single-family properties to municipal sewer rather than relying on septic tanks inside the Jordan Lake and Upper Neuse watersheds.
member_justifications.key_quote: Getting homes off septic and onto city sewer protects water quality in our watershed.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supports the individual homeowner's request while critiquing North Carolina's statutory ban on proactive municipal annexation for forcing piecemeal satellite pockets across service boundaries.
member_justifications.key_quote: It speaks to the awkward situation that the state legislature has put municipalities in and not being able to proactively annex land.

development_cases.location: 734 South Miami Boulevard, 1220 Lynn Road, and 101 Spring Street
development_cases.scale: Up to 320 apartment units and 2,000-7,000 sq ft of commercial/public/civic space on 25.565 acres (3 parcels)
development_cases.zoning_change: RU-5 to PDR 12.75 (Falls/Jordan Lake Watershed Protection District B) with Textual Development Plan

proffers.affordable_housing: At least 5% of units at 80% AMI or below for 30 years (increased from 3% at Planning Commission; term extended on dais from 20 to 30 years)
proffers.environmental_tree: 7% tree preservation; 200-ft Lick Creek stream buffer (100 ft each side); 100-year storm detention ponds; 100% native trees for required landscaping where allowed (up from 25%); Energy Star certification for primary residential buildings
proffers.transit_infrastructure: Circular turnaround bulb at end of Spring Street built to City standards; left-turn lane at Lynn Road driveway; sidewalk/multi-use path if NCDOT requests; high-visibility pedestrian crosswalks subject to Transportation approval
other_proffers: 2,000-7,000 sq ft of commercial, public, or civic space
Prohibited uses: clubs/lodges, wireless communication facilities, drive-throughs, and convenience stores with gas sales
Unspecified monetary contribution to Durham Public Schools mentioned at hearing without a stated dollar amount

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supports Urban Tier infill that avoids expanding Durham's urban footprint, argues traffic impacts are shared across urban neighborhoods, and welcomes walkable retail alongside proffers improved under Planning Commission pressure.
member_justifications.key_quote: This is Urban Tier infill inside our existing footprint, bringing walkable retail and more units than what could be built by right.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Maintains that upholding Durham's Urban Growth Boundary requires denser infill inside the boundary rather than outward sprawl, praising the long-term hold developer and added attainable housing over a 217-unit by-right option.
member_justifications.key_quote: If we're serious about our Urban Growth Boundary, we have to say yes to building up on infill parcels inside it.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supports the project's density, transit access, and retail mix in principle, but votes no because routing roughly 20% of traffic onto narrow, unimproved Spring Street violates Vision Zero safety goals, alongside Lick Creek headwater erosion, deforestation, Planning Commission opposition (7-4 among voting members), and a D-grade (13/22) comprehensive plan score.
member_justifications.key_quote: Spring Street is a country road... we're not on track with Vision Zero... it's not going to be a safe place.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Explains that he negotiated dais concessions on Energy Star and buffers to improve the project if it passed, yet votes nay because cut-through street design, failing stream buffer policies along Lick Creek, and zero parkland dedication fail his 3Ds standard and comprehensive plan protections.
member_justifications.key_quote: We need to manage the process of change... stream buffers, that's another one of these policies in the comprehensive plan that is determined to not be consistent... I have the same heartburn and the same concerns that Council Member Cook expressed.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Weighs real concerns over Spring Street against the site's Mixed Use Neighborhood designation, genuine commercial/civic square footage, 30-year affordable units, half-mile transit access, and superior infill outcome compared to 217 by-right units.
member_justifications.key_quote: Spring Street isn't ideal, but inside the urban growth boundary with true mixed uses and 30-year affordability, this beats the 217-unit by-right alternative.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Votes nay citing neighborhood testimony about dismissive treatment of resident Wanda Waiter by the developer and insufficient community benefit.
member_justifications.key_quote: The reported treatment of Ms. Waiter and lack of genuine benefit to existing neighbors make this a no for me.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Shares hesitation over narrow Spring Street and condemns disrespectful conduct toward neighbors, but supports Urban Tier infill as essential 'puzzle pieces' toward a 15-minute community.
member_justifications.key_quote: We have to connect these puzzle pieces inside the urban tier if we ever want to build a true 15-minute community.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session April 18, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council's April 18, 2024 work session featured major pre-budget presentations on a proposed $200M 2024 General Obligation Bond referendum ($85M parks/aquatics and $115M streets/sidewalks), a $28.5M Classification and Compensation Study moving salaries to the 60th market percentile, and proposed FY25 water, sewer (+6.1%), and stormwater rate adjustments. Members also scrutinized Lofts at Southside Phase 3/4 financing gaps, permanent affordability on DCLT infill lots, and an emergency propane leak evacuation briefing on Angier Avenue. A heated disagreement erupted under Other Matters when DeDreana Freeman sought $41,000 for the Heart of a Champion summer camp, prompting debate over procurement equity and mid-year earmarks.

agenda_items.title: Council Announcements and Safety Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton initially opened the meeting and recognized his upcoming North Carolina League of Municipalities presidency before Mayor Leonardo Williams arrived and condemned recent gunfire outside an occupied Durham apartment complex.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Items (Items 19, 24, 27)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page presented priority scheduling additions covering Water/Sewer rate presentations (Item 19), Stormwater rate briefings (Item 24), and updated materials on the Wake Olive Apartments case (Item 27). Council approved accepting the priority items 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Comments on Youth Funding and Community Issues
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Residents Jacqueline Wagstaff, Jeremy Burgren, and Jay Dunston addressed Council on youth summer programming, community safety, and municipal transparency.

agenda_items.title: Questions on Items 2, 3, 6, and 15 (Dacian Ave, DCLT Lots, Lofts at Southside, RRFBs)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members examined Item 2 (Dacian Ave street closure requested by Javiera Caballero), Item 3 (Durham Community Land Trust 99-year affordability across 5 lots flagged by Carl Rist), Item 6 (Lofts at Southside Phase 3/4 $8M financing gap using ARPA and 9%/4% LIHTC questioned by Chelsea Cook and Carl Rist), and Item 15 (17 Rectangular Rapid Flashing Beacons at school and trail crossings supported by Rist, Freeman, and Cook).

agenda_items.title: 2024 General Obligation Bond Referendum Package ($200M)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget and Infrastructure staff presented a $200M GO Bond package split between $85M for Parks and Recreation ($43M Wheels Aquatic Center and $42M East End/Long Meadow Pool) and $115M for Streets and Sidewalks ($60M new sidewalks, $45M paving/repairs, $10M unpaved roads), projecting a 2.51-cent average and 3.45-cent peak property tax impact. While DeDreana Freeman questioned the omission of explicit green/sustainability bond components, a majority gave thumbs-up to advance the package toward the May 20 Council meeting.

agenda_items.title: Classification and Compensation Study Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Consultants Jim Rondengruber and Annette Haffner presented the comprehensive Classification and Compensation Study carrying a $28.5M total budget impact to position municipal pay at the 60th market percentile, widen step spreads from 4% to 5%, raise minimum living wages from $19.58 to $21.59/hr (by July 31), address -17.6% police and -7.8% fire market lags, and cap executive raises at 5%. Council members questioned implementation timing, step compression, and unionized/frontline parity.

agenda_items.title: Proposed FY25 Water and Sewer Rates (+6.1%)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Water Management Director Don Greeley outlined a proposed 6.1% water and sewer rate increase for FY25 to finance long-term capital pressures including Jordan Lake partnership infrastructure ($600M), PFAS treatment upgrades ($30M), and dam rehabilitation ($70-85M).

agenda_items.title: 3639 Angier Avenue Propane Leak and Evacuation Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson briefed Council on the active emergency response and neighborhood evacuation following a propane leak at 3639 Angier Avenue, detailing fire, police, and sheltering coordination.

agenda_items.title: Proposed FY25 Stormwater Rates
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works Director Marvin Williams briefed Council on proposed FY25 stormwater rate adjustments needed to sustain drainage maintenance, flood mitigation, and regulatory compliance.

agenda_items.title: Request for $41,000 Heart of a Champion Summer Camp Allocation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DeDreana Freeman requested placing a $41,000 mid-year funding item for the Heart of a Champion summer camp at Cornwallis onto a formal agenda, sparking sharp debate with Mayor Williams, Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Javiera Caballero over bypassing competitive RFPs and prior budget deadlines while Chelsea Cook and Nate Baker supported bringing the item forward for a public vote.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Advanced to May 6 General Business Agenda

agenda_items.title: Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee Nomination and May 6 Agenda Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council recorded a Participatory Budgeting Steering Committee nomination for Raven Smith and reviewed the summary of items slated for the May 6, 2024 regular meeting before adjourning without a separate formal agenda-settling roll-call vote.

votes.item_title: Accept City Manager's Priority Items (April 18, 2024)
votes.notes: Added priority briefings for Item 19 (Water/Sewer rates), Item 24 (Stormwater rates), and Item 27 (Wake Olive supplemental info).
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager Wanda Page presented her priority updates for the April 18 work session, incorporating budget-related utility rate briefings under Items 19 and 24 as well as supplemental information for the Wake Olive development case under Item 27. Council raised no objections to adding these presentations to the afternoon schedule. A motion to accept the City Manager's priority items passed unanimously 7-0 by voice vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session April 18, 2024
disagreements.issue: Process and Equity of $41,000 Mid-Year Summer Camp Allocation Request
disagreements.summary: Council clashed during Other Matters over whether to advance a single-organization $41,000 request for the Heart of a Champion camp at Cornwallis without a competitive process.
disagreements.side_a_position: Place the $41,000 request on the May 6 agenda so Council can openly debate urgent summer programming for Cornwallis youth.
side_a_arguments: Cornwallis public housing families face immediate summer engagement needs that cannot wait another budget cycle.
Other community programs received mid-year or targeted city support, making an open Council vote appropriate.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose unvetted, ad hoc mid-year grants to individual organizations outside competitive procurement.
side_b_arguments: Singling out one organization invites dozens of equally deserving nonprofits to request unbudgeted mid-year earmarks.
A formal competitive Youth Fund in FY25 ensures fairness, accountability, and consistent evaluation.
disagreements.resolution: The item was placed onto the May 6 General Business Agenda (Item 25), where it subsequently failed 3-4.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session April 18, 2024
disagreements.issue: 2024 General Obligation Bond Package Scope and Sustainability Inclusion
disagreements.summary: Council Member DeDreana Freeman questioned excluding dedicated green/climate sustainability components from the $200M Parks and Streets GO Bond package favored by the majority.
disagreements.side_a_position: Include explicit green infrastructure or sustainability investments within the 2024 GO Bond referendum rather than deferring them.
side_a_arguments: Earlier bond planning discussions contemplated green and climate resilience priorities that disappeared from the final $200M split.
Addressing climate infrastructure alongside aquatics and paving aligns with City sustainability commitments.
disagreements.side_b_position: Keep the $200M bond tightly focused on $85M in aquatic/park facilities and $115M in streets and sidewalks within manageable tax impacts.
side_b_arguments: Residents prioritized sidewalk construction, road paving, unpaved street upgrades, Wheels Aquatic Center, and East End/Long Meadow pools.
Expanding bond categories further would raise the projected 2.51-cent average / 3.45-cent peak tax rate impact.
disagreements.resolution: A Council majority gave thumbs-up to advance the $200M Parks ($85M) and Streets/Sidewalks ($115M) bond package toward the May 20 Council meeting.
