meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting April 15, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: At its April 15, 2024 regular meeting, the Durham City Council passed the Consent Agenda, approved the Wheels Roller Skating Rink operator contract (7-0) and a Resolution in Support of Immigrant Communities (7-0), rezoned Trellis Durham RTP to convert an extended-stay hotel into 122 apartments (7-0), and adopted the FY24-25 Annual Action Plan and HUD grant ordinances (7-0). The evening's centerpiece was a contentious public hearing on Wake Olive Apartments, a proposed 218-unit annexation and PDR 17.92 rezoning along Wake Forest Highway that had received a unanimous 10-0 denial recommendation from the Planning Commission. After heavy neighborhood testimony, late proffers, and an abandoned referral motion by Chelsea Cook, Council voted 2-5 to defeat Wake Olive Apartments.

agenda_items.title: Civic Proclamations (DPR Centennial, Telecommunicators, Firefighters, Black Maternal Health, Alcohol Awareness)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Williams presented proclamations marking the Durham Parks and Recreation Centennial, National Public Safety Telecommunications Week, Firefighters Day, Black Maternal Health Week, and Alcohol Awareness Month.

agenda_items.title: Council Member Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chelsea Cook and Nate Baker spoke on Passover, Gaza, gun violence, and a recent library bomb threat; Javiera Caballero and DeDreana Freeman discussed the Senior Games, State of the City, and farmers markets; Carl Rist and Mark-Anthony Middleton noted five recent shootings and DPD Chief Andrews' update; and Mayor Williams addressed youth gun violence including a 16-year-old victim and local culinary/community initiatives.

agenda_items.title: Priority Update and Consent Agenda (Items 1-14, 16-26, 32)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff noted Item 26 (DCHC MPO FY22-23 annual report) as an informational priority item requiring no separate vote. Council pulled Items 15 and 31 for separate consideration and approved the remaining Consent Agenda unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Wheels Roller Skating Rink Operator Contract (Durham City Skating LLC / United Skates)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following public comment from Gideon Bueno criticizing a reduced skating floor footprint and $22,000 annual base rent structure, staff clarified concession revenue sharing and facility investment terms with United Skates affiliate Durham City Skating LLC. Council approved the operator contract 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Resolution in Support of Immigrant Communities in Durham
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Javiera Caballero introduced a resolution affirming municipal support for immigrant residents alongside state and local advocates including Rep. Ricky Hurtado and Pablo Friedman. All seven Council members adopted the resolution unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Zoning: Wake Olive Apartments (5247 & 5255 Wake Forest Hwy)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and Redeeming Development Group LLC presented a 12.16-acre annexation and rezoning from RR/RS-20 to PDR 17.92 for up to 218 apartments—including 13 income-restricted units (7 at 60% AMI, 6 at 80% AMI) for 30 years, Green Building certification, EV chargers, native plantings, and a 10-ft multi-use path—following a 10-0 Planning Commission denial recommendation. Thirteen neighborhood speakers opposed the project over NC 98 traffic congestion, rural peripheral location, and Lick Creek watershed strain; after Chelsea Cook introduced and withdrew a motion to refer back to Planning Commission and an applicant staff-referral request lacked consensus, Council voted 2-5 to reject the annexation and UEA.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: Trellis Durham RTP (2011 Residence Inn Blvd)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Blue Ocean representatives Toby Coleman and Evan Gallant presented a 23.103-acre OI(D) graphic-to-textual rezoning converting a former extended-stay hotel into 122 apartment units with 10-0 Planning Commission backing. Chelsea Cook and DeDreana Freeman pressed the applicant on existing mortgage covenants that prevented dedicated income-restricted units and on avoiding resident displacement, before joining a unanimous 7-0 approval.

agenda_items.title: FY24-25 Annual Action Plan and HUD Grant Project Ordinances (CDBG, HOME, ESG, HOPWA)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson presented the FY24-25 Annual Action Plan and four federal grant ordinances totaling $2,130,000 (CDBG), $1,400,000 (HOME), $180,000 (ESG), and $1,160,000 (HOPWA). Advocates from the Coalition to End the HIV Epidemic (Dr. Haley Cunningham and Lenea Foster) urged $1M in additional local housing funding for people living with HIV before Council unanimously adopted all five motions.

agenda_items.title: Substantial Amendments to FY2017-2023 Annual Action Plans & Granville County HOPWA Addition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented substantial amendments reallocating prior-year CDBG funds and formally adding Granville County to the Durham Eligible Metropolitan Statistical Area (EMSA) for FY21-22 HOPWA administration. Council adopted all three implementing motions 7-0.

votes.item_title: Adopt Consent Agenda (Items 1-14, 16-26, 32)
votes.notes: Items 15 and 31 pulled for separate discussion and votes.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Williams confirmed that Items 15 (Wheels Roller Skating Rink operator contract) and 31 (Resolution in Support of Immigrant Communities) had been pulled from the Consent Agenda for separate presentations and public comment. Item 26 (DCHC MPO annual report) remained on consent as an informational priority item requiring no extra action. With no additional pulls requested by Council or residents, the remaining consent items passed 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 15: Approve Wheels Roller Skating Rink Operator Contract with Durham City Skating LLC
votes.notes: Contract with United Skates affiliate following work-session and meeting review of floor size and rent structure.
votes.discussion_detail: Community member Gideon Bueno urged Council to reject or revise the Wheels Roller Skating Rink operator agreement with Durham City Skating LLC (United Skates), criticizing a smaller skating floor area and $22,000 annual rent structure compared with past public expectations. Parks and Recreation and General Services staff clarified the capital investment obligations, revenue-sharing tiers, and programming commitments that underpin the public-private partnership. Council members acknowledged community passion for the historic rink's reopening while expressing confidence in staff's negotiated terms. All seven members voted aye to approve the operator contract.

votes.item_title: Item 31: Adopt Resolution in Support of Immigrant Communities in Durham
votes.notes: Introduced by Javiera Caballero in response to state legislative proposals including HB 10.
votes.discussion_detail: Council Member Javiera Caballero presented the Resolution in Support of Immigrant Communities alongside advocates from the Governor's Advisory Council on Hispanic/Latino Affairs, Rep. Ricky Hurtado, and community members such as Pablo Friedman. Speakers stressed how state enforcement mandates like House Bill 10 erode trust between immigrant families, municipal agencies, and local law enforcement, underscoring the City's commitment to safe and inclusive services. Council members expressed unanimous solidarity with Durham's immigrant residents and local legal defense efforts. The resolution passed 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 27 (Wake Olive Apartments): Approve Annexation Ordinance and Utility Extension Agreement
votes.notes: 5247 & 5255 Wake Forest Hwy (Redeeming Development Group LLC); Cook moved at 02:44:57 to refer back to Planning Commission and withdrew at 03:00:55; subsequent applicant request for staff referral lacked consensus.
votes.discussion_detail: Wake Olive Apartments proposed annexing and rezoning 12.16 acres on NC 98 (Wake Forest Highway) from RR/RS-20 to PDR 17.92 for 218 apartments, following a unanimous 10-0 denial vote from the Planning Commission. Thirteen nearby residents opposed the project due to extreme traffic congestion along two-lane Wake Forest Highway, auto-dependent separation from services and transit, and potential watershed impacts on Lick Creek. Although the developer proffered 13 income-restricted units (7 at 60% AMI, 6 at 80% AMI) for 30 years, EV chargers, native landscaping, and a 10-foot path, opponents on Council criticized post-Planning Commission proffers, lack of mixed commercial/civic uses, and far-flung sprawl outside established infrastructure corridors. After Chelsea Cook withdrew a motion to return the case to Planning Commission and the applicant's request for staff referral lacked consensus, Mayor Williams and Mark-Anthony Middleton voted aye while Caballero, Baker, Rist, Freeman, and Cook voted nay, defeating the annexation 2-5 and rendering the companion zoning and consistency votes moot.

votes.item_title: Item 28a (Trellis Durham RTP): Adopt Zoning Map Change OI(D) Graphic to OI(D) Textual Development Plan
votes.notes: 23.103 acres at 2011 Residence Inn Blvd converting former extended-stay hotel into 122 apartment units.
votes.discussion_detail: Blue Ocean representatives Toby Coleman and Evan Gallant requested replacing an older graphic development plan at 2011 Residence Inn Boulevard with a textual OI(D) plan enabling adaptive reuse of a former extended-stay hotel into 122 apartment homes, supported 10-0 by the Planning Commission. Chelsea Cook and DeDreana Freeman questioned why income-restricted units were omitted and sought assurance against displacing current long-term extended-stay occupants, to which the applicant explained existing Freddie Mac/federal mortgage restrictions prohibited formal income-restriction covenants while market rents would remain naturally modest without demolition. Appreciating the adaptive reuse of an existing building near RTP, Council approved the rezoning 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 28b (Trellis Durham RTP): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Zoning Consistency Statement
votes.notes: Statutory consistency finding for Trellis Durham RTP.
votes.discussion_detail: Following unanimous passage of the Trellis Durham RTP adaptive-reuse rezoning, Council considered the statutory NCGS 160D-605 consistency and reasonableness statement prepared by Planning staff. No members raised additional comments on the finding. The consistency statement passed 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 29a: Adopt Draft FY2024-25 Annual Action Plan for HUD Programs
votes.notes: Federal entitlement plan required for CDBG, HOME, ESG, and HOPWA allocations.
votes.discussion_detail: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson presented the FY24-25 Annual Action Plan governing how Durham invests federal entitlement grants across affordable housing development, homelessness prevention, neighborhood revitalization, and supportive services. During the public hearing, Dr. Haley Cunningham and Lenea Foster of the Coalition to End the HIV Epidemic urged Council to pair federal HOPWA funds with $1 million in local resources to stabilize housing for people living with HIV. Council thanked the advocates and moved forward with the required federal filing, adopting the Annual Action Plan 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 29b: Adopt FY24-25 HUD Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) Project Ordinance ($2,130,000)
votes.notes: CDBG grant project ordinance totaling $2,130,000.
votes.discussion_detail: Companion to the Annual Action Plan, Council voted on the grant project ordinance appropriating $2,130,000 in FY24-25 Community Development Block Grant funds for eligible low- and moderate-income housing and public service activities. Staff noted the amounts reflected HUD entitlement estimates subject to minor final federal adjustments. The ordinance passed 7-0 without dissent.

votes.item_title: Item 29c: Adopt FY24-25 HUD HOME Investment Partnerships Grant Project Ordinance ($1,400,000)
votes.notes: HOME grant project ordinance totaling $1,400,000.
votes.discussion_detail: Council next voted on the grant project ordinance establishing $1,400,000 in FY24-25 HOME Investment Partnerships funding for affordable rental production, rehabilitation, and CHDO set-asides. Staff confirmed consistency with the City's housing priorities outlined in the Annual Action Plan. Council adopted the ordinance 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 29d: Adopt FY24-25 HUD Emergency Solutions Grant (ESG) Project Ordinance ($180,000)
votes.notes: ESG grant project ordinance totaling $180,000.
votes.discussion_detail: Council considered the $180,000 FY24-25 Emergency Solutions Grant project ordinance supporting emergency shelter operations, street outreach, and rapid re-housing programs. No separate debate occurred following the consolidated public hearing. All seven members voted aye to pass the ordinance 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 29e: Adopt FY24-25 HUD Housing Opportunities for Persons With AIDS (HOPWA) Grant Project Ordinance ($1,160,000)
votes.notes: HOPWA grant project ordinance totaling $1,160,000 (Mayor misread as $160,000 when reading the motion).
votes.discussion_detail: Council voted on the final Item 29 ordinance appropriating $1,160,000 in FY24-25 HOPWA funding for regional housing assistance serving low-income households affected by HIV/AIDS (verbally misread by the Mayor as $160,000 while reading from the agenda motion for Item 29e). Coalition advocates earlier requested supplemental local funding in the upcoming City budget cycle to address waitlists. Council adopted the federal HOPWA grant ordinance 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 30a: Approve Substantial Amendments to FY2017-18 through FY2022-23 Annual Action Plans
votes.notes: Reprogrammed unspent CDBG funds across multiple prior-year HUD plans.
votes.discussion_detail: Staff presented substantial amendments covering six prior HUD Annual Action Plans (FY17-18 through FY22-23) to reallocate unused CDBG balances to active affordable housing and community development priorities before federal timeliness penalties accrue. No members of the public signed up to oppose the reallocations during the public hearing. Council approved the substantial amendments 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 30b: Authorize City Manager to Execute Documents for CDBG Reallocations
votes.notes: Implementing authorization tied to Item 30a.
votes.discussion_detail: Following adoption of the substantial amendments, Council voted to authorize the City Manager to execute HUD submissions and subrecipient agreements implementing the prior-year CDBG reallocations. Staff confirmed all transfers complied with HUD citizen-participation requirements. The authorization passed 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 30c: Add Granville County to Durham EMSA for FY2021-22 HOPWA Funding
votes.notes: Expanded regional HOPWA service geography to include Granville County.
votes.discussion_detail: Staff requested formal approval to include Granville County within the Durham Eligible Metropolitan Statistical Area (EMSA) for administering FY2021-22 HOPWA regional housing assistance, aligning municipal grant borders with updated federal metropolitan definitions. No objections were raised by Council or speakers. The motion passed unanimously 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting April 15, 2024
disagreements.issue: Wake Olive Apartments Annexation & Rezoning (Item 27)
disagreements.summary: Council voted 2-5 to deny annexing and rezoning 12.16 acres along Wake Forest Highway for 218 apartments after a 10-0 Planning Commission denial recommendation and intense neighbor pushback.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve Wake Olive Apartments to expand workforce housing and capture late developer proffers in East Durham.
side_a_arguments: East Durham needs additional multifamily apartments including 13 income-restricted units at 60% and 80% AMI.
The applicant added green building, EV, multi-use path, and affordability proffers and argued infrastructure could be extended.
Repeatedly denying applicants after proffer updates risks perceptions of unpredictability.
disagreements.side_b_position: Deny annexation/rezoning due to peripheral auto-dependent location, infrastructure/traffic gaps, missing mixed uses, and post-Planning Commission changes.
side_b_arguments: Two-lane NC 98/Wake Forest Highway and Lick Creek watershed face severe strain without transit service or commercial/civic uses.
Submitting major design and affordability revisions after a 10-0 Planning Commission denial undermines public review.
The site's scale and peripheral separation conflicted with Comprehensive Plan place-type expectations.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and Utility Extension Agreement failed 2-5, defeating the project.

development_cases.location: 5247 & 5255 Wake Forest Highway (NC 98, East Durham, adjacent to Neal Middle School)
development_cases.scale: Up to 218 apartment units on 12.16 acres (2 parcels)
development_cases.zoning_change: RR and RS-20 to PDR 17.92

proffers.affordable_housing: 13 income-restricted units (at least 7 at 60% AMI and 6 at 80% AMI or less, including at least 3 two-bedroom units) for 30 years
proffers.environmental_tree: No stream crossings; 100-ft riparian buffer on each side of stream with buildings kept beyond 100 ft; Green Building certification (NGBS Bronze+, Energy Star 75+, or LEED); at least 3 EV charging spaces; native plantings; stormwater commitments
proffers.transit_infrastructure: 10-ft multi-use path across NC 98 frontage; road improvements at 2 entrances onto Hwy 98; exploratory talks on footpath connection to Neal Middle School
other_proffers: Maximum building height 70 ft tapered to 40 ft or less at rear and sides
Unspecified monetary contribution to Durham Public Schools mentioned by applicant without a dollar amount

member_justifications.stance_summary: Highlights severe Hwy 98 infrastructure deficiencies and Triassic soil erosion risks, criticizes framing green building certifications as a substitute for sensitive land stewardship, and argues a site bordering Neal Middle School should anchor a cohesive mixed-use village concept rather than isolated apartments.
member_justifications.key_quote: I looked at this as anything that's close to the school is an opportunity to really build like a village concept there, and I wanted more out of this project.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Acknowledges post-Planning Commission proffers and supports higher residential density within Mixed Use Neighborhood areas, but opposes this proposal because it provides zero commercial or non-residential uses at a strategic location.
member_justifications.key_quote: I'm most concerned about the place type map and the fact there is not a mix of uses here... I feel like we need something better at this location that would have a mix of uses.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Argues it is unfair to force a single project to fix long-standing regional infrastructure deficits after the City accepted its application fees, interprets Mixed Use Neighborhood across a broader area where apartments diversify nearby single-family and townhome stock, and credits the applicant's post-PC proffers.
member_justifications.key_quote: We cannot put the entire burden of regional infrastructure on one developer after taking their application.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Thanks community speakers on waterway impacts, criticizes submitting sweeping proffer revisions eight months after the Planning Commission's 10-0 denial without sending the revised plan back for PC review, and opposes the site's transportation, walkability, and single-use flaws.
member_justifications.key_quote: We have these projects that come before us vastly changed from when they went in front of our Planning Commission... we don't get an opportunity to hear our appointed experts' opinions on these actual projects.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Contrasts Wake Olive sharply with Aura 751; cites Planning Commissioners Trap, Valentine, and CE regarding environmental sensitivity and warns that a deep, single-use apartment tract along Neal Middle School would sever future street connectivity and block a cohesive Mixed Use Neighborhood from ever materializing.
member_justifications.key_quote: It would essentially create a 1,000-foot deep barrier along the border of Neal Middle School... completely precluding this larger area from developing in a manner consistent with the future place types map as a mixed-use neighborhood.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Distinguishes Wake Olive from infill apartments near existing commercial corridors like Sharon Road or Aura 751; warns that approving isolated car-dependent apartments far out on NC 98 locks in an unsustainable development pattern for surrounding parcels.
member_justifications.key_quote: The no is where it is on 98; if it was closer in it would make a lot more sense to me... what this project does will influence whatever else happens around it.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Praises the 'good cop, bad cop' dynamic between Planning Commission denials and Council negotiations for extracting stronger proffers, indicates willingness to refer back for mixed-use exploration, and ultimately votes aye.
member_justifications.key_quote: That back-and-forth pressure with the Planning Commission has consistently helped us get stronger commitments out of applicants.

development_cases.location: 2011 Residence Inn Boulevard (near NC 54 & NC 55)
development_cases.scale: 122 multifamily apartment units (extended-stay hotel conversion) on 23.103 acres
development_cases.zoning_change: OI(D) Graphic Development Plan to OI(D) Textual Development Plan (Falls/Jordan Watershed Protection District B, Major Transportation Corridor I-40)

proffers.transit_infrastructure: NC 54 right-of-way dedication
other_proffers: Restricted exclusively to multifamily residential uses
Unit count capped at 122 units

member_justifications.stance_summary: Accepts that pre-existing mortgage covenants bar formal rent-restriction proffers following an earlier staff submittal error, notes projected Class B rents near 80% AMI, and urges outreach with Housing for New Hope to support existing extended-stay residents.
member_justifications.key_quote: Given the pre-existing loan constraints, I encourage connecting with Housing for New Hope to make sure current residents aren't left behind.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Praises the resource and environmental savings of adaptive reuse over greenfield construction, while pressing staff on the pre-submittal error and seeking protections for current extended-stay residents and families.
member_justifications.key_quote: Adaptive reuse saves enormous resources compared to new construction, though I want to make sure vulnerable extended-stay residents are protected.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supports repurposing an existing hotel into multifamily housing and encourages deeper partnership with the City on transitional housing conversions.
member_justifications.key_quote: Reusing existing hotel buildings is a practical way to create needed housing, and I hope to see more partnership around transitional units.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Highlights the Planning Commission's unanimous 10-0 approval and supports organic adaptive reuse of existing commercial structures into housing.
member_justifications.key_quote: A 10-0 Planning Commission recommendation for organic adaptive reuse of an existing building is an easy yes.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session April 4, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: At the April 4, 2024 work session, Council excused Javiera Caballero's upcoming April 18 absence (7-0) and settled the April 15 agenda (7-0) after debating a member-initiated UDO text amendment proposal and eight pulled consent items. Nate Baker's proposal for a Council resolution directing a UDO public park dedication text amendment failed to win four thumbs-up as colleagues urged vetting through the Joint City County Planning Committee with advance draft text. During consent review, Chelsea Cook and Baker questioned 30-year versus permanent affordability on Reinvestment Partners' $3.2M 312 E. Umstead SRO project, Bloomberg paper-streets work, Aetna employee benefits, two DPD-housed HEART positions, Wheels Skating Rink terms, and the Amtrak lot lease termination for the Durham Rail Trail.

agenda_items.title: Council Announcements, Park Dedication UDO Proposal, and Absence Excusal
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Nate Baker proposed a Council resolution initiating a UDO text amendment requiring public park land dedication, sparking procedural pushback from colleagues who wanted draft text reviewed in advance and routed through JCCPC, causing the request to stall without four thumbs-up. Carl Rist also referenced Durham's 2021 Lights Out bird-safety resolution, and Council voted 7-0 to excuse Javiera Caballero's April 18 absence.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Excused Caballero absence 7-0; Baker UDO resolution failed to gain consensus

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page confirmed there were no priority items to add for the April 4 work session.

agenda_items.title: Public Comments on Gun Violence, CHHF, and Global Issues
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Darrell Langley addressed gun violence intervention and Charles Hamilton Houston Foundation mentorship, while Jeremy Burgren spoke about Eric Holland, gun violence, and Gaza.

agenda_items.title: Review of Items 4, 5, 6, 7, 12, 15, 16, and 24
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chelsea Cook pulled multiple consent items for staff questioning, including Item 4 (Bloomberg paper-streets grant), Item 5 (Housing for New Hope 3rd Amendment), Item 6 (DPS PAL 1st Amendment), Item 12 (Aetna employee benefits, joined by Caballero and Freeman), Item 15 (Wheels United Skates operator contract, later pulled to April 15 separate vote), Item 16 (Governor's Crime Commission grant funding two HEART positions housed via DPD), and Item 24 (NCDOT Amtrak lot lease termination for the Durham Rail Trail park). On Item 7 ($3.2M ARPA loan to Reinvestment Partners for 17 SROs at 312 E. Umstead), Cook, Rist, and Baker pressed Director Reginald Johnson on 30-year versus permanent affordability protections.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Advanced to April 15 agenda (Item 15 flagged for separate vote)

agenda_items.title: Durham-Chapel Hill-Carrboro MPO FY22-23 Annual Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DCHC MPO Executive Director Doug Plachcinski briefed Council on the MPO's administrative transition from the City of Durham to Central Pines Regional Council, noting Durham provides roughly 58% of local dues with 40% board voting share alongside $75M in regional Durham transportation projects.

agenda_items.title: BPAC Nomination and April 15 Council Agenda Settling
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council nominated Christopher Perlstein to the Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Commission (BPAC) and voted 7-0 to settle the April 15, 2024 regular meeting agenda.

votes.item_title: Excuse Absence of Council Member Javiera Caballero for April 18, 2024 Work Session
votes.notes: Excused upcoming April 18 work session absence.
votes.discussion_detail: Council Member Javiera Caballero requested an excused absence in advance for the April 18, 2024 work session due to a scheduling conflict. Under Council rules requiring formal excusal votes for anticipated absences, a colleague moved and seconded to grant the excusal. All seven members voted aye by voice vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session April 4, 2024
disagreements.issue: Process for Member-Initiated UDO Public Park Dedication Text Amendment
disagreements.summary: Nate Baker sought Council consensus to initiate a UDO park-land dedication text amendment directly at the work session, while a majority declined to back it without advance draft text and Joint City County Planning Committee review.
disagreements.side_a_position: Initiate a Council resolution immediately to explore mandatory public park dedication in the UDO.
side_a_arguments: Durham lacks sufficient public park acquisition as rapid residential growth accelerates.
Placing the resolution on a future agenda begins formal staff and committee analysis promptly.
disagreements.side_b_position: Require advance written text and coordination through JCCPC and the ongoing UDO rewrite rather than spontaneous verbal requests.
side_b_arguments: Text amendments carry joint City-County governance obligations through JCCPC rather than unilateral Council initiation.
Members had not seen drafted resolution language ahead of the work session, and staff capacity is focused on the comprehensive UDO rewrite.
disagreements.resolution: Baker's request failed to receive four thumbs-up and was not placed on the April 15 agenda.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session April 4, 2024
disagreements.issue: 30-Year vs. Permanent Affordability on 312 E. Umstead SRO Loan (Item 7)
disagreements.summary: Council members questioned whether a $3.2M ARPA loan to Reinvestment Partners for 17 SRO units at 312 E. Umstead should lock in permanent affordability rather than a 30-year period.
disagreements.side_a_position: Push for permanent affordability covenants on heavily subsidized nonprofit/ARPA housing investments.
side_a_arguments: Covering $3.2M for 17 SRO units equates to major public subsidy per door that warrants perpetual affordability.
Expiring 30-year terms create future displacement cliff risks.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain the 30-year standard agreement used in the current ARPA underwriting to close the transaction before federal deadlines.
side_b_arguments: Community Development staff noted Reinvestment Partners is a mission-driven nonprofit unlikely to flip the property and warned renegotiating closing terms could delay ARPA obligation deadlines.
Adding unilateral covenant changes late in deal structuring risks project delays.
disagreements.resolution: Item 7 remained on the April 15 Consent Agenda as structured, with staff noting affordability duration policy as an ongoing Council priority.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting April 1, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: At its April 1, 2024 regular meeting, the Durham City Council approved the Consent Agenda (7-0), voted 6-1 to amend the revised Equal Business Opportunity Program (EBOP) ordinance by striking the word 'aspirational' before 'goals' over Mark-Anthony Middleton's dissent, and adopted the amended EBOP ordinance and policy (7-0). Council unanimously approved Aura 751 (350 apartments with 22 income-restricted units on NC 751) after adding a marked-crosswalk commitment at Buck Crossing despite a 9-0 Planning Commission denial, and unanimously approved the 1324 Bungalow Avenue annexation. A third annexation case, the 28.57-acre Lee Valley development, faced sharp questions over missing Transit-Oriented Area commercial/civic uses and unresolved Wendell Road collector alignment before the applicant requested a continuance to September 3, 2024.

agenda_items.title: Fair Housing Month, Community Development Week, and International Women's Day Proclamations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Williams issued proclamations recognizing Fair Housing Month, National Community Development Week, and International Women's Day.

agenda_items.title: Council Member Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Carl Rist commented on City Hall landscaping and March Madness; Javiera Caballero spoke on Church World Service and March Madness; Mark-Anthony Middleton addressed the Baltimore Key Bridge collapse and spring holidays; and Mayor Williams noted his visit with Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott, recent child shootings, the Black Mayors Coalition in Memphis, and NCCU's SIPS Academy.

agenda_items.title: Priority Items (None) and Consent Agenda (Items 1-10, 12-18)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With no priority items added, Council pulled Item 11 (EBOP Ordinance) for amendment and adopted the remaining Consent Agenda items 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Revised Equal Business Opportunity Program (EBOP) Ordinance and Policy
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Carl Rist moved to amend the revised EBOP ordinance by striking the adjective 'aspirational' before 'goals,' backed by City Attorney Fred Lamar's opinion that 'goals' remain legally defensible unlike unlawful quotas. Mark-Anthony Middleton dissented on the amendment to avoid altering staff-vetted language, before joining a 7-0 vote on the amended ordinance and policy.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Zoning: Aura 751 / R 751 (NC 751)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Applicant counsel Cal Cunningham and Trinsic Acquisition Company presented an 11.92-acre annexation and rezoning from RR to PDR 30.594 for up to 350 apartments, offering 22 income-restricted units (11 at 80% AMI, 11 at 60% AMI) for 30 years, Green Building certification, 10 EV chargers, a 75-ft buffer, natural heritage preservation, an off-site sidewalk gap closure, and an added dais proffer for a Buck Crossing marked crosswalk subject to NCDOT approval. Despite a 9-0 Planning Commission denial recommendation and four objecting neighbors citing traffic and density, Council approved all three motions 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Initial Zoning: 1324 Bungalow Avenue
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Moved ahead of Item 21 by consent, Council reviewed a 0.82-acre voluntary annexation and direct RS-20 zoning translation for CWH Properties LLC at 1324 Bungalow Avenue. All three companion votes passed unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Zoning: Lee Valley (Wendell Rd & George King Rd)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Nil Ghosh and Jeremy Medlin presented a 28.57-acre RS-20-to-RCD rezoning for 310-340 quadplex, multiplex, and apartment units with 3% at 80% AMI (updated to 30 years) and $53,500 for DPS, which the Planning Commission had backed 8-5. After resident Ronnie Covington and Council members Baker, Rist, Freeman, and Caballero objected to missing Transit-Oriented Area commercial/civic uses, private streets, and an unresolved Wendell Road collector-street 'island,' the applicant requested and received an informal continuance to September 3, 2024 with the public hearing held open.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Continued to September 3, 2024 at applicant's request (no vote)

agenda_items.title: Cornwallis Summer Camp Agenda Item Thumbs-Up and Committee Room Return
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DeDreana Freeman secured Council thumbs-up to bring forward a future discussion item on Cornwallis summer camp programming, and Mayor Williams announced the April 9 State of the City address and upcoming return of work sessions to the Committee Room.

votes.item_title: Item 11 Amendment: Strike 'Aspirational' Before 'Goals' in Revised EBOP Ordinance
votes.notes: City Attorney Fred Lamar confirmed removing 'aspirational' before 'goals' remained legally compliant.
votes.discussion_detail: Following debate initiated at the March 21 work session, Council Member Carl Rist moved to amend the revised EBOP ordinance by removing the modifier 'aspirational' before 'goals,' arguing that calling participation benchmarks 'aspirational' unnecessarily weakens the City's public commitment to Underutilized Business Enterprise inclusion. City Attorney Fred Lamar advised Council that 'goals' remains legally distinct from unlawful quotas under federal disparity jurisprudence, meaning the edit carried no added legal exposure. Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton voted nay, cautioning against altering staff-crafted disparity ordinance language on the dais, while the other six members voted aye to carry the amendment 6-1.

votes.item_title: Item 11a: Adopt Revised Equal Business Opportunity Program (EBOP) Ordinance as Amended
votes.notes: Updated City contracting equity ordinance.
votes.discussion_detail: After passing Carl Rist's textual amendment 6-1, Council voted on the full revised Equal Business Opportunity Program ordinance updating municipal contracting outreach and UBE participation goals following Durham's disparity study. Mark-Anthony Middleton joined the majority on final passage to affirm the City's broader contracting equity framework despite opposing the wording edit. The amended ordinance passed 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 11b: Authorize City Manager to Establish EBOP Implementation Policy
votes.notes: Companion administrative policy authorization to Item 11a.
votes.discussion_detail: Council next voted on the companion authorization empowering the City Manager to adopt administrative policies and procedures implementing the newly amended EBOP ordinance across City departments. Staff confirmed the policy updates align procurement scoring, bid tracking, and compliance enforcement with the ordinance changes. All seven members voted aye 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 20a (Aura 751): Approve Annexation Ordinance and Utility Extension Agreement with Trinsic Acquisition Company LLC
votes.notes: 11.92 acres along NC 751; property owners Charles & Brenda Beckon and Katherine Booth Butler.
votes.discussion_detail: Trinsic Acquisition Company LLC and counsel Cal Cunningham presented the voluntary annexation and Utility Extension Agreement for 11.92 acres along NC 751, proposing up to 350 apartments adjacent to existing suburban infrastructure and major employers. Despite four neighboring speakers raising traffic and density concerns and the Planning Commission's earlier 9-0 denial vote, Council cited substantial post-Planning Commission improvements, including 22 income-restricted units (half at 60% AMI, half at 80% AMI) for 30 years, a 75-foot buffer, natural heritage protection, and an off-site 5-foot sidewalk connection. At the dais, Cunningham also added a marked crosswalk commitment at Buck Crossing subject to NCDOT approval. Council unanimously approved the annexation and UEA 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 20b (Aura 751): Adopt Zoning Map Change (RR to PDR 30.594)
votes.notes: Includes 22 affordable units for 30 years, Green Building certification, 10 EV chargers, and 75-ft setback.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the annexation vote, Council approved rezoning the 11.92-acre Aura 751 tract from Rural Residential (RR) to Planned Development Residential (PDR 30.594) with the revised textual development plan and the new dais crosswalk proffer. Council members praised the developer's inclusion of deeper 60% AMI units, natural heritage conservation buffers, EV charging infrastructure, and pedestrian link closures along NC 751 as decisive improvements over the version rejected by the Planning Commission. All seven members voted aye to adopt the rezoning 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 20c (Aura 751): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Zoning Consistency Statement
votes.notes: Statutory consistency finding for Aura 751.
votes.discussion_detail: Pursuant to NCGS 160D-605, Council voted on the statutory statement affirming that the Aura 751 PDR 30.594 zoning map amendment is consistent with the Comprehensive Plan's housing and connectivity goals and reasonable in the public interest. Staff confirmed the consistency finding reflected all committed elements on the record. The motion passed 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 22a (1324 Bungalow Ave): Approve Annexation Ordinance and Utility Extension Agreement with CWH Properties LLC
votes.notes: 0.82-acre single-parcel annexation moved ahead of Item 21.
votes.discussion_detail: Council moved Item 22 ahead of the longer Lee Valley case to expedite a straightforward 0.82-acre voluntary annexation and Utility Extension Agreement at 1324 Bungalow Avenue with CWH Properties LLC. Planning staff noted the parcel already sits surrounded by existing infrastructure and attracted no neighborhood opposition at the public hearing. Council approved the annexation and UEA 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 22b (1324 Bungalow Ave): Approve Initial Zoning Map Change (RS-20 County to RS-20 City)
votes.notes: Direct RS-20 residential zoning translation.
votes.discussion_detail: Council considered the companion initial zoning ordinance directly translating 1324 Bungalow Avenue from Durham County RS-20 to City RS-20 upon annexation. Staff confirmed no density expansion or change of use was proposed beyond standard residential zoning parity. Council adopted the initial zoning 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 22c (1324 Bungalow Ave): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Zoning Consistency Statement
votes.notes: Statutory consistency finding for 1324 Bungalow Ave.
votes.discussion_detail: Council voted on the formal NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement confirming that the direct RS-20 initial zoning translation at 1324 Bungalow Avenue aligns with the Comprehensive Plan. No additional questions were raised. The consistency statement passed 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting April 1, 2024
disagreements.issue: Deleting 'Aspirational' Before 'Goals' in Revised EBOP Ordinance (Item 11)
disagreements.summary: Council voted 6-1 to amend the Equal Business Opportunity Program ordinance by striking the word 'aspirational' before 'goals,' with Mark-Anthony Middleton dissenting.
disagreements.side_a_position: Remove 'aspirational' so the City's minority and women business participation benchmarks stand clearly as firm municipal goals.
side_a_arguments: Calling equity targets 'aspirational' dilutes accountability and signals weaker resolve to underutilized businesses.
The City Attorney confirmed 'goals' does not constitute an illegal quota and remains fully defensible.
disagreements.side_b_position: Preserve staff-drafted 'aspirational goals' phrasing without late dais edits.
side_b_arguments: Disparity-study attorneys and Equity & Inclusion staff carefully chose wording to insulate Durham's program from legal challenge.
Second-guessing staff drafting on the dais creates unnecessary risk.
disagreements.resolution: Amendment passed 6-1, and the full revised EBOP ordinance then passed 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting April 1, 2024
disagreements.issue: Lee Valley Rezoning Transit-Oriented Area Compliance and Collector Street Design (Item 21)
disagreements.summary: A majority of Council members questioned Lee Valley's omission of commercial/civic space, private streets, and an isolated Wendell Road collector segment, contrasting with Mark-Anthony Middleton's support for advancing East Durham housing.
disagreements.side_a_position: Require Transit-Oriented Area (TOA) projects to deliver real mixed commercial/civic uses, public street grids, and coherent Wendell Road collector alignment.
side_a_arguments: The Comprehensive Plan's TOA place type expects neighborhood-serving commercial/civic elements rather than pure residential sprawl.
Private streets and a disconnected collector-road island along Wendell Road fall short of multimodal connectivity standards.
disagreements.side_b_position: Recognize the 8-5 Planning Commission approval, affordability proffers, and DPS contribution as sufficient grounds to support needed East Durham housing.
side_b_arguments: The project provides 310-340 multiplex and apartment homes, 30-year 80% AMI affordability, and $53,500 for Durham Public Schools.
Strict insistence on every TOA ideal can stall viable housing near planned transit corridors.
disagreements.resolution: Sensing insufficient support for immediate approval, applicant representatives requested and received a continuance to September 3, 2024.

development_cases.location: NC 751 near I-40 interchange and Streets at Southpoint
development_cases.scale: Up to 350 multifamily apartment units on 11.92 acres (2 parcels)
development_cases.zoning_change: RR (Residential Rural) to PDR 30.594 (Falls/Jordan Watershed Overlay District B, Major Transportation Corridor I-40)

proffers.affordable_housing: 22 income-restricted units (11 at 60% AMI and 11 at 80% AMI) for 30 years (upgraded post-Planning Commission from 11 at 80% AMI for 20 years)
proffers.environmental_tree: Minimum 2.29 acres existing tree preservation; protection of adjacent Natural Heritage Area; primary residential and community amenity buildings certified to a National Green Building Standard; 10 EV charging stations; enhanced stormwater controls up to the 100-year storm event; 100% native tree plantings
proffers.transit_infrastructure: 10-foot shared-use path along NC 751 frontage plus 30-foot right-of-way dedication; off-site 5-foot sidewalk connection (approx. 50-100 yards) north to Streets at Southpoint commercial/transit; dais commitment for marked crosswalk across NC 751 at Buck Crossing Drive subject to NCDOT approval
other_proffers: 75-foot primary building setback from northern single-family neighbors (increased from 60 ft)
Minimum 4-story building height

member_justifications.stance_summary: Supports adding multifamily rental diversity in a predominantly for-sale housing corridor within walking distance of Aldi, Target, and bus routes. Praises the developer's post-Planning Commission proffers meeting 18 of 22 comprehensive plan policies, Green Building commitment, and 22 affordable units despite wishing state law allowed stronger inclusionary zoning.
member_justifications.key_quote: I think this is exactly what we need in an area that is heavily commercial. It connects residents, it has a strong affordable housing commitment.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Evaluates the rezoning through his '3Ds' framework (density, diversity, and design), noting the car-centric NC 751 context, missing north/west street stub connections, and preference for perpetual affordability. Ultimately votes aye because the post-Planning Commission upgrades deliver rare Green Building standards, 6% affordability with half at 60% AMI, walkability to grocery and greenways, plus an added dais commitment for a marked crosswalk across NC 751 at Buck Crossing.
member_justifications.key_quote: There are some important things in this proposal that we don't often see in proposals: the Green Building standards, the connectivity, the actual walkability to a grocery store.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Initially wanted more affordable units or transitional building heights, but supports the case because post-Planning Commission changes added setbacks, Natural Heritage Area conservation, and Green Building proffers, and longstanding Black property owners are responsibly stewarding the land. Urges developers to present full proffers at the Planning Commission stage rather than waiting until Council.
member_justifications.key_quote: They responded in kind to the Planning Commission's concerns and made substantial improvements before bringing this back before us.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Highlights the off-site 5-foot sidewalk gap closure allowing residents to walk about half a mile to Aldi and under a mile to transit. Emphasizes respect for Planning Commission and BPAC feedback while concluding the developer's post-PC proffers directly resolved those concerns.
member_justifications.key_quote: Closing that sidewalk gap makes it truly walkable to groceries and transit.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Argues 350 apartments with 22 income-restricted units serve Durham far better than 17 by-right single-family homes. Credits the Planning Commission's 9-0 denial vote with prompting stronger proffers and rejects excluding multifamily rental housing from single-family neighborhoods.
member_justifications.key_quote: Twenty-two deeply affordable units in a high-opportunity corridor beats 17 by-right single-family homes any day.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Expresses frustration that Durham must rely on private developers to close sidewalk gaps and wait on NCDOT approvals, while arguing that increasing housing supply across price points lowers exclusivity and densifying near Southpoint helps attract stronger regional transit investment.
member_justifications.key_quote: Increasing our housing supply near commercial centers like Southpoint is how we make Durham less exclusive and build the case for better transit.

development_cases.location: 1324 Bungalow Avenue
development_cases.scale: 1 parcel and right-of-way totaling 0.82 acres (1 unit)
development_cases.zoning_change: RS-20 County to RS-20 City (Falls/Jordan Lake Watershed Overlay District B)

development_cases.location: 5412 & 5416 Wendell Road and 5529 & 5533 George King Road
development_cases.scale: 310 to 340 units (quad-format townhomes, duplexes, and multiplex/apartments; 12 DU/acre minimum) on 28.57 acres (6 parcels)
development_cases.zoning_change: RS-20 to RCD (Residential Compact with Development Plan); 1 parcel (REID 141615) RS-20 County to RS-20 City for lift station

proffers.affordable_housing: 3% of final unit count at 80% AMI for 30 years (corrected on dais from 20-year typo)
proffers.environmental_tree: More than double required open space; stormwater controls for the 100-year storm event with more than one stormwater system; native plant species for required landscaping
proffers.transit_infrastructure: Right-of-way dedication for adopted collector streets; pump/lift station designed to go offline when future regional lift station west of George King Road is built
other_proffers: Architectural commitments ensuring varying unit sizes
Active amenity elements

member_justifications.stance_summary: Questions the reliance on internal private streets and opposes the lack of mixed uses under his 3Ds framework. Quoting Planning Commissioner CE, states he will vote no because approving a solely residential development on 28+ acres inside a designated Transit Opportunity Area (TOA) omits commercial, civic, or non-residential components required by the comprehensive plan.
member_justifications.key_quote: Reserving or committing to some civic or non-residential component would bring the proposal closer to the intent for the TOA Place Type... I'll be voting no on this one.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Highlights concerns about creating an isolated 'island' pocket of existing homes sandwiched between Wendell Road and the proposed collector street alignment. Later recommends a continuance at 02:51:26 so the applicant can coordinate street alignment and adjacent planning with the neighboring Lee Village Center project rather than facing defeat.
member_justifications.key_quote: We need to avoid creating an isolated island of existing homes without coordination with the neighboring Lee Village Center alignment.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Objects to forfeiting commercial and mixed-use opportunity inside a Transit Opportunity Area and raises alarm over isolating neighboring parcels, specifically citing adjacent landowner concerns.
member_justifications.key_quote: I'm deeply concerned about losing commercial mixed-use potential in a transit area while boxing in existing neighbors.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Agrees with Baker against abandoning the Transit Opportunity Area mixed-use vision and flags inadequate safe pedestrian crosswalks and bus access across NC 54. Leans no because collector alignments and neighboring site plans remain too much in flux.
member_justifications.key_quote: I share the concern about giving up on the Transit Opportunity Area mix of uses when so much around the collector streets is still in flux.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Argues the demise of Durham's Light Rail project altered the Transit Opportunity Area premise, backs the Planning Commission's 8-5 approval recommendation, and declines to hold one applicant's vote hostage to separate neighboring developments.
member_justifications.key_quote: With the Light Rail gone, the context for the TOA has changed, and I'm ready to support the Planning Commission's approval tonight.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Views the comprehensive plan as guiding rather than mandatory and expresses skepticism that ground-floor retail is automatically viable on every site, though he welcomes continuing the hearing to September 3 so collector-street coordination can produce a stronger plan.
member_justifications.key_quote: The comprehensive plan is a guide, not law, though a continuance could help align the collector streets with the adjacent site.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Procedures Committee Meeting March 22, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: At the March 22, 2024 Durham City Council Procedures Committee meeting—facilitated by a committee chair addressed as Madam Chair before returning the floor to Mayor Leonardo Williams to adjourn—the committee unanimously approved the minutes from its January 31, 2020 meeting by voice vote, with no split or contested votes taken during the session. City Attorney Kim Rehberg presented a comprehensive rewrite of the Council's Code of Ethics, explaining that the existing 1995 code (amended in 2010 and 2018 via Resolutions 10099 and 8145) was disjointed and proposed narrowing it exclusively to City Council members while separating city employees (covered under HRM 800-series policy) and moving appointed boards and commissions into Attachment A. Rehberg walked through draft provisions covering conflicts of interest, a peer-city-aligned gift policy, financial and personal-relationship disclosures, and internal Council enforcement mechanisms, followed by revised Council procedures on special meetings, attendance and five-absence vacancy rules, and remote participation for non-voting debate. The committee also discussed codifying simple-majority (four-member) consent at work sessions for Council member-initiated agenda items rather than a two-thirds threshold, and agreed to reconvene at a later date rather than rushing adoption before the June 17 budget vote.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Microphone Orientation, and Roll Call
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The committee called the meeting to order at 2:39 p.m., noted traffic delays, and reviewed the operation and mute controls of the chamber's new microphone system, with Council Member Carl Rist testing his mic. Following brief staff introductions, roll call began with Mayor Leonardo Williams, Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton, Council Member Carl Rist, and Council Member Javiera Caballero recorded before a gap in the transcript.

agenda_items.title: Approval of January 31, 2020 Committee Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The chair noted that the Procedures Committee had last met on January 31, 2020 and requested a motion to approve those minutes. After a motion was made and staff clarified that copies of the minutes had been circulated by email, the committee approved the minutes unanimously by voice vote.

agenda_items.title: Overview of Council Procedures and Revised Code of Ethics
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Attorney Kim Rehberg reviewed the history of the Council's procedures and ethics code, referencing the February 16 Council budget retreat discussion on due process and conflicts of interest and confirming she personally drafted the comprehensive rewrite. She explained that the existing 1995 code—modified by Resolutions 10099 (2010) and 8145 (2018)—was cobbled together and conflated Council members with city employees and appointed boards, proposing instead a standalone Council ethics resolution while covering employees under HRM's 800-series policy and moving boards and commissions to Attachment A.

agenda_items.title: Draft Code of Ethics Walkthrough: Conflicts, Gifts, Disclosures, and Enforcement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Rehberg walked through conflict-of-interest standards, a gift policy aligned with Professor Bell's model code and North Carolina peer cities, and disclosure rules, noting prior Council questions about disclosing personal relationships with city staff. She also reviewed Section 4 (pages 7–11), which adds explicit internal Council enforcement and disciplinary provisions that had been largely absent from the existing code.

agenda_items.title: Council Procedures: Special Meetings, Attendance, and Remote Participation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a truncated middle portion of the transcript, Rehberg reviewed procedures for suspending rules, modifying the regular calendar, and calling special meetings (by the mayor, city manager, or any four Council members) as defined in the City Charter. She presented expanded attendance rules linking excessive unexcused absences to ethics discipline and reiterating the charter's five-consecutive-absence vacancy rule, alongside a new remote participation policy allowing remote remarks and work session debate while noting statutory limits against counting remote members for quorum or voting.

agenda_items.title: Council-Initiated Agenda Items, Next Steps, and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Rehberg flagged the need to add a work-session order of business to resolve bifurcated agenda rules and sought committee direction on Council member-initiated resolutions and presentations. Committee members favored codifying their longstanding practice of requiring simple-majority (four-member) consent at a work session rather than a two-thirds threshold, agreed to reconvene rather than rush completion before the June 17 budget vote, and turned the floor back to Mayor Leonardo Williams to adjourn at 4:27 p.m.

votes.item_title: Approval of January 31, 2020 Procedures Committee Minutes
votes.notes: Passed unanimously by voice vote ('All in favor, say aye... Any opposed? Motion passes unanimously'). Mover and seconder were not identified by name in the transcript digest. Roll call at 00:01:50–00:01:55 confirmed Mayor Leonardo Williams, Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton, Council Member Carl Rist, and Council Member Javiera Caballero before a transcript gap, and opening remarks at 00:00:13 noted 'we're all here'.
votes.discussion_detail: Before the vote, a member asked whether copies of the January 31, 2020 minutes were available in the room and was informed they had been sent by email.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session March 21, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: At its March 21, 2024 work session, the Durham City Council excused three members' July 25 absences (7-0), suspended rules to approve a $133,094 NC 911 radio grant and DHA Commerce Street HOME ordinances (7-0), and voted to hold a closed session on a legal settlement demand (7-0). Members debated several major policy issues, including an unusual push by newer Council members to modify FY25 Budget Development Guidelines for earlier compensation-study data and flat-dollar pay-equity models, developer responsibility in the $2.93M SE Durham Watershed Improvement Plan, and striking 'aspirational' before 'goals' in the EBOP ordinance. The session ended with an emotional clash between Council members over City Hall front-door locking procedures and fire-code capacity limits ahead of settling the April 1 agenda (7-0).

agenda_items.title: Council Announcements and July 25 Absence Excusal Votes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following brief announcements, Council voted 7-0 in three separate motions to excuse upcoming July 25, 2024 work session absences for Carl Rist, Javiera Caballero, and DeDreana Freeman.

agenda_items.title: Durham Police Department Lifesaving Recognition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council and Police leadership recognized Senior Police Officer May and Officer Mueller for performing lifesaving CPR during a critical medical emergency.

agenda_items.title: Priority Items, Rule Suspension for Items 10 & 24, and Closed Session Motion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council accepted the City Manager's and City Attorney's priority items (7-0), suspended rules (7-0) to immediately pass an NC 911 radio grant (Item 10) and DHA Commerce Street HOME grant ordinances (Item 24), and approved entering Closed Session at the end of business under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3) regarding a settlement demand.

agenda_items.title: Public Comments from Jeremy Burgren and Donald Reigns
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Jeremy Burgren addressed community policing and municipal transparency, while Donald Reigns of the Durham Council of the Blind highlighted accessibility and transit needs for blind and visually impaired residents.

agenda_items.title: Bid Report, FY25 Budget Development Guidelines (Item 6), and McKinney Square ARPA Loan (Item 9)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chelsea Cook questioned Item 4 (February Bid Report) regarding GS 143-129 bidding thresholds, a sole-source pump vendor, and Dell contract default. On Item 6 (FY25 Budget Development Guidelines), Cook, Nate Baker, Carl Rist, and DeDreana Freeman pressed for earlier classification/compensation study data and flat-dollar equity scenarios while Mark-Anthony Middleton, Javiera Caballero, and Mayor Williams defended the Manager's standard calendar and process; on Item 9 (McKinney Square), members probed 30-year versus permanent affordability and the $27M City/County ARPA match.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Kept Item 6 on April 1 Consent Agenda after discussion

agenda_items.title: Interlocal Agreement for Southeast Durham Watershed Improvement Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented an ILA splitting costs ($2.022M City and $910,000 County) for the Southeast Durham Watershed Improvement Plan. Nate Baker and Chelsea Cook questioned using taxpayer funds to remediate sediment pollution linked to private development while Mayor Williams and Mark-Anthony Middleton stressed the City's duty to protect streams and residents regardless.

agenda_items.title: Equal Business Opportunity Program (EBOP) Sunset Extension and Revision
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Equity & Inclusion staff reviewed the EBOP ordinance update, sparking debate between Carl Rist—who objected to characterizing UBE participation benchmarks as 'aspirational goals'—and Mark-Anthony Middleton and staff defending the existing legal framing.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Advanced to April 1 Consent Agenda (later pulled April 1)

agenda_items.title: Durham Destination Master Plan Briefing (Discover Durham)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Discover Durham CEO Susan Amey presented the Destination Master Plan alongside three proposed state legislative requests, including adjusting local occupancy tax redistribution formulas (4%/2%). Council members asked questions about tourism equity, worker pay, and convention center/cultural asset priorities.

agenda_items.title: Board Nominations, April 1 Agenda Settling, and City Hall Access Debate
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council recorded nominations for Larry Dale McKeller, Ben Goldberg, and Lorenzo A. Pedro, settled the April 1 agenda 7-0, and then engaged in a tense exchange after DeDreana Freeman and Chelsea Cook criticized City Hall front doors being locked and 7:00 PM public-comment limits while Mayor Williams and Mark-Anthony Middleton cited fire-code capacity and security rules before entering Closed Session.

votes.item_title: Excuse Absence of Council Member Carl Rist for July 25, 2024 Work Session
votes.notes: Part of summer work session absence excusals.
votes.discussion_detail: During Council Announcements, Carl Rist disclosed an upcoming scheduling conflict for the July 25, 2024 summer work session and requested formal excusal. Council members noted multiple summer absences later prompted consideration of rescheduling that work session entirely. All seven members voted aye by voice vote to excuse Rist's absence.

votes.item_title: Excuse Absence of Council Member Javiera Caballero for July 25, 2024 Work Session
votes.notes: Excused July 25 absence.
votes.discussion_detail: Council Member Javiera Caballero similarly requested an excused absence in advance for the July 25, 2024 work session. Following the procedural vote for Carl Rist, a motion to excuse Caballero was seconded without objection. The motion passed unanimously 7-0 by voice vote.

votes.item_title: Excuse Absence of Council Member DeDreana Freeman for July 25, 2024 Work Session
votes.notes: Third member excused for July 25, 2024.
votes.discussion_detail: Council Member DeDreana Freeman also requested excusal for the July 25, 2024 work session, marking three members scheduled to be away on that date. Members noted the cluster of absences would likely warrant rescheduling the July work session at a later date. Council voted 7-0 by voice vote to excuse Freeman.

votes.item_title: Accept City Manager's Priority Items (March 21, 2024)
votes.notes: Included priority scheduling for Items 10 and 24.
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager Wanda Page presented her priority adjustments for the March 21 work session, requesting immediate Council action on Item 10 (North Carolina 911 Board radio grant) and Item 24 (HOME grant ordinances for DHA Commerce Street) due to external closing deadlines. Council raised no objections to placing those items on priority status. The motion to accept the Manager's priority items passed 7-0 by voice vote.

votes.item_title: Suspend Rules for Immediate Action on Items 10 and 24
votes.notes: Allowed binding grant and ordinance votes during a work session.
votes.discussion_detail: To approve binding grant and project ordinance measures outside a regular business meeting, staff requested suspension of Council's normal work-session rules for Items 10 and 24. Explaining that both state grant execution and DHA financial closing timelines could not wait until April 1, leadership called the suspension motion. All seven Council members voted aye 7-0 by voice vote.

votes.item_title: Item 10: Approve NC 911 Board Grant Agreement for Emergency Communications Radios ($133,094.24)
votes.notes: Immediate approval granted under suspended rules.
votes.discussion_detail: Emergency Communications staff requested execution of a $133,094.24 grant agreement from the North Carolina 911 Board to fund replacement and interoperable emergency dispatch radios. Immediate Council approval ensured the City met the state's grant acceptance window without forfeiture. No members expressed concerns with the grant terms, and the motion passed 7-0 by voice vote.

votes.item_title: Item 24: Adopt HOME Grant Project Ordinances (FY16-17 through FY22-23) for DHA Commerce Street Closing
votes.notes: Cleared federal HOME funding ordinances required for Durham Housing Authority Commerce Street closing.
votes.discussion_detail: Community Development staff explained that multiple prior-year HOME Investment Partnerships project ordinances (FY16-17 through FY22-23) required technical alignment to allow the Durham Housing Authority's Commerce Street affordable housing transaction to close on schedule. Waiting until April 1 would have delayed closing commitments for the downtown DHA development. Council passed the HOME grant project ordinances unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Receive City Attorney's Priority Item (Closed Session Litigation/Settlement Request)
votes.notes: Accepted City Attorney's priority request for Closed Session consultation.
votes.discussion_detail: City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg requested adding a priority item for Closed Session attorney-client consultation concerning a legal settlement demand against the City. Accepting the item onto the agenda preceded the formal statutory motion required under North Carolina Open Meetings Law. Council voted 7-0 by voice vote to receive the City Attorney's priority item.

votes.item_title: Motion to Hold Closed Session Under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3) at Conclusion of Business
votes.notes: Statutory closed session to consult with City Attorney on a settlement demand; convened after public business around 03:51:10.
votes.discussion_detail: Pursuant to North Carolina General Statute 143-318.11(a)(3), Council considered entering Closed Session at the conclusion of open work-session business to preserve attorney-client privilege while reviewing a pending settlement demand. The City Attorney read the statutory citation into the record before the chair called the question. Council approved the closed-session motion 7-0 by voice vote and entered closed session after completing agenda settling.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 21, 2024
disagreements.issue: FY25 Budget Development Guidelines: Compensation Data Timing and Flat vs. Percentage Equity Models (Item 6)
disagreements.summary: Newer Council members pushed to update budget guidelines for earlier Classification and Compensation Study access and flat-dollar raise scenarios, while senior members defended the City Manager's standard schedule.
disagreements.side_a_position: Accelerate release of raw compensation study findings and analyze flat-dollar or equity-weighted raises for lower-paid workers.
side_a_arguments: Waiting until mid-April or May compresses Council's ability to evaluate a $28M+ pay overhaul and union wage priorities.
Flat-dollar increases lift frontline workers disproportionately compared to across-the-board percentage raises.
disagreements.side_b_position: Preserve the Manager's established budget calendar and avoid directing unvetted pay structures mid-process.
side_b_arguments: HR consultants require full quality control before releasing salary study scenarios to Council and staff.
Altering formal budget guidelines late risks disrupting departmental budget preparation.
disagreements.resolution: Item 6 remained on the April 1 Consent Agenda without formal amendment, while staff committed to bringing the compensation briefing on April 18.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 21, 2024
disagreements.issue: Developer Accountability in Southeast Durham Watershed Improvement Plan (Item 17)
disagreements.summary: Council members differed over whether public funds should finance $2.93M in Southeast Durham watershed remediation or if private developers should bear greater responsibility.
disagreements.side_a_position: Require stronger developer accountability rather than relying on public tax/utility dollars to fix sediment pollution.
side_a_arguments: Rapid greenfield construction in Southeast Durham generated severe erosion into Lick Creek and adjacent basins.
Spending $2.022M in City funds and $910k in County funds subsidizes damage caused by inadequate site enforcement.
disagreements.side_b_position: Proceed with the joint City-County watershed plan immediately to address legacy and ongoing stream degradation.
side_b_arguments: Downstream residents and ecosystems need remediation regardless of whether blame spans historical and current projects.
Enforcing new UDO rules proceeds separately from executing existing basin-wide stabilization.
disagreements.resolution: Item 17 advanced to the April 1 Consent Agenda as drafted.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 21, 2024
disagreements.issue: EBOP Ordinance 'Aspirational Goals' Language (Item 11)
disagreements.summary: Carl Rist objected to retaining 'aspirational' before 'goals' in the revised Equal Business Opportunity Program ordinance, opposed by Mark-Anthony Middleton and staff.
disagreements.side_a_position: Strike 'aspirational' so municipal contracting equity benchmarks carry stronger normative force.
side_a_arguments: Labeling goals 'aspirational' undermines accountability to local minority- and women-owned businesses.
Legal counsel should verify whether simple 'goals' terminology suffices without softening language.
disagreements.side_b_position: Retain staff's vetted disparity-study phrasing to protect the ordinance legally.
side_b_arguments: Staff and disparity attorneys drafted the phrase carefully to distinguish goals from prohibited quotas.
Changing legal terms without full review risks jeopardizing program durability.
disagreements.resolution: Item 11 stayed on the April 1 Consent docket from the work session, but Rist successfully pulled and amended it 6-1 at the April 1 Council meeting.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session March 21, 2024
disagreements.issue: City Hall Front Door Locking, Fire-Code Capacity, and Public Comment Cutoffs
disagreements.summary: At the close of open session, Council members clashed sharply over locking City Hall doors after hours and restricting in-person public entry.
disagreements.side_a_position: Keep City Hall accessible to residents attending public meetings rather than locking front doors prematurely or capping access at 7:00 PM.
side_a_arguments: Residents attempting to attend evening meetings encountered locked entrances, chilling democratic participation.
Public institutions must prioritize open entry and transparent accommodation for late-arriving workers.
disagreements.side_b_position: Enforce fire-marshal occupancy limits, building security protocols, and established public-comment deadlines.
side_b_arguments: Chamber overcrowding triggers binding fire-code capacity violations and safety risks for attendees and staff.
Security staff must manage perimeter access consistently once chambers reach overflow limits or normal operating cutoff times.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Mayor Williams directed staff to enforce fire-code and security protocols while managing overflow accommodations.
