meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting March 18, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: The March 18, 2024 Durham City Council meeting centered on a nearly three-hour FY2024-25 Budget & CIP Public Hearing featuring dozens of residents and unionized workers advocating for an Office of Survivor Care, a $25/hr municipal minimum wage (UE Local 150), police and fire pay/retiree benefits, park remediation ($5M), Vision Zero transit, and eviction diversion. Council accepted priority items referring Item 14 back to DPD (7-0), passed the Consent Agenda (7-0), and unanimously approved the 3411 & 3417 Pickett Road annexation and RS-20 translation (7-0) following a brief procedural clash over off-topic remarks. Finally, Council debated Sharon Road Apartments (260 units on Wake Forest Hwy) at length before approving the annexation and UEA 4-3 and the PDR 10.62 zoning map change 6-1.

agenda_items.title: 50th Durham CROP Hunger Walk and Omega Zeta Chapter 50th Anniversary
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Williams presented proclamations celebrating the 50th anniversary of the Durham CROP Hunger Walk and the 50th anniversary of the Omega Zeta Chapter of Omega Psi Phi Fraternity, attended by Justice Mike Morgan.

agenda_items.title: Council Announcements and Transit Employee Recognition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chelsea Cook highlighted Meals on Wheels and Ramadan food drives with the Zakat Foundation; Mark-Anthony Middleton and Mayor Williams reported on National League of Cities federal advocacy on ARPA deadlines and PFAS funding; and Williams honored National Transit Employee Day, recognizing over 230 GoDurham and 59 Access workers and Campus Hills CPR lifesavers.

agenda_items.title: Priority Items (Item 14 Referred; Item 22 Updated) and Consent Agenda (Items 1-13, 15-18)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council voted 7-0 to accept City Manager priority updates referring Item 14 (Governor's Crime Commission grant) back to DPD and recording Sharon Road Apartments (Item 22) proffer/fiscal updates (3% tax growth estimate and $35,500 DPS contribution), then approved the remaining Consent Agenda 7-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Priority Items accepted 7-0; Consent Agenda passed 7-0

agenda_items.title: FY2024-25 Budget and FY2025-30 Capital Improvement Program Public Hearing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Sixty-three residents signed up under two-minute speaking limits for the FY25 budget hearing, chaired in part by Mark-Anthony Middleton while Mayor Williams rested his voice. Major advocacy coalitions called for creating an Office of Survivor Care (Prescriptions for Repair/Durham CAN/Dr. Henry Rice), raising minimum city pay to $25/hr and reclassifying Solid Waste (UE Local 150), closing 166 DPD and 31 DFD vacancies with improved pay and retiree health coverage (FOP/PBA), dedicating $5M for park heavy-metal remediation plus Walltown/Northgate small area planning, advancing Vision Zero and fare-free transit (Bike Durham), funding Don't Waste Durham's ReUse Hub, and expanding eviction diversion.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Initial Zoning: 3411 & 3417 Pickett Road
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a 2.93-acre voluntary annexation and direct RS-20 zoning translation at 3411 and 3417 Pickett Road for Linda S. Davis and Paridon C. Davis, marking Durham's first direct-translation case reviewed by the Planning Commission (10-0 approval) under updated state legislation. During discussion, Mayor Williams ruled DeDreana Freeman out of order when she thanked earlier budget speakers rather than addressing Pickett Road, before Council voted 7-0 on all three motions.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Zoning: Sharon Road Apartments (4862 Wake Forest Hwy)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Sharon Road Wake Forest Land LLC requested annexing and rezoning 24.87 acres from CN(D)/RS-20/RR to PDR 10.62 for 260 apartments, adding 1% at 100% AMI for 30 years atop 5% at 80% AMI, a 10-ft path to Walgreens, 24% tree cover, 4 EV chargers, and $35,500 for DPS after a 9-4 Planning Commission approval vote. Eleven neighboring residents opposed the project over Lick Creek sediment, blasting, and NC 98 traffic; Council split over private-driveway connectivity loopholes, Nollan/Dolan limits on an $80k-$100k off-site ADA crosswalk, and avoiding a de facto East Durham moratorium, ultimately passing annexation 4-3, rezoning 6-1, and consistency 7-0.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Annexation Passed 4-3; Zoning Passed 6-1; Consistency Passed 7-0

votes.item_title: Accept City Manager's Priority Items (March 18, 2024)
votes.notes: Referred Item 14 (Governor's Crime Commission grant) back to DPD and added fiscal/DPS proffer updates ($10k to $35,500) to Item 22.
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager Wanda Page presented priority docket changes prior to taking up the Consent Agenda, notably recommending that Item 14 (a Governor's Crime Commission grant application) be referred back to the Durham Police Department for further refinement. She also supplied updated cost-benefit estimates (3% tax-base growth) and an increased Durham Public Schools contribution (from $10,000 to $35,500) for Item 22, Sharon Road Apartments. Council raised no objections to the Manager's adjustments and adopted the priority items 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 21a (3411 & 3417 Pickett Road): Approve Annexation Ordinance and Utility Extension Agreement
votes.notes: 2.93 acres with property owners Linda S. Davis and Paridon C. Davis.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff presented the voluntary annexation and Utility Extension Agreement covering 2.93 acres at 3411 and 3417 Pickett Road for owners Linda S. Davis and Paridon C. Davis, noting 10-0 Planning Commission endorsement. During the discussion window, Mayor Williams ruled DeDreana Freeman out of order when she attempted to thank earlier FY25 budget public-hearing speakers rather than commenting on Pickett Road. Turning back to the merits with no resident opposition, Council voted 7-0 to approve the annexation and UEA.

votes.item_title: Item 21b (3411 & 3417 Pickett Road): Approve Initial Zoning Map Change (RS-20 County to RS-20 City)
votes.notes: First direct-translation initial zoning reviewed by Planning Commission under new state law.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff noted that 3411 and 3417 Pickett Road represented the first direct County-to-City RS-20 zoning translation routed through the Planning Commission under revised North Carolina statutory procedures, earning a unanimous 10-0 recommendation. Because the proposal maintained identical single-family RS-20 rules without density increases, Council had no substantive land-use objections. All seven members voted aye to adopt the initial zoning 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 21c (3411 & 3417 Pickett Road): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Zoning Consistency Statement
votes.notes: Statutory consistency finding for Pickett Road initial zoning.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the Pickett Road annexation and initial RS-20 zoning approvals, Council voted on the required NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement affirming alignment with the Durham Comprehensive Plan. No members requested further discussion. The consistency statement passed 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 22a (Sharon Road Apartments): Approve Annexation Ordinance and Utility Extension Agreement
votes.notes: 24.87 acres at 4862 Wake Forest Hwy with Sharon Road Wake Forest Land LLC (260 apartments).
votes.discussion_detail: Sharon Road Apartments drew nearly two hours of debate over annexing and extending municipal utilities to a 24.87-acre tract at 4862 Wake Forest Highway for 260 apartments, following a 9-4 Planning Commission endorsement. Eleven East Durham residents opposed the project, pointing to Lick Creek watershed turbidity, rock blasting impacts, and pedestrian hazards along NC 98. Supporters Williams, Middleton, Caballero, and Rist argued the parcel satisfied 23 of 25 Comprehensive Plan policies, sat adjacent to Walgreens with a committed 10-foot shared-use path, provided 6% income-restricted units (5% at 80% AMI plus 1% at 100% AMI added at the meeting) for 30 years, and warned against imposing an unlawful de facto moratorium on East Durham housing. Dissenters Baker, Cook, and Freeman objected to private-driveway connectivity loopholes, Lick Creek erosion, and the absence of an $80,000-$100,000 ADA crosswalk across NC 98 (which staff noted was constrained by Nollan/Dolan nexus rules), resulting in a 4-3 annexation approval.

votes.item_title: Item 22b (Sharon Road Apartments): Adopt Zoning Map Change to PDR 10.62
votes.notes: Baker and Cook opposed the discretionary UEA/annexation (Item 22a) while voting aye on the zoning map change once annexation passed.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately after approving the Sharon Road Apartments annexation and Utility Extension Agreement 4-3, Council voted on the companion rezoning from CN(D)/RS-20/RR to Planned Development Residential (PDR 10.62) incorporating the expanded 6% affordability commitment, 24% tree preservation, 4 EV chargers, 10-foot pedestrian path to Walgreens, and $35,500 DPS contribution. Having registered their core opposition against extending municipal utilities on the discretionary annexation vote, Nate Baker and Chelsea Cook joined the majority on the resulting zoning map motion to ensure enforceable textual conditions attached to the development. Only DeDreana Freeman maintained a nay vote, yielding a 6-1 approval.

votes.item_title: Item 22c (Sharon Road Apartments): Adopt NCGS 160D-605 Zoning Consistency Statement
votes.notes: Statutory consistency finding for Sharon Road Apartments.
votes.discussion_detail: Council concluded action on Item 22 by voting on the statutory NCGS 160D-605 consistency and reasonableness statement supporting the PDR 10.62 zoning designation. Consistent with standard procedure following final rezoning passage, all seven Council members voted aye 7-0.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting March 18, 2024
disagreements.issue: Sharon Road Apartments Annexation, Off-Site Crosswalk, and Lick Creek Protection (Item 22)
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-3 on annexing 24.87 acres on Wake Forest Highway for 260 apartments, pitting infill housing and commercial adjacency against off-site pedestrian safety, driveway connectivity, and Lick Creek impacts.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve annexation and PDR 10.62 zoning based on Comprehensive Plan policy compliance, commercial adjacency, and added proffers.
side_a_arguments: Project met or exceeded 23 of 25 Comprehensive Plan policies and connects via a 10-ft path directly to neighboring Walgreens retail.
Updated UDO erosion controls apply and the developer added 1% at 100% AMI alongside 5% at 80% AMI (30 years) plus $35,500 for DPS.
Legal staff cautioned that Nollan/Dolan limits an off-site $80k-$100k ADA signalized crossing and blanket denials risk a de facto East Durham moratorium.
disagreements.side_b_position: Deny the discretionary annexation and Utility Extension Agreement due to unsafe NC 98 pedestrian crossings, private-driveway connectivity, and watershed impacts.
side_b_arguments: Without an ADA-accessible crosswalk across Wake Forest Highway/Sharon Road, bus riders and walkers face severe safety hazards.
Counting a private driveway as street connectivity circumvents public street standards, and blasting/grading threaten Lick Creek.
Buffer, green-building, and affordability commitments fell short of the site's environmental risks.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and UEA passed 4-3, followed by 6-1 approval of the PDR 10.62 zoning ordinance.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting March 18, 2024
disagreements.issue: Ruling Public-Hearing Remarks Out of Order and Chamber Fire-Code Access
disagreements.summary: Mayor Williams ruled DeDreana Freeman out of order during the Pickett Road hearing for thanking budget speakers, and later addressed resident frustration over locked doors tied to chamber capacity limits.
disagreements.side_a_position: Allow Council members broader latitude to acknowledge residents waiting through long hearings and keep chamber access open.
side_a_arguments: Residents who stayed for hours to participate in civic hearings deserve Council acknowledgment and unobstructed building entry.
Strict gavel enforcement on non-substantive thank-yous feels unduly punitive toward colleagues.
disagreements.side_b_position: Enforce germaneness rules during statutory zoning public hearings and uphold fire-marshal occupancy lockouts.
side_b_arguments: Council rules require remarks during an advertised zoning hearing to stay strictly germane to the specific land-use case on the floor.
Fire-code capacity caps legally require limiting entry once chambers reach maximum occupancy.
disagreements.resolution: Procedural ruling stood during the Pickett Road item, and Mayor Williams reiterated fire-code capacity protocols after the Sharon Road vote.

proffers.dps_cash: $35,500 donation to Durham Public Schools ($500 per projected student; increased from $10,000)
proffers.affordable_housing: 6% of units income-restricted for 30 years: 5% at 80% AMI and 1% at 100% AMI (1% at 100% AMI added at hearing)
proffers.environmental_tree: Minimum 24% tree coverage (above code minimum); native tree plantings; 100-ft stream buffers; reduced from 2 stream crossings to 1 combined vehicular/utility crossing; stormwater control measures and active open space outside stream buffers; 4 EV charging stations; subject to new UDO mass grading and erosion rules
proffers.transit_infrastructure: 10-foot shared-use path along NC 98 and Sharon Road frontages connecting to existing sidewalk up to Walgreens; turn lanes in both directions on Sharon Road; right-in/right-out access on NC 98 and full access on Sharon Road aligned with Ravenstone
other_proffers: Maximum building height limits and recreational open space
Declined off-site crosswalk/ADA ramp/audible signal package at NC 98 & Sharon Rd ($80k-$100k cost) and declined NGBS certification

member_justifications.stance_summary: Cook opposed annexation, questioning the dropped off-site ADA crosswalk at NC 98 and Sharon Road, the lack of a full TIA, and the severe turbidity observed in Lick Creek. She argued the added 1% at 100% AMI is income-restricted rather than affordable under Durham's definition, and pressed the developer on stream crossings and creek protection.
member_justifications.key_quote: You talked about adding a single percentage point of—and I want to be very clear—that's income restricted, it's not affordable housing at 100% as per our definition, but most of the commentary that you got from the commission was about that environmental impact and about that traffic study.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Rist probed whether street impact fees could help fund pedestrian crossing improvements at NC 98 and Sharon Road and asked staff how blasting damages and Planning Commission no-vote records are handled before voting in favor of the project.
member_justifications.key_quote: It's a question about blasting and responsibility for addressing the costs to homeowners from blasting... other cities provide like a fund or some way to ensure that homeowners are not harmed.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Freeman voted against both annexation and rezoning (the lone nay on rezoning), criticising the omission of ADA-compliant crosswalk ramps and signals on a 45-50 mph road as discriminatory against non-drivers and raising concerns about Community Development staffing for long-term affordability monitoring.
member_justifications.key_quote: I had a question just regarding the ADA compliance package—I'm concerned that it sounds like discrimination against anyone who's not in a vehicle with ADA compliance around what we're doing and planning.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Middleton supported the 9-4 Planning Commission recommendation, praising the 6% 30-year affordability proffer and arguing that denying applications meeting newly tightened UDO rules amounts to an unfair de facto moratorium after taking application fees. He contended transit follows density and the proposal was superior to past suburban developments.
member_justifications.key_quote: If we're going to have a de facto moratorium in an area, if we're not going to do any more development, then we have to say that at the beginning of the process—we can't take an application fee, go through the whole process knowing full well that we are operating under a de facto moratorium.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Williams voted in favor, citing supply-and-demand economics and legal limits that prevent the city from forcing developers to build off-site crosswalks not directly connected to the site. He welcomed the fees, paths, and proffers secured at no direct cost to taxpayers.
member_justifications.key_quote: I can't force someone to do something that's not connected to their site... so I appreciate all of the fees we did get already because it helps continue to fund this entire process.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Although Baker stated he supported apartments on the site in principle and praised the idea of a pedestrian crossing, he opposed annexation because the project lacked NGBS green building certification, relied on private parking-lot driveways to bypass public street connectivity rules, kept open space under private HOA control, and sat amid unsustainable auto-centric sprawl in southeast Durham without planned transit.
member_justifications.key_quote: As we have seen in southeast Durham, we have not been building a sustainable, inclusive, walkable city... this site is situated within the chaos that has been created in southeast Durham, and that makes this a really difficult decision.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Caballero voted in favor, emphasizing North Carolina's preemption limits on local exactions (such as off-site crosswalks and NCDOT's 96% highway funding mandate) and arguing council must judge each rezoning incrementally against the Comprehensive Plan. Because the project met 23 of 25 policies and sat next to walkable commercial uses like Walgreens and shopping centers, she supported approval.
member_justifications.key_quote: A rezoning is for the case in front of me, and this is better because it is adjacent to commercial, it is going to be walkable in a much better way than some of the other things that we have approved, so I will be supporting it.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session March 7, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: At the March 7, 2024 work session, all seven Council members met to review consent agenda items, hear the GoDurham FY 2023 Annual Report, and set the agenda for the upcoming regular meeting. Council passed three procedural motions unanimously (7-0) to accept and enter an attorney-client closed session and to settle the upcoming meeting agenda, while debating pulled items on board/commission attendance, 30-year affordable housing expirations, and 911 alternate routing with Fayetteville. Transportation Director Sean Egan also briefed Council on GoDurham's 19% ridership growth, operator safety and wage increases, 18 electric buses on order, and future funding pressures for fare-free transit once federal pandemic aid expires.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Council Announcements, and Closed Session Priority Request
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members shared updates on federal HUD officials visiting Durham Housing Authority properties including McDougle Terrace, upcoming proposals for the 505 Chapel Hill Street site, and Mayor Leonardo Williams's attendance at the Yale CEO & Mayors Summit in Washington, D.C. City Attorney requested a closed session at the end of regular business under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3) regarding a settlement demand for an unfiled liability action.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Approved 7-0 (two procedural motions for closed session)

agenda_items.title: Public Comment: Council Decorum and Youth Investment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident Donna Stanback criticized council members for making derogatory remarks toward residents who spoke on infrastructure, environment, and the comprehensive plan at the March 4 meeting. D'Warren Langley urged Council to prioritize boys and young men of color in the upcoming budget and policy decisions.

agenda_items.title: Boards, Committees, Commissions, and Task Forces CY 2023 Annual Attendance Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pulled by Carl Rist and Leonardo Williams; City Clerk staff explained that members below 50% attendance are contacted by email, phone, and letter before formal removal. Rist and Williams questioned whether Durham maintains too many boards and commissions (29 managed by the Clerk) and suggested an audit of board necessity and quorum impacts, while the City Attorney reviewed state conflict-of-interest rules (N.C.G.S. 14-234.3) restricting council votes on nonprofit contracts.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Forwarded on Consent Agenda (no work session vote)

agenda_items.title: Trails at Twin Lakes Apartment Homes Multifamily Housing Revenue Bonds ($5.1M)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pulled by Nate Baker; Community Development Director Reginald Johnson confirmed the 30-year affordability period follows NCHFA Low-Income Housing Tax Credit QAP rules and that Durham is only serving as the IRS-required conduit jurisdiction for DHA-issued bonds with no city debt or city funds. Baker, Carl Rist, and DeDreana Freeman urged staff to build a comprehensive database tracking all income-restricted and proffered affordable units—including bedroom counts and expiration dates—to prepare for 15- and 30-year affordability cliffs.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Forwarded on Consent Agenda (no work session vote)

agenda_items.title: 911 Alternate Call Routing Interlocal Agreement with City of Fayetteville
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pulled by Mark-Anthony Middleton; Emergency Communications Director Randy Beeman clarified that the agreement is a statewide ESInet requirement among 127 PSAPs solely for catastrophic facility incapacity while staff relocate to a backup center, not for daily staffing shortages as media reports had implied. DeDreana Freeman and Middleton reiterated support for statewide efforts to classify 911 telecommunicators as first responders.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Forwarded on Consent Agenda (no work session vote)

agenda_items.title: ARPA Project Right-of-Way Tree Watering Contract (Jumping Buddies LLC dba Pit Stop Pressure Washing)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pulled by Nate Baker; General Services Assistant Director Kevin Lilly and Urban Forestry Supervisor Dan Hickey explained that summer tree watering coincides with peak mowing and pruning workloads and past attempts to use seasonal hires failed. City Manager Wanda Page noted that one-time ARPA funds are well suited for contracted deployment.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Forwarded on Consent Agenda (no work session vote)

agenda_items.title: ARPA Project Right-of-Way Tree Planting Contract (Davis Landscape Ltd.)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pulled by Nate Baker; staff explained that the ~$900 per-tree unit price reflects larger balled-and-burlapped street trees with higher survival rates than bare-root stock (which costs roughly one-third as much), and covers purchase, transport, warehousing, installation, and a one-year replacement warranty.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Forwarded on Consent Agenda (no work session vote)

agenda_items.title: GoDurham Fiscal Year 2023 Annual Report Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Director Sean Egan reported a 19% ridership increase (+910,000 trips, second-highest in NC), restoration to 100% of 2020 service levels in January 2024, operator wage increases above $19.65/hr, protective barriers on 100% of buses, and 18 battery-electric buses ordered for 2026 via federal/state grants. Council members questioned operator safety against assaults and gunfire, preventable crash rates, and how Durham will sustain fare-free service once federal COVID funds run out after FY25 (with a $374,000 County DIME block grant covering ~20% of fare loss).

agenda_items.title: Upcoming Work Session Requests, State of the City, Board Nominations, and Settling the Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council gave informal consensus for April work session presentations by Justice Matters, Sister Cities of Durham (Kunshan MOU), and Discover Durham, and Javiera Caballero and Mayor Williams previewed the April 9 State of the City and a tri-board City-County-DPS housing task force. City Clerk reported two board nominations, and Council voted to settle the upcoming meeting agenda (Consent 1-18; GBA Public Hearings 20-22) before recessing to closed session.

votes.item_title: Accept City Attorney's Priority Item to Hold a Closed Session
votes.notes: Vote conducted by raising left hand at Mayor's request to separate priority-item acceptance from the statutory closed session motion.
votes.discussion_detail: The City Attorney presented one priority item requesting a closed session at the end of regular business for attorney-client consultation. Mayor Leonardo Williams noted that he had previously waited until the end of meetings and reminded Council that two separate motions are required: one to accept the priority item onto the agenda and a second reciting the statutory closed-session basis. Council members promptly moved, seconded, and approved accepting the City Attorney's priority item by a unanimous show of hands with all seven members present.

votes.item_title: Hold Closed Session Pursuant to N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3) for Attorney-Client Consultation
votes.notes: Closed session held at the conclusion of the work session concerning handling of a settlement demand for a yet-to-be-filed liability action.
votes.discussion_detail: Following acceptance of the priority item, the City Attorney read the formal statutory language to hold a closed session pursuant to North Carolina General Statute 143-318.11(a)(3) for attorney-client consultation concerning the handling of a settlement demand for a yet-to-be-filed liability action. Mayor Williams entertained a motion on the language as read. Council approved the motion unanimously by voice vote with no debate, scheduling the closed session for the end of the work session.

meetings.title: Durham City Council March 4, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: At the March 4, 2024 regular meeting, City Council voted 2-4 to reject a three-year renewal contract with SoundThinking, Inc. for the ShotSpotter gunshot detection system following extensive public opposition and debate over the Duke Wilson Center pilot evaluation. Council also voted 4-2 to annex and extend utilities to Olive Branch Reserve North (280 townhomes and duplexes) over unanimous 10-0 Planning Commission opposition and neighborhood warnings about Martin Branch Creek sediment pollution, before approving the rezoning ordinance and consistency statement 6-0. In addition, Council unanimously (6-0) adopted the Consent Agenda and approved two other West Durham rezonings: Old West Farms Durham (Alabama Ave wedding venue) and Aura Green Hill (440 multifamily units including 39 affordable units on Hillsboro Road).

agenda_items.title: Proclamations and Excused Absence of Council Member DeDreana Freeman
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members read proclamations recognizing March 2024 as American Red Cross Month (Chelsea Cook), March 20, 2024 as Meatout Day (Carl Rist), and April 2024 as Arab American Heritage Month (Mark-Anthony Middleton). Council then voted 6-0 to excuse DeDreana Freeman's absence and reminded residents to bring photo ID for the March 5 primary election.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Adoption
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams read the Consent Agenda covering board appointments, sales tax distribution interlocal agreement, Justice Matters and El Centro Hispano contracts, HOPWA amendment, ARPA wealth-building contract, parks and street maintenance contracts, the 2023 Q4 crime report, and transit/IT contracts, with Item 17 held on the General Business Agenda.

agenda_items.title: Contract with SoundThinking, Inc. for ShotSpotter Gunshot Detection Response Services
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chief Patrice Andrews, Analytical Services Manager Jason Schiess, and Dr. Philip Cook were available as nearly 20 residents and advocates spoke overwhelmingly against renewing ShotSpotter, citing the Wilson Center report showing 91% of ShotSpotter-only alerts were unconfirmed and no statistical gains in arrests or gun violence reduction. Council members Cook, Baker, Rist, and Caballero argued the data did not justify the multi-year expenditure (~$658,500) and urged preventive investments, while Mayor Williams and Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton defended the 1.2-minute faster response time and potential life saved.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Failed 2-4 (Williams and Middleton Aye; Baker, Caballero, Cook, Rist Nay)

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation and Zoning Map Change: Olive Branch Reserve North
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mill Creek Residential requested annexation, a utility extension agreement, and rezoning of 87.7 acres (48.1 developable acres) on Olive Branch Road from RR to PDR 3.700 for up to 280 rental townhomes and duplexes, raising its affordability proffer at the hearing to 6% (17 units) for 30 years at 80% and 100% AMI alongside stream buffers and a 300-ft wildlife corridor. Over a dozen residents, Preserve Rural Durham members, and Neuse Riverkeeper Samantha Krop opposed the project, citing Martin Branch Creek turbidity at 40x state limits, 10-0 Planning Commission denial, traffic, and EMS response delays.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Annexation/UEA Passed 4-2 (Baker, Cook Nay); Rezoning & Consistency Passed 6-0

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: Old West Farms Durham (903 Alabama Ave & 805/809 Trent Dr)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Applicants Brian and Melissa O'Hara sought rezoning from RU-5(2) and CG to CG(D) to adaptive-reuse the historic 80-year-old West Durham Pentecostal Church as a wedding venue and potential wine bar, proffering a 5-year non-demolition commitment and adding prohibitions on nightclubs and simple convenience stores at the hearing. Neighborhood working group members supported the plan while requesting traffic calming at the Green/Oakland/Alabama/Trent intersection; one neighbor asked for a short deferral to tighten parking-lot landscaping.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: Aura Green Hill (3438, 3454, 3456 Hillsboro Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Trinsic Residential requested rezoning 12.6 acres from PDR 59.102 and IL to PDR 34.923—incorporating two adjacent motel parcels into a previously approved site—for up to 440 multifamily and townhouse-style apartment units, retaining 39 affordable units (60%, 80%, and 100% AMI for 30 years), a 50-ft public park buffer, green building certification, and $123,000 for DPS. Watts Hospital-Hillandale Neighborhood Association representatives supported the 8-0 Planning Commission-recommended project and noted a $35,000 verbal developer commitment for Sprunt Avenue speed humps.

votes.item_title: Excuse Absence of Council Member DeDreana Freeman
votes.notes: DeDreana Freeman requested an excused absence prior to the meeting.
votes.discussion_detail: During roll call at the start of the March 4 meeting, the City Clerk noted that Council Member DeDreana Freeman had requested an excused absence. Following ceremonial proclamations, Mayor Leonardo Williams entertained a motion to formally accept Freeman's excused absence. The motion was moved, seconded, and approved unanimously (6-0) via the Clerk's electronic voting system.

votes.item_title: Authorize Three-Year Contract with SoundThinking, Inc. for ShotSpotter Gunshot Detection Services (Item 17)
votes.notes: Clerk announced motion failed 4-2 (4 Nays, 2 Ayes; DeDreana Freeman absent/excused). Public speakers cited ~$658,500 3-year total cost (transcript ASR truncated the Mayor's reading of the contract amount).
votes.discussion_detail: Following the Duke Wilson Center evaluation, more than 15 residents and advocates (including Damon Williams, Samuel Scarboro, Leslie St. Dre, Brittany Price, Kesha Mallette, and Elle Gent) urged Council to reject the three-year ShotSpotter renewal, while East Durham resident and city employee Wilma Oliver spoke in favor. Council Members Chelsea Cook, Nate Baker, Carl Rist, and Javiera Caballero argued against renewal, emphasizing that 91% of ShotSpotter-only alerts were unconfirmed, 50 of 52 gunshot-wound incidents already had 911 calls, regression analysis showed no gains in arrests, evidence collection, or witness interviews, focus group residents lacked trust in the tool, and resources were better invested in 911 staffing, prevention, and HEART. Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton and Mayor Leonardo Williams argued in favor, contending ShotSpotter reduced median response time by 1.2 minutes, potentially saved a life, had backing from Police Chief Patrice Andrews, the Sheriff, and NCCU, and helped an understaffed police force (~120 vacancies). The motion failed 2-4, ending the city's ShotSpotter contract.

votes.item_title: Annex Olive Branch Reserve North and Authorize Utility Extension Agreement with MCRT SFR Investments LLC (Item 25, Motion 1)
votes.notes: Planning Commission had recommended denial 10-0. At the hearing, Mill Creek Residential increased its affordable housing proffer from 3% for 10 years at 80% AMI to 6% (17 units) for 30 years (3% at 80% AMI, 3% at 100% AMI).
votes.discussion_detail: Mill Creek Residential sought annexation, utility extension, and rezoning of 87.7 acres along Olive Branch Road for up to 280 townhouse and duplex rentals, committing to preserve ~45% of the site (including a 300-ft wildlife corridor and 100-ft stream buffers), 24% tree canopy, 100-year storm detention, $23,000 for DPS, and 17 income-restricted units for 30 years. Over a dozen neighbors, Preserve Rural Durham advocates, and Neuse Riverkeeper Samantha Krop testified against the project due to severe sediment pollution in Martin Branch Creek (40x state turbidity standards), blasting impacts on nearby wells, traffic congestion on Olive Branch Road, EMS response delays, and the 10-0 Planning Commission denial. Nate Baker and Chelsea Cook voted No, arguing the car-centric development violated the Comprehensive Plan, added heavy traffic and environmental risk, and offered 100% AMI units outside the plan's 30-80% AMI affordability definition. Middleton, Caballero, Rist, and Williams voted Aye, noting the project was consistent with 22 of 25 comp plan policies, triggered stricter new UDO erosion controls, funded road improvements, and avoided 129 high-priced by-right single-family homes on wells and septic.

votes.item_title: Adopt Ordinance Amending UDO to Rezone Olive Branch Reserve North to PDR 3.700 (Item 25, Motion 2)
votes.notes: Took property out of Residential Rural Falls/Jordan District B (County jurisdiction) and established PDR 3.700 Falls/Jordan District B (City jurisdiction) after annexation passed 4-2.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately following the 4-2 approval of the Olive Branch Reserve North annexation and utility extension agreement, Council took up the companion UDO zoning map change ordinance establishing PDR 3.700 City jurisdiction zoning in place of County Residential Rural zoning. After extensive public testimony and Council debate on environmental safeguards, roadway improvements, and housing mix during the consolidated public hearing, all six members present voted Aye on the zoning ordinance once the annexation had been approved.

votes.item_title: Adopt Consistency Statement for Olive Branch Reserve North Rezoning (Item 25, Motion 3)
votes.notes: Adopted statutory consistency statement pursuant to N.C.G.S. 160D-605.
votes.discussion_detail: As required by North Carolina General Statute 160D-605 following approval of the Olive Branch Reserve North zoning map amendment, Council considered the statutory consistency statement. Staff had reported that the PDR 3.700 designation matched the Mixed Residential Neighborhood and Recreation/Open Space place types and 22 of 25 applicable Comprehensive Plan policies. Council moved, seconded, and adopted the consistency statement 6-0.

votes.item_title: Adopt Ordinance Amending UDO to Rezone Old West Farms Durham to CG(D) (Item 26, Motion 1)
votes.notes: Rezones 0.61 acres at 903 Alabama Ave and 805/809 Trent Dr from RU-5(2) and CG to CG(D) with 5-year non-demolition commitment for the historic church.
votes.discussion_detail: Applicants Brian and Melissa O'Hara requested CG(D) zoning to preserve and convert the 80-year-old West Durham Pentecostal Church at 903 Alabama Avenue into a Carolina Grove wedding/event venue and potential wine bar. Their attorney Keenan Conder added two additional prohibited uses (nightclubs and simple convenience stores) at the hearing on top of prior proffers limiting height, signage, and demolition for five years. Neighborhood working group members Dan Welch, Tom Clark, and Kathy Shipp spoke in support (requesting traffic calming at Green/Oakland/Alabama/Trent), while neighbor John Wood supported the concept but asked for a short deferral on parking landscaping; Conder confirmed landscaping and impervious-surface reductions would be enforced at site plan review, and Council approved the rezoning 6-0.

votes.item_title: Adopt Consistency Statement for Old West Farms Durham Rezoning (Item 26, Motion 2)
votes.notes: Staff recommended updating the Place Type Map to Neighborhood Services upon approval.
votes.discussion_detail: Following approval of the Old West Farms Durham zoning map change, Council considered the statutory consistency statement under N.C.G.S. 160D-605. Because the CG(D) zoning differed from the property's Transit Opportunity Area and Established Residential place type designations, planning staff recommended updating the place type designation to Neighborhood Services. Council moved, seconded, and passed the consistency statement unanimously 6-0.

votes.item_title: Adopt Ordinance Amending UDO to Rezone Aura Green Hill to PDR 34.923 (Item 27, Motion 1)
votes.notes: Rezones 12.599 acres at 3438, 3454, 3456 Hillsboro Rd from PDR 59.102 and IL to PDR 34.923 for up to 440 multifamily/townhouse-style units; Planning Commission recommended 8-0.
votes.discussion_detail: Collier Marsh represented Trinsic Residential in expanding a previously approved January 2023 project by incorporating two adjacent motel parcels along Hillsboro Road to build up to 440 multifamily and townhouse-style apartment units. The proposal maintained 39 income-restricted units (13 each at 60%, 80%, and 100% AMI for 30 years), a 50-foot public-access park buffer, no increase in impervious surface, green building certification, and a $123,000 DPS donation. Watts Hospital-Hillandale Neighborhood Association representatives Doc Doyle and Tom Miller spoke in favor and highlighted a verbal $35,000 developer commitment toward Sprunt Avenue traffic calming; Council approved the rezoning 6-0.

votes.item_title: Authorize Utility Extension Agreement with Trinsic Acquisition Company LLC for Aura Green Hill (Item 27, Motion 2)
votes.notes: Companion utility extension agreement for Aura Green Hill.
votes.discussion_detail: As the second motion on the Aura Green Hill application, Council considered authorizing the City Manager to enter into a utility extension agreement with Trinsic Acquisition Company LLC for the 12.599-acre Hillsboro Road development. Consistent with the Transit Opportunity Area designation and the 8-0 Planning Commission recommendation, Council approved the utility extension agreement 6-0.

votes.item_title: Adopt Consistency Statement for Aura Green Hill Rezoning (Item 27, Motion 3)
votes.notes: Adopted statutory consistency statement pursuant to N.C.G.S. 160D-605.
votes.discussion_detail: Concluding action on Item 27, Council voted on the statutory consistency statement required under N.C.G.S. 160D-605 for the Aura Green Hill rezoning. Staff confirmed the PDR 34.923 zoning was consistent with the Transit Opportunity Area designation on the Place Type Map. The motion passed unanimously 6-0, and Council adjourned at 11:20 PM.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council March 4, 2024
disagreements.issue: Renewal of ShotSpotter (SoundThinking, Inc.) Gunshot Detection Contract (Item 17)
disagreements.summary: Council split 2-4 on whether to execute a new three-year contract with SoundThinking, Inc. for ShotSpotter acoustic gunshot detection in a three-square-mile area after reviewing the independent Duke Wilson Center pilot evaluation.
disagreements.side_a_position: Do not renew the ShotSpotter contract and redirect city resources toward 911 staffing, HEART, and preventive community investments.
side_a_arguments: 91% of ShotSpotter-only alerts (752 of 825) had no confirmed gunfire evidence, creating ~2.3 extra Priority 2 two-car dispatches per day.

50 of 52 gunshot-wound incidents already generated 911 calls, and regression analysis showed no statistically significant gains in arrests, evidence collection, or witness interviews from faster 911 response.
The evaluation could not establish any reduction in overall gun violence, and focus-group/public feedback showed strong community opposition and distrust in East Durham.
Company lobbying tactics (including social media ads targeting council members) and moving goalposts from violence reduction to response speed undermined confidence.
disagreements.side_b_position: Approve the three-year ShotSpotter renewal as an investigative and rapid-response tool alongside HEART and DPD.
side_b_arguments: ShotSpotter reduced median Priority 2 gunshot response time by 1.2 minutes (3.6 minutes at the 90th percentile) and plausibly saved one shooting victim's life via faster officer first aid.
79% of shooting incidents in the pilot area were initiated by ShotSpotter without an initial 911 call, and ShotSpotter-only calls produced 7 arrests and 71 evidence recoveries.
Police Chief Patrice Andrews, the Sheriff, North Carolina Central University, and some East Durham residents supported keeping the tool while DPD faces ~120 officer vacancies.
Durham implemented strict guardrails preventing stops/detentions based solely on ShotSpotter alerts, avoiding over-policing abuses seen in other cities.
disagreements.resolution: Motion to renew failed 2-4; the ShotSpotter contract was not renewed.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council March 4, 2024
disagreements.issue: Olive Branch Reserve North Annexation and Density vs. Environmental & Infrastructure Impacts (Item 25)
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-2 on annexing and extending utilities to an 87.7-acre Mill Creek Residential townhome/duplex project on Olive Branch Road after a 10-0 Planning Commission recommendation for denial and heavy opposition from Preserve Rural Durham and the Neuse Riverkeeper.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve annexation and rezoning to secure environmental protections, 17 income-restricted rentals, roadway upgrades, and duplex/townhome housing diversity.
side_a_arguments: The proposal meets 22 of 25 Comprehensive Plan policies, preserves 45% of the site (300-ft wildlife corridor and 100-ft stream buffers), and will be governed by Durham's stricter 2023 UDO erosion/mass-grading rules.
Denying the rezoning invites by-right development of 129 expensive single-family homes ($600K-$800K+) on wells and septic with fewer protections and no developer-funded NCDOT road improvements.
The developer increased its proffer at the hearing to 6% (17 units) income-restricted for 30 years (3% at 80% AMI, 3% at 100% AMI) plus $23,000 for DPS without city subsidy.
disagreements.side_b_position: Deny the annexation and rezoning due to Comprehensive Plan inconsistency, severe sedimentation in Martin Branch Creek, and unmitigated car-centric sprawl.
side_b_arguments: The Planning Commission voted unanimously (10-0) to recommend denial because the single-use development is miles from groceries/transit and entrenches auto-dependent sprawl.

Martin Branch Creek is already severely impaired (measured at 40x state turbidity limits), and Southeast Durham faces cumulative impacts from 41 active developments, blasting damage, overcrowded schools, and 13-minute EMS response times.
100% AMI units do not meet the Comprehensive Plan's affordable housing target (30-80% AMI) and are insufficient to offset the environmental and infrastructure costs.
disagreements.resolution: Annexation and utility extension agreement passed 4-2; Council then voted 6-0 on the companion zoning ordinance and consistency statement.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Baker voted against annexation (before voting aye on zoning/consistency once annexed), calling rapid clear-cutting in southeast Durham an environmental catastrophe and referencing riverkeeper Samantha Krop's turbidity measurements in Martin Branch. Citing the unanimous 10-0 Planning Commission denial, he argued the isolated residential subdivision is disconnected, car-centric sprawl inconsistent with the Mixed Residential Neighborhood place type.
member_justifications.key_quote: It's hard to describe it as anything but corporate developer pillaging of the land, of the environment... what we are replacing valuable forest and farmland out there with is the most unsustainable, car-centric, climate-denying development that we could possibly be building.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Cook opposed annexation, highlighting severe cumulative impacts on waterways, schools, and traffic—1,200 to 2,100 daily trips from this site alone alongside nearby approved subdivisions—and warning that commercial walkability will never materialize if all surrounding land is developed purely residentially. She also noted the 3% at 100% AMI proffer falls outside Durham's formal affordable housing definition.
member_justifications.key_quote: We cannot rely on commercial and walkability things coming to this area when literally all of the land is being developed for residential... what we haven't seen today is anything that really tackles the huge impact that this is going to have on the area.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Rist welcomed the developer's upgraded proffer extending affordability to 6% for 30 years (3% at 80% AMI and 3% at 100% AMI), asking staff whether 100% AMI meets the Comprehensive Plan's affordability target before supporting the project.
member_justifications.key_quote: We've now increased it to a total of 6% with 3% at 80% AMI, 3% at 100% AMI, and we've increased that deed restriction to 30 years.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Middleton supported annexation and rezoning, pushing back against what he viewed as a de facto moratorium in southeast Durham after the council had already adopted residents' proposed UDO erosion and tree-preservation rules. He argued that rejecting projects with environmental and affordable proffers only leaves high-priced by-right single-family homes on wells and septic.
member_justifications.key_quote: If any council member thinks that a moratorium is the appropriate approach, then vote no... every yes we say is no to something else, and I don't want large high-priced single family homes on septic, on wells out there if I have to choose.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Caballero supported the proposal as an '88% project' meeting or exceeding 22 of 25 applicable Comprehensive Plan policies. She emphasized that the private affordable units, native tree plantings, and state-road improvements represent incremental progress far superior to adjacent older subdivisions or by-right single-family homes.
member_justifications.key_quote: They brought us an 88% project... we incrementally in rezonings have to get slowly better and slowly better, and that is what this project does.

member_justifications.stance_summary: Williams argued against letting 'perfect be the enemy of good', noting 40 of 88 acres remain undeveloped and praising the developer's added post-Planning Commission proffers. He concluded that 280 townhome/duplex rentals with affordable units and road/environmental commitments are clearly preferable to 129 by-right single-family homes.
member_justifications.key_quote: This is a situation where perfect is the enemy of good... 129 single family homes versus what's been offered, for me that's common sense, so I'll be supporting.

meetings.title: City Council Budget Retreat - March 1, 2024 - 9:00 a.m.
meetings.executive_summary: During the full-day FY 2024-25 Budget Retreat (presided over in the morning by Mayor Pro Tempore Mark-Anthony Middleton until Mayor Leonardo Williams arrived), Council reviewed the refreshed Strategic Plan dashboard, Budget Community Conversations findings, $104M in FY25 general CIP requests, $610M in potential November 2024 General Obligation Bond concepts, and ARPA obligations ($1.1M remaining unobligated). In directional straw polls on seven deferred Council budget requests plus one late addition, Council greenlit up to $50,000 for summer Council internships, honoring the pay-and-class study, and $250,000 for Justice Matters' Immigrant Legal Defense Fund, while rejecting recurring funding for 360 Heart of a Champion, referring Hayti Reborn ($3M ask) to staff, and seeing three items withdrawn. Council also clashed over draft FY25 budget guidelines regarding whether employee raises should be tiered rather than a flat 5% across-the-board, and whether to pursue a 2024 GO Bond alongside expected tax increases for staff pay.

agenda_items.title: Strategic Plan Refresh and Public Dashboard Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Strategy and Performance staff Sherry Mehta and Cesalie Hamilton presented the 2023-2026 Strategic Plan structure (5 goals, 15 objectives, 41 initiatives), quarterly DSAP accountability reviews, and the new public dashboard launched in January 2024. Nate Baker and Carl Rist asked about alignment with the Comprehensive Plan and requested clearer outcome-based performance measures by the June update.

agenda_items.title: FY 2024-25 Budget Community Conversations Report (ETR Services)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dr. Jen Gathings and Kesha Martin (ETR Services) presented qualitative findings from four resident budget conversations (255+ attendees, ~60% people of color, ~50% newly engaged), where Affordable Housing (52 highest-priority votes) and Infrastructure/sidewalks/transit (64 highest-priority votes) dominated, alongside prevention-focused Public Safety/HEART and competitive city pay. Council members discussed how to integrate qualitative findings with the Resident Survey and avoid participants speaking on behalf of communities other than their own.

agenda_items.title: FY 2025 Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Christina Reaves outlined $104M in general capital FY25 department requests, $150.1M in enterprise requests (Water & Sewer $126M, Stormwater $24M, Solid Waste $100K), and $16.7M for fleet replacement. Javiera Caballero and DeDreana Freeman requested that staff present the rubric scoring of CIP projects at a public work session before May, and noted a slide swap between Economic Prosperity and Environmental prioritization descriptions.

agenda_items.title: Municipal General Obligation (GO) Bond Exploration (~$610M Portfolio) & Debt Profile
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Department heads presented potential GO Bond buckets totaling ~$610M: $147.4M ($113M unfunded) for 31 miles of sidewalks (Sean Egan), ~$130M for EV charging/efficiency/solar sustainability projects (Stacy Poston), ~$315M-$415M for a new Durham Convention Center and headquarters hotel financing gap (Jori Propst), and Splash & Play aquatic/park redevelopments at Long Meadow, East End, and former Wheels/Merrick-Moore (Wade Walcutt), alongside an update on the fully allocated 2019 $95M housing bond (Reginald Johnson) and a debt capacity briefing by Finance Director Tim Flora. Mayor Pro Tempore Middleton questioned floating a 2024 bond alongside tax hikes for employee pay, while other members debated Convention Center living-wage requirements, park remediation, and June LGC deadlines.

agenda_items.title: American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) Funding Status Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy City Manager Bertha Wimbush reported that $52.8M (including $2M in interest earnings) of Durham's $52M ARPA allocation and interest is obligated, leaving $1.1M unobligated ahead of the December 31, 2024 federal obligation deadline. Council members asked whether the remaining $1.1M could support eviction diversion or rental assistance if tied to COVID-era eligibility periods.

agenda_items.title: City Council Budget Requests — Phase 2 (Deferred/Yellow Items Review)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Facilitated by BMS analyst Lindsay Gavin via non-binding directional straw polls (Green/Red): Council greenlit up to $50,000 for summer Council internships (amended down from $98,500), confirmed honoring the pay-and-class study, and added $250,000 for Justice Matters' Immigrant Legal Defense Fund (2-year extension requested by Caballero). Three requests were withdrawn ($1M first-time homebuyer DPA by Rist, HEART 24-hour team expansion by Caballero, and $25/hr city minimum wage by Baker), while 360 Heart of a Champion ($41,000) received only 1 Green (Cook) and Hayti Reborn Justice Movement ($3M) was referred to Community Safety staff without a dollar figure.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Non-binding straw polls only (no formal votes)

agenda_items.title: FY 2024-25 Budget Guidelines and Employee Pay Plan Structure
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Christina Reaves presented draft budget guidelines maintaining current rates for Debt Service (11.5¢), Solid Waste (5.59¢), Dedicated Housing (3.38¢), Transit (3.75¢), and BID (7¢), allowing a general fund property tax increase (above 31.55¢) to cover pay study market adjustments, capping Water/Sewer (+6.2%) and Stormwater (+$1.55/mo) rate hikes, and proposing 5% average pay-for-performance/step increases across General, Police, and Fire plans (3% part-time). Baker, Rist, and Cook questioned moving general step plans to 5% and urged modeling tiered/graduated raises, while Middleton, Williams, and City Manager Wanda Page argued pay-plan redesigns were outside the market study's scope and could delay raises past June 30; Council reached no formal vote on tax caps.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / Guidelines deferred to upcoming work session and April vote

disagreements.meeting_title: City Council Budget Retreat - March 1, 2024 - 9:00 a.m.
disagreements.issue: FY 2024-25 Budget Guidelines: Uniform 5% Step/Pay-for-Performance Increases vs. Graduated/Tiered Compensation Design
disagreements.summary: Council members disagreed over draft budget guidelines proposing 5% average pay-for-performance and step-plan increases across general, police, and fire employees alongside market adjustments, and whether to cap potential property tax increases now.
disagreements.side_a_position: Explore graduated or flat-dollar raise structures favoring lower-paid workers and review exact fiscal numbers before locking 5% guideline language.
side_a_arguments: Awarding a uniform percentage gives larger dollar raises to top earners than front-line workers; a flat-dollar or tiered model (like Charlotte's 2.5% cap at top tiers) would be more equitable.
Council had not yet seen the full fiscal cost numbers for bumping the general step plan from 4.8%/4% to 5% on top of market adjustments.
disagreements.side_b_position: Keep the existing pay-plan design with 5% step/performance guidelines for FY25 to deliver raises on time by June 30, and defer any structural pay-plan redesign to a future budget cycle.
side_b_arguments: Altering the pay-plan structure is a multi-month classification/redesign project that was not part of the market study's charge and would jeopardize adopting a balanced budget by June 30.
Every employee group—from public works to fire drivers—expects step values and market adjustments to be honored immediately without delaying raises.
Staff still needs Council feedback on maximum acceptable tax-rate increases (noting 1¢ generates ~$4.1M-$4.2M) when balancing market pay adjustments.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken at the retreat; staff will refine numbers and return the draft Budget Guidelines to a March work session ahead of an April formal vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: City Council Budget Retreat - March 1, 2024 - 9:00 a.m.
disagreements.issue: Timing of a 2024 General Obligation Bond Referendum Amid Pay-Study Tax Pressures
disagreements.summary: Council members expressed differing views on whether to place a major GO Bond package (~$300M-$610M across sidewalks, parks, sustainability, and potentially a Convention Center) on the November 2024 ballot given concurrent tax increases needed for employee pay.
disagreements.side_a_position: Defer the GO Bond referendum to 2025 or later to prioritize employee compensation and avoid stacking multiple tax increases in 2024.
side_a_arguments: Funding the employee pay study will already require a substantial property tax increase in FY25, making it difficult to ask voters for bond debt simultaneously.
More time is needed to mount a public education campaign and evaluate whether borrowing substantially accelerates project delivery beyond current CIP pacing.
disagreements.side_b_position: Continue evaluating a 2024 GO Bond package (and public-private/county partnerships for the Convention Center) to address urgent sidewalk, park, and climate backlogs.
side_b_arguments: Sidewalks, safer streets, affordable housing, and neighborhood parks are top resident priorities, and current 2.5 miles/year sidewalk pacing would take 170 years without bond acceleration.
A Convention Center and headquarters hotel partnership with the County and private sector could expand sales and occupancy tax capacity, provided jobs meet living-wage or union standards.
disagreements.resolution: Staff noted that final project selections and a Council resolution would be needed by June 2024 for LGC approval if pursuing a November 2024 ballot referendum; no decision was finalized.

disagreements.meeting_title: City Council Budget Retreat - March 1, 2024 - 9:00 a.m.
disagreements.issue: Direct Line-Item Council Grants to Nonprofits (360 Heart of a Champion & Hayti Reborn Justice Movement)
disagreements.summary: Council debated whether to include Council-initiated recurring grants for 360 Heart of a Champion ($41,000) and Hayti Reborn Justice Movement ($3M) in the FY25 budget guidelines.
disagreements.side_a_position: Support funding 360 Heart of a Champion (at least for one year) and Hayti Reborn's peer-to-peer violence prevention work.
side_a_arguments: Youth summer programming and community-led violence prevention address root causes of gun violence and fill gaps Parks & Recreation cannot cover alone.
Hayti Reborn is asking for $3M over three years ($1M/year) to match County/federal support, and Community Safety staff can set metrics.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject ad hoc recurring line-item earmarks for individual nonprofits without competitive vetting and fiduciary controls.
side_b_arguments: Granting recurring budget lines to specific organizations bypasses competitive RFP/ARPA due diligence and sets an unsustainable precedent when dozens of youth nonprofits have similar needs.
A $3M commitment to one organization is fiscally unrealistic for the City's budget without staff vetting and integration into existing Community Safety operations.
disagreements.resolution: In non-binding straw polls, 360 Heart of a Champion failed to advance (1 Green [Cook], rest Red), and Hayti Reborn was referred to Community Safety staff for analysis without a dollar amount.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session Feb 22, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: At the February 22, 2024 work session (with Chelsea Cook excused absent), Council approved adding the 2023 Q4 Crime Report and the Duke Wilson Center ShotSpotter evaluation as priority presentations (6-0) and entered an attorney-client/real-property closed session at the close of business (6-0). Council heard emotional public comment from GoDurham bus drivers whose Route 8 bus was fired upon in November, received a Haw River Assembly briefing on stream trash traps and erosion control, and reviewed the FY24 Q2 Financial Report showing a projected $7.4M General Fund positive variance driven by vacancy savings. Police Chief Patrice Andrews reported a 3.79% drop in violent crime alongside a 134% surge in motor vehicle thefts and 76% sworn staffing, before Dr. Philip Cook presented the Wilson Center's ShotSpotter findings showing faster response times and 71 evidence recoveries but no detectable productivity gain on 911 calls and 91% unconfirmed ShotSpotter-only alerts.

agenda_items.title: Manager's Priority Items (Items 16 & 24) and City Attorney Introduction
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Wanda Page requested adding Item 16 (2023 Q4 Crime Report) and Item 24 (Duke Wilson Center ShotSpotter Evaluation presentation) as priority items, which Council approved 6-0. City Attorney Kimberly Rehberg introduced new assistant city attorney Sarah Laws, and Mayor Williams read the Consent Agenda (pulling Item 7 himself and Item 17 for Nate Baker).

agenda_items.title: Public Comment: Ceasefire Accountability, Youth Funding, and GoDurham Bus Driver Safety
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Speakers Jeremy Bergren and D'Warren Langley addressed local gun violence, poverty, and Charles Hamilton Houston Foundation youth mentorship funding. Later in the session, GoDurham drivers Julian Mack and Sarah Maxwell described Mack's Route 8 bus being shot up in November 2023 and demanded stronger DPD/DA accountability and safety protections for drivers; Mayor Williams pledged to follow up with staff and the transit contractor.

agenda_items.title: ARPA Project: Road to Wealth Building Project
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pulled by Mayor Williams to check on implementation readiness; Deputy City Manager Bertha Wimbush noted the program spans four sessions with organizer Larry Hester in attendance. Williams said he would connect directly with Hester offline to support community partnerships.

agenda_items.title: Haw River Assembly Presentation on Plastic Pollution and Trash Traps
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Requested by Carl Rist; Madison Haley and Haw Riverkeeper Emily Sutton presented data showing over 40,000 pieces of mostly styrofoam and plastic litter captured in the Third Fork Creek trash trap and plans for a Northeast Creek trap. They urged fencing major commercial litter sources, adopting wildlife-friendly biodegradable erosion control in city projects and the UDO despite state plastic-ban preemption, and expanding public storm-drain education.

agenda_items.title: FY 2023-24 Second Quarter Financial Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Christina Reaves projected a $7.4M positive General Fund variance ($5.9M expenditure savings largely from $4.3M personnel vacancies) and positive variances across Water/Sewer, Transit ($4.1M), Solid Waste, Stormwater ($7.6M), DPAC, and Inspections, offset by a -$326K Parking Fund deficit. Carl Rist questioned how long unfilled vacant FTEs remain budgeted, and Manager Wanda Page explained the city budgets less than 100% of authorized positions to account for anticipated vacancies.

agenda_items.title: 2023 Fourth Quarter Crime Report Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief Patrice Andrews reported a 3.79% drop in violent crime and ~14% decline in robberies (including robberies targeting Hispanic victims), alongside 49 homicides, an 11.8% rise in confirmed shootings (with victims down 13.6%), a 134% jump in auto thefts, a 71.4% homicide clearance rate, and 76% sworn staffing. She detailed 7 violent incidents on GoDurham buses (3 cleared by arrest, 2 pending warrants, and the November shooting still open) and noted 79% of gunshot incidents were initiated by ShotSpotter without 911 calls.

agenda_items.title: Wilson Center ShotSpotter Pilot Evaluation Presentation and Public Feedback
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dr. Philip Cook (Duke/Wilson Center) presented the independent evaluation of Durham's 2023 ShotSpotter pilot: 1,447 alerts (57% ShotSpotter-only), 20% overall confirmation rate (twice as high for 911 calls), 1.2-minute median response-time gain, 7 ShotSpotter-only arrests, 71 evidence recoveries, and 1 life plausibly saved, but no measurable gain in arrests/evidence/witnesses on 911 calls and unknown impact on overall gun violence. Following split comments from Jevonte Dunston (pro) and Abdul Nasser of Campaign Zero (con), Council debated the findings and placed Item 17 on the March 4 General Business Agenda.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Item 17 placed on March 4 GBA (no work session vote)

agenda_items.title: Board Nominations, Settled Agenda Report, and Closed Session Motion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Clerk nominated Glenda Jang (Durham Affordable Housing Implementation Committee) and Asme Kou (Human Relations Commission), and City Manager Wanda Page reported the settled March 4 agenda (Consent 1-16, 18-21; GBA 17; Public Hearings 25-27). Council then voted 6-0 to enter closed session under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5) regarding real property contract negotiations.

votes.item_title: Approve City Manager's Priority Items (Items 16 and 24)
votes.notes: Vote conducted by raising hands. Chelsea Cook was granted an excused absence.
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager Wanda Page presented two priority items for the February 22 work session: adding a 20-minute presentation for Item 16 (2023 Fourth Quarter Crime Report) and adding Item 24 (the Wilson Center's independent ShotSpotter evaluation presentation) to the agenda packet for approximately 20 minutes. Mayor Williams entertained a motion to approve the Manager's priority items. Council moved, seconded, and approved adding both presentations unanimously (6-0) by a show of hands.

votes.item_title: Hold Closed Session Pursuant to N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5) for Real Property Negotiation Instructions
votes.notes: Closed session held in the committee room to seek instruction in negotiating material terms of a proposed real property acquisition/purchase/option/exchange/lease contract. Chelsea Cook absent/excused.
votes.discussion_detail: At the conclusion of the work session—after Baker confirmed Item 17 (ShotSpotter contract) should move to the March 4 General Business Agenda and the City Manager reported the settled agenda—Mayor Williams called for a closed session under Item 35. Assisted by the City Attorney/Clerk, the Mayor read the statutory motion under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5) to seek instruction on negotiating material terms for a real property contract. Council moved, seconded, and passed the motion unanimously (6-0) by voice vote before moving upstairs to the committee room.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session Feb 22, 2024
disagreements.issue: Interpretation of the Duke Wilson Center ShotSpotter Pilot Evaluation (Items 17 & 24)
disagreements.summary: Following Dr. Philip Cook's presentation of the Wilson Center evaluation, Council members diverged in how they weighed ShotSpotter's response-time gains against its opportunity costs and null impact on 911 investigative productivity.
disagreements.side_a_position: Question the cost-effectiveness and opportunity costs of ShotSpotter given null investigative productivity findings and limited community support.
side_a_arguments: Faster 911 response times under ShotSpotter produced no detectable improvement in arrests, evidence collection, or witness interviews.
In addition to the $225,000+ contract cost, ShotSpotter generated 2.3 extra two-car Priority 2 dispatches per day (2% of citywide Priority 2 deployments), creating officer opportunity costs.
The impact on overall gun violence could not be determined, and focus-group residents voiced skepticism about spending priorities.
disagreements.side_b_position: View the evaluation as validating ShotSpotter as an effective response tool that should not be unfairly judged on gun-violence prevention.
side_b_arguments: Proponents and SoundThinking never claimed ShotSpotter would reduce gun violence; it was intended as a response tool and succeeded in cutting median response time by 1.2 minutes (5:11 in Q4).

ShotSpotter-only alerts produced 7 arrests (+32%), nearly doubled evidence collection cases, and plausibly saved one victim's life—making it worth the ~$200K/year cost just as Council funds HEART without proof of lives saved.
Durham's strict guardrails prevented Chicago-style over-policing, and residents in high-gunfire areas asked for police protection.
disagreements.resolution: Council placed Item 17 (three-year SoundThinking renewal contract) on the March 4, 2024 General Business Agenda for formal deliberation and vote.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Feb 19 2024
meetings.executive_summary: At its February 19, 2024 regular meeting, Durham City Council issued proclamations for Future Business Leaders of America Week and Local Government Communications, heard announcements on the budget retreat's GFOA award, Vision Zero, and Ellerbe Creek sediment runoff, and read a 43-item Consent Agenda alongside General Business Item 46. Following hours of deliberations and public engagement (with middle segments omitted in the digest), Council voted 5-2 to adopt Item 46, a resolution supporting a ceasefire and an end to violence between Israel and Palestine, with Mayor Leonardo Williams and Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton voting no. After passage, Mayor Williams declined to entertain Council Member DeDreana Freeman's motion to amend the resolution to include the word 'genocide,' adjourning the meeting at 12:54 AM.

agenda_items.title: Mayoral Proclamations and Council Announcements on Budget, Vision Zero, and Ellerbe Creek
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams proclaimed FBLA Week (Feb 11–17) and Durham's first Local Government Communications recognition. Council members recognized budget staff for earning the GFOA Distinguished Budget Presentation Award (Chelsea Cook), noted multi-department Vision Zero street-design talks and county coordination over Ellerbe Creek sediment runoff (Nate Baker), and reminded residents about early voting and photo ID rules before City Attorney Kim Rehberg and the Clerk reported no priority items.

agenda_items.title: Reading of Consent Agenda Items 1–43 and Item 46
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Williams read the consent docket spanning board appointments, 2023 commission annual reports, surplus property conveyance to Durham Community Land Trustees (Item 17), a non-discrimination ordinance amendment (Item 24), stormwater/watershed agreements (Items 27, 35, 36), bike/pedestrian and Woodcroft Parkway contracts (Items 32–33), water survey bill credits (Item 37), annexations/rezonings/text amendment (Items 40–43), and Item 46; the consent vote occurred during the middle portion omitted from the transcript digest.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / Consent vote omitted in digest truncation

agenda_items.title: Resolution Supporting a Ceasefire and an End to Violence Between Israel and Palestine
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Williams recounted convening a confidential 'team of intellectual rivals' (imams, rabbis, Christian leaders, and activists) and explained he would release a separate mayoral statement rather than vote for a prescriptive resolution he feared would divide Durham. Chelsea Cook moved and Williams seconded the motion to adopt Item 46, which passed 5-2 with Williams and Mark-Anthony Middleton voting no; DeDreana Freeman then requested to amend the passed resolution to add the word 'genocide,' which Mayor Williams ruled out of order post-vote.

votes.item_title: Adopt Agenda Item 46: Resolution Supporting a Ceasefire and an End to Violence Between Israel and Palestine
votes.notes: Clerk announced: 'The motion passes five to two with Mayor Williams and Mayor Pro Tem Middleton voting no.'
votes.discussion_detail: Chelsea Cook moved and Leonardo Williams seconded passage of Item 46; the electronic vote passed 5-2 with Williams and Mark-Anthony Middleton voting no. Williams subsequently declined to entertain DeDreana Freeman's post-vote request to add 'genocide' to the adopted text.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Feb 19 2024
disagreements.issue: Adoption and Language of Ceasefire Resolution (Item 46) and Post-Vote 'Genocide' Amendment
disagreements.summary: Council split 5-2 over adopting a formal ceasefire resolution regarding Israel and Palestine, and subsequently clashed over DeDreana Freeman's post-vote request to amend the resolution to include the term 'genocide.'
disagreements.side_a_position: Adopt Item 46 as a formal City Council resolution calling for a ceasefire and end to violence (with Freeman further advocating explicit inclusion of the word 'genocide').
side_a_arguments: Council Member Chelsea Cook drafted the resolution language to reflect constituent pain and establish an official council stance.
Passing the resolution demonstrates moral leadership and solidarity with residents calling for a ceasefire.
DeDreana Freeman argued after passage that failing to name 'genocide' ignored the reality and power dynamics raised by residents.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose adopting a prescriptive council resolution while issuing a separate mayoral statement, and bar post-vote amendments once the resolution passed.
side_b_arguments: Mayor Leonardo Williams argued the Council lacks power to enact foreign policy and feared a formal resolution would tear the community apart as in 2018.
Williams preferred a non-unanimous vote reflecting Durham's diversity and releasing his own statement shaped by his confidential small-group dialogue.
After passage, Williams refused Freeman's amendment request on procedural grounds because the council had already negotiated for four months and voted.
disagreements.resolution: Item 46 passed 5-2 at 05:49:02; Freeman's post-vote amendment request was not entertained, and the meeting adjourned at 12:54 AM.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat 2/16/2024
meetings.executive_summary: At the February 16, 2024 Durham City Council Budget Retreat, City Manager Wanda Page opened with a lighthearted 'Smart Bull AI' presentation framing Durham's ~2,600-employee workforce, community listening feedback on streets, sidewalks, parks, and affordable housing, and property-tax revenue constraints (one cent generating ~$4.1 million). ETC Institute's Jason Morado then presented the annual resident satisfaction survey, showing top ratings for libraries, fire/EMS response, utilities, and employee courtesy alongside >40% dissatisfaction with street maintenance, sidewalks, public schools, and bicycle facilities. In the closing compensation-study discussion, Council debated whether to include ~$4.6 million in pay-plan design changes (such as raising step increases from 4% to 5%) without additional comparable data or targeted equity tiers for lower-paid workers, ultimately giving informal 6-member consensus to model the presented $28 million package while returning on March 1 with supplemental wage and equity data.

agenda_items.title: City Manager's FY 2024-25 Budget Framing and Community Conversation Priorities
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams and Budget Director Christina Reardon welcomed Council before City Manager Wanda Page used a 'Smart Bull AI' skit to highlight priorities for Durham's ~2,600 city employees, the ongoing compensation and classification study, and four community conversations emphasizing streets, sidewalks, recreation, and affordable housing. She noted property taxes comprise ~47% of city revenue and one cent on the tax rate generates ~$4.1M.

agenda_items.title: Annual Resident Satisfaction Survey Presentation (ETC Institute)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Jason Morado of ETC Institute reviewed survey findings showing highest resident satisfaction with library services, fire and life safety, city employee customer service, water/sewer utilities, fire response time, and EMS quality. At least 40% of respondents expressed dissatisfaction with four areas: city street maintenance, sidewalk quality, public schools, and bicycle facilities.

agenda_items.title: Compensation Study Market Adjustments and 4%-to-5% Step Policy Debate
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following truncated middle presentations, Council debated the $28M employee compensation estimate and two policy changes totaling ~$4.6M, including boosting annual step increases from 4% to 5% (~$3M–$3.3M). DeDreana Freeman and another colleague sought municipal comparables, racial-equity breakdowns, and $25/hour minimum scenarios rather than uniform percentage gains, while other members gave six nods of informal consensus to model the staff package immediately and revisit equity/lower-tier adjustments on March 1.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Budget Retreat 2/16/2024
disagreements.issue: Structure and Cost of Employee Pay Plan Policy Changes (4%-to-5% Step Increase vs. Targeted Equity Tiers)
disagreements.summary: During the budget retreat's closing compensation-study discussion, Council members disagreed over whether to advance ~$4.6 million in pay-plan design changes—particularly increasing general step raises from 4% to 5%—without first reviewing municipal comparables and targeting larger increases toward lower-paid workers.
disagreements.side_a_position: Hold off on or restructure the ~$4.6M policy changes (including the 4%-to-5% step increase) until staff provide municipal comparables, racial equity data, $25/hour minimum modeling, and options favoring lower-wage employees.
side_a_arguments: A flat 5% raise gives far more dollars to someone earning $150/hour than someone earning $19/hour and lacks flexibility to target workers facing the steepest cost-of-living barriers.
The $4.6M in policy design changes (~$3M–$3.3M for the 4%-to-5% shift) lacked comparable data from peer municipalities and could be deferred while focusing first on market adjustments.
disagreements.side_b_position: Give staff immediate direction to include the $28M market and policy-change package in budget models so pay raises stay on schedule while returning with requested data on March 1.
side_b_arguments: Delaying budget-modeling direction risks stalling employee pay relief during the current budget cycle.
The consultant's market study and established budget process already allow Council to adjust specific ranges once final study figures arrive.
disagreements.resolution: Six members gave informal nods of consensus at 07:48:16 to advance staff modeling of the presented $28M package while requesting follow-up wage and equity data for the March 1 retreat.
